“_Assez!_” said Poirot. “I will not be the _rabat-joie_—the
kill-joy! Go to Yardly Chase, and wear your diamond. But I pray
of you, be careful.”

He saw her to the door. When he returned to the room his face was
grave.

“What is it?” I asked. “You don’t believe in that cock-and-bull
story of the god’s eye, do you?”

“No,” said Poirot. “But I believe in the Chinaman.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that he was a very real person. I saw him from the window
while you were describing him to me. He was following Miss Marvell.
And he was a Chinaman.”

“You don’t say so! What shall we do?”

“Nothing. It is Miss Marvell’s affair. I have given her my advice,
and she has refused it. Now we must wait.”

But I could see that Poirot was not satisfied. He spent the morning
pacing up and down, his eyebrows twitching from time to time.

Finally he announced his intention of going out.

“To the _Magnificent_?” I asked.

“No, to the offices of _Society Gossip_. I wish to see the writer
of that article.”

He was out for some hours. When he returned, he looked more
perplexed than ever. He flung himself into a chair.

“_Enfin!_” he remarked. “I have seen the lady—a certain Miss
Shelter. It was she who wrote the article. It seems that she was
given the information by a ‘friend.’ She could not, or would not,
mention his name. But I have found out one thing. The article was
published at the special request of someone.”

“Who?”

“Gregory Rolf.”

“The husband?” I cried in surprise.

“Precisely. Now what can have been his motive? To get a good
advertisement for his wife? Perhaps. But there may be more in it
than that.”

He sat silent for a minute or two, then he looked up at me.

“Hastings, I’m going to Yardly Chase.”

“When?”

“To-morrow. I shall go down to the village and stay at the inn.
There is a something in this case that I do not like. We will see!”

Next morning saw us on our way to Yardly Chase. It was a beautiful
old house, and the village of Yardly was a typical English village.
We put up at the “Yardly Arms,” a small but comfortable inn.

Poirot was restless. He could not sit still. He insisted on going
for a walk, and our walk led us past the gates of the Chase.

As we were passing, a car drove out. In it were a man and a woman.
The man was driving. He was a tall, dark man with a somewhat
dissipated face. The woman was fair and very beautiful.

“Lord and Lady Yardly,” whispered Poirot.

They did not notice us, and the car sped on.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I must see Lady Yardly. I have a feeling—a
feeling in here”—he tapped his forehead—“that she is the key to the
whole mystery.”

“But how will you manage it?” I asked.

“Wait. I have my methods.”

He would say no more.

That evening, after dinner, he suddenly announced that he was going
up to the Chase.

“But they don’t know you,” I protested.

“I have my card,” he replied.

I followed him, somewhat skeptically. When we reached the house,
he asked to see Lady Yardly.

The servant hesitated.

“I’m afraid her ladyship is at dinner, sir.”

“It is a matter of great importance,” said Poirot. “Will you give
her my card?”

The man took it and went away. In a few minutes he returned.

“Will you come this way, please?”

He led us into a small, daintily-furnished morning-room. A few
minutes later, Lady Yardly entered. She was even more beautiful
at close quarters than she had been in the car.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she said, with a charming smile. “I have heard
of you, of course. What can I do for you?”

Poirot bowed.

“I must apologize for this intrusion, milady. But I am here on a
matter of some urgency. It concerns—the Star of the East.”

The smile died out of Lady Yardly’s face. She went very pale.

“The Star of the East?” she repeated. “What about it?”

“You are aware, no doubt, that Miss Mary Marvell is expected here
to-morrow?”

“Yes, I believe so.”

“And that she is bringing with her a diamond known as the Western
Star?”

Lady Yardly nodded.

“The two diamonds, milady, are said to be the two eyes of a temple
god. There is a legend that they will be stolen and returned to the
temple.”

Lady Yardly sank into a chair.

“It is true, then!” she whispered. “The letters—the threats——”

“You, too, have received letters, milady?” asked Poirot, his eyes
gleaming.

She nodded.

“I had the first one a week ago. I thought it was a joke. But then
came the others. And to-night—to-night——” She broke off, shuddering.

“What happened to-night?”

“A Chinaman—I saw him in the garden. He was looking in through the
window. Oh, Monsieur Poirot, I am frightened—terribly frightened!”

“Calm yourself, milady,” said Poirot. “I am here. I will protect
you. But you must tell me everything. Where is the diamond now?”

“It is in my jewel-case, in my bedroom.”

“And Lord Yardly? Does he know of these letters?”

“No. I—I didn’t want to worry him. He has enough to worry him as
it is.”

“I see. Now, milady, I have a request to make. Will you allow me
to see the diamond?”

Lady Yardly hesitated.

“It is very late——”

“It is a matter of life and death, milady.”

She rose.

“Very well. I will fetch it.”

She left the room. Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens. Both diamonds are in
danger. What does it mean? Is it a real attempt to steal them, or
is there some deeper mystery?”

Before I could answer, a piercing shriek rang through the house.

“_Mon Dieu!_” cried Poirot. “What was that?”

He rushed to the door, I followed him. We ran out into the hall.
At the foot of the stairs we saw Lady Yardly. She was leaning
against the banisters, her face ghastly.

“The diamond!” she gasped. “It’s gone! The Chinaman—I saw him!”

She fainted.

In a moment the house was in an uproar. Servants appeared from
nowhere. Lord Yardly came running out of the dining-room.

“What’s the matter? What’s happened?” he cried.

Poirot explained briefly. Lord Yardly’s face turned a dull,
purplish red.

“The diamond stolen? By a Chinaman? Nonsense! It’s impossible!”

“I saw him, George,” moaned Lady Yardly, who was recovering. “He
was at the window—he snatched it from me!”

“We must search the grounds at once!” cried Lord Yardly. “Come,
Monsieur Poirot!”

The search was fruitlessly continued for some time. No trace of
the thief was found.

Next morning, Poirot was very silent. He spent a long time
examining the room from which the diamond had been stolen. It was
Lady Yardly’s bedroom. The window was open, and there were marks
on the sill.

“A very clever thief,” he remarked to me. “He must have been as
agile as a cat.”

“But the Chinaman, Poirot? Lady Yardly saw him!”

“_Oui_, she saw him. And I saw a Chinaman in London. It is all
very mysterious.”

That afternoon, Miss Mary Marvell and her husband arrived. When
they heard the news, Miss Marvell was almost beside herself with
terror.

“My diamond!” she cried. “It will be the next! I know it! Oh,
Gregory, what shall we do?”

“Don’t worry, Mary,” said Rolf, soothingly. “We’ll take every
precaution. Monsieur Poirot is here, and he’ll see that nothing
happens.”

But despite all precautions, the blow fell that evening.

We were all in the drawing-room after dinner. Miss Marvell was
wearing the Western Star. Suddenly, the lights went out. There
was a sound of a scuffle, a muffled cry, and then silence.

When the lights came on again, Miss Marvell was lying on the floor.
The diamond was gone!

“The Chinaman!” she gasped, as we helped her up. “He was here—in
the room!”

Once more, a search was made, but with no result. The thief had
vanished into thin air.

Lord Yardly was distraught.

“Two diamonds stolen in two days! It’s incredible! What are the
police doing?”

“The police, milord, are doing their best,” said Poirot. “But this
is no ordinary theft. It is the work of a master-mind.”

He beckoned to me, and we went to his room.

“Hastings,” he said, “the time has come to use the little grey
cells. What do we know?”

“We know that two diamonds have been stolen by a Chinaman,” I
replied.

“_Do_ we know that? Or do we only think we know it? Let us examine
the facts. First, the letters. They were received by both ladies.
Second, the Chinaman. He was seen by me in London, by Lady Yardly
at the Chase, and by Miss Marvell in the drawing-room. Third, the
thefts themselves. Both diamonds were stolen under almost
impossible circumstances.”

“What are you getting at, Poirot?”

“I am getting at the truth, _mon ami_. And the truth is often
stranger than fiction. Tell me, Hastings, what did you think of
Lady Yardly?”

“She’s a very beautiful woman,” I said.

“And a very unhappy one, I think. Did you notice her face when I
mentioned the Star of the East? She was terrified. Why?”

“Because of the threats, I suppose.”

“Perhaps. Or perhaps because of something else. And what of
Gregory Rolf? Why did he have that article published in _Society
Gossip_?”

“To get publicity for his wife, as you said.”

“But was that the only reason? Think, Hastings. The article
mentioned both diamonds. It suggested a comparison between them.
Why?”

“I don’t know.”

“Neither do I—yet. But I have a suspicion. A very strong
suspicion.”

He would say no more.

The next day, Poirot was busy. He had several interviews with the
different members of the party. He even went up to London for a
few hours.

When he returned, his face was set.

“I have it, Hastings!” he cried. “The whole thing is clear to me
now. The pieces of the puzzle fit together perfectly.”

“Who is the thief?” I asked.

“Wait. You shall see. I have invited everyone to meet me in the
morning-room at five o’clock. Then all will be revealed.”

At five o’clock, we were all assembled. Lord and Lady Yardly, Miss
Marvell and Gregory Rolf. They all looked anxious and expectant.

Poirot stood before them, his hands behind his back.

“Messieurs, Mesdames,” he began, “you are all wondering why I have
called you here. It is to tell you the truth about the theft of
the two diamonds.”

There was a tense silence.

“First,” said Poirot, “let us deal with the Chinaman. He was a
very useful person, this Chinaman. He was the scapegoat, the bogey-man
used to frighten you. But did he really exist? I saw a Chinaman in
London, it is true. But he was a very ordinary Chinaman, a poor
man who had been paid to follow Miss Marvell. He knew nothing of
any diamonds. As for the Chinaman seen at Yardly Chase—he was a
myth, a creature of the imagination!”

“But I saw him!” cried Lady Yardly.

“And I!” added Miss Marvell.

“_Pardon_, milady, but you did not see a Chinaman. You saw what
you expected to see. In your case, it was a shadow—a trick of the
light. In the case of Miss Marvell, it was even simpler. The lights
were turned out by someone in the room. In the darkness, anything
is possible.”

“Then who stole the diamonds?” asked Lord Yardly.

“There was only one diamond, milord,” said Poirot quietly.

“Only one? What do you mean?”

“I mean that the Star of the East and the Western Star are one and
the same stone!”

A gasp of astonishment went round the room.

“Impossible!” cried Rolf. “I bought the Western Star in San
Francisco three years ago.”

“_Oui_, Monsieur, you bought a diamond. But it was not the Western
Star. It was a clever imitation. The real Western Star—which is,
as I have said, the Star of the East—was all the time in the
possession of Lady Yardly.”

Lady Yardly gave a low cry and buried her face in her hands.

“But how did you know?” I asked.

“It was simple, _mon ami_. I discovered that three years ago, when
Lady Yardly was in America, she was—shall we say?—very friendly
with Monsieur Rolf. She was also in need of money. Her husband,
milord Yardly, had been somewhat—extravagant. She decided to sell
the Star of the East. She sold it to Monsieur Rolf. But she could
not let her husband know. So she had a copy made, and it was this
copy that she kept.”

“And the theft?” asked Lord Yardly, his voice shaking.

“The theft was a staged affair. Lady Yardly, hearing that Miss
Marvell was coming to the Chase with the diamond—the real diamond—was
terrified that the truth would come out. She knew that a comparison
of the two stones would reveal the fraud. So she decided to ‘lose’
her diamond before Miss Marvell arrived. The letters, the
Chinaman—they were all part of the plot to make the theft seem
real.”

“And Miss Marvell’s diamond?” I asked.

“That was stolen by someone else,” said Poirot, his eyes fixed on
Gregory Rolf. “Someone who knew the truth, and who saw a chance
to get his hands on the real diamond. That someone was you,
Monsieur Rolf!”

Rolf started forward, his face pale with rage.

“It’s a lie!” he shouted.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I have proof. I have been to London, and
I have seen the man who made the copy of the diamond for Lady
Yardly. He identified you, Monsieur Rolf, as the man who
commissioned him to do the work—not for Lady Yardly, but for
yourself! You see, you had already sold the real diamond, and you
needed a copy to give to your wife as a wedding present!”

Rolf collapsed into a chair.

“You have been very clever, Monsieur Poirot,” he muttered. “Too
clever for me.”

“And so,” said Poirot, turning to the others, “the mystery is
solved. The diamond will be returned to its rightful owner—the
temple in China from which it was stolen many years ago. It is
the only way to end the curse.”

Lord Yardly stepped forward.

“Monsieur Poirot, I don’t know how to thank you. You have saved
my family from a great scandal.”

“It is nothing, milord,” said Poirot. “It was a small matter for
the little grey cells.”

And as we walked back to the inn, Poirot turned to me with a
twinkle in his eye.

“You see, Hastings? The simplest explanation is always the best.
But I must admit, the Chinaman was a touch of genius—even if he
didn’t exist!”

“I see. ‘The Star of the West’ and ‘the Star of the East.’ Both
coming to Yardly Chase on Friday next! It’s a bit of a coincidence,
isn’t it, Monsieur Poirot?”

“The letters! The letters!” Poirot’s face was very grave. “They
warn you of the loss of _your_ diamond?”

“Yes.”

“And you think that the Yardly diamond is also in danger?”

“I shouldn’t be surprised. Say, Monsieur Poirot, don’t you think
I’d better go down there? It seems to me that it’s up to us to
guard the stones.”

Poirot pondered.

“_Écoutez_, madame! I will do my best. But I should feel more
comfortable if you would allow me to keep the diamond for you
until Saturday.”

“I’m sorry, but I really can’t. I want to wear it. Gregory’s so
set on it.”

“I understand. Then we must see what can be done. I shall find
means to see Lord Yardly.”

“That will be easy. I’ll give you a letter of introduction.”

“_Merci_, madame. I will do my best for you.”

With a charming smile, Miss Marvell rose and prepared to go. I
opened the door for her, and she passed out. When I returned,
Poirot was sitting with his eyes closed. He looked very grave.

“A weird story, Hastings.”

“Extraordinary!” I cried. “And you think there’s anything in it?”

“I do not know. But it is interesting—very interesting. One thing
puzzles me. Why did she come to me?”

“Because she was afraid, I suppose.”

“_M’yes_—but there is something—something behind it all. I wonder
now——”

He did not finish his sentence. Suddenly he turned to me.

“Hastings, I’m going to have a look at that Yardly diamond. I’ll
run down to Yardly Chase this afternoon. I’ve no doubt Lord Yardly
will be glad to see me. You can come too, if you like.”

I jumped at the chance.

Yardly Chase was a magnificent old place, and Lord Yardly proved
a most charming host. He was a tall, thin man, with a somewhat
dissipated face, and a certain air of _laisser-aller_. We found
him in the library, and after Poirot had explained his errand and
presented Miss Marvell’s letter, he was all attention.

“This is a most extraordinary story,” he said. “I’d heard something
of the kind before, but I always looked on it as a bit of a joke.
I’ll show you the ‘Star of the East’ if you like.”

He went to a safe in the wall, and after some fumbling with the
combination, he drew out a small leather case. Opening it, he
displayed a magnificent diamond, which, as far as I could judge,
was the exact double of the one we had seen that morning.

“It is a beautiful stone,” murmured Poirot. “And you have no fear
for its safety, milord?”

Lord Yardly laughed.

“Not the slightest. I’ve lived too long in the East to be scared
by tales of temple gods and Chinamen. I’m only too glad to have
the stone at all—if I’d had my way, it would have been sold long
ago. But it’s an heirloom, and I can’t touch it.”

“But you could if you were in—financial difficulties, could you
not?” asked Poirot delicately.

Lord Yardly’s face clouded.

“I suppose I could—if I could prove they were sufficiently
serious. But, thank Heaven, it hasn’t come to that yet. And now,
Monsieur Poirot, you must stay and have some tea.”

As we were finishing our tea, Lady Yardly came in. She was a
tall, dark woman, with a somewhat tragic face. She seemed rather
surprised to see us, and Lord Yardly explained our presence.

“It’s all very interesting,” she said, but her voice was cold and
indifferent. “I suppose Gregory Rolf and his wife are really
coming on Friday?”

“Yes, it’s all settled,” said Lord Yardly. “I’m looking forward
to seeing Gregory again. It’s some years since we met.”

“I didn’t know you knew him,” I said.

“Oh, yes, I met him out in California three years ago. He’s a
charming fellow.”

As we drove back to London, Poirot was very silent.

“What are you thinking about?” I asked at last.

“I am thinking, Hastings, that there are more things in this case
than meet the eye. Why did Miss Marvell come to me? Why did she
want to wear the diamond at Yardly Chase? And why was Lady Yardly
so cold and indifferent?”

“Perhaps she’s jealous of Miss Marvell’s beauty,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But I think there is more than that. I think, Hastings,
that we are on the eve of a very big mystery.”

And with that I had to be content.

Friday came at last. Poirot and I went down to Yardly Chase by an
afternoon train. We found the house full of people, and the
excitement was intense. Miss Marvell and her husband had already
arrived, and everyone was talking about the two diamonds.

At dinner, the two stones were the centre of attraction. Miss
Marvell wore hers on a long platinum chain, and Lady Yardly wore
hers in a magnificent diamond necklace. They were, as far as one
could see, identical.

After dinner, we all adjourned to the drawing-room. The evening
passed pleasantly enough, but I noticed that Poirot was very
alert. He seemed to be watching everyone and everything.

Suddenly, about eleven o’clock, the lights went out. There was a
moment of dead silence, and then a woman’s scream rang out.

“The diamond! My diamond!”

It was the voice of Lady Yardly.

In a moment the lights were on again. Lady Yardly was standing in
the middle of the room, her hand to her throat. The diamond
necklace was still there, but the great central stone, the “Star
of the East,” was gone!

Everyone was in a state of the wildness. Lord Yardly was beside
himself with rage and excitement.

“The Chinaman!” he cried. “It must have been the Chinaman!”

But there was no sign of any Chinaman. The doors and windows were
all securely fastened.

Poirot was the only one who remained calm. He went over to Lady
Yardly and spoke to her in a low voice.

“Do not distress yourself, milady. We shall find your diamond.”

Then he turned to the rest of us.

“I must ask you all to remain in this room for a few minutes. I
wish to make a little investigation.”

He went out of the room, and we waited in silence. In about ten
minutes he returned. He was carrying something in his hand.

“Is this your diamond, milady?” he asked, holding out a large
stone.

Lady Yardly gave a cry of joy.

“Yes! Yes! Where did you find it?”

“I found it in the garden, just outside the window,” said Poirot.

“But the windows were all fastened!” cried Lord Yardly.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “That is why I found it in the garden.”

“I don’t understand,” said Lord Yardly.

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “The diamond was not stolen by
a Chinaman. it was stolen by someone in this room.”

A gasp of astonishment went round the room.

“And that someone,” continued Poirot, “is—Miss Mary Marvell!”

There was a moment of dead silence. Everyone looked at Miss
Marvell, who had turned deathly pale.

“It’s a lie!” she cried. “I never touched the diamond!”

“Then how do you explain this?” asked Poirot, holding up a small
piece of silk. “I found this caught in the window-latch. It is of
the same material as your dress.”

Miss Marvell looked at her dress. A small piece was indeed missing.

“I—I must have caught it on something,” she stammered.

“And how do you explain this?” continued Poirot, holding up a
small bottle. “I found this in your room. It is a powerful
anaesthetic.”

Miss Marvell burst into tears.

“I didn’t do it! I tell you I didn’t do it!”

“Then who did?” asked Poirot.

“I did!”

The voice came from the doorway. We all turned. There, standing in
the doorway, was Gregory Rolf.

“I stole the diamond,” he said. “I wanted the money. I’m in
terrible debt, and I thought I could sell the stone and no one
would be any the wiser.”

“But how did you do it?” asked Lord Yardly.

“It was easy enough,” said Rolf. “I knew the combination of the
safe—I’d seen you open it the other day. I waited until the lights
went out—I’d arranged that with a confederate—and then I took the
stone. I thought I could throw the blame on the Chinaman.”

“And Miss Marvell?” asked Poirot.

“She knew nothing about it,” said Rolf. “I used her dress to make
it look as if she’d done it, and I put the anaesthetic in her
room to make it look as if she’d been drugged.”

“A very clever plot,” said Poirot. “But not quite clever enough
for Hercule Poirot.”

Lord Yardly was furious.

“You scoundrel!” he cried. “I’ll have the law on you for this!”

But Rolf only laughed.

“You can’t,” he said. “The diamond is mine!”

“Yours?”

“Yes. Lady Yardly gave it to me three years ago in California. It
was a—a token of her affection. I’ve had it ever since. The one
you had in the safe was a paste replica.”

Lord Yardly turned to his wife. She was deathly pale.

“Is this true?” he asked.

Lady Yardly bowed her head.

“Yes,” she whispered. “It is true.”

Lord Yardly was silent for a moment. Then he turned to Rolf.

“Get out!” he said. “Get out of my house, and never let me see
your face again!”

Rolf laughed, and went out of the room. Miss Marvell followed him,
still sobbing.

When they had gone, Lord Yardly turned to Poirot.

“I don’t know how to thank you, Monsieur Poirot. You have saved
me from a very great misfortune.”

“It was nothing, milord,” said Poirot. “A mere matter of the
little grey cells.”

As we drove back to London, I asked Poirot how he had discovered
the truth.

“It was very simple, Hastings. I knew from the first that there
was something wrong. Why did Miss Marvell come to me? To create an
alibi, of course. She wanted me to believe in the Chinaman story,
so that when the diamond was stolen, I should at once suspect
him. And the letters—they were too much like a detective story.
No, I knew that the whole thing was a plot between her and her
husband. But I did not know the truth about Lady Yardly until I
saw her face when the diamond was mentioned. Then I knew that she
had something to hide. And when I saw the diamond in the safe, I
knew at once that it was a paste replica. It had not the fire of
the real stone. After that, it was easy enough to guess the
rest.”

“But what about the piece of silk and the anaesthetic?” I asked.

“Ah, those!” Poirot chuckled. “I found them, it is true, but I
did not find them where I said I did. I found the silk in Miss
Marvell’s room, and the anaesthetic in her husband’s bag. I merely
used them to force a confession.”

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I know it, Hastings. I know it.”

“In effect, it is a very curious coincidence,” murmured Poirot.
“But—if I understand you, madame—you are still determined to go
down to Yardly Chase with your diamond?”

“I’m certainly not going to let a lot of Chinks and a few
threatening letters keep me from showing off my ‘Western Star’ to
all the folks. Lord Yardly is an old friend of Greg’s, and—well,
Gregory’s a bit of a collector himself, and he’s just crazy to
compare the two stones.”

Poirot sighed.

“I only hope you will have no reason to regret it, madame.”

“I’ll take my chances, Monsieur Poirot.” She rose. “And if
anything _does_ happen—well, I’ve got you to fall back upon.”

“I shall be at your service, madame. But I would have preferred
to prevent rather than to—remedy.”

“That’s so like a doctor, isn’t it? Well, good-bye, Monsieur
Poirot.”

And with a sunny smile, she left us.

I looked at Poirot. He was frowning.

“Hastings, I should like to know one thing. Who is it that sends
out these letters?”

“The Chinaman, of course.”

“_Y-es_,” said Poirot doubtfully. “But—it is very curious.
_Society Gossip_ only appeared yesterday. The third letter was
delivered yesterday also. It would have been more natural if the
news in _Society Gossip_ had prompted the third letter—but the
letters began _before_ the paragraph appeared. Still, it is
unimportant. Let us look at it from another point of view. Who
benefits if the diamond is stolen?”

“The insurance company, if they don’t have to pay,” I suggested.

Poirot shook his head.

“No, no, my friend. The person who _possesses_ the diamond, if it is
well insured. That is what I was thinking. But she is rich—this
Mary Marvell. And yet—one never knows! The more one has, the more
one wants. And then, there is the husband. He might be in low
water. But I do not think so.”

“And there’s another possibility,” I said. “Suppose the letters
are a hoax—and that someone is really planning to steal the jewel.
They would use the ‘Chinaman’ story to put people on the wrong
scent.”

“That is possible,” agreed Poirot. “But if so, why the reference
to the full moon? That is very specific.”

He was silent for a moment, then he looked up with a twinkle in
his eye.

“_Enfin_, we shall see what Friday brings! In the meantime,
Hastings, I think a little visit to the _Magnificent_ might not
be out of place.”

“To see Gregory Rolf?”

“Precisely. I should like to see the man who bought a diamond for
a tenth of its value from a frightened ‘Chink’ in San Francisco.”

We found Gregory Rolf at the hotel. He was a big, handsome man,
with a certain flamboyant charm, but there was something about him
I didn’t quite like—a touch of the ‘bounder’ perhaps. He greeted
us heartily.

“Glad to know you, Monsieur Poirot! Mary told me she’d been to see
you. I tell her it’s all bunkum—those letters, I mean. Some crank
who’s read too many detective stories, that’s my opinion.”

“And the Chinaman who delivered them?” asked Poirot.

Rolf laughed.

“Oh, that! Probably some fellow from a laundry dressed up. They’ll
do anything for a bit of a lark in this country.”

“You are not afraid for the diamond, then?”

“Not a bit! I’ve told Mary to leave it in the safe here, but she’s
set on wearing it at Yardly Chase. Women are like that, you know.”

“I see. And you yourself—you are also going to Yardly Chase?”

“Yes, we’re going down on Friday. Lord Yardly’s a good sort—and
between you and me, I think he’s a bit hard up. He’s keen on this
film idea.”

“I understand. Well, Monsieur Rolf, I will not detain you. I wish
you a pleasant visit.”

As we left the hotel, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Mr. Gregory Rolf?”

“I didn’t like him much,” I confessed. “There’s something—I don’t
know—a bit too ‘shrewd’ about him.”

“He is a man of business, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “And now, let
us see if we can find out something about Lord and Lady Yardly.”

It was not difficult. The Yardlys were well known in society.
Lord Yardly was a typical sporting peer, with more ancestors than
brains. Lady Yardly, before her marriage, had been Maude St. John,
a girl of good family but no money. They had been married for
about ten years and had two children.

“Nothing very helpful there,” I remarked, after we had gathered
these facts.

“Perhaps not,” said Poirot. “And yet—three years ago, the Yardlys
were in California. And three years ago, Gregory Rolf was in
California. And three years ago, Mary Marvell’s husband—to be—bought
a diamond from a ‘Chink’ in San Francisco. It is a small world,
Hastings!”

The following day, Thursday, passed without incident. But on Friday
morning, just as we were finishing breakfast, the door opened and
a lady was ushered in.

She was tall and dark, with a pale, distinguished face and
haunting, melancholy eyes. She was dressed in deep mourning.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she asked.

“I am Hercule Poirot, madame. At your service.”

“I am Lady Yardly.”

I started, and Poirot bowed.

“Please sit down, Lady Yardly. This is my friend, Captain
Hastings.”

She acknowledged my presence with a slight bow, and then turned
to Poirot.

“Monsieur Poirot, I have come to you in great distress. I—I
scarcely know how to begin.”

“Take your time, madame,” said Poirot kindly. “You are in trouble
about—a diamond?”

She started.

“How did you know? Oh, I suppose it is in the papers! That
paragraph in _Society Gossip_——”

“I have heard of it, yes. But tell me your story in your own
words.”

Lady Yardly twisted her fingers nervously.

“It—it is the Star of the East—the diamond that has been in my
husband’s family for generations. It is supposed to have a curse
upon it. And now—I have had threatening letters.”

“Similar to those received by Miss Mary Marvell?”

“You know about those? Yes, they are almost identical. They say
the diamond must be returned—that ‘the two eyes of the god must
meet.’ It is terrifying!”

“And when did you receive these letters, madame?”

“The first one came three days ago. The second yesterday. And
this morning—this morning I found a third one on my dressing
table!”

“And was it also delivered by a Chinaman?”

Lady Yardly shook her head.

“I don’t know. I didn’t see anyone. It—it just appeared.”

Poirot looked at her thoughtfully.

“And Lord Yardly? What does he say to all this?”

“He—he doesn’t know. I haven’t told him. He has been so worried
lately about—about money matters. I didn’t want to add to his
troubles. But I am so frightened, Monsieur Poirot! What shall I
do?”

“The diamond—it is at Yardly Chase?”

“Yes. We are going down there this afternoon. Miss Marvell and her
husband are coming to stay with us.”

“I know. Now, Lady Yardly, I will give you the same advice I gave
to Miss Marvell. Give the diamond into my keeping until the danger
has passed.”

A look of almost physical pain passed over Lady Yardly’s face.

“I—I cannot do that, Monsieur Poirot.”

“Why not?”

“Because—because it is not here. It is at Yardly Chase, in the
safe.”

“Then let me go down with you to Yardly Chase. I can guard it
there.”

Lady Yardly hesitated.

“I—I don’t know what my husband would say. He—he is very proud.
He might not like the idea of a—a private detective.”

“Tell him I am an old friend,” suggested Poirot. “Or—wait! I have
a better idea. I will come down as a guest of Miss Marvell. She
has already asked me to help her.”

Lady Yardly looked relieved.

“That would be much better. Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. You have
taken a great weight off my mind.”

She rose and held out her hand.

“We shall expect you this evening, then?”

“I shall be there, madame.”

When she had gone, I looked at Poirot.

“Well, this is getting complicated! Two diamonds, two sets of
threatening letters, and two ladies who won’t part with their
jewels!”

“It is very symmetrical, is it not?” said Poirot. “The two eyes of
the god—they are both in danger. And they are both to meet at
Yardly Chase on the night of the full moon.”

“And that’s to-night!” I cried.

“Precisely. We have no time to lose, Hastings. Pack a bag. We go
to Yardly Chase by the afternoon train.”

Yardly Chase was a magnificent old place, but it had a neglected,
run-down air. Lord Yardly, a big, bluff man with a red face and
a loud voice, received us with hearty, if somewhat forced,
hospitality.

“Glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot! Any friend of Mary’s is welcome
here. She’s a great girl, isn’t she? And Gregory—he’s a white man!
We’re going to do great things together, I can tell you.”

It was evident that Lord Yardly was pinning his hopes on the film
deal to restore the family fortunes.

Miss Marvell and her husband had already arrived. Mary was in high
spirits, but I thought Gregory Rolf looked a little uneasy. Lady
Yardly was pale and quiet, and I noticed that she and Rolf
avoided each other’s eyes.

Dinner was a somewhat strained affair. Lord Yardly talked
incessantly about the film deal, while Mary Marvell sparkled and
chattered. But beneath it all, there was a sense of impending
trouble.

After dinner, we all gathered in the big hall. It was a dark,
shadowy place, lit only by the flickering light of the fire and
a few candles.

“Well,” said Lord Yardly, rubbing his hands together. “Here we are!
The night of the full moon! Where are those Chinamen of yours,
Mary?”

“Don’t, George!” said Lady Yardly, with a shiver. “It’s not a
subject for joking.”

“Nonsense, my dear! It’s all a pack of rubbish. Let’s see the
diamonds! That’ll scare ‘em away!”

Mary Marvell laughed and drew her diamond from her neck. It shone
with a cold, brilliant light.

“And yours, Lady Yardly?” asked Gregory Rolf.

Lady Yardly hesitated, then she too produced a jewel-case. She
opened it, and there, lying on a bed of blue velvet, was a diamond
almost identical to Mary Marvell’s.

“The two eyes of the god!” whispered Poirot.

Suddenly, the lights went out.

There was a moment of dead silence, then a woman’s scream rang
out through the hall.

“The diamond! The diamond! He’s got it!”

It was Lady Yardly’s voice.

I heard the sound of a scuffle, then a door slammed.

“Quick! The lights!” cried Lord Yardly.

Someone struck a match, and then the candles were relit.

Lady Yardly was standing by the table, her hand to her throat.
The jewel-case lay open and empty.

“He—he came out of the shadows!” she gasped. “A Chinaman! He
snatched it and ran!”

“Which way?” cried Lord Yardly.

“Through that door!” She pointed to a small door that led to the
terrace.

Lord Yardly and Gregory Rolf rushed out. I was about to follow
them, when Poirot’s hand fell on my arm.

“Stay here, Hastings. There is nothing to be done—out there.”

“But the thief!”

“The thief is long gone, _mon ami_.”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“You are sure it was a Chinaman, madame?”

“Oh, yes! I saw his face—his horrible, yellow face!”

“I see. And you, Miss Marvell? Your diamond—it is safe?”

Mary Marvell gave a little gasp and clutched at her neck.

“Yes—yes, I have it here. Oh, it’s too terrible! Poor Lady
Yardly!”

At that moment, Lord Yardly and Rolf returned. They were both
out of breath and empty-handed.

“Not a sign of him!” panted Lord Yardly. “He must have disappeared
into the woods.”

“I’ll call the police,” said Gregory Rolf.

“No—wait!” said Poirot.

He stepped forward into the centre of the room.

“I do not think the police will be necessary.”

“What do you mean?” cried Lord Yardly.

“I mean,” said Poirot slowly, “that I know who stole the diamond.”

There was a moment of stunned silence.

“You know?” gasped Lady Yardly. “But—but you saw! It was a
Chinaman!”

“It was not a Chinaman, madame,” said Poirot. “It was someone
much nearer home.”

He turned to Mary Marvell.

“Miss Marvell, may I see your diamond for a moment?”

She looked surprised, but she handed it to him. Poirot took it to
one of the candles and examined it closely.

“As I thought,” he murmured.

Then he turned to Lady Yardly.

“Lady Yardly, three years ago, when you were in California, you
met Mr. Gregory Rolf, did you not?”

Lady Yardly turned deathly pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. You were—shall we say—a little indiscreet? And
Mr. Rolf was—shall we say—a little opportunistic? He had letters
of yours—letters that Lord Yardly must never see.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Gregory Rolf, stepping forward.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I think not. Lady Yardly, you had no money
of your own. But you had the ‘Star of the East.’ And so, you made
a bargain. You gave the diamond to Mr. Rolf in exchange for your
letters. But the diamond was an heirloom—it could not be missed.
And so, Mr. Rolf had a paste replica made for you. It was that
replica that was ‘stolen’ tonight.”

“And the ‘Western Star’?” I asked, bewildered.

“The ‘Western Star’ _is_ the ‘Star of the East,’” said Poirot.
“Mr. Rolf gave it to his wife as a wedding present. He is a man
who likes to keep things in the family!”

“But the letters?” cried Mary Marvell. “The threatening letters?”

“They were sent by Mr. Rolf himself,” said Poirot. “He wanted to
create a ‘legend’ for the diamond, so that no one would suspect its
true origin. And tonight, he staged the ‘theft’ of the replica, so
that Lady Yardly could tell her husband it was gone, and no one
would ever be the wiser.”

“It’s not true!” sobbed Lady Yardly, sinking into a chair.

“It is true, madame,” said Poirot gently. “But do not despair.
Lord Yardly need never know the truth. Mr. Rolf, I think you will
return the ‘Western Star’ to Lady Yardly. And in return, she will
not prosecute you for the ‘theft’ of the replica.”

Gregory Rolf looked at Poirot, then at his wife, then at Lord
Yardly. His face was a mask of fury. But he knew he was beaten.

Without a word, he took the diamond from Poirot’s hand and flung
it onto the table. Then he turned and strode out of the room.

Mary Marvell looked at the diamond, then at Lady Yardly, then at
Poirot. Then, with a little shrug of her shoulders, she followed
her husband.

Lord Yardly looked from one to the other, his face a picture of
bewilderment.

“I—I don’t understand,” he stammered. “What’s happened? Where’s
the Chinaman?”

“There was no Chinaman, my lord,” said Poirot. “It was just—a
little drama—staged for your benefit. But everything is all
right now. Lady Yardly has her diamond back.”

He picked up the ‘Western Star’ and handed it to Lady Yardly.

“I think, madame,” he said, “that it would be better if you kept
it in a—more secure place—in future.”

Lady Yardly took the diamond, her eyes filling with tears.

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot,” she whispered. “Thank you.”

As we walked back to our rooms, I looked at Poirot.

“Well, that was a surprise! I never suspected Gregory Rolf.”

“Did you not, Hastings? To me, it was very clear. The ‘Chinaman’
was too—how shall I say?—too ‘theatrical.’ And the timing of the
letters—it was all too convenient. No, it was a clever plan—but
not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

And with a little smile of satisfaction, he went into his room
and closed the door.

“It _is_ a curious coincidence,” said Poirot. “And _you_ believe the
story of the temple god?”

“Well, I don’t know. Gregory does. He says he’s always felt there
was some story attached to the stone. And the letters, you see!
They came from a _Chinaman!_ That is what I’m afraid of!”

“And you think that when you and Lady Yardly meet on Friday, the
two stones will be together for the first time for—how many
hundreds of years?”

“That’s it,” said Miss Marvell.

“_Eh bien_, madame, I do not like it. It bodes no good! No, I do
not like it at all!”

“What can I do?”

“Stay in London. Do not go to Yardly Chase.”

“No, I must go. If I didn’t, it would look as if I were afraid of
the letters, and—well, Gregory’s just set on my going, and he
doesn’t believe in the letters anyway. He just laughs at them.”

“_Assez!_” said Poirot. “I have warned you. At any rate, you will
be on your guard, madame? If a Chinaman should appear, do not stop
to argue with him. Fly! Scream! Run!”

“I will,” promised Miss Marvell.

When she had gone, Poirot sat for some time in deep thought.

“What do you think of it, Hastings?” he asked at last.

“It’s a most romantic story,” I said.

“_Mais oui_, it is indeed! And yet—I wonder!” He looked at me
sharply. “Does it not strike you as being a little _too_ romantic?
A little too like—what do you call it—a ‘film’ plot?”

“And yet, the letters,” I argued.

“Ah! the letters!”

“They were _printed_,” I said. “That looks like a genuine attempt
at concealment.”

“Or the reverse! It is very easy to print. It is not so easy to
disguise your own handwriting. Is it possible that the letters
were written by some one who had no need to disguise his
handwriting?”

I did not quite follow him.

“You mean——?”

“I mean, Hastings, that I should like to know a little more about
Mr. Gregory B. Rolf.”

“He is a very well-known actor, isn’t he?”

“_Oui._ But his name has been coupled with Lady Yardly’s—three years
ago—in California. At the time when the diamond was bought from
a Chinaman. Why from a Chinaman? Because it was a stolen stone?
But if so, why all this _mise-en-scène_ about the temple god? It
savours of the cinema, Hastings—the cinema!”

“But why should he wish to steal his own wife’s diamond?” I
suggested.

“Why, indeed? Unless it is—not his wife’s diamond!”

“What do you mean?”

“Suppose it is _not_ insured for fifty thousand pounds? Suppose
it is a—paste?”

“In that case, why all this bother?”

“Ah! that is what we have to find out. But here is another visitor.”

This time it was a man. A tall, handsome, dark-haired man, whom
I recognized as Gregory Rolf. He apologized for his intrusion.

“I’m really very sorry, Monsieur Poirot,” he began. “But I felt I
must come and see you. My wife’s been here, hasn’t she?”

Poirot bowed.

“She’s been worrying about those letters. She’s a bit high-strung,
and she’s taken it into her head that they are genuine. I can’t
persuade her they’re a hoax. Some silly kid’s joke, I expect.”

“So you do not believe in the story of the god’s eye, Monsieur
Rolf?” asked Poirot, with a smile.

“Not a bit of it! The whole thing’s a fake. My wife’s a bit of a
child, Monsieur Poirot. She likes the romantic side of life.”

“You do not think there is any danger of the diamond being stolen?”

“Not a bit! Why, I’ve got my eye on it all the time. And believe
me, it’s a pretty sharp one! No, I’ve just come along because I
want to ask you to—well, not to encourage her in this idea. It
just wears her out. You understand?”

“I understand,” said Poirot. “And yet—I should advise her to stay
in London.”

“Oh, she’s quite safe. I’ll look after her. And the Yardlys will
take care of her too. We’re going down there on Friday.”

“I’m sure you’ll look after her very well, Monsieur Rolf,” said
Poirot. “You were in California, I believe, when you bought the
diamond?”

“Yes. I got it for a song from a Chink. I think he’d stolen it.”

“And you were acquainted with Lady Yardly at the time?”

Mr. Rolf’s face went a shade darker.

“I met her once or twice. She’s a very beautiful woman.”

“Well, Monsieur Rolf, I wish you a pleasant visit to Yardly Chase.”

When he had gone, Poirot shook his head.

“He is a very good actor, that one,” he remarked. “But I think he
is also a very clever man. It is a pity he did not stay a little
longer. I should have liked to have asked him about his collection
of Chinese curios!”

The following day brought a surprise. A lady, heavily veiled, was
announced. She proved to be none other than Lady Yardly.

She was a tall, beautiful woman, with a somewhat haggard face and
restless, unhappy eyes.

“I have come to you in great distress, Monsieur Poirot,” she began.
“I—I have been receiving such strange letters.”

She drew from her bag a sheet of paper. It was exactly the same as
the ones we had already seen.

“The great diamond which is the right eye of the god must return
whence it came.”

“You too?” cried Poirot.

“Then you know? You have seen letters like this before?”

“I have seen them, milady. When did you receive this?”

“It was left at my house in Town by hand—by a Chinaman, the butler
says.”

“And you have the diamond, the Star of the East, with you?”

“No, it is at Yardly Chase.”

“Then you must go down there at once, milady, and see that it is
safe.”

“That is what I mean to do. Lord Yardly is there now. He is very
anxious to see you, Monsieur Poirot. Could you come down with me?”

“I will come with pleasure, milady. Hastings, you will accompany
us?”

“Delighted,” I said.

“Then we will start by the afternoon train.”

“And—Lord and Lady Yardly are going to be there on Friday next?”
queried Poirot.

“Why, yes!”

“And you think that it is all a plot to get you both together,
so that the ‘Western Star’ and the ‘Eastern Star’ can be stolen
at the same time?”

“It seems so to me.”

“And you have no idea of who could be at the bottom of it?
Have you no enemies?”

“Only the usual professional jealousies, Monsieur Poirot.
Gregory says it’s all a frame-up to get a bit of free
advertisement. But I don’t know. It’s that Chinaman that
scares me.”

“Well, madame, I shall be happy to do what I can. But I
confess I should prefer your staying in London for the
present.”

“I’m afraid that’s not possible. We’re all booked up.”

“Then I will do my best for you. If I can, I will come
down to Yardly Chase myself on Friday.”

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, if you only would! I should feel
so much safer.”

With a charming smile, Miss Marvell rose and prepared to
depart.

“And the diamond, madame? You will not leave it with me?”

“I guess not, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll keep it in the hotel
safe.”

“_Assez bien_! But be very careful, I implore of you.”

He saw her to the door. When he returned, he was looking
grave.

“What do you think of it all, Poirot?” I asked.

“It is a very curious case, Hastings. Very curious
indeed. A film star, a diamond, a Chinaman—it is like a
_cinéma_ drama, is it not?”

“But do you think it is a hoax?”

“I do not know. It might be. But that story of the
diamonds—the two eyes of the god—it is an old one. It
has been used in many a story. It is a classic!”

“Then you think it is a fake?”

“Not necessarily. Truth is often more classic than
fiction. But tell me, Hastings, what did you think of the
lady?”

“She is very charming—and very beautiful.”

“Is she? I should not have said so. She has the face of
a child—yes. But her eyes—they are the eyes of a woman
who has seen much, and who knows how to get what she
wants. She is a very clever woman, our Miss Mary Marvell.”

“And her husband? What of him?”

“Ah! Gregory Rolf! He is a very handsome man, is he not?
And a very successful one. I wonder——”

“What?”

“I wonder why he is so anxious to go to Yardly Chase.
It is a long way from London.”

“He says it is for business.”

“_Peut-être_! But I should like to know more of this
Gregory Rolf. He is a man of many parts, I think.”

The door opened and a tall, handsome man entered. It was
Gregory Rolf himself. He apologized for his intrusion,
explaining that he had come to fetch his wife.

“She’s gone, Mr. Rolf,” I said. “She left about five
minutes ago.”

“Oh, I must have missed her. Well, no matter. I’ll go
back to the hotel. I suppose she’s told you all about
this nonsense of the letters?”

“She has,” said Poirot. “What is your opinion of them,
Monsieur?”

Rolf laughed.

“Publicity, Monsieur Poirot! Just publicity! Mary’s a
wonderful little woman, but she’s got a perfect craze
for being in the limelight. She’s been feeling a bit
neglected lately—the public’s been a bit cold—so she
thought she’d start a little excitement. That’s all.”

“You think there is no danger, then?”

“Not a bit of it! Why, I’ve had letters like that myself
before now. Every one in our profession gets them. It’s
all part of the game.”

“Then you are not afraid for the diamond?”

“Not in the least. It’s well insured, anyway!”

He laughed again, shook hands with us both, and departed.

“There,” I said. “You see! Even her husband thinks it’s
a hoax.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But I—I am not so sure. There is
something about this case—something that I do not like.
Wait—I will see if I can find out anything about those
Yardlys.”

He went to his bookcase and took down a large volume.

“Yardly. Baron Yardly. Tenth Baron. Married Maude,
daughter of the late John S. Emerson of New York. One
son, born 1912. One daughter, born 1914. Residences:
Yardly Chase, Hants; 100, Park Lane, W. Um! Not much
there. But wait—here is something.”

He had picked up a small book from the table.

“This is a ‘Who’s Who’ of the film world. Let us see.
Rolf—Gregory. Born 1888. Married Mary Marvell 1921.
Films: ‘The Heart of a Rose,’ ‘The Desert Song,’ etc.
Wait—here is something else. ‘Was in California in 1919.’
That was the year Lady Yardly was there. I wonder——”

He broke off.

“What are you going to do, Poirot?”

“I am going to Yardly Chase, Hastings. There is some
mystery here—and I mean to get to the bottom of it.”

“_Épatant!_” murmured Poirot. “Without doubt a romance of the first
water.” He turned to Mary Marvell. “And you are not afraid, madame?
You have no superstitious terrors? You do not fear to introduce
these two Siamese twins to each other lest a Chinaman should appear
and, hey presto! whisk them both back to China?”

His tone was mocking, but I fancied that an undercurrent of
seriousness lay beneath it.

“I don’t believe that Lady Yardly’s diamond is anything like as
good a stone as mine,” said Miss Marvell. “Anyway, I’m going to
see.”

“Just now,” I said, with a quiet, confident air. “And hers, like
yours, were from a Chinaman. Is it not so?”

Lady Yardly sat like one turned to stone.

“It is true,” she murmured. “There is something very terrible in
this. Can you help me? What did you tell Miss Marvell?”

“Wait a moment, Lady Yardly. You had three letters, I presume?”

“Yes.”

“And they arrived at the same time as hers?”

“I don’t know when hers arrived. My first came three weeks ago,
the second a week later, and the third only this morning.”

“What did they say?”

“That the diamond which was the right eye of the god must return.”

“And the last one?”

“Threatened that it would be taken from me on Friday—at the full
of the moon.”

I nodded.

“The same date, you see. And it was left by a Chinaman?”

“No, they all came by post.”

“Ah!” I ejaculated. “That is a new point. And have you the diamond
with you?”

She shook her head.

“It is at Yardly Chase. We never bring it to London. It is too
valuable.”

“You have it with you now, I think?”

“No, no, I tell you.”

She seemed strangely agitated.

“Lady Yardly, I’m sure I’m right. You’re afraid of its being stolen.
You’ve brought it up to put it in a place of safety.”

I saw that I had been too precipitate. She rose to her feet, her
eyes flashing.

“I’ve already told you, sir, that I have not the diamond with me.
I came to see Monsieur Poirot. As he is not here, I will not
trouble you further.”

She moved towards the door.

“Lady Yardly! One moment!”

It was Poirot’s voice. He had entered the room at that moment,
unknown to either of us.

He bowed to her with his best manner.

“_Madame_,” he said, “I can help you, if you will allow me. It is
not the diamond you have in your hand, then? No? Ah, _pardon!_ I
am wrong. I see that it is only your handkerchief. But sit down,
I pray of you. My friend has told you that I know something of this
affair?”

“He says that Mary Marvell has been here.”

“That is so, madame. She also has received letters from a
Chinaman.”

“My letters were not from a Chinaman,” said Lady Yardly.

“_Pardon_! They were from one who wished to be thought a Chinaman,”
corrected Poirot. “The letters to Miss Marvell were printed; yours,
I think, were written in a disguised hand?”

“How did you know that?”

“_Ma foi_, madame, it is my business to know things. I will tell
you even more. Your diamond is at this moment—at Yardly Chase.”

“Yes.”

“And it was not you who suggested to your husband that he should
ask the Rolfs down to the Chase?”

“I? No, indeed. It was my husband’s own idea.”

“I thought as much,” said Poirot. “And he is very anxious that
Miss Marvell should bring her diamond with her?”

“He thought it would be such a good thing for the two stones to be
compared,” said Lady Yardly, with a certain amount of hesitation.

“I see,” said Poirot. “Then it was he who wrote to the papers about
them?”

“I believe so.”

Poirot looked at her for a long time, then he shook his head
gently.

“I wouldn’t go back to Yardly Chase just yet, if I were you, Lady
Yardly.”

“But I must. We have a big house-party for the week-end.”

“Then I, too, must go to Yardly Chase. It is very simple.”

“But, Monsieur Poirot——”

“I go as a friend of yours, you understand? A friend of your past
life in California. It is a little lie, but it will do no one any
harm.”

“It would be impossible to deceive my husband,” she murmured. “He
is—he has a very difficult temper.”

“Leave that to me, madame. I can be very discreet.”

Lady Yardly rose.

“Then I will leave everything in your hands, Monsieur Poirot.”

She went out.

“_Et voilà_!” said Poirot. “The plot thickens.”

“I was right, then,” I said. “She _had_ the diamond with her?”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, no, _mon ami_, she had not. But she is a very unhappy woman.
I should like to help her.”

“And Lord Yardly?”

“I should like to help _him_ too. A pair of very difficult
characters, if I am not mistaken.”

“But what about the Chinaman?” I asked.

“The Chinaman,” said Poirot, “is a very interesting person. I
wonder if we shall see him at Yardly Chase?”

I laughed.

“You’re joking, Poirot.”

“Not at all. I have a feeling that we shall. It is a very strange
story, Hastings.”

“It’s like a melodrama,” I said.

“It is very like a melodrama,” agreed Poirot. “And like most
melodramas, it is not quite what it seems.”

He would say no more, and I was left to wonder what he meant.

The following Friday saw us on our way to Yardly Chase. We had
been invited to spend the week-end there, and Poirot had been
introduced to Lord Yardly as an old friend of his wife’s.

Lord Yardly was a big, bluff man, with a hearty manner and a
somewhat choleric temperament. He seemed to be very fond of his
wife, but there was a certain amount of tension between them.

The other guests included the Rolfs, and several people whom I did
not know.

Miss Marvell was looking more like a child than ever, and she wore
the “Western Star” on every possible occasion.

Lady Yardly, on the other hand, was very quiet and subdued. She
hardly ever wore her diamond, and when she did, she seemed uneasy.

The first evening passed off without incident. Poirot was at his
best, and kept everyone amused with his stories.

But the next day, the atmosphere changed. It was the day of the
full moon.

I noticed that Poirot was very watchful. He seemed to be
everywhere at once, and his eyes were never still.

After dinner, we all went into the drawing-room. It was a large,
oak-panelled room, with a big fireplace at one end.

Lord Yardly was talking to Gregory Rolf, while Mary Marvell was
showing her diamond to some of the other guests.

Lady Yardly was sitting by herself in a corner of the room. She
looked very pale and nervous.

Suddenly, the lights went out.

There was a moment of silence, and then a woman’s scream.

“My diamond!” cried Mary Marvell. “Someone has taken my diamond!”

There was a sound of a scuffle, and then the lights came on again.

Mary Marvell was standing in the middle of the room, her hand to
her throat. The “Western Star” was gone.

Everyone began to talk at once. Lord Yardly was furious, and
Gregory Rolf was trying to comfort his wife.

Poirot, however, was perfectly calm. He was looking at the floor
near where Mary Marvell had been standing.

“The window!” he cried suddenly. “Look at the window!”

One of the long French windows was open.

“A Chinaman!” cried one of the guests. “I saw a Chinaman!”

“Nonsense!” said Lord Yardly. “How could a Chinaman get in here?”

“I tell you I saw him!” insisted the guest. “He was wearing a
pigtail and a long silk robe.”

Poirot went over to the window and looked out.

“The marks of feet,” he said. “Very small feet. It is possible.”

He turned back to the room.

“And you, Lady Yardly?” he asked. “You have your diamond?”

Lady Yardly’s hand went to her neck.

“Yes,” she said. “It is here.”

She drew it out from beneath her dress. The “Star of the East”
sparkled in the light.

“It is a mercy they did not take both,” said Lord Yardly. “But
this is a most serious matter. I shall call the police at once.”

“Wait a moment, my lord,” said Poirot. “Before you call the
police, I should like to ask a few questions.”

“Questions? What questions? The thing’s as plain as a pikestaff.
Some rascally Chinaman has broken in and stolen the diamond.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But there are one or two things that I
do not understand.”

He turned to Mary Marvell.

“Madame, you were wearing the diamond when the lights went out?”

“Yes.”

“And you felt someone take it from your neck?”

“Yes. I felt a hand, and then the chain broke.”

“I see. And you, Lady Yardly, you were sitting in that corner?”

“Yes.”

“Did you see anything?”

“No. It was quite dark.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “the lights were only out for a few
seconds. It was a very quick piece of work.”

He began to walk up and down the room, his hands behind his back.

“A very quick piece of work,” he repeated. “And a very clever
one. But not quite clever enough.”

He stopped in front of Gregory Rolf.

“Mr. Rolf, you were standing near your wife when the lights went
out?”

“Yes. I tried to grab the fellow, but he was too quick for me.”

“I see. And you, Lord Yardly, you were standing near the
fireplace?”

“Yes. I was talking to Rolf here.”

“I see,” said Poirot again.

He went over to the window and picked something up from the floor.

“What is that?” asked Lord Yardly.

“A piece of silk,” said Poirot. “Black silk. From a Chinaman’s
robe, perhaps?”

He looked at it closely, then put it in his pocket.

“Now,” he said, “I think we may call the police.”

The police arrived a short time later, but they could find no
trace of the thief. The footprints outside the window led across
the lawn to the shrubbery, and then disappeared.

The next morning, Poirot and I were sitting in the library.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “what do you make of it?”

“It is a very pretty problem, Hastings. A very pretty problem
indeed.”

“Do you think it was a Chinaman?”

“Who knows? It is possible. But there are other possibilities.”

“What do you mean?”

“Think, Hastings. Who would benefit from the theft of the diamond?”

“The thief, of course.”

“But who is the thief? Is it a real Chinaman, or someone
pretending to be a Chinaman?”

“The guest said he saw a pigtail.”

“A pigtail can be easily made. And a silk robe too.”

“But the footprints?”

“Small feet, Hastings. Very small feet. Like those of a woman,
perhaps?”

I stared at him.

“A woman? You mean Lady Yardly?”

“Or Miss Marvell herself.”

“But why should she steal her own diamond?”

“Insurance, Hastings. Fifty thousand pounds is a large sum of
money.”

“But she’s rich!”

“One can never be too rich. And then there is the other diamond.
The ‘Star of the East.’”

“What about it?”

“It is still here. Why did the thief not take that one too?”

“Perhaps he didn’t have time.”

“Perhaps. Or perhaps he only wanted one of them.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will have a little talk with Lady Yardly.”

He left the room, and I was left to my own reflections.

A few minutes later, he returned. He was looking very grave.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have discovered something very important.”

“What is it?”

“Lady Yardly’s diamond is a paste.”

“A paste? You mean it’s a fake?”

“Exactly. It is a very good fake, but it is a fake nonetheless.”

I was thunderstruck.

“But how? When? Who could have switched it?”

“That is what I intend to find out.”

He went to the door and called Lord Yardly.

“My lord, I should like to speak to you for a moment.”

Lord Yardly came in, looking very harassed.

“Well, Poirot, what is it now? Any more news about the diamond?”

“Yes, my lord. I have some very serious news. Lady Yardly’s
diamond is a fake.”

Lord Yardly stared at him in disbelief.

“A fake? What nonsense! It’s been in the family for generations.”

“It may have been, my lord. But the stone that Lady Yardly is
wearing now is not the real ‘Star of the East.’”

Lord Yardly’s face turned a deep red.

“Are you suggesting that my wife is a liar?”

“I am suggesting nothing, my lord. I am merely stating a fact.”

“I don’t believe it! I’ll have it examined by a jeweler at once.”

“That would be a very good idea,” said Poirot. “But in the
meantime, I have another question to ask you.”

“Well?”

“Did you know that your wife was being blackmailed?”

Lord Yardly’s jaw dropped.

“Blackmailed? What the devil are you talking about?”

“I have reason to believe that Lady Yardly has been receiving
threatening letters for some time.”

“Who from?”

“That I do not know. But I suspect it has something to do with the
diamond.”

Lord Yardly sank into a chair.

“This is terrible,” he muttered. “First the theft, and now this.”

“Do not despair, my lord. Hercule Poirot is on the case.”

He turned to me.

“Hastings, I want you to go to London and find out everything you
can about Gregory Rolf’s past life. Especially his time in
California three years ago.”

“Right you are, Poirot.”

I left at once, and spent the next two days in London, making
enquiries. I found out a good deal about Gregory Rolf. He had
indeed been in California three years ago, and had been involved
in a scandal with a prominent socialite.

When I returned to Yardly Chase, I told Poirot what I had learned.

“Ah!” he said. “It is as I thought. The plot is becoming much
clearer.”

“But who is the blackmailer?”

“I think I know, Hastings. But I must be sure.”

He went to the drawing-room, where everyone was assembled.

“Mesdames et Messieurs,” he said, “I have a few things to say to
you.”

Everyone fell silent.

“The theft of the ‘Western Star’ was a very clever piece of work,”
he began. “But it was not as clever as the person who planned it.”

He looked around the room.

“The letters, the Chinaman, the footprints—all were part of a
carefully laid plan. A plan to hide the fact that the diamond had
already been stolen.”

“What do you mean?” asked Gregory Rolf.

“I mean, Mr. Rolf, that the ‘Western Star’ was not stolen on
Friday night. It was stolen several days before.”

“That’s impossible!” cried Mary Marvell. “I was wearing it when
the lights went out!”

“Were you, madame? Or were you wearing a paste copy?”

Mary Marvell turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do, madame. I think you and your husband planned
this whole thing together.”

“How dare you!” shouted Gregory Rolf.

“Calm yourself, monsieur. I have proof.”

He took the piece of black silk from his pocket.

“This silk,” he said, “did not come from a Chinaman’s robe. It

production. It—it was just like what you’ve described.”

“A Chinaman?” I asked.

She nodded.

“Yes. He—he seemed to know everything. He knew about the diamond—the
‘Star of the East.’ He said it must return to the god.”

“And you have had others?”

“Yes. One every week. The last one came yesterday. It said that
if I did not give up the diamond it would be taken from me at the
full of the moon.”

“That is Friday next,” I said.

“Yes,” she whispered.

I felt a thrill of excitement.

“And you have the diamond with you?”

“No, it is at Yardly Chase. We—we are very poor, Monsieur Hastings.
My husband has been very—unfortunate. The diamond is the most
valuable thing we possess. I—I have been tempted to sell it, but
I could not bring myself to do so. It is an heirloom.”

“I understand,” I said sympathetically. “But you have it still?”

“Yes.” She hesitated. “But I am afraid—horribly afraid. I feel as
though some one were watching me all the time—as though, wherever
I go, there is a Chinaman behind me.”

I could not help a slight smile.

“I think you will find that Monsieur Poirot will be able to dispel
your fears, Lady Yardly,” I said. “He is a most remarkable man.”

“I hope so,” she said. “I have heard such wonderful things of him.”

At that moment the door opened, and Poirot entered. He started
slightly on seeing our visitor.

“Lady Yardly,” I said, “this is Monsieur Poirot.”

He bowed over her hand.

“_Enchanté_, milady. I was not expecting this honour.”

Lady Yardly turned to him.

“Monsieur Poirot, I am in great trouble. Captain Hastings has been
telling me that you already know something of my story.”

Poirot looked at me.

“Ah!” he said. “And what has the good Hastings been telling you?”

I recounted briefly what had passed.

“_Bien, bien_,” said Poirot. “And you have the letters with you,
milady?”

“I have the last one.” She drew it from her bag.

Poirot took it and studied it with interest.

“_Parfait!_” he murmured. “The same paper—the same printing. This
is very interesting.”

He looked at Lady Yardly.

“Tell me, milady, have you ever been to California?”

I saw a sudden flush leap into her cheeks.

“Yes,” she said. “I was there three years ago.”

“And you met a Mr. Gregory Rolf there?”

The flush deepened.

“I—I may have done so. I met a great many people.”

“I see,” said Poirot. He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“And what is it you want me to do, milady?”

“I—I don’t know. I am so frightened. Can you help me?”

“I will do my best, milady. But I must have all the facts. You say
the diamond is at Yardly Chase?”

“Yes.”

“And you are going there on Friday?”

“We are there now. I only came up to town for the day.”

“I see. Well, milady, I think the best thing will be for me to come
down to Yardly Chase on Friday. Then I can see for myself what is
happening.”

“Oh, would you? That would be so kind of you!”

“It is a pleasure, milady. And now, if you will excuse me, I have
a little business to attend to.”

He escorted her to the door. When he returned, he looked at me
with a whimsical smile.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of our two clients?”

“It’s a most extraordinary coincidence!” I said. “Both of them
having these letters from a Chinaman.”

“_Coincidence_—it is a large word, _mon ami_! There is more in this
than meets the eye.”

“You think there is a real Chinaman?”

“I think there is a real diamond,” said Poirot. “And I think there
is a real mystery. But as to the Chinaman—_on verra_!”

On the following Friday, we set out for Yardly Chase. It was a
long journey, and we did not arrive until late in the afternoon.
Lord Yardly met us at the station. He was a tall, fair man, with
a somewhat vacant expression.

“Glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “My wife’s been in a
terrible state of nerves lately. All this talk about Chinamen and
diamonds—it’s enough to drive anyone crazy.”

“It is a most remarkable story, milord,” said Poirot.

“Oh, I don’t believe a word of it myself,” said Lord Yardly. “But
if it makes her feel any better to have you here, I’m delighted.”

We drove to the Chase, a magnificent old house set in a large park.
Lady Yardly was waiting for us in the hall. She looked pale and
anxious.

“I’m so glad you’ve come!” she said.

She led us into the drawing-room, where we found Mary Marvell and
Gregory Rolf. They had arrived earlier in the day.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Miss Marvell, “so you’ve come after
all? I thought you said you weren’t interested in hoaxes?”

“I am always interested in diamonds, madame,” said Poirot.

“And in Chinamen?” asked Gregory Rolf with a laugh.

“Especially in Chinamen,” said Poirot.

Dinner was a somewhat strained affair. Lord Yardly was obviously
trying to be a good host, but he was clearly worried about his wife.
Lady Yardly herself was very quiet, and Miss Marvell and Gregory
Rolf seemed to be the only ones who were enjoying themselves.

After dinner, we all went into the drawing-room. Lady Yardly had
the diamond with her, and she showed it to us. It was a magnificent
stone, but, as Miss Marvell had said, it was not as large as the
“Western Star.”

“It’s a beautiful stone, Lady Yardly,” said Miss Marvell. “But I
think mine is a little better, don’t you?”

She drew out her own diamond and held it up to the light. The two
stones shone with a brilliant fire.

“They are both very fine,” said Poirot.

Suddenly, the lights went out. There was a moment of complete
darkness, and then a scream from Lady Yardly.

“The diamond!” she cried. “It’s gone!”

When the lights came on again, Lady Yardly was standing in the
middle of the room, her hand to her throat. The diamond was gone.

“The window!” cried Gregory Rolf. “Look!”

One of the long French windows was standing open. He rushed to it
and looked out.

“There’s some one there!” he shouted. “A man—running!”

He leapt out of the window and disappeared into the darkness. Lord
Yardly followed him.

“Oh, my diamond! My diamond!” moaned Lady Yardly.

Poirot was examining the window.

“A very neat piece of work,” he murmured.

In a few minutes, Lord Yardly and Gregory Rolf returned. They were
both breathless.

“He got away,” said Rolf. “He was too quick for us. But I saw him—it
was a Chinaman!”

“A Chinaman?” cried Lady Yardly. “I knew it! I knew it!”

“Are you sure it was a Chinaman, Mr. Rolf?” asked Poirot.

“Positive! I saw his pigtail flying as he ran.”

“I saw him too,” said Lord Yardly. “At least, I saw a figure in
the darkness. It might have been a Chinaman.”

“This is very serious,” said Poirot. “We must call the police at
once.”

“I’ve already done so,” said Lord Yardly. “They should be here any
minute.”

The police arrived shortly afterwards, and a thorough search of
the grounds was made, but no trace of the thief could be found.

The next morning, Poirot and I were sitting in the library.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, “what do you make of it?”

“It seems clear enough,” I said. “The Chinaman did it. He’s been
threatening to take the diamond for weeks, and now he’s done it.”

“And Miss Marvell’s diamond?” asked Poirot. “Why did he not take
that too?”

“Perhaps he didn’t have time,” I suggested.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But there is another possibility.”

“What is that?”

“That there never was a Chinaman.”

“But Gregory Rolf saw him! And Lord Yardly saw a figure!”

“Mr. Rolf says he saw a Chinaman. Lord Yardly says he saw a figure.
There is a difference, _mon ami_.”

“But the window was open!”

“_Oui_, the window was open. But who opened it? And who turned out
the lights?”

“You think it was an inside job?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that it is time I had a little talk with
Lady Yardly.”

He sent for her, and she came into the library, looking even paler
than she had the night before.

“Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, “I want you to tell me the truth.”

“The truth?” she gasped. “What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that I do not believe in your Chinaman.
I think you know more about the disappearance of the diamond than
you have told us.”

Lady Yardly burst into tears.

“It’s true!” she sobbed. “It’s true! There was no Chinaman. I—I
took the diamond myself.”

“You took it?” I cried. “But why?”

“Because I had to!” she moaned. “I was being blackmailed. Gregory
Rolf—he knew about—about something that happened in California
three years ago. He told me that if I didn’t give him the diamond,
he would tell my husband.”

“So you gave it to him?” asked Poirot.

“Yes. He told me to make up the story about the Chinaman, and the
letters. He said he would arrange the whole thing.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And the lights?”

“He turned them out. He said it would make it look more
realistic.”

“And the man he saw running away?”

“There was no man. He just made that up.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And where is the diamond now?”

“He has it. He said he would sell it and give me some of the money.”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we should have a word with Mr. Rolf.”

But Gregory Rolf was nowhere to be found. He had disappeared
during the night, and with him, of course, the diamond.

“Well,” I said, “it seems he’s got away with it.”

“Not quite,” said Poirot.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that I took the precaution of changing the
diamonds yesterday afternoon. The stone that Mr. Rolf has is a
very good imitation. The real ‘Star of the East’ is in my pocket.”

He drew the diamond out and held it up. It sparkled brilliantly in
the sunlight.

“But how did you know?” I asked.

“My dear Hastings, it was quite simple. The letters—they were too
perfect. They were like something out of a book. And then there
was the story of the two diamonds. It was too convenient. I
suspected from the first that it was a plot to steal the diamonds.
And when I saw Gregory Rolf, I was sure of it. He is a very good
actor, but he is not a very good criminal.”

“And Miss Marvell?” I asked. “Was she in it too?”

“I do not think so,” said Poirot. “I think she was as much a victim
as Lady Yardly. She believed the story of the Chinaman, and she
was afraid for her own diamond.”

“But why did she come to you?”

“Because she was worried. And because, like everyone else, she
wanted the advice of the great Hercule Poirot!”

He smiled and put the diamond back in his pocket.

“And now, Hastings, I think we should return the ‘Star of the East’
to Lord Yardly. He will be very glad to have it back.”

And so the mystery of the “Western Star” was solved. It was a
clever plot, but it was not clever enough for Hercule Poirot.

“You see, Hastings,” he said, as we were driving back to London,
“it is always the same. People think they can deceive me, but they
forget one thing.”

“What is that?” I asked.

“The little grey cells, _mon ami_! The little grey cells!”

“She has just left. As I was saying, if she, as the holder of one
of the twin diamonds, has received a mysterious series of warnings,
you, as the holder of the other stone, must necessarily have done
the same. You see how simple it is? I am right, then, you have
received these strange communications also?”

For a moment she hesitated, as though in doubt whether to trust me
or not, then she bowed her head in assent with a little smile.

“That is so,” she acknowledged.

“Were yours, too, left by hand—by a Chinaman?”

“No, they came by post; but, tell me, has Miss Marvell undergone
the same experience, then?”

I recounted to her the events of the morning. She listened
attentively.

I saw her to her car, and returned to the room, to find Poirot
already there. I told him at once what had happened.

“_Tiens!_” he ejaculated. “So Lady Yardly too, has received
letters of a similar nature? And she is coming to Yardly Chase for
the week-end?”

“Miss Marvell is going there too,” I replied.

Poirot was silent for a space. Then he looked up.

“Tell me, Hastings, what was your impression of Lady Yardly?”

I thought.

“A beautiful woman, of a very high-spirited and somewhat reckless
type, I should say. Not at all like Miss Marvell.”

Poirot nodded.

“And what did you make of her story? Did it strike you as—as
authentic?”

“Why, certainly! Why should it not?”

“I don’t know. There is something—something which eludes me. I
cannot yet see the connection. Tell me, Hastings, did she say
anything about her husband?”

“Not a word.”

“And you did not see the letters she had received?”

“No, she had destroyed them.”

“_C’est dommage._” Poirot sighed. “I would have liked much to see
those letters.”

“But you have seen those of Miss Marvell.”

“_Oui_, but it is the others that I want. However, it cannot be
helped. We must wait and see what Friday brings forth.”

Friday came, but it brought nothing to us in London. On Saturday
morning, however, a telegram arrived from Yardly Chase. It was
from Lord Yardly and ran as follows:

“DIAMOND STOLEN LAST NIGHT. PLEASE COME AT ONCE.”

I was for starting at once, but Poirot was more leisurely.

“Wait, _mon ami_, let us first see what the morning papers have
to say. They may have more details.”

The papers, however, had nothing. They were full of the visit of
the American film stars to Yardly Chase, and of the house-party
there.

“Very well,” said Poirot, “let us start for Yardly Chase.”

We reached our destination about midday. It was a magnificent old
place, and Lord Yardly, a tall, thin man with a tired face, met
us at the station.

“It’s a most mysterious business, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as
he drove us to the house. “My wife is in a terrible state. She
insists that it’s some Chinese plot.”

“And you, _milord_?”

Lord Yardly shrugged his shoulders.

“I don’t know what to think. It certainly seems very strange.
Last night, about ten o’clock, my wife was in her sitting-room
dressing for dinner, when she suddenly saw a Chinaman’s face
peering in at the window. She screamed, and he disappeared. We
all rushed in, but could find no trace of him. Then, about an hour
later, when we were all at dinner, there was another scream from
upstairs. We rushed up, and found my wife’s maid fainted on the
floor, and the diamond—which my wife had left on the dressing-table—gone!”

“And the window?” asked Poirot.

“It was wide open. The thief must have climbed up by the ivy.”

“And you found no trace of him?”

“None. It was a very dark night, and he would have no difficulty
in escaping.”

“And Miss Marvell’s diamond?” I asked. “Was that stolen too?”

“No, Miss Marvell has her jewel with her. She had it on at dinner.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is curious.”

We had arrived at the house by this time, and Lord Yardly led the
way into the library.

“I’ll send for my wife,” he said. “She will be able to tell you
more than I can.”

Lady Yardly appeared in a few minutes. She looked pale and
agitated, and her eyes were red with weeping.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she cried, “it is too terrible! My poor
diamond! It is gone—gone!”

“Calm yourself, I pray you, madame,” said Poirot soothingly. “Tell
us exactly what happened.”

Lady Yardly’s account was substantially the same as her husband’s.
She had seen the Chinaman at the window, and later the diamond
had been stolen from her dressing-table while she was at dinner.

“And your maid, madame? What has she to say?”

“Poor girl, she is quite prostrate. She says she heard a noise
at the window, and then a man—a Chinaman—sprang into the room.
He hit her a blow on the head, and that is all she remembers.”

“I see,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “And you, madame, you saw the
Chinaman at the window earlier in the evening?”

“Yes, I am certain of it. I shall never forget that face—it was
horrible!”

Poirot turned to Lord Yardly.

“You have sent for the police, _milord_?”

“Yes, they have been here this morning. But they could find
nothing.”

“And Miss Marvell? Is she still here?”

“Yes, she and Mr. Rolf are staying until Monday.”

“I should like to see them,” said Poirot.

Miss Marvell and her husband were found in the garden. Gregory
Rolf was inclined to be facetious.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “your warnings didn’t seem to
have much effect. The Chink has got the Yardly diamond, but he
hasn’t got ours yet.”

“Not yet, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot quietly.

“And he won’t either,” said Miss Marvell. “I’m taking good care
of mine.”

She held up her hand, on which the “Western Star” was flashing.

“I see,” said Poirot. “You are wearing it.”

“Yes, and I don’t intend to take it off.”

“Quite right, madame,” said Poirot. “It is the only safe way.”

He turned to Gregory Rolf.

“And you, monsieur, you have no fears for your wife’s safety?”

“Not I! I guess I can look after her all right.”

“I am sure you can,” said Poirot politely.

He turned back to the house.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, as we walked towards the library,
“what do you think of it all?”

“It seems a very clear case,” I said. “The Chinaman has got one of
the diamonds, and he will certainly try for the other.”

“You think so?”

“It seems obvious.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “And yet—there are one or two things
which I do not quite understand.”

“What are they?”
