“For one thing, why did the Chinaman only take the Yardly diamond?
Miss Marvell’s diamond is just as valuable, and it was in the
same house.”

“But it was not so easy to get at,” I pointed out. “Miss Marvell
had it on her person.”

“That is true. But the Chinaman could have waited. He had already
waited three years, according to Mr. Rolf.”

“Perhaps he was afraid of being caught.”

“Perhaps. And then there is the matter of the letters. Why did
the letters to Lady Yardly come by post, while those to Miss
Marvell were left by hand?”

“I don’t see that that matters much.”

“Perhaps not. But it is a point. And then there is the perfume.”

“The perfume?”

“Yes, the perfume of joss-stick. Lady Yardly noticed it on her
letters. Did Miss Marvell notice it on hers?”

“I don’t know. She didn’t say so.”

“No, she didn’t. I should like to ask her.”

He turned back and found Miss Marvell still in the garden.

“One moment, madame,” he said. “The letters you received—did they
have any particular perfume?”

Miss Marvell looked surprised.

“Perfume? No, I don’t think so. I didn’t notice any.”

“Thank you, madame,” said Poirot.

He returned to me.

“You see, Hastings? No perfume. That is another point.”

“I don’t see that it leads anywhere,” I said.

“Perhaps not. But we shall see. Now I should like to see the
maid.”

The maid was a pretty, dark-haired girl, still very much upset.
Her story was simple. She had heard a noise at the window, and
on going to see what it was, a man had jumped into the room and
struck her down. She had seen his face—it was the face of a
Chinaman.

“And then?” asked Poirot.

“I don’t remember anything more, sir, until I found them all
standing round me.”

“I see. And the diamond? Where was it?”

“It was on the dressing-table, sir. Her ladyship had just taken
it off.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you.”

He turned to Lord Yardly.

“Is it possible to see the room where the theft took place?”

“Certainly.”

Lord Yardly led the way upstairs to a large, luxuriously
furnished room. Poirot went straight to the window.

“It is a long drop to the ground,” he said, looking out.

“Yes, but the ivy is very strong.”

Poirot nodded. He examined the window-sill closely, but
apparently found nothing. Then he turned to the dressing-table.

“The diamond was here, you say?”

“Yes.”

Poirot looked at the table for a moment, then he picked up a
small bottle of perfume.

“Lady Yardly’s?” he asked.

“Yes.”

Poirot sniffed at it.

“_C’est exquis!_” he murmured.

He put the bottle down and turned to Lord Yardly.

“Well, _milord_, I think I have seen all I want to see for the
present. I should like to have a few words with Lady Yardly
alone.”

“Certainly,” said Lord Yardly. “I will go and find her.”

He left the room, and Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it now?”

“I don’t know,” I said. “It’s a very strange business.”

“It is,” said Poirot. “Very strange.”

Lady Yardly came into the room at that moment. She looked
anxious and tired.

“You wanted to see me, Monsieur Poirot?”

“Yes, madame. I wanted to ask you one or two questions.”

“Yes?”

“You told me the other day that you had destroyed the letters you
received. Is that so?”

“Yes, it is.”

“You are quite sure?”

“Of course I am sure. Why do you ask?”

“Because I thought you might have forgotten. It is a pity. They
might have been very useful.”

“I am sorry,” said Lady Yardly.

“And the perfume, madame? You are sure it was the perfume of
joss-stick?”

“Oh, yes, I am sure of that.”

“I see. And now, madame, I have one more question to ask you.
A very important one.”

“What is it?”

“Where is the diamond?”

Lady Yardly started.

“Where is it? Why, it is stolen, of course!”

“Is it, madame?”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, madame, that I do not believe the diamond was stolen by
a Chinaman.”

“Then who stole it?”

“I think, madame, that you know that better than I do.”

Lady Yardly turned very pale.

“I—I don’t understand you,” she stammered.

“I think you do, madame. I think you know very well where the
diamond is.”

Lady Yardly sank into a chair.

“What do you mean?” she whispered.

“I mean, madame, that there was no Chinaman at the window last
night. There was no Chinaman who struck your maid. It was all a
story, invented by you.”

“Monsieur Poirot!”

“It is no use, madame. I know the truth. You have the diamond
yourself.”

Lady Yardly began to sob.

“It is true,” she moaned. “It is true. But I had to do it! I had
to!”

“Why, madame?”

“Because I was being blackmailed. Gregory Rolf—he knew something—something that happened three years ago in California. He
threatened to tell my husband if I didn’t give him the diamond.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And so you invented this story of the
Chinaman to account for the disappearance of the diamond?”

“Yes. I didn’t know what else to do. He was so cruel—so
relentless.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And the letters? You wrote them yourself?”

“Yes. I thought it would make the story more believable.”

“And the perfume? The perfume of joss-stick?”

“I put it on the paper to make it seem more like the East.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And Miss Marvell’s letters? Did you write
those too?”

“No, I don’t know anything about them. I suppose Gregory Rolf
wrote those himself.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, madame, I think you had better tell
your husband the truth.”

“Oh, no, no! I couldn’t! He would never forgive me!”

“I think he would, madame. It is better to tell the truth than
to live a lie.”

Lady Yardly sobbed for a few minutes, then she looked up.

“Perhaps you are right, Monsieur Poirot. I will tell him.”

“That is right, madame,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will
excuse us, I think we will be going.”

As we drove back to the station, I turned to Poirot.

“How did you know, Poirot?” I asked. “How did you know she had
the diamond?”

“It was the perfume, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “The perfume of
joss-stick. Lady Yardly said her letters were scented with it.
But Miss Marvell’s were not. Why should the Chinaman scent one
set of letters and not the other? It was not logical. And then,
when I saw the perfume on Lady Yardly’s dressing-table—it was
not joss-stick, it was a very expensive French perfume. But
it was the same perfume that I had noticed on the letters she
brought to my rooms.”

“But she said they were scented with joss-stick!”

“Exactly, _mon ami_. She said so because she wanted to make the
story more believable. But she made a mistake. She forgot that
Hercule Poirot has a very good nose!”

“And the Chinaman at the window?”

“There was no Chinaman, _mon ami_. Lady Yardly saw what she
wanted to see. And the maid—she was in the plot too, no doubt.”

“And what about Gregory Rolf?”

“Ah, Gregory Rolf! He is a clever man, that one. He knew about
Lady Yardly’s secret, and he used it to get the diamond. He
probably wrote the letters to his wife himself, to make her think
she was in danger too. It was a very clever plot.”

“And the diamond? What will happen to it?”

“I think, _mon ami_, that Lord Yardly will find it in a very
unexpected place. And I think that Gregory Rolf will find that
England is not a very safe place for him!”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you have done it again!”

“_Oui, mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was a very simple case. A
matter of the little grey cells—and a very good nose!”

And he settled back in his seat with a look of great satisfaction.

I saw her to the door. Just as she was about to step into her car,
Poirot himself returned. I introduced him.

“Ah! Monsieur Poirot,” she cried. “I have been to you for advice.
Your friend, Captain Hastings, has told me all about Miss Marvell
and her letters. They’re the same as mine. It’s all very
disturbing, isn’t it?”

“Most certainly it is. Let us return to my rooms. I have one or
two questions to ask of you, Lady Yardly.”

She shook her head.

“I’m so sorry—I’ve a dozen engagements. I really must get off.
Captain Hastings has all the facts.”

“But it would be a satisfaction to me to hear them from yourself.”

“Wait. I have an idea. Why not come down to Yardly Chase for the
week-end? We shall have quite a party there. Miss Marvell and her
husband are coming, you know. You will be able to talk it over
then, and I can show you the diamond.”

“You are most kind, Lady Yardly. I shall be delighted.”

“That’s settled then. Friday next.”

She drove off. I noticed Poirot looking after the car with a
peculiar expression.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” he said, as we went upstairs again. “You
have been busy! You have made progress! You have interviewed Lady
Yardly in my absence.”

I laughed.

“Yes, I flatter myself I did rather well. I went to the root of
the matter at once.”

And I told him my deductions. Poirot smiled.

“_Pas mal_! Only, you should have noticed the smell of the
joss-stick. It was very strong.”

“How did you know? I did not tell you!”

“I smelt it—in the air as I came in! Also, I have been to the
offices of _Society Gossip_. The editor is an old friend of mine.
I have learned several things of interest.”

He took a turn or two round the room.

“_Voyons!_ What have we? Two diamonds, both of the same size and
shape—both forming the eyes of a Chinese god—one in the East, one
in the West. Both are threatened at the same time. The full of the
moon is on Friday next. On that day both the owners of the
diamonds will be under the same roof. Why? Because Gregory Rolf,
husband of the one, was a friend of the other, three years ago in
the States. This Gregory Rolf—it is a man of a certain
shrewdness—one who would see that two and two make four. Is it
not so?”

“Then you think he is at the bottom of it all?”

“I think nothing, _mon ami_. But there are possibilities, are there
not?”

“But if the Chinaman is a myth——”

“Who said he was a myth? Not I. There may be a Chinaman—or there
may not. We shall see.”

“Anyway, the mystery will be solved on Friday.”

“On the contrary, on Friday the mystery begins!”

I looked at him, but he refused to say more.

“In the meantime,” he remarked, “I shall make certain little
investigations. And you, Hastings, you will have the goodness to
look up all that is to be found out about Yardly Chase.”

The next few days passed quickly. I found out a good deal about
the history of the Yardly diamond. It had been in the family for
some generations, and there was no doubt as to its being a very
fine stone.

I also learnt that Lord Yardly was at the end of his tether
financially. He had been a great gambler in his youth, and the
estates were heavily mortgaged. Lady Yardly had been a Miss Edith
Saville, a well-known beauty.

On the Friday morning Poirot and I started for Yardly Chase. It
was a wonderful old place, and in the setting of the spring woods
was like a dream of the past.

Lord Yardly met us at the station. He was a man of about fifty,
with a pleasant, somewhat vacant face, and an easy-going manner.

“Glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “My wife has been
telling me about this business. A bit of a joke, what? Those
screen people have to get up some kind of a stunt, you know, to
keep themselves in the public eye. Though I must say I’m a bit
surprised at Edith’s taking it seriously.”

He laughed. I noticed that his laugh was a little hollow.

“We’ll go up to the house in the car. Most of the party is there
already. Gregory Rolf and his wife, you know. They’re quite a
feature in their way.”

As we drove along, Poirot began to talk of the diamond.

“My wife’s got it on her now,” said Lord Yardly. “She doesn’t often
wear it, but she thought she’d like to to-night. It’s a fine stone,
you know—the best we’ve got. Must have cost a lot of money when
it was bought.”

“It’s an heirloom, isn’t it?” I asked.

“Oh, yes. Been in the family for years. I don’t know where it
originally came from—India, I suppose.”

We reached the house, and were soon in the midst of a gay party.
Lady Yardly was a charming hostess. She looked very beautiful in
a simple evening gown of black velvet, which showed off the
brilliant diamond at her throat to perfection.

Mary Marvell, too, was looking her best. She was wearing her own
diamond, and the two stones were certainly very similar.

After dinner, we all gathered in the big hall. The conversation
naturally turned on the jewels.

“They’re wonderfully alike,” said Gregory Rolf, looking from one
to the other. “It’s a pity they can’t be seen together.”

“Why not?” said Lady Yardly. “Let’s put them on the table here,
side by side.”

She unfastened her own diamond and laid it on the table. Mary
Marvell followed suit.

We all crowded round. The two stones were indeed very similar in
size and shape, though it seemed to me that Lady Yardly’s had a
slight yellowish tinge.

“A wonderful pair,” murmured Poirot. “It is a pity they should
ever be separated.”

“Well, they won’t be for long, if the Chinaman has his way!” laughed
Gregory Rolf.

As he spoke, the lights suddenly went out. For a moment there was
a dead silence. Then a woman’s scream rang out, followed by the
sound of a heavy fall.

I felt Poirot’s hand on my arm.

“_Vite_, Hastings! The switch—where is it?”

I felt my way along the wall, and in a moment the lights were on
again.

A strange sight met our eyes. Lady Yardly was lying on the floor in
a dead faint. Mary Marvell was standing by the table, her face
ashen.

But the diamonds had vanished!

“So you’ve seen her,” Poirot said, with his eyes twinkling, on
his return.

“Seen who?” I asked, as though my mind was far away.

“_La belle dame_, Lady Yardly. You had a charming _tête-à-tête_,
_hein_? Come, _mon ami_, do not be so mysterious. I know it all.”

“How can you? You were out!”

“_Vraiment_! But have I not told you that the good Mrs. Murchison
has a tongue? A most excellent woman—one whom I have no
hesitation in recommending for the post of a _concierge_ in Paris.”

“Well, since you know, there’s no more to be said. But I told
Lady Yardly everything. She’s had letters, too.”

“_Tiens!_ Is it so? And what did she say?”

I recounted our conversation. Poirot listened with an air of
repressed excitement.

“And she had not the letters with her? No? _Dommage!_ And she
thinks they were scented with joss-stick? That is interesting!
Very interesting! And the ‘Western Star’—did she say she had it
with her? No? _Tant pis!_”

“She didn’t say anything about it,” I replied, “but it’s a diamond
exactly like Miss Marvell’s, and it’s the other eye of the god.”

“So the story goes. A very pretty story! I should like to see
these two stones together. It would be a sight for the gods—or
at least for the one god whose eyes they were! And we are to be
of the party, Hastings?”

“Are we? I didn’t know.”

“But yes! I have seen Lord Yardly at his club. We are most
amiably invited for Friday.”

“I’m glad of that,” I said, “for I’m really beginning to feel
nervous about the whole thing. It’s so—so uncanny.”

Poirot shook his head.

“_Pas du tout_, my friend. It is as simple as A B C. But it is
very interesting—very!”

The Friday found us at Yardly Chase, a fine old mansion that had
been in the family for centuries. Lord Yardly was a typical
Englishman of the old school, bluff and hearty, and a keen
sportsman. Lady Yardly was a charming hostess.

The other guests were Mary Marvell and her husband.

I must confess that I felt a certain amount of excitement. It was
the night of the full moon. Would the Chinese thief really make
his appearance? Or was it all a hoax as Gregory Rolf had
suggested?

Dinner was a somewhat silent meal. We were all, I think, a little
under the influence of the approaching climax.

After dinner we assembled in the big hall. The moon was shining
brightly through the high windows.

Suddenly there was a cry from Lady Yardly. She was standing by the
window.

“Look!” she cried. “Look there!”

We all rushed to the window. Outside on the terrace a dark figure
was standing. It was the figure of a man, and as he turned his
face towards us in the moonlight, we saw that he was a Chinaman.

With a cry of “The diamond! The diamond!” Lady Yardly fell
fainting to the floor.

Her husband rushed to her side.

“My God! The diamond’s gone!” he cried.

We looked at Lady Yardly’s neck. The magnificent diamond she had
been wearing was no longer there.

In the confusion that followed, the Chinaman disappeared. We
searched the gardens and the park, but no trace of him was to be
found.

Poirot, who had remained strangely quiet, now came forward.

“A most interesting occurrence,” he remarked. “Most interesting.
And now, if you will permit me, I will have a little talk with
Lady Yardly.”

He was absent for about half an hour. When he returned his face
bore a look of satisfaction.

“Everything is as I thought,” he said. “A very simple case.”

“Simple!” I cried. “When a man disappears into thin air, and a
diamond is stolen before our very eyes!”

“Precisely, _mon ami_. It is the simplicity of it that is so
charming. But come, we must return to London. I have much to do.”

On our way back in the train, Poirot was very uncommunicative. To
all my questions he only replied with a smile.

“Wait, Hastings, wait. All will be revealed in good time.”

The next morning, to my surprise, Poirot announced that he was
going to call on Miss Mary Marvell.

“But why?” I asked. “She hasn’t lost her diamond.”

“Not yet, _mon ami_, not yet. But who knows? The full moon, it
lasts for more than one night.”

We found Miss Marvell in her suite at the _Magnificent_. She
seemed very much upset by the news of the robbery at Yardly
Chase.

“It’s too terrible!” she cried. “And to think that my diamond may
be the next! I’m so frightened, Monsieur Poirot. What shall I
do?”

“Be calm, madame,” said Poirot. “I have everything in hand. But I
must ask you one question. Where is your diamond now?”

“It’s in the hotel safe. I put it there as soon as we got back
last night.”

“Good. Now, if you will be so kind as to fetch it. I wish to
examine it.”

Miss Marvell left the room and returned in a few minutes with a
small jewel-case. She opened it and handed the diamond to Poirot.

He took it to the window and examined it closely. Then he handed
it back to her.

“Thank you, madame. It is as I thought. And now, if you will
excuse us, we must be going.”

As we left the hotel, I turned to Poirot.

“Well?” I asked. “What did you find out?”

“I found out, Hastings, that the ‘Western Star’ is a very fine
diamond—but it is not the diamond that Miss Marvell showed me
the other day!”

“What!” I cried. “You mean it’s a fake?”

“Precisely. A very good imitation, but a fake nevertheless.”

“But then—who has the real diamond?”

“Ah, that is the question! But I think I can answer it. Come, we
must go back to our rooms. I expect a visitor.”

We had not been back ten minutes when the door opened and Gregory
Rolf was shown in. He looked pale and anxious.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’ve just heard that you’ve been to
see my wife. What is this about the diamond being a fake?”

Poirot smiled.

“It is quite true, Mr. Rolf. The stone Miss Marvell has now is a
paste imitation.”

Rolf sank into a chair.

“Then it’s gone!” he groaned. “The real diamond has been stolen!”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot quietly, “the real diamond has not
been stolen—because it was never in Miss Marvell’s possession!”

Rolf stared at him.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Mr. Rolf, that you never bought the ‘Western Star’ in San
Francisco. You bought a very good imitation, and you gave it to
your wife as a wedding present. You see, you were not as rich then
as you are now.”

Rolf went very white.

“How did you know?” he whispered.

“It was very simple. When I saw the stone the first time, I knew
it was a fake. But I did not say so. I wanted to see what would
happen. And what happened? Lady Yardly came to see me. She, too,
had a diamond. And her diamond was real!”

“Lady Yardly’s diamond was real?” I cried.

“Certainly. It was the ‘Star of the East.’ And then I began to
think. Why should two diamonds, one real and one fake, be so
closely connected? And then I remembered the story of the two
eyes of the god. One went West, the other East. The ‘Star of the
East’ was in the possession of the Yardly family. The ‘Western
Star’ was bought by Mr. Rolf in San Francisco. San Francisco is in
the West. You see?”

“But I don’t understand,” I said. “If Miss Marvell’s diamond was a
fake, why did she get the blackmailing letters?”

“She didn’t,” said Poirot. “_She_ wrote them herself!”

“What!”

“Yes. She wanted the advertisement. She knew the story of the
Yardly diamond, and she thought it would be a fine piece of
publicity if it were thought that she had the twin stone, and that
it was being claimed by a Chinese gang. So she invented the letters
and the Chinaman.”

“But what about Lady Yardly?” I asked. “She had the real diamond,
and it was stolen.”

“Was it?” said Poirot. “I think not. Let us ask Lady Yardly
herself. She is in the next room.”

He went to the door and opened it. Lady Yardly came in. She was
crying.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she sobbed, “I can’t keep it up any longer!
You are too clever for me.”

“Tell us, madame,” said Poirot kindly.

“It was three years ago,” she said. “In California. I—I was very
foolish. I met Gregory Rolf. I was attracted by him. I—I gave
him some money—and I gave him the diamond to sell for me. I
was in debt, you see. He brought me back a paste imitation, and
I have worn it ever since. My husband never knew.”

“And the robbery?” I asked.

“It was a pretense. I knew Mary Marvell was coming, and I knew
she had a diamond which she claimed was the twin to mine. I was
afraid that if the two stones were seen together, mine would be
discovered to be a fake. So I arranged the robbery. I—I was the
Chinaman!”

“You!” I cried.

“Yes. I had a Chinese costume which I had used in some private
theatricals. I put it on, and—well, you know the rest.”

Poirot turned to Gregory Rolf.

“And you, monsieur? What have you to say?”

Rolf stood up. He looked very old and tired.

“I have nothing to say,” he said. “I was a scoundrel. I took the
diamond and I sold it. I—I have never been able to get it
back.”

Poirot nodded.

“I thought as much. Well, the matter is now in the hands of Lord
Yardly. I have told him everything.”

At that moment the door opened and Lord Yardly entered. He went
straight to his wife and took her in his arms.

“It’s all right, my dear,” he said. “I know everything. And I
forgive you.”

He turned to Poirot.

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. You have saved my wife’s honour.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot. “A mere matter of the little grey
cells.”

And so the mystery of the “Western Star” was solved. But I still
think that Poirot was a little hard on poor Mary Marvell. After
all, she only wanted a little advertisement!

“Then you’ll tell him what I’ve said, won’t you? I wish now I had
not destroyed the letters. It might have been better to have kept
them. Is it true, Captain Hastings, that Miss Marvell and her
husband are coming down to us on Friday?”

“Quite true,” I replied. “And she is bringing her diamond, too.”

Lady Yardly gave a start.

“I only hope she doesn’t lose it!” she exclaimed, with an attempt
at lightness. “Though if the stories are true, she’s not likely to,
is she?”

I smiled as I saw her out. Poirot arrived back soon after her
departure. I recounted all that had occurred. He listened with
great attention.

“So Lady Yardly has had these letters, too? And the perfume of the
East was about them—_eh_? That is very interesting.”

He paced the room for a few moments, then he stopped.

“I must see those letters of Miss Marvell’s again, Hastings. Give
them to me, _mon ami_.”

I handed them to him, and he took them to the window, examining
them minutely.

“Nothing,” he said at last. “Absolutely nothing. Not even a trace
of a smell. It is curious, that!”

I thought so too. Was it possible that Lady Yardly’s imagination
had led her to perceive a non-existent perfume? My meditations
were interrupted by Poirot.

“One thing is certain, Hastings. The drama is being played—the
actors are already on the stage. Now, what do you think of Lady
Yardly?”

I described her as best I could.

“A beautiful woman, you say? And a woman of the world. It is
different from our little Mary Marvell—who is also a woman of the
world, but who does not show it. Our Mary, she is ‘the girl next
door’—or what you will! But she has the _tête_ of a business
woman, _allez_! And Lady Yardly, she is unhappy, you say? Why?
Is it that she fears to lose her diamond? Or is it something else?”

“I think she’s a very sensitive woman,” I replied. “The thought of
any mystery or danger would naturally tell on her.”

Poirot shook his head.

“There is more than that, Hastings. Now I, Hercule Poirot, have a
little idea. It is a very little one—so little that I do not care
to speak of it. I must have more information. I must know the past
history of Lady Yardly.”

“If you really want to know it,” I said, “I might be able to find
out something from Mary Cavendish. She’s an old friend of Lady
Yardly’s.”

“An excellent idea! See her at once, _mon ami_. I have other
matters to attend to.”

I did as he requested, and returned about two hours later. Poirot
was sitting in his chair, his eyes closed, his fingertips joined.

“Well?” he asked, without moving.

“I have found out several things. In the first place, Lord Yardly
is a bit of a stick. He’s very proud of his name and his
ancestors. As for Lady Yardly, she had a bit of a reputation three
years ago—some story about a young Californian whom she had met
out there. Some people say she was actually in love with him.
Then, suddenly, the thing was hushed up. They say her husband paid
a big sum of money to some one. Anyhow, they’ve been living quite
happily ever since. But people haven’t forgotten.”

“The young Californian—was it Gregory Rolf?”

“It was.”

“_Tiens!_ This is very interesting. And the diamond, ‘the Star of
the East’—when did Lord Yardly give her that?”

“He didn’t give it to her. It’s an heirloom. It’s been in the
family for generations.”

“_Vraiment?_” Poirot’s eyes flew open. “And you are sure of that,
Hastings?”

“Absolutely. Mary Cavendish was quite positive on the point.”

“Then we have a very pretty problem, _mon ami_! Now, tell me, what
do you think of Gregory Rolf?”

“A very handsome man—but a trifle loud, perhaps. Not quite a
gentleman.”

“I agree with you. He is—how do you say?—a little ‘thick.’ And
now, Hastings, we must prepare for our journey to Yardly Chase.”

“We are going there?” I cried, surprised.

“But certainly. I have received an invitation from Lord Yardly.”

He showed me a letter. It was a brief, almost curt, note, asking
Poirot to come down on Friday and stay for a few days.

“It seems he, too, has been hearing about me,” said Poirot, with a
twinkle. “Well, Hastings, we shall see what we shall see! I have
a little idea—a very little one—but it grows, _mon ami_, it grows!”

I felt at my most important as I showed her to the door.

“I may rely on you to tell Monsieur Poirot everything, then?” she
asked, with a charming smile.

“Of course! You may depend upon me.”

“And you think that there is something in it—something more than
a joke?”

I smiled at her again, and we shook hands once more.

“Indeed I do,” I said. “There’s some deep-laid plot at work, that’s
my opinion.”

I had hardly closed the door behind her when Poirot came in.

“_Bon jour_, Hastings! How do we go on? Have you had a visitor in
my absence?”

I recounted at some length my interview with Lady Yardly. Poirot
listened with the greatest attention.

“_Tiens! Tiens!_” he remarked. “You have indeed been busy! And
nothing more? No little details of any sort?”

“Well—nothing that I noticed,” I said.

“_Pas de parfum_—eh?”

“By Jove, Poirot! You are a wizard! I’d forgotten all about that.
How did you know? Yes, she did mention a curious smell about the
letters.”

“Ah! _Le parfum d’Orient_—_l’encens_—the joss-stick—_hein_?”

I nodded.

“Exactly. But how did you know?”

“I have a nose, _mon ami_, and it is at present telling me quite
plainly that a lady who uses a certain very expensive and very
individual perfume has been in this room within the last half-hour.
The same perfume, _mon cher_, that was used by Miss Mary Marvell!”

“Impossible!” I cried. “Lady Yardly’s perfume was quite different.”

“_Vraiment?_” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Then you did not notice it
after all! Or perhaps you are right—she may have used another.
But let us proceed. Have you seen this morning’s paper?”

He handed me a sheet of the _Daily Mail_.

“Listen to this: ‘Diamond Robbery at the Magnificent. Miss Mary
Marvell’s Famous Jewel Stolen.’”

“What?” I cried. “But it was here—in this room—not an hour ago!”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “And yet it has been stolen! A very
pretty little problem, is it not?”

“But how—where—when?”

“That, _mon cher_, is what we are about to discover.”

When my friend returned, I enjoyed telling him the tale of what
had occurred during his absence. He cross-questioned me rather
sharply over the details of our conversation and I could read
between the lines that he was not best pleased to have been absent.
I also fancied that the dear old fellow was just the least inclined
to be jealous. It had become rather a pose with him to consistently
belittle my abilities, and I think he was chagrined at finding no
loophole for criticism. I was secretly rather pleased with myself,
though I tried to conceal the fact for fear of irritating him. In
spite of his idiosyncrasies, I was deeply attached to my quaint
little friend.

“Wait till to-morrow, _mon ami_. _Alors_, we shall see what we
shall see.”

Lord Yardly arrived on the morrow. He was a great, big,
red-faced, simple-looking man, and he seemed considerably
mystified.

“Got your wire, Monsieur Poirot. Here I am. What is it all about?
Has someone been trying to rob my wife?”

Poirot leant back in his chair, half closing his eyes.

“That is what I want to find out from you, _milord_. Has she had
any threatening letters?”

Lord Yardly stared.

“Not that I know of. She would have told me if she had.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Oh, quite. We have no secrets from each other.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “And yet she has been to see me,
_monsieur_.”

“My wife? Here? When?”

“Yesterday afternoon.”

Lord Yardly’s face went a dark, angry red.

“I don’t believe it,” he said. “She was at Yardly Chase
yesterday.”

“And yet she was here!” persisted Poirot.

Lord Yardly’s look changed from anger to bewilderment.

“Look here, Monsieur Poirot, what do you mean? You must be
mistaken.”

Poirot did not answer. He merely took a little note-book from his
pocket, and consulted it.

“Is she not a tall, dark lady, with flashing eyes and a pale
proud face?”

Lord Yardly nodded.

“And she was wearing a long coat of blue velvet with a high grey
fur collar?”

Lord Yardly’s jaw dropped.

“That’s her favourite coat,” he admitted. “But I could have
sworn she was at the Chase.”

“Then you were mistaken,” said Poirot dryly. “Now, _milord_,
listen to me. If you wish to save your diamond, you must tell me
the whole truth.”

Lord Yardly looked at him for a moment, then he gave a short,
bitter laugh.

“The truth? I wish I knew it! There’s some mystery about that
diamond, I know. It’s been in the family for generations, and
yet—well, I’ve heard rumors.”

“What rumors?”

“That it was a paste imitation, and that the real stone had been
sold years ago. I don’t believe it, of course—but it’s a
queer thing that my wife won’t let me have it valued.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “Now we are getting at it. Tell me, _milord_,
did you ever hear of a man named Gregory Rolf?”

Lord Yardly’s face darkened.

“Rolf? The actor? Yes, I’ve heard of him. Why?”

“He was a friend of your wife’s, was he not, in California three
years ago?”

“I believe he was. I didn’t know her then, of course. But what has
all this to do with the diamond?”

“Everything,” said Poirot. “Now, _milord_, I have a piece of
advice to give you. Go home at once. Tell your wife that I have
told you everything. Tell her that the danger is great, and that
she must give the diamond into my keeping. You understand?”

Lord Yardly shook his head.

“I don’t understand a bit. But I’ll do as you say. I can see
you’re serious.”

“I am very serious,” said Poirot gravely.

When Lord Yardly had gone, I turned to Poirot.

“What is it all about? I don’t understand in the least.”

“Neither do I, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye.
“But I am beginning to have an idea. A very small idea—it is only
just beginning to sprout.”

“But why did you tell Lord Yardly to say you knew everything?”

“To see what his wife would do, of course. It is what you call a
bluff.”

“And Gregory Rolf? What has he to do with it?”

“Ah, that is the most interesting part of the whole business. He
knew Lady Yardly in California, you see. And he is the husband
of Mary Marvell. It is a very pretty little problem.”

“But the Chinaman?”

“Ah, the Chinaman! I am not so sure about the Chinaman. He is a
very useful person, the Chinaman. He can be anywhere at any time.
He is the _deus ex machina_ of the detective story.”

“You think he is a myth?”

“I think he is a very convenient person to have about. But come,
Hastings, we must not waste time. We have much to do.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to the hotel _Magnificent_. I have a little business
to transact there.”

I followed him, wondering what his next move would be. At the
_Magnificent_, he asked for Mr. Gregory Rolf. We were shown up
to his sitting-room. Miss Marvell was there also. They both
seemed surprised to see us.

“I have come, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot, “to ask you a few
questions.”

Gregory Rolf looked at him with a slight frown.

“Questions? What about?”

“About the diamond you bought in San Francisco three years ago.”

Rolf’s face went a shade paler.

“What about it?” he asked.

“I want to know the name of the man you bought it from.”

“I don’t know his name. I told you he was a Chinaman.”

“And you bought it for a tenth of its value?”

“Yes. I told you that too.”

“And you never had any suspicions?”

“Why should I? I thought I was getting a bargain.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And you didn’t know that it was the
famous ‘Western Star’?”

“No. I only found that out later.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “Now, Mr. Rolf, I have one more
question. Have you ever seen Lady Yardly’s diamond, the ‘Star of
the East’?”

Rolf shook his head.

“No. I’ve heard of it, of course, but I’ve never seen it.”

“That is strange,” said Poirot. “Because I have reason to believe
it is the exact twin of your wife’s diamond.”

Rolf laughed.

“Well, I guess that’s just a coincidence.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse me, I will
take my leave.”

As we went down in the lift, I turned to Poirot.

“What was the point of all those questions?”

“To see how he would take them, _mon ami_. He is a very good
actor, Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“You think he was lying?”

“I am sure of it. But why? That is the question. Why should he
lie about such a simple thing?”

“Perhaps he really doesn’t know the man’s name.”

“Perhaps. But I think not. And now, Hastings, we have one more
visit to pay.”

“Where to?”

“To a certain firm of jewellers in Bond Street.”

At the jewellers, Poirot had a long conversation with the manager.
I could not hear what they were saying, but Poirot seemed very
pleased when he came out.

“What did he tell you?” I asked.

“He told me what I wanted to know, _mon ami_. And now, we must
wait. The full moon is on Friday. On Friday evening, we shall go
to Yardly Chase.”

“To Yardly Chase?”

“Yes. I have been invited by Lord Yardly. He is very anxious
about his diamond, you see.”

“And Miss Marvell? Is she going too?”

“Oh yes. She and her husband are to be there. It will be a very
interesting party, Hastings. A very interesting party indeed.”

The intervening days passed slowly. I was full of excitement and
curiosity. Poirot, on the other hand, was unusually quiet. He
spent a good deal of time in thought, and he refused to discuss
the case with me.

On Friday afternoon we traveled down to Yardly Chase. It was a
magnificent old house, set in a large park. Lord Yardly met us
at the station. He looked anxious and harassed.

“Glad you’ve come, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “My wife is in a
terrible state of nerves. She won’t leave her room.”

“And the diamond?” asked Poirot.

“She has it with her. She won’t let it out of her sight.”

When we arrived at the house, we were shown to our rooms. A little
later, we went down to the drawing-room. Miss Marvell and Gregory
Rolf were there, looking very much at home. Miss Marvell was
dressed in a wonderful gown of pale green, and the ‘Western Star’
flashed on her breast.

Lady Yardly did not appear until dinner-time. She looked pale and
agitated, and her eyes were constantly wandering towards the door.
She was wearing a magnificent diamond necklace, with a large stone
in the center.

“The ‘Star of the East’,” whispered Poirot to me.

The dinner was a somewhat strained affair. Lord Yardly tried to
keep up a conversation, but his wife was obviously not listening.
Miss Marvell and Gregory Rolf talked about their latest film, but
they, too, seemed a little uneasy.

After dinner we went into the library. It was a large, oak-paneled
room, with French windows opening onto the terrace. The moon was
at the full, and its light flooded the room.

Suddenly, there was a sound outside. A low, chanting voice,
singing a strange, oriental melody. We all froze.

“What’s that?” gasped Lady Yardly.

Gregory Rolf went to the window and looked out.

“There’s someone out there!” he cried. “A man in a long robe—a
Chinaman!”

He threw open the window and dashed out. We followed him onto the
terrace. The garden was empty. There was no sign of any Chinaman.

“He must have gone into the shrubbery,” said Rolf, pointing to a
clump of bushes at the end of the terrace.

We all ran towards the bushes. As we did so, a loud scream rang
out from the library. We rushed back.

Lady Yardly was standing in the middle of the room, her hand
clutched to her throat. Her necklace was gone.

“It’s gone!” she cried. “The diamond! He took it!”

“Who took it?” asked Lord Yardly.

“The Chinaman! He came in through the window while you were all
outside. He snatched it from my neck and ran out again.”

“But we were just outside the window!” cried Gregory Rolf. “We
must have seen him.”

“He was too quick for you,” said Lady Yardly, sinking into a
chair. “He was like a shadow.”

At that moment, Mary Marvell gave a sharp cry.

“My diamond! It’s gone too!”

We all looked at her. Her dress was torn, and the ‘Western Star’
had vanished.

“He must have taken it at the same time,” she sobbed. “I didn’t
even feel him do it.”

Lord Yardly turned to Poirot.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot? What do you make of this? Both diamonds
stolen under our very noses!”

Poirot did not answer. He was looking at the floor near the
window. He stooped down and picked something up. It was a small,
curiously shaped piece of silk.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of a Chinaman’s robe, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “It seems
our friend was in a hurry.”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“Tell me, madame, did you see the man’s face?”

“No. He had a mask on. But I could see his eyes—they were slanted,
like a Chinaman’s.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And you, Miss Marvell? Did you see him?”

“No. I only felt him snatch the jewel.”

Poirot nodded.

“It is all very clear,” he said. “The god has reclaimed his eyes.”

Lord Yardly groaned.

“This is terrible! What are we going to do?”

“We must call the police, of course,” said Gregory Rolf.

“The police?” said Poirot. “Ah, _mon ami_, I think we can do
better than that. If you will all come with me into the small
drawing-room, I think I can explain everything.”

We followed him into the next room. Poirot closed the door and
turned to face us.

“Now,” he said, “I will tell you what really happened. But first,
I must ask Lady Yardly a question. Madame, where is the ‘Star of
the East’?”

Lady Yardly stared at him.

“I told you! It was stolen!”

“No, madame,” said Poirot. “It was not stolen. It was never here
to-night.”

“What do you mean?” gasped Lord Yardly.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the stone Lady Yardly was wearing
to-night was a paste imitation. The real diamond was sold three
years ago.”

There was a dead silence. Lord Yardly looked at his wife. Her
head was bowed, and she was weeping silently.

“Is this true, Maude?” he asked in a low voice.

“Yes,” she whispered. “I had to. I was being blackmailed.”

“By whom?”

She didn't answer. Poirot stepped forward.

“By a man who knew her secret, _milord_. A man she had met in
California three years ago. A man named Gregory Rolf.”

Everyone turned to look at the actor. He was standing by the
window, his face a mask of indifference.

“This is absurd!” he said. “I never blackmailed anyone in my
life.”

“Oh yes, you did,” said Poirot. “You knew that Lady Yardly had
been—shall we say, indiscreet—while she was in California. You
had some letters of hers, and you used them to force her to give
you the diamond.”

“That’s a lie!” cried Rolf.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why you sold
a large diamond to a firm of jewellers in Bond Street three years
ago—a stone that corresponds exactly to the ‘Star of the East’.”

Rolf didn't answer. His face had gone a sickly grey.

“But what about the ‘Western Star’?” I asked. “Miss Marvell’s
diamond? That was stolen to-night too.”

“No, Hastings,” said Poirot. “That diamond was not stolen either.
It is still in this room.”

He walked over to Mary Marvell and held out his hand.

“If you please, madame.”

With a trembling hand, Mary Marvell reached into her bodice and
drew out the ‘Western Star’.

“I don’t understand,” I said. “Why did she pretend it was
stolen?”

“Because her husband told her to,” said Poirot. “It was all part
of his plan. He knew that the ‘Star of the East’ was a paste
imitation, and he wanted to make sure that no one would find out.
So he arranged this little drama of the Chinaman. He even
blackmailed Lady Yardly into helping him. She was to pretend her
diamond was stolen, and Mary Marvell was to do the same. That way,
the loss of the ‘Star of the East’ would be explained, and no one
would ever know it was a fake.”

“But the letters?” I asked. “The threatening letters?”

“All written by Mr. Rolf, of course. He even went so far as to
dress up as a Chinaman and chant outside the window, to give his
story more color.”

Lord Yardly turned to Rolf. His face was white with rage.

“You scoundrel! You’ve ruined my wife’s life, and you’ve tried to
cheat me out of my family diamond!”

“He hasn’t cheated you, _milord_,” said Poirot. “I have been in
communication with the jewellers in Bond Street. They still have
the ‘Star of the East’. It was never sold, only pledged as
security for a loan. I have arranged for it to be returned to you
on payment of the debt.”

Lord Yardly’s face cleared.

“Monsieur Poirot, I don’t know how to thank you!”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot, with a modest wave of his hand.
“A mere matter of the little grey cells.”

As we were driving back to London, I turned to Poirot.

“How did you know it was Gregory Rolf?”

“It was the letters, _mon ami_. The letters to Miss Marvell were
left by hand—by a Chinaman. But the letters to Lady Yardly came
by post. Why the difference? Because Mr. Rolf could easily dress
up as a Chinaman in London, but he couldn’t do it in the country
without being noticed. And then there was the perfume—the
joss-stick. It was too much, _mon ami_. It was what you call
over-acting. And Gregory Rolf is, as I said, a very good actor.”

“And what will happen to him now?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that Lord Yardly will not prosecute. For
the sake of his wife’s reputation, he will let the matter drop.
As for Mr. Rolf and his wife, I think they will find it convenient
to return to America as soon as possible.”

He sighed and leaned back in his seat.

“It has been a most interesting case, Hastings. Most interesting.
But I think, in the future, I shall stick to more mundane
crimes. Romanticism, it is very fatiguing for the little grey
cells.”

“I have told you—it is the psychology that matters. No more, _mon
ami_.”

Early next morning Lord Yardly arrived. He was a large-built,
hearty-looking man, and appeared quite ready to enter into the
spirit of the thing. I fancy he thought it was some new-fangled
private detective’s method of advertisement.

“I got your wire,” he explained. “Hope I haven’t come too late. My
wife’s been quite worried about these letters, though I told her
to pay no attention to them. Some practical joker, I expect. What
do you say to that, Monsieur Poirot?”

“The letters are identical with those received by Miss Mary
Marvell.”

Lord Yardly gave a long whistle.

“What? The film star? Then there is something in it after all. And
she’s coming down to us to-morrow. Well, that is a coincidence.”

“You have the diamond with you, my lord?”

“Not likely. I’m not such a fool. It’s in the bank.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“Then I may suggest that you go and fetch it, and that you bring
it here?”

Lord Yardly stared.

“What for?”

“So that I may compare it with the ‘Western Star.’”

“But she hasn’t brought it with her?”

“She will do so to-morrow. If you will bring yours here this
afternoon, I can then go with you to the bank and see it safely
returned.”

Lord Yardly hesitated.

“I suppose you know what you’re talking about,” he said at last.
“It’s a bit of a nuisance, but if you really think it’s necessary,
I’ll go and get the thing.”

He left us, and Poirot turned to me.

“What do you think of him, Hastings?”

“A very pleasant fellow. I liked him.”

“_Moi aussi_,” said Poirot. “He is what you call ‘a good fellow,’
_n’est-ce pas_?”

“Quite. And a typical John Bull.”

“_C’est ça_! A typical John Bull.”

He sat down and began to hum a little tune.

“It is interesting, _n’est-ce pas_?” he said, after a minute or
two.

“What?”

“The whole thing. You noticed, _mon ami_, that Lord Yardly’s version
differs slightly from his wife’s?”

“How?” I asked, surprised.

“She told us she had destroyed the letters. He says she was
worrying about them.”

“That’s only natural. She wouldn’t want to worry him, so she would
say she had destroyed them, while all the time she was really
bothered.”

“_Peut-être_,” said Poirot. “But did you notice another thing? He
was quite surprised when I told him that Mary Marvell was coming
to Yardly Chase to-morrow.”

“Well, what of it? He’s a busy man. I dare say he doesn’t bother
about his wife’s guests.”

“It is possible,” said Poirot, but he did not look convinced.

In the afternoon Lord Yardly returned with the jewel. It was a
magnificent stone, a little larger than the “Western Star,” but
extraordinarily like it in every other way. Poirot examined it
critically.

“A beautiful stone,” he murmured. “And you have the history of it,
_milord_?”

“It’s been in the family for some generations. My great-great-
grandfather brought it from the East. There was some story about
its having been the eye of an idol, but I’ve always looked upon
that as a bit of a yarn.”

“And you are not afraid of its being stolen?”

“Not I!” said Lord Yardly. “No Chinaman will get into Yardly Chase.
We’re too well-guarded for that.”

“The diamond is usually kept there?”

“No, it’s only there for a few days at a time. It spends most of
the year in the bank. My wife likes to have it for some of our big
house-parties.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, we will return it to the bank at once.
I am satisfied.”

We went together and saw the jewel safely deposited.

On our return to the rooms, I found Poirot in a state of great
excitement. He was walking up and down, his eyes sparkling with
glee.

“_Mon cher_,” he cried, “everything is arranged. We go down to
Yardly Chase to-morrow!”

“What?” I cried. “How did you manage it?”

“A little word to Lord Yardly. I have business in that part of the
world—the case of the missing bonds, you remember? He is a most
hospitable man. He has invited us both.”

“This is great!” I said. “I’ve always wanted to see the Chase.”

Next day saw us on our way. Our host met us at the station in his
car, and in a few minutes we were being whirled through the
magnificent park.

Yardly Chase was a grand old building, parts of it dating from the
thirteenth century. We were warmly welcomed by Lady Yardly, and
met the other guests. Miss Marvell and her husband had already
arrived, and we found them in the great hall. Gregory Rolf was
regaling the company with stories of the “Wild West.” Miss Marvell
was looking her best in a wonderful gown of some shimmering
material. She wore the “Western Star” on a long platinum chain.

I noticed that Lady Yardly was looking pale and tired. She seemed
to be watching the other woman with a kind of fearful fascination.

After dinner we were all sitting in the hall. The huge log fire
threw flickering shadows on the walls. It was a beautiful and
peaceful scene.

Suddenly, without any warning, the lights went out. The room was
plunged in darkness. There were several exclamations of surprise,
and then a woman’s scream.

“The diamond! The diamond! It’s gone!”

It was Mary Marvell’s voice.

In a moment there was a scene of the wildest confusion. People
were running to and fro, and voices were raised in excitement. At
last a servant appeared with a candle, and we were able to see
each other’s faces.

Mary Marvell was standing in the middle of the room, her hand to
her throat. The chain was there, but the diamond had vanished.

“What’s happened? What’s happened?” cried Lord Yardly, appearing
on the scene.

In a few words he was told. He was at once the man of action.

“Lock all the doors!” he shouted. “No one must leave the house.
Gregory, come with me. We’ll search the grounds.”

I turned to Poirot. He was sitting quite still in his chair, a
faint smile on his face.

“Well?” I cried. “Aren’t you going to do something?”

“What should I do, _mon ami_?”

“But the diamond! It’s been stolen!”

“It would seem so,” said Poirot.

“And you sit there and do nothing!”

“What can I do? The lights go out—it is very simple. In the
darkness, someone snatches the jewel. Who? That is the question.”

“It must be one of the Chinamen!” I cried.

“Did you see a Chinaman, Hastings?”

“No, but——”

“Then why should you think it was a Chinaman?”

“Because of the letters! And the person who snatched it must have
been very quick and very silent.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Very quick and very silent.”

At that moment Gregory Rolf and Lord Yardly returned. They had
found no one in the grounds.

“The fellow must have got away,” said Rolf. “But how did he get in?
All the doors and windows were fastened.”

“That is the mystery,” said Lord Yardly.

We spent the rest of the evening in a state of great excitement.
The police were sent for, and a thorough search of the house was
made, but no trace of the diamond could be found.

Next morning Poirot and I were up early. We found Mary Marvell in
the breakfast-room. She was looking very pale and had obviously
had a bad night.

“It’s too terrible!” she wailed. “My beautiful diamond! I shall
never see it again!”

“Do not despair, madame,” said Poirot. “I have a little idea.”

“You have? What is it?”

“I cannot tell you yet. But I am not without hope.”

As soon as we were alone, I turned to Poirot.

“What is your idea?” I asked.

“It is very simple, _mon ami_. I am going to have a little talk
with Lady Yardly.”

“Lady Yardly? What has she to do with it?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

We found Lady Yardly in the morning-room. She looked even more
wan and haggard than she had on the previous evening.

“Monsieur Poirot,” she said, “this is a terrible business. I feel
responsible, in a way, as it happened in my house.”

“Do not distress yourself, madame,” said Poirot. “I have every
hope of recovering the jewel. But first, I must ask you a few
questions.”

“Certainly. What is it you want to know?”

“Lady Yardly, have you ever seen Gregory Rolf before?”

I saw her start. A faint flush rose to her cheeks.

“Why—why do you ask that?”

“Because I have a reason. You knew him in America, did you not,
three years ago?”

She hesitated for a moment, and then bowed her head.

“Yes,” she whispered. “I knew him.”

“And he—he was interested in the Yardly diamond?”

She looked up at him, her eyes wide with fear.

“How did you know?”

“It was a guess,” said Poirot. “A very simple guess. And now,
madame, I will tell you what I think happened. Three years ago,
you were in America. You met Gregory Rolf. You were—shall we say—
indiscreet? You had a friendship with him. And you told him the
story of the Yardly diamond. Am I right?”

She did not answer, but her silence was sufficient.

“Gregory Rolf is a man who knows the value of jewels,” continued
Poirot. “He saw the possibilities of the Yardly diamond. He began
to blackmail you. He threatened to tell your husband of your
indiscretion unless you gave him the diamond.”

“No, no!” she cried. “It wasn’t like that!”

“Then how was it?”

“I—I can’t tell you.”

“Then I must tell you. You gave him the diamond. But you could not
let your husband know. So you had a clever imitation made. That
is what you have been wearing lately. The real stone was in the
possession of Gregory Rolf. He gave it to his wife as a wedding
present.”

I gasped. Could this be true?

“But the letters?” I cried. “What about the letters?”

“The letters were a clever ruse on the part of Gregory Rolf. He
wanted to create an atmosphere of mystery—to make it appear that
a Chinese gang was after the diamonds. Then, when the time was
ripe, he would steal his wife’s diamond—which was really the Yardly
diamond—and everyone would believe it had been taken by the
Chinamen.”

“But why should he want to steal his own wife’s diamond?” I asked.

“Because it was insured for fifty thousand pounds, _mon ami_! It
was a very clever plot. He would have the diamond, and the
insurance money as well!”

“But how did the lights go out?”

“That was also very simple. Gregory Rolf had arranged it. He knew
exactly where the switch was. In the darkness, he snatched the
jewel from his wife’s neck. He knew she would scream, and that
would add to the effect.”

“But Lady Yardly?” I asked. “What was her part in it?”

“She was a victim,” said Poirot. “She was being blackmailed by Rolf.
He had told her of his plan, and had forced her to help him. She
was to receive similar letters, and to pretend that she was also
in danger. It was her part to make the whole story seem more
plausible.”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“Is it not so, madame?”

She buried her face in her hands and sobbed.

“Yes, yes! It is all true. He’s a devil—a devil! I’ve been in his
power for years. I didn’t know what to do.”

“And the diamond?” I asked. “Where is it now?”

“It is in Gregory Rolf’s pocket,” said Poirot. “If you will go and
find him, Hastings, and tell him that I should like a little word
with him, I think we shall find that he is quite ready to restore it.”

I was about to leave the room when the door opened and Gregory Rolf
himself walked in. He looked from one to the other of us, a
defiant look on his face.

“Well?” he said. “What’s all this about?”

“It is about the Yardly diamond, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot. “I think
you have it in your pocket. Will you be so good as to give it to
me?”

For a moment I thought Rolf would show fight, but he saw that the
game was up. With a curse, he drew the diamond from his pocket and
flung it on the table.

“Take it!” he cried. “And much good may it do you!”

He turned and strode out of the room.

Poirot picked up the jewel and handed it to Lady Yardly.

“There, madame,” he said. “Your family diamond is restored to you.
And I think you need have no more fear of Mr. Gregory Rolf. I
have a few words to say to him which will, I think, ensure his
speedy departure from this country.”

Lady Yardly took the diamond, her eyes shining with gratitude.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“By being more careful in the future, madame,” said Poirot, with
a little bow. “And by remembering that the ‘Western Star’ and the
‘Star of the East’ are better kept apart.”

When we were back in London, I asked Poirot one question.

“How did you know, Poirot? What was it that first gave you the
clue?”

“It was the psychology, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, tapping his
forehead. “The psychology of the individual. I knew that Miss
Marvell was a very shrewd woman. She would not be easily deceived.
If she had received those letters, she would have come to me at
once. But she didn’t. She waited until the third letter arrived.
Why? Because she wanted to make sure that the story was well
established. And then, there was the perfume on Lady Yardly’s
letters. It was the same perfume that Miss Marvell uses. That was
a very great mistake on the part of Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“I see,” I said. “And what about the Chinaman?”

“There was no Chinaman, Hastings. He was a creature of Mr. Rolf’s
imagination. A very useful creature, but, like all creatures of
the imagination, he lacked reality.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s been a most interesting case.”

“It has had its points,” said Poirot. “But it was not of the most
difficult. For a man of my abilities, it was—what do you call it?—
a ‘piece of cake’!”

And with a little chuckle, he settled himself in his chair and
closed his eyes.

“No, no, _mon ami_, do not ask me. You would find my explanations
far too simple. It is the simple things that you never see! For
the present we will say no more. Friday will soon be here.”

I thought he was right. Friday was not long in coming, and I
confess that I was more than a little excited. Lord Yardly duly
appeared at Poirot’s rooms, but he proved to be a difficult subject.
He was a tall, loosely-built man, with a red face and a loud voice.
He appeared at first to be inclined to take the whole thing as a
joke.

“What’s all this about, eh? My wife’s been worrying me to death
lately about this diamond of ours. Says someone’s going to steal
it. Who? Why? What for? I told her it was all bunkum.”

Poirot explained carefully. Lord Yardly’s face grew more serious
as the little Belgian proceeded.

“Wait a minute. You say Mary Marvell has had these letters too?
By Jove, that’s queer! Mary Marvell. I haven’t seen her for years.
Not since I was in the States.”

“The lady is coming to Yardly Chase to-day, milord.”

“What? Mary Marvell? Here? I didn’t know it. My wife didn’t say
a word about it.”

“It appears that Mr. Gregory Rolf has business with you, milord.”

“Oh, Rolf! Yes, I remember him. A great big fellow. So he’s Mary
Marvell’s husband, is he? I’d forgotten.”

His face had become very thoughtful. I wondered what memories the
name of Gregory Rolf had conjured up.

“It is my advice, milord, that you should place the diamond in my
keeping for the next few days.”

“No, no, I won’t do that. It’s been in our family for over a
hundred years, and it isn’t going to leave it now.”

Poirot sighed.

“Then I can do no more. You will at least take every precaution,
milord?”

“Of course, of course. We’ve got a first-rate safe at the Chase.
The diamond’s kept there as a rule. I’ll see that it’s put back
there at once.”

“You are going back now?”

“By the 12.15.”

“You will permit us to accompany you, milord? We could return this
evening.”

“Delighted, I’m sure. Glad to have you.”

We had a very pleasant journey down. Lord Yardly was a most
agreeable companion, and he and I were soon deep in a discussion
on the merits of various breeds of hunters.

Yardly Chase was a magnificent old place, and as we drove up the
long avenue of oaks I felt that it was a fit setting for the drama
that was about to be played.

We were met at the door by Lady Yardly. She looked pale and
anxious, and her eyes sought those of Poirot with an almost
piteous appeal.

“Oh, I am so glad you have come!” she cried. “The most terrible
thing has happened.”

“What is it?” cried Lord Yardly. “Not the diamond?”

“No, no, but Gregory Rolf and his wife have arrived, and—and——”

“And what?”

“Mary Marvell’s diamond has been stolen!”

“Stolen?” we all cried in one breath.

“Yes. It’s too dreadful. They were only here an hour when it
happened.”

“How did it happen?” asked Poirot.

“They were all in the drawing-room. Mary had the diamond on a
chain round her neck. Suddenly the lights went out. There was a
scream from Mary, and when the lights were turned on again the
diamond was gone!”

“And the windows?” asked Poirot. “Were they open?”

“Yes, it was a very warm day.”

“And did anyone see anything?”

“Mary says she saw a dark figure—a Chinaman—spring out of the
window.”

“A Chinaman!” cried Lord Yardly. “Then it’s true after all.”

“It certainly looks like it,” I said.

We followed Lady Yardly into the drawing-room. Miss Marvell was
sitting on a sofa, looking very white and shaken. Gregory Rolf was
standing by her, his face grim and set.

“This is a pretty business, Lord Yardly,” he said, as we entered.
“My wife’s diamond has been stolen under your roof.”

“I’m sure I’m very sorry, Rolf,” said Lord Yardly. “It’s a most
unfortunate occurrence.”

“Unfortunate! I should say it was! That diamond was worth fifty
thousand pounds.”

“I’m sure I don’t know what to say,” murmured Lord Yardly. “We
must send for the police at once.”

“The police have already been sent for,” said Gregory Rolf. “But
I don’t expect they’ll find much. That Chinaman’s probably miles
away by now.”

I looked at Poirot. He was standing in the middle of the room,
his eyes darting from one face to another.

“You saw the Chinaman, madame?” he asked, turning to Mary Marvell.

“Yes, yes. I saw his face quite clearly in the moonlight. It was
horrible—horrible!”

“In the moonlight?” said Poirot. “But I thought you said the
lights were out?”

“So they were. But the moon was shining in through the window.”

“I see. And you, Mr. Rolf, did you see him too?”

“No. I was at the other end of the room. By the time I got to the
window he had disappeared.”

“And you, Lady Yardly?”

“I saw nothing. I was so startled when the lights went out.”

“And Lord Yardly was not in the room?”

“No, I had only just arrived.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. He walked over to the window and
looked out. “It is a long drop to the ground. A man would have to
be very agile to jump out of that window without hurting himself.”

“Oh, these Chinamen are like cats!” said Gregory Rolf.

“Possibly,” said Poirot. He turned back into the room. “And now,
Lord Yardly, if I might suggest it, it would be as well to see if
your diamond is safe.”

“Good heavens!” cried Lord Yardly. “I’d forgotten all about it.”

He hurried out of the room, and we all followed him. He led the
way to a small room which he used as a study. In the corner of the
room was a large safe. Lord Yardly drew a key from his pocket and
opened it. He reached his hand into the back of the safe and drew
out a small velvet-lined box. He opened it—and a cry of relief
broke from his lips.

The Star of the East was there, its many facets catching the light
and throwing it back in a thousand fires.

“Thank God!” he said. “At least that’s safe.”

He was about to replace the box in the safe when Poirot's hand
suddenly shot out and took it from him.

“You permit, milord?”

He walked over to the window and examined the stone with the same
care he had bestowed on Mary Marvell’s diamond. Suddenly he gave
a low whistle.

“What is it?” I asked.

Poirot did not answer. He was still looking at the stone. Then he
turned to Lord Yardly.

“Milord, I have a request to make. Will you allow me to take this
stone back to London with me?”

“What? Certainly not!”

“I think it would be as well,” said Poirot quietly. “If the
thieves have been successful in one case, they will certainly try
their luck in the other.”

“I can look after my own property, thank you,” said Lord Yardly
stiffly.

“As you please,” said Poirot. He handed the box back to Lord Yardly.
“But if you will take my advice, you will not leave that stone in
the safe to-night.”

“Where would you have me put it?”

“Give it to Lady Yardly to wear.”

“That’s not a bad idea,” said Lord Yardly. “What do you say, Maude?”

“If you think it’s best, George,” said Lady Yardly. Her voice was
low and trembling.

“Very well, then, that’s settled.”

We returned to the drawing-room, where we found the police had
arrived. They were headed by Inspector Japp, an old friend of
Poirot’s.

Japp was a brisk, energetic little man, and he soon had the whole
story from Mary Marvell and her husband. He then proceeded to
examine the window and the ground outside, but he found no traces
of the thief.

“It’s a mysterious business,” he said to Poirot. “What do you
make of it?”

“It is certainly very curious,” said Poirot. “Tell me, Japp, have
you ever known a Chinaman to be a successful thief in this
country?”

“Can’t say I have. They mostly stick to opium dens and that sort
of thing.”

“Exactly. It is a point to be remembered.”

We spent the rest of the afternoon in a fruitless search of the
house and grounds. As evening approached, the atmosphere became
tense and expectant. We were all thinking of the full moon and the
threat contained in the letters.

Dinner was a quiet and rather dismal meal. Lady Yardly was
wearing the Star of the East, and its brilliance seemed to mock
the anxious faces around the table.

After dinner we all adjourned to the drawing-room. The windows
were shut and the curtains drawn. Lord Yardly was restless and
kept pacing up and down the room. Mary Marvell was sitting on the
sofa, her eyes fixed on the Star of the East. Gregory Rolf was
standing by the fireplace, his face as grim as ever.

Suddenly, without any warning, the lights went out. There was a
stifled cry from Lady Yardly, followed by a sound of scuffling and
then a loud crash.

“The lights! The lights!” cried Lord Yardly.

Gregory Rolf struck a match, and in another moment the room was
flooded with light.

Lady Yardly was lying on the floor in a dead faint. Her neck was
bare. The Star of the East was gone!

At the same moment we saw that one of the windows was wide open,
the curtains blowing in the breeze.

“He’s got it!” cried Lord Yardly. “The Chinaman!”

He rushed to the window and looked out.

“There he goes!” he shouted. “I can see him running across the
lawn!”

He leapt out of the window and we all followed him. We could see
a dark figure running towards the woods at the end of the garden.
We chased him as fast as we could, but he was too quick for us. He
disappeared into the shadows of the trees, and though we searched
for over an hour we could find no trace of him.

We returned to the house, tired and discouraged. Lady Yardly had
recovered from her faint and was sitting in a chair, her face
buried in her hands.

“It’s gone!” she moaned. “The family diamond—gone!”

“Don’t worry, Maude,” said Lord Yardly, though he looked pretty
shaken himself. “We’ll get it back. Japp’s got the police out
searching the whole countryside. They’re bound to catch him.”

“I’m not so sure,” said Gregory Rolf. “These Chinamen are
slippery customers.”

Poirot had been very quiet during all this. He was now sitting in
a corner of the room, his eyes half closed. I went over to him.

“Well, Poirot, what do you think of it now?”

He opened his eyes and looked at me.

“I think, my friend, that it is time we returned to London.”

“To London? But what about the diamond?”

“The diamond, Hastings, will be found in good time. For the
present, there is nothing more for us to do here.”

I was surprised, but I knew from experience that it was no use
arguing with Poirot when he had made up his mind. We took our
leave of the Yardlys and the Rolfs and caught the last train back
to town.

The next morning Poirot was up early. When I came down to
breakfast I found him sitting at the table, surrounded by a pile
of newspapers.

“Well, Poirot, any news?”

“Much news, Hastings. The papers are full of the Great Diamond
Mystery. It is the sensation of the hour.”

“And have the police found any trace of the Chinaman?”

“None whatever. And I do not think they will.”

“Why not?”

“Because, _mon ami_, there is no Chinaman!”

“No Chinaman? But we all saw him!”

“You saw a dark figure, Hastings. That is all. In the moonlight,
and in the excitement of the moment, it was easy to imagine it was
a Chinaman.”

“But Mary Marvell saw his face!”

“Ah, Mary Marvell! That is another matter altogether.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that Mary Marvell is a very clever actress.
She is used to playing a part.”

“You mean she lied?”

“I think it is more than possible.”

“But why should she lie? And what about the other diamond—the one
that was stolen from Lady Yardly?”

“That, too, was a part of the play.”

“I don’t understand you, Poirot.”

“It is very simple, _mon ami_. But before I explain, we must
have a little talk with Lady Yardly.”

“With Lady Yardly? But she is at Yardly Chase.”

“No, she is in London. I took the liberty of telephoning her this
morning and asking her to call on us. She should be here at any
moment.”

Sure enough, a few minutes later Lady Yardly was announced. She
looked even more pale and haggard than she had the day before.

“You wished to see me, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked, as she sank
into a chair.

“Yes, madame. I wished to talk to you about the Star of the East.”

Lady Yardly sighed.

“It is gone, Monsieur Poirot. There is no more to be said.”

“On the contrary, madame, there is a great deal to be said. To
begin with, the Star of the East was not stolen by a Chinaman.”

Lady Yardly started.

“Not stolen by a Chinaman? But we all saw him!”

“You saw what you were intended to see, madame. But the Star of
the East was never in any danger from a Chinaman. It was in danger
from a much more formidable person.”

“Who?”

“From yourself, madame.”

Lady Yardly turned as white as a sheet.

“From me? What do you mean?”

“I mean, madame, that you yourself took the diamond from the safe
and—no, I am wrong. You did not take it from the safe. You had
already disposed of it some years ago!”

Lady Yardly gasped and fell back in her chair. Poirot went on in
the same quiet, pitiless voice.

“Three years ago, when you were in the United States, you met a
man—a man called Gregory Rolf. You were—shall we say—a little
indiscreet. You gave him certain letters. Later, he began to
blackmail you. You had no money of your own, so you gave him the
Star of the East. He had it replaced by a clever imitation, and it
was this imitation that you have been wearing ever since.”

Lady Yardly buried her face in her hands and began to sob.

“It’s true—it’s true! Oh, Monsieur Poirot, what am I to do?”

“The truth, madame, is always the best course. But let us finish the
story. Mr. Gregory Rolf is not only a blackmailer, but he is also
a very clever and ambitious man. He married Mary Marvell, and he
determined to use her as a means of getting back the real diamond
without any suspicion falling on himself. He invented the story of
the two twin diamonds and the temple god. He sent the anonymous
letters to his wife and to you. He even arranged for a ‘Chinaman’
to be seen lurking about. Then, at the right moment, he ‘stole’
the diamond from his wife—or rather, she ‘stole’ it from herself.
It was all a part of the plan to make the story of the Chinese
thieves seem real. Then, when he came to Yardly Chase, he intended
to steal the Star of the East from you. He knew it was an imitation,
but he also knew that if it were stolen, the insurance company
would pay the full value of the real stone. It was a very pretty
piece of work!”

“But how did you find out?” I asked, amazed.

“It was the letters that first made me suspicious,” said Poirot.
“They were so very—theatrical! And then, when I saw the Star of
the East, I knew at once that it was a fake. It was a good fake,
but it did not deceive the eyes of Hercule Poirot. After that, it
was only a matter of putting the pieces together.”

“And what is to be done now?” asked Lady Yardly, looking up at him
with tear-filled eyes.

“That, madame, is for you to decide. If you tell the truth to Lord
Yardly, I think you will find him more forgiving than you expect.
He is a good man, and he loves you.”

“I will tell him,” said Lady Yardly firmly. “I will tell him
everything.”

She rose and gave Poirot her hand.

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. You have been very kind.”

After she had gone, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my ‘simple’ explanation?”

“It was marvellous, Poirot! Simply marvellous!”

“_Du tout_,” said Poirot. “It was merely a matter of using the
little grey cells. But come, let us go and have some lunch. All
this talk of diamonds has made me very hungry.”

And that is how Hercule Poirot solved the mystery of the “Western
Star.”

Lord Yardly, I may add, showed no particular resentment at being
summoned to my friend’s rooms. He was a tall, thin man, with
something of the appearance of a horse-dealer, and a somewhat
vacuous expression.

“I understand that you’ve been interesting yourselves in some
business of my wife’s,” he said, as he seated himself. “The usual
fright about nothing, I suppose? Some nervous joke or other?”

Poirot looked at him.

“Lord Yardly, your wife has received letters from a Chinaman
threatening her with the loss of the Yardly diamond.”

“The Star of the East, eh? My wife mentioned it to me. I thought
it was a practical joke—nothing more. After all, the stone is safe
in the bank, and not even at the Chase.”

“Then you must be aware that it was not Lady Yardly’s intention
to keep it in the bank?”

“Eh? What’s that?”

“She told Captain Hastings here only yesterday that she intended
bringing the diamond to Yardly Chase for Miss Mary Marvell to see.”

Lord Yardly gave a long, low whistle.

“By Jove, that’s risky! If there really is anything in these
Chinese rumours. I’ve heard something of the sort myself from the
States. It was in San Francisco—where we were three years ago.
There was some talk about a diamond that had been stolen from an
idol’s head. Some one said mine was like it. I laughed at the time,
but——” He broke off, looking from one to the other of us. “Do you
think there really is something in it?”

Poirot nodded.

“I do. And I want you, Lord Yardly, to do me a favour.”

“Anything you like, Monsieur Poirot. I’m only too anxious to keep
the diamond safe.”

“Then I want you to go to the bank and bring it back here with
you.”

“But——”

“You will do it?”

“Of course, if you think it’s necessary. But I really can’t see
why.”

“The reason is simple. I want to see the diamond. It is possible
that I may find out something from it which will give us a clue.”

Lord Yardly rose.

“Well, if you say so. I’ll go at once. It’s not far to the bank.”

He returned in less than half an hour, and handed a small shagreen
case to Poirot.

The latter opened it. On a bed of white velvet lay a magnificent
stone. For a few minutes Poirot studied it in silence, then he
closed the case and handed it back to Lord Yardly.

“Thank you, _milord_. I am satisfied. It is as I thought.”

“You have found a clue?”

“I have found what I wanted to know. I would advise you to return
the diamond to the bank as quickly as possible.”

“I’ll go now. But tell me, Monsieur Poirot, what do you think of
these letters?”

“I think, _milord_, that they are a very serious matter. But I
hope that we shall be able to circumvent the thieves. One thing
more—it would be as well if you said nothing to Lady Yardly of
your visit to me.”

“Certainly. But why?”

“Because, _milord_, she is already in a state of nervous tension.
It is better not to worry her further.”

Lord Yardly nodded.

“I understand. Good-morning, Monsieur Poirot.”

And he left us.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked, as the door closed behind him. “What is
it you have found out?”

“_Mon ami_, I have found out that Lady Yardly is a very clever
woman. But not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait, Hastings, wait! The plot thickens. We must be ready for all
emergencies.”

The next few days passed without any further developments. Then,
on the Friday morning, Poirot received a telegram:

“Diamond stolen last night. Please come at once. Yardly.”

Poirot’s eyes flashed.

“The game is afoot! Quick, Hastings, we must catch the 10.15 to
Yardly Chase.”

We arrived at the little station shortly after mid-day, and were
met by a car which whirled us up to the house. Lord Yardly received
us in the library. He looked pale and haggard.

“It’s gone!” he said, as we entered. “The Star of the East has
vanished!”

“Tell us all about it,” said Poirot.

“It happened last night—about ten o’clock. We were all in the
drawing-room—my wife, Miss Marvell, and Rolf. Suddenly the lights
went out. There was a sound of a scuffle, a cry from my wife, and
then the lights came on again. Lady Yardly was lying on the floor
faintly, and the diamond was gone from her neck!”

“And the thief?”

“He had vanished. But a window was open, and on the gravel outside
we found a pigtail! It must have been a Chinaman!”

“A pigtail!” Poirot’s voice was full of interest. “And what did
you do?”

“I telephoned to the police at once. They are here now, but they
haven’t found any trace of the thief.”

“And Miss Marvell? Is her diamond safe?”

“Yes. She hadn’t got it on at the time.”

“I see. And where is Lady Yardly now?”

“In her room. She’s had a terrible shock.”

“I should like to see her,” said Poirot.

Lord Yardly led the way upstairs. Lady Yardly was lying on a couch
in her boudoir. She looked very pale and fragile.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she cried, as we entered, “can you help us?
It was all so horrible! That awful Chinaman!”

“Calm yourself, madame,” said Poirot soothingly. “Tell me exactly
what happened.”

She repeated her husband’s story, adding a few details.

“I felt a hand at my throat—a cold, thin hand—and then the necklace
was wrenched away. I think I must have fainted then.”

“And you saw the man?”

“Only a shadow—a dark, crouching figure. But I saw the pigtail!”

Poirot nodded.

“I see. And now, madame, I have a request to make. I should like
to see the pigtail.”

Lord Yardly fetched it from a drawer. It was a long, black pigtail,
undoubtedly of Chinese origin. Poirot examined it closely, then
laid it down.

“A very interesting clue,” he remarked. “And now, if you will
permit, I should like to examine the drawing-room.”

We went downstairs. The drawing-room was a large, well-proportioned
room, with three long windows opening on to the terrace. Poirot
examined the window that had been found open, then stepped out
on to the terrace. The gravel was somewhat disturbed, but there
were no clear footprints.

“The rain last night has washed them away,” said Lord Yardly.

Poirot nodded. He was looking at the ground with a preoccupied
air. Suddenly he stooped and picked up something. It was a small,
glittering object.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of glass,” said Poirot. “From the chandelier, I imagine.”

He replaced it in his pocket, and we returned to the house. In the
hall we met Gregory Rolf. He looked worried and anxious.

“This is a bad business, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “What do you
make of it?”

“It is a very curious case,” replied Poirot. “But I have hope.
And now, Lord Yardly, if you will excuse me, I should like to
have a few words with Miss Marvell.”

He found the actress in the morning-room. She was looking pale and
nervous.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she cried, “do you think I’m safe? That
awful Chinaman! He’ll be after my diamond next!”

“Do not be afraid, madame,” said Poirot. “I have taken precautions.
Where is your diamond now?”

“In the hotel safe deposit in London. I didn’t bring it down after
all. Gregory wouldn’t let me.”
