“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “The good Mr. Rolf is a man of sense.
But tell me, madame, when did you decide not to bring the diamond?”

“On Wednesday night. Gregory and I talked it over, and he said it
wasn’t worth the risk.”

“I see. And you have not seen it since then?”

“No.”

“Thank you, madame. That is all I wanted to know.”

He turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, I think we may return to London. There is
nothing more to be done here.”

I was astonished, but I followed him to the car. As we drove to
the station, I broke out:

“But, Poirot, you’re not going to leave things like this? What
about the diamond? What about the Chinaman?”

“Patience, Hastings, patience! I have seen all I want to see.
The case is almost complete.”

“But who is the thief?”

“Ah, that is a question! But I think I can tell you one thing.
There is no Chinaman!”

“No Chinaman? But the pigtail?”

“A very clever piece of stage property, _mon ami_. No, the thief
is much nearer home than China.”

“You mean——”

“I mean that the Star of the East was stolen by some one in the
house. Some one who knew all about the letters and the Chinese
story.”

“But who?”

“That is what we shall see. And now, _mon cher_, I have a little
experiment to make. We will not go back to London just yet. We
will stay at the inn in the village for a few hours.”

We spent a weary afternoon at the “Yardly Arms.” Poirot seemed
buried in thought, and would hardly speak a word. At last, about
six o’clock, he rose.

“And now, Hastings, we will return to the Chase. I think the time
has come to reveal the truth.”

We found the whole party assembled in the library. Lord and Lady
Yardly, Miss Marvell, and Gregory Rolf. Poirot walked into the
middle of the room.

“Mesdames and messieurs,” he said, “I have come to tell you who
stole the Star of the East.”

There was a tense silence. Every eye was fixed on the little man.

“The theft of the diamond,” continued Poirot, “was a very clever
piece of work. It was planned to look like a Chinese vendetta.
The letters, the pigtail, the darkening of the room—all were
designed to lead the mind in one direction. But there were several
points that did not fit in. For instance, the letters to Lady
Yardly were not left by hand, but came by post. Why? Because the
person who sent them could not risk being seen in the guise of
a Chinaman. Then, the diamond was stolen while Lady Yardly was
wearing it. A very risky proceeding for a common thief. But for
someone else—not risky at all.”

He paused, and his eyes swept the room.

“I have discovered that the diamond known as the Star of the East
was not in the bank at all. It was in Lady Yardly’s possession all
the time. She had it with her in London when she came to see me.”

Lord Yardly started.

“But she told me——”

“She told you it was in the bank, _milord_, because she did not
want you to know that she had been wearing it. You see, she was
being blackmailed.”

Lady Yardly gave a low cry.

“Yes, madame, I know all. Three years ago, in California, you
met a man. You were—shall we say, indiscreet? That man had your
letters. He used them to extort money from you. At last you had
no more money. Then he demanded the diamond. You were desperate.
You knew that your husband would never forgive you if he knew the
truth. So you hit upon a plan. You would pretend that the diamond
had been stolen by the Chinese gang of whom you had heard. You
sent the letters to yourself—and to Miss Marvell, to make the
story more plausible. Then, last night, you staged the robbery.
You turned out the lights, you dropped the pigtail which you had
provided, and you pretended to faint. It was very simple—and very
effective.”

“But the diamond?” cried Lord Yardly. “Where is it now?”

“The diamond, _milord_, is in the possession of the man who was
blackmailing your wife. He was here last night. He is here now.
That man is Gregory Rolf!”

A gasp of astonishment went round the room. Gregory Rolf started
forward, his face livid.

“It’s a lie!” he shouted.

“Is it?” said Poirot calmly. “Then perhaps you will explain how
this piece of glass came into your possession?”

He held out the small object he had picked up on the terrace.

“It is not a piece of glass, _mon ami_. It is a diamond—a very
small diamond from the setting of the Star of the East. It must
have been jarred loose when you wrenched the necklace from Lady
Yardly’s neck. I found it on the terrace where you dropped it as
you made your escape.”

For a moment Gregory Rolf stood like a stag at bay. Then, with
a sudden movement, he dashed for the window. But Poirot was too
quick for him. He tripped him up, and in another moment Lord
Yardly and I had secured him.

“And the diamond?” asked Lord Yardly.

Poirot reached into Rolf’s pocket and drew out a small leather
pouch. Inside was the Star of the East.

“There is your diamond, _milord_. And now, I think, we had better
send for the police.”

Lady Yardly had buried her face in her hands.

“Can you ever forgive me, George?” she sobbed.

Lord Yardly went to her and took her in his arms.

“It’s all right, Maude. We’ll forget all about it. The diamond is
safe, and that’s all that matters.”

As we drove back to London that evening, I looked at Poirot with
unfeigned admiration.

“You’re a marvel, Poirot! How did you know it was Rolf?”

“_Mon ami_, it was the psychology! Rolf is a man who likes to
play the hero. He is also a man who is always in need of money.
When I saw the two diamonds, I realized that they were identical.
That gave me the clue. Rolf had seen the Star of the East in
California, and he knew its history. He used that knowledge to
blackmail Lady Yardly. When he heard that Miss Marvell was coming
to England with the Western Star, he saw his chance. He would
steal the Star of the East and make it look like the work of the
Chinese. He even used his own wife as an unconscious tool. It was
a very pretty scheme—but he forgot the little gray cells of Hercule
Poirot!”

And the great detective tapped his forehead with a smile of
infinite satisfaction.

I was on tenterhooks to know what his plans were, but he would give
me no further information. In fact, he seemed to have forgotten
all about the matter. He sat in his chair, a look of beatific
content on his face, occasionally humming a little tune and now
and then breaking out into a few words of some popular song. I
must say he had a most excruciating voice. I can only suppose that
he was following some train of thought of his own.

The next morning, about eleven o’clock, we were interrupted by the
arrival of a visitor. It was none other than Lord Yardly himself.
He was a tall, thin, aristocratic-looking man, with a slight stoop
and a pleasant, if somewhat weary, face. He did not seem particularly
pleased at having been summoned to London.

“I got your wire, Monsieur Poirot, but I really can’t imagine why
you sent it. I was just coming up to town in any case to-day. My
wife’s been worrying me to death about some ridiculous letters
she’s been getting. I told her she was a fool to take any notice
of them.”

Poirot looked at him with an air of mild reproof.

“One cannot be too careful, _milord_. You have the letters with
you?”

“Maude’s destroyed them. She’s such a nervous woman. But they
were just the same as those Miss Marvell’s been getting. I believe
the whole thing’s a plant of some kind.”

“A plant?”

“Yes. Some sort of advertisement for this film of theirs. That’s
what I think.”

“Then you do not believe in the legend of the Star of the East?”
asked Poirot.

“Oh, I know it’s a good story. I’ve often told it myself. My great-
grandfather brought the stone home from China. There’s a tradition
it’s been in the family ever since. But as for all this about
temple gods and Chinamen—well, it’s just the sort of thing these
film people would get up.”

Poirot’s eyes narrowed.

“Then you have no intention of taking any precautions, _milord_?”

“Precautions? What precautions? I’m going to have the stone in a
safe at Yardly Chase. If any Chinaman tries to get it, he’ll have
his work cut out, that’s all.”

“And you are not afraid of its being stolen?”

“Not in the least.”

“Then why have you come to see me?” asked Poirot with a smile.

Lord Yardly looked a little confused.

“Well, to tell you the truth, I’m not as easy in my mind as I’d
like to be. My wife’s so nervous. She’s got it into her head that
something’s going to happen. And then there’s this business of
Mary Marvell. If she’s had letters too——”

“It is certainly a curious coincidence,” murmured Poirot. “Tell me,
_milord_, what do you know of Mr. Gregory Rolf?”

“Rolf? Oh, I believe he’s a very decent fellow. Met him in the
States three years ago when I was out there. He’s been very helpful
to me over several little matters. In fact, it was through him I
got into touch with this film company.”

“I see. And you have no reason to—to—dislike him?”

Lord Yardly looked surprised.

“Dislike him? No, not at all. Why should I?”

“I merely wondered. And your wife? She was with you in the States,
I think?”

“Yes. We both met him there. He was very civil to us.”

“I see.”

Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he rose.

“_Eh bien, milord_, I will not detain you any longer. But I should
like to ask you one thing. You will permit me to come down to Yardly
Chase on Friday?”

“Why, certainly, if you’d like to. But I’m afraid you’ll find it
a very dull party. Just ourselves and the Rolfs.”

“On the contrary, I think I shall find it most interesting. _À
vendredi, milord_.”

Lord Yardly took his departure. Poirot turned to me with a twinkle
in his eye.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of the situation now?”

“It seems to me that Lord Yardly is a very sensible man,” I
replied. “He isn’t going to be scared by any nonsense about
Chinamen.”

“And yet he is not quite easy in his mind. He has come to me! He
was wise—that _milord_!”

“But what do you think of it all, Poirot?”

“I think, _mon ami_, that we have here a very pretty little problem.
And I think that on Friday we shall see some developments.”

“You really think the diamonds will be stolen?”

“I think it is more than likely.”

“But how? And by whom?”

“Ah, that is what we are going to find out. In the meantime, I
must make certain inquiries.”

And Poirot disappeared into his bedroom, leaving me to my own
reflections. I must confess I was more than a little puzzled. What
was the connection between the two diamonds? And why were Mary
Marvell and Lady Yardly both receiving these mysterious letters?
It seemed as though some secret society was at work. And then there
was Gregory Rolf. What part did he play in the mystery? I felt
sure that Poirot suspected something, but what it was I could not
imagine.

Friday came at last. We took the afternoon train to Yardly Chase.
It was a beautiful old house, set in a magnificent park. Lord
Yardly met us at the station in his car.

“Glad you could come, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “We’re just
sitting down to tea. The Rolfs arrived this morning.”

In the drawing-room we found Lady Yardly and her guests. Mary
Marvell was looking more like a child than ever in a simple white
frock. Gregory Rolf was as handsome and debonair as ever.

Lady Yardly greeted us with a smile.

“I’m so glad you could come, Monsieur Poirot. I feel much safer
now you’re here.”

“You are very kind, madame,” said Poirot with a bow.

Tea was a cheerful meal. Every one seemed in the best of spirits.
Even Lady Yardly appeared to have forgotten her fears. After tea,
Lord Yardly took us for a stroll in the grounds.

“It’s a fine old place, isn’t it?” he said. “I’d hate to have to
part with it. But things are pretty difficult nowadays.”

“I can well imagine it, _milord_,” said Poirot. “And this film—it
will help?”

“I hope so. It’s a good deal of money.”

We returned to the house for dinner. It was a gala occasion. Mary
Marvell was wearing her famous diamond, and Lady Yardly also wore
hers. The two stones were certainly very similar.

“They’re a wonderful pair, aren’t they?” said Gregory Rolf. “It’s
a pity they should be separated.”

“They won’t be for long, if the stories are true,” said Mary
Marvell with a laugh.

Lady Yardly shivered.

“Don’t!” she said. “It makes me feel quite creepy.”

After dinner we went into the drawing-room. The windows were open,
and the scent of the flowers came in on the soft night air. It was
the night of the full moon.

Suddenly, a strange thing happened. From the garden there came the
sound of a low, wailing cry. It was a weird, unearthly sound that
made my blood run cold.

“What was that?” gasped Lady Yardly.

Gregory Rolf sprang to his feet.

“It sounded like—like a Chinaman!” he cried.

We all rushed to the window. Outside, the moonlight was as bright
as day. But there was no one to be seen.

“It must have been an owl,” said Lord Yardly. “They make the most
extraordinary noises sometimes.”

“No, no,” cried Mary Marvell. “It wasn’t an owl. It was a human
voice. I’m sure of it.”

We searched the garden, but could find nothing. We returned to the
drawing-room, feeling a little shaken.

“I think I’ll go to bed,” said Lady Yardly. “I feel quite tired.”

“A good idea,” said her husband. “We’re all a bit jumpy to-night.”

We all retired to our rooms. But I, for one, could not sleep. I
sat by my window, looking out into the night. Everything was still
and silent.

Suddenly, I heard a sound. It was a low, muffled cry. It seemed to
come from Lady Yardly’s room, which was next to mine.

I sprang to my feet and rushed into the corridor. At the same
moment, Poirot appeared from his room.

“What is it?” I gasped.

“I do not know, _mon ami_. But we must find out.”

We hurried to Lady Yardly’s door. It was locked. Poirot hammered
on it.

“Lady Yardly! Lady Yardly! Are you there?”

There was no answer. We heard the sound of a struggle within.

“Quick, Hastings! We must break it down!”

Together we threw ourselves against the door. It gave way with a
crash. We burst into the room.

The scene that met our eyes was a strange one. Lady Yardly was
lying on the floor, unconscious. Beside her stood a man in Chinese
dress. He held a knife in his hand.

As we entered, he sprang towards the window.

“Stop him!” cried Poirot.

I rushed forward, but he was too quick for me. He leapt onto the
windowsill and vanished into the night.

Poirot was at Lady Yardly’s side.

“She is not hurt,” he said. “Only a slight faint. But—look!”

He pointed to her neck. The diamond was gone.

“The Star of the East!” I cried. “It has been stolen!”

“And not only that,” said Poirot. “Look at the window.”

On the windowsill lay a small piece of paper. On it was written
in printed letters:

“The eye of the god has returned.”

“But how did he get in?” I asked. “The door was locked.”

“The window was open,” said Poirot. “He must have climbed up the
ivy.”

We raised Lady Yardly and placed her on the bed. In a few minutes
she opened her eyes.

“What happened?” she moaned.

“The diamond, madame,” said Poirot. “It has been stolen.”

“Oh, my God!” she cried. “I knew it! I knew it!”

We spent the rest of the night in a state of great excitement.
The police were summoned, and a search was made for the thief. But
no trace of him could be found.

The next morning, Poirot and I were sitting in the drawing-room.
Gregory Rolf and Mary Marvell were also there. They were both
greatly distressed by the theft.

“It’s a terrible thing,” said Gregory Rolf. “I can’t believe it’s
really happened.”

“And to think that my diamond might be next!” said Mary Marvell.

“Do not distress yourself, madame,” said Poirot. “I think I can
promise you that your diamond will not be stolen.”

“How can you be so sure?” asked Gregory Rolf.

“Because, _mon cher_, I know who the thief is.”

We all stared at him in amazement.

“You know?” I cried. “Who is it?”

Poirot smiled.

“It is very simple, _mon ami_. If you will all come with me to the
library, I will explain everything.”

We followed him into the library. Lord Yardly was already there,
looking very grim.

“Now, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “What is all this about? You say
you know who the thief is?”

“I do, _milord_.”

“Then who is it? Out with it!”

Poirot looked round at the assembled company.

“The thief,” he said slowly, “is none other than—_milady_ herself!”

There was a moment of stunned silence. Then Lady Yardly sprang to
her feet.

“What!” she cried. “How dare you!”

“It is true, madame,” said Poirot calmly. “You stole your own
diamond.”

“But why?” I gasped. “Why should she do such a thing?”

“Because, _mon ami_, the diamond was not hers to steal. Or rather,
it was not the real diamond.”

“What do you mean?” asked Lord Yardly.

“I mean, _milord_, that the Star of the East was sold three years
ago. What Lady Yardly has been wearing is a paste replica.”

Lord Yardly turned to his wife. His face was pale.

“Is this true, Maude?” he asked.

Lady Yardly buried her face in her hands and began to sob.

“Yes,” she moaned. “It’s true. I had to do it. I was in debt—terribly
in debt. And Gregory Rolf—he knew. He blackmailed me.”

“Gregory Rolf?” I cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It was Mr. Rolf who bought the diamond three
years ago. He has had it ever since. The story of the Chinese god
and the twin diamonds was all a clever invention of his to cover
up the fact that he already had the stone.”

“But what about the letters?” I asked. “And the Chinaman last
night?”

“The letters were written by Mr. Rolf himself,” said Poirot. “He
sent them to Miss Marvell and Lady Yardly to create an atmosphere
of mystery and fear. And the Chinaman—that was Mr. Rolf too. He is
an actor, remember. It was easy for him to disguise himself.”

“But why did he do it?” I asked. “If he already had the diamond,
why go to all this trouble?”

“Because, _mon ami_, he wanted to steal the other diamond—the Star
of the West. He knew that if he could create a situation where
both diamonds were supposed to be in danger, he would have a
chance to get his hands on Miss Marvell’s stone. He staged the
theft of Lady Yardly’s diamond to make it seem that the threat was
real. He hoped that Miss Marvell would be so frightened that she
would give her diamond to him for safe keeping. And then—_hey
presto!_—he would have both stones.”

“But you stopped him, Poirot!” I cried.

“_Oui, mon ami_. I saw through his little game from the beginning.
The story of the twin diamonds was a little too romantic, even for
me. And when I saw the two stones, I knew that they were not
identical. Lady Yardly’s stone was a clever imitation. I suspected
the truth then, and my inquiries confirmed it.”

Gregory Rolf stood up. He was no longer the handsome hero of
romance. He looked like a trapped animal.

“You’re very clever, Monsieur Poirot,” he said with a sneer. “But
you can’t prove anything.”

“On the contrary, _mon cher_,” said Poirot. “I have the real Star
of the East in my pocket. I found it in your room this morning.”

He drew the diamond from his pocket and held it up. It sparkled
brilliantly in the sunlight.

Gregory Rolf made a sudden dash for the door, but the police were
waiting for him. He was led away, followed by Mary Marvell, who
was in a state of collapse.

Lord Yardly turned to his wife.

“Maude,” he said softly. “Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I was afraid,” she whispered. “I thought you’d never forgive me.”

“My dear,” he said, taking her hand. “We’ve both made mistakes.
But we’ll start again.”

Poirot and I walked out into the garden.

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “You’ve done it again. But how did you
know the diamond was in Rolf’s room?”

“I didn’t, _mon ami_,” said Poirot with a twinkle in his eye.
“It was a little bluff. But it worked, did it not?”

I laughed.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot.”

“_Oui, mon ami_,” he said modestly. “I am indeed.”

“Not now, I pray you. Let us not confuse the mind. And observe that
‘Peerage’—how you have replaced him! See you not that the tallest
books go in the top shelf, the next tallest in the row beneath,
and so on. Thus we have order, _method_, which, as I have often
told you, Hastings——”

“Exactly,” I said hastily, and put the offending volume in its
proper place.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


Lord Yardly turned out to be a cheery, loud-voiced sportsman with
a rather red face, but with a good-humoured bonhomie about him that
was distinctly attractive and made up for any lack of mentality.

“Extraordinary business this, Monsieur Poirot. Can’t make head or
tail of it. Seems my wife’s been getting odd kind of letters, and
that this Miss Marvell’s had ’em too. What does it all mean?”

Poirot handed him the copy of _Society Gossip_.

“First, _milord_, I would ask you if these facts are substantially
correct?”

The peer took it. His face darkened with anger as he read.

“Damned nonsense!” he spluttered. “There’s never been any romantic
story attaching to the diamond. It came from India originally, I
believe. I never heard of all this Chinese god stuff.”

“Still, the stone _is_ known as ‘The Star of the East.’”

“Well, what if it is?” he demanded wrathfully.

Poirot smiled a little, but made no direct reply. “What I would
ask you to do, _milord_, is to place yourself in my hands. If you
do so unreservedly, I have great hopes of averting the catastrophe.”

“Then you think there’s actually something in these wild-cat
tales?”

“Will you do as I ask you?”

“Of course I will, but——”

“_Bien!_ Then permit that I ask you a few questions. This affair
of Yardly Chase, is it, as you say, all fixed up between you and
Mr. Rolf?”

Lord Yardly rose to take his departure. “Then I’ll see you on Friday, Monsieur Poirot? You’ll come down to the Chase with the others?”
“I shall be enchanted, _milord_,” replied Poirot with a bow. When he had gone, my friend sat for a long time in silence, his eyes fixed on the ceiling. At last he spoke. “The situation is of a most interesting, Hastings. Consider the actors in our little drama. We have the beautiful film star with her diamond, and the noble lady with hers. We have the husband who is—how do you say—_aux abois_? Debt, it is a hard taskmaster. And then we have the mysterious Chinaman, who flits in and out like a shadow. It is a well-constructed play, is it not? But who is the author? That is what we must find out. We go to Yardly Chase on Friday, _mon ami_. It is there that the curtain will rise on the final act.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “The full moon, it is on Friday. Today is Wednesday. If it pleases you, _milord_, we will accompany you to Yardly Chase to-morrow. It is essential that I am on the spot to observe—and to protect. We must ensure that the Star of the East remains in its setting.” Lord Yardly looked somewhat taken aback by this sudden proposal, but he eventually gave a short, bluff laugh. “By all means, Monsieur Poirot. If you’re set on it, come along. We’ve plenty of room, and it’ll be a change from London for you. We’ll take the 11.15 from Paddington.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “It is a situation of the most delicate. Now, milord, I have a request to make of you. On Friday, when Miss Marvell and her husband arrive at Yardly Chase, I wish to be there also. It may be that my presence will act as a—how shall we say?—a deterrent to those who would seek to interfere with the ‘eyes of the god.’ You can arrange this? A friend of yours, perhaps? And one thing more—where, precisely, is the Star of the East kept at this moment?”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And the jewel itself, is it at Yardly Chase at this moment?”

“Yes,” replied his lordship. “In the safe there. Maude—my wife, you know—is very nervous about it since she got those letters. She wanted me to bring it up to London and put it in the bank, but I told her it was safe enough. We’ve got a good safe, and plenty of servants.”

“Nevertheless,” said Poirot gravely, “I would advise you to be careful. The full of the moon, it is on Friday. If you will permit, I should like to be at Yardly Chase on that day.”

“Delighted, my dear fellow, delighted!” cried Lord Yardly. “Come down on Friday morning and stay for the weekend. The Rolfs are coming too, you know.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, _milord_, I have a request to make
of you. It is that you will allow me and my friend Hastings to
visit Yardly Chase on Friday. It is, as I have remarked, the night
of the full moon. If the god is to reclaim his eye, it is then that
he will strike. We should like to be there to—how do you say?—see
the fun.” Lord Yardly laughed heartily. “By all means, Monsieur
Poirot! Delighted to have you. It’ll be a bit of a house party,
anyway. The Rolfs are coming, you know. We’ll see if your ‘little
grey cells’ can beat the Chinese.” He took his departure, still
chuckling, leaving Poirot looking after him with a very grave
expression indeed.

“I comprehend,” said Poirot. He remained a moment or so in thought,
then rose briskly to his feet. “You return to Yardly Chase at once?
_Bien!_ Say no word to anyone—to _anyone_ mind—but expect us there
this evening. We will arrive shortly after five.”

“All right, but I don’t see——”

“_Ça n’a pas d’importance_,” said Poirot kindly. “You will that I
preserve for you your diamond, _n’est-ce pas_?”

“Yes, but——”

“Then do as I say.”

A sadly bewildered nobleman left the room.

  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

“A thousand pardons for this intrusion, Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, with a flourish of his hat. “Your husband, he has been so kind as to invite us to view the glories of Yardly Chase. To an old man like myself, whose life is spent in the fogs of London, this—this is a vision of the past! _Mes enfants_, you have a home of great history.” Lady Yardly looked at her husband, a slight frown marring her brow. Lord Yardly, taking his cue from Poirot, broke in somewhat awkwardly: “Yes, yes, quite so. Told M. Poirot he must come down and see the place for himself. Thought a night in the country would do him good.”

“I have taken the liberty, Lady Yardly, of accepting your husband’s most kind invitation,” said Poirot, with a flourish and a deep bow. “The history of your family, it has always interested me. And the jewel—ah, the jewel! It is a legend, is it not? I am a humble admirer of the beautiful.” Lady Yardly’s eyes flickered to her husband, a shadow of apprehension crossing her face, but she recovered herself quickly. “We are delighted to see you, Monsieur Poirot,” she said graciously. “Though I fear my husband has been over-anxious. He believes—well, you know what he believes about our poor diamond.”

He advanced with a series of little bows. “A thousand apologies for our intrusion, milady! But Lord Yardly, he was so kind as to permit that I—who have the passion for the history and the antiquities—should view your so beautiful home before the arrival of the great stars of the cinema.” Lady Yardly’s face cleared, and she extended a hand graciously. Lord Yardly, recovering his composure, joined in the welcome, though I could see he was still profoundly puzzled by Poirot’s sudden appearance and his previous injunctions of secrecy.

“I have taken the liberty, Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, bowing low over
her hand, “of accepting your husband’s hospitality. The matter of
which we spoke—it is of a gravity! And since the full of the moon is
so near, I thought it well to be on the spot.” Lady Yardly’s face
clouded, and she shot a quick look of reproach at her husband. “I
see,” she said slowly. “You are very kind, Monsieur Poirot. But I
fear you have had your journey for nothing. I have decided to think no
more of the matter.” “A wise decision, Madame,” said Poirot. “But I,
I have a little hobby. I collect ‘sensations.’ And this story of the
two diamonds, it is a sensation of the most premier order!”

“A thousand apologies for this intrusion, Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, bowing low. “Your husband was kind enough to suggest that I might be of some small service in a matter of—shall we say, the ancestral safety? Since I was in the neighborhood, I ventured to present myself. I trust that you will forgive the suddenness of our arrival.” Lady Yardly’s eyes flickered for a moment towards me, then back to Poirot; she seemed a trifle confused, but she rose with grace. “Monsieur Poirot is always welcome,” she said. “My husband did not tell me he was expecting you, but no matter. You will stay the night, of course? I will tell the butler to prepare rooms for you and Captain Hastings.”

“All my excuses! It is that I investigate still this affair of Miss
Marvell’s. She comes to you on Friday, does she not? I make a
little tour first to make sure that all is secure. Also I wanted
to ask of Lady Yardly if she recollected at all the postmarks on
the letters she received?”

Lady Yardly shook her head regretfully. “I’m afraid I don’t. It is
stupid of me. But, you see, I never dreamt of taking them
seriously.”

“You’ll stay the night?” said Lord Yardly.

“Oh, _milord_, I fear to incommode you. We have left our bags at
the inn.”

“That’s all right.” Lord Yardly had his cue. “We’ll send down for
them. No, no—no trouble, I assure you.”

Poirot permitted himself to be persuaded, and sitting down by Lady
Yardly, began to make friends with the children. In a short time
they were all romping together, and had dragged me into the game.

“_Vous êtes bonne mère_,” said Poirot, with a gallant little bow,
as the children were removed reluctantly by a stern nurse.

Lady Yardly smoothed her ruffled hair.

“I adore them,” she said with a little catch in her voice.

“And they you—with reason!” Poirot bowed again.

“Look at this, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, extending his hand. “It’s
from Gregory Rolf. Read it.”

Poirot read the telegram aloud:

“Just heard from Mary. She’s had another letter. Full moon to-night.
She’s scared to death. Am bringing her down to you by the six-thirty.
Hope you can put us up. Rolf.”

“By the six-thirty! Then they will be here at any moment!”

A car was heard outside, and we heard the sound of voices in the
hall. Gregory Rolf and his wife were ushering themselves in.

Miss Marvell was a very different being from the cool, self-possessed
young woman of this morning. She was trembling with nervousness,
and her face was deathly pale. She clutched Poirot by the arm.

“It’s coming—it’s coming! I know it! Oh, Monsieur Poirot, do
something! Save me!”

“_Tranquillisez-vous_, madame. I am here. All will be well.”

Gregory Rolf looked over at Lord Yardly. “Hope we’re not intruding,
but Mary was just set on coming. She’s got the idea that she’ll be
safe here with you.”

“Why, of course! Delighted to have you. But I’m afraid the Chase
isn’t the safest place in the world to-night.”

“You’ve had a letter too?” Miss Marvell turned to Lady Yardly.

“Yes.”

“And the diamond—the Star of the East?”

“It is in my jewel-case in my room,” said Lady Yardly.

“Mine is here,” said Miss Marvell, indicating her bosom. “I’m not
going to let it out of my sight for a moment.”

“_Bien_,” said Poirot. “Then we are all together. We will have a
pleasant little dinner, and then—we shall see what we shall see.”

Dinner was a somewhat strained meal. Every one was more or less
apprehensive. Both the diamonds were being worn by their respective
owners, and the flash and sparkle of them was almost dazzling.

After dinner we all sat together in the hall. The large doors were
locked and bolted.

The night was a beautiful one, and the moon, now at its full,
shone in through the high uncurtained windows.

Poirot was the life and soul of the party. He told stories, he
mimicked, he was altogether his most enchanting self.

Suddenly, without any warning, the lights went out.

We were in total darkness.

There was a muffled cry, then the sound of a scuffle, and a heavy
fall.

“_Mon Dieu!_” cried Poirot. “The switch! Where is the switch?”

Gregory Rolf’s voice called out: “I’ve got it! Here it is!”

The next moment the lights sprang on again.

We all stood as though turned to stone.

In the middle of the room, Lady Yardly lay unconscious. At her
throat, the Star of the East was gone!

Her husband flew to her side. Miss Marvell was screaming
hysterically.

“It’s gone! My diamond! It’s gone too!”

She pointed to her neck. The chain was there, but the great stone
had vanished!

At that moment there was a loud knocking at the door.

“Open! Open in the name of the law!”

Gregory Rolf went to the door and undid the bolts.

Two men stepped into the room.

“I am Inspector Miller from Scotland Yard, and this is Sergeant
Benton. We have reason to believe that a daring robbery was to
be attempted here to-night.”

“You’re a bit late, Inspector,” said Gregory Rolf grimly. “The
diamonds have gone.”

“Both of them?”

“Both of them.”

The Inspector’s face fell.

“That’s bad. We’ve been shadowing a couple of suspicious-looking
Chinamen all day, but they’ve given us the slip in the woods
round here. We only got here a few minutes ago.”

Lord Yardly was bending over his wife. She opened her eyes.

“The Chinaman,” she moaned. “The Chinaman—at the window.”

We all looked towards the window. One of the panes was broken.

“That’s how he got in,” said the Inspector. “And he must have
got away the same way. Lord Yardly, if you’ll stay with her
ladyship, I’ll take my man and search the grounds.”

“I’ll come with you,” said Gregory Rolf.

The three men hurried out.

Lord Yardly carried his wife up to her room. Miss Marvell, still
sobbing, followed them.

Poirot and I were left alone.

My friend was strangely silent. He was looking at the floor.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “the Chinaman has won after all.”

He did not answer. He was still looking at the floor. Suddenly
he stooped and picked up something.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A small piece of black silk, Hastings. Look.”

He held it out on the palm of his hand. It was a tiny fragment,
torn, it seemed, from a sleeve.

“The Chinaman!” I cried.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “Perhaps.”

He walked over to the window and examined the broken pane.

“A neat job,” he remarked. “Very neat.”

He turned back into the room.

“Hastings, did you notice anything about the lights?”

“Only that they went out.”

“Yes, but _how_ did they go out? They did not flicker. They
went out—_pouf_!—like that.”

“The main switch, I suppose.”

“Exactly. And where is the main switch, Hastings?”

“I don’t know. In the hall somewhere, I suppose.”

“No, it is in the small room off the hall—the room where the
overcoats are kept.”

“Then someone must have been there?”

“Precisely.”

“But who?”

“That is what we must find out. Come, Hastings, there is no
time to be lost.”

He led the way out of the hall, but instead of going towards the
cloak-room, he went upstairs.

He paused for a moment outside Lady Yardly’s door, then tapped
lightly.

Lord Yardly opened it.

“How is Lady Yardly?” asked Poirot.

“She is better, thank you. The shock was great, of course.”

“May I speak to her for a moment?”

Lord Yardly hesitated, then drew back to let us pass.

Lady Yardly was lying on a couch. She looked very pale and
suffering.

“Madame,” said Poirot softly, “I have a question to ask you.
When the lights went out, did you feel anyone’s hand at your
throat?”

“Yes,” she whispered. “A cold, thin hand. It seemed to—to
_slither_ over my skin.”

“And then?”

“Then I saw the Chinaman. He was standing by the window. The
moonlight was full on him. He had a long knife in his hand.
I—I think I fainted then.”

“I see. Thank you, madame.”

As we went out, we met Gregory Rolf and the Inspector. They had
found no trace of the thieves.

“The woods are very thick,” said the Inspector. “They could
easily hide. But we’ve got the local police on the look-out.
They won’t get far.”

Gregory Rolf went into his wife’s room. The Inspector remained
with us.

“A bad business, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “I’d have given a
lot to have caught those fellows.”

“You think they were Chinamen?” asked Poirot.

“Well, her ladyship says so, doesn’t she? And we’ve been
shadowing two of them all day.”

“True,” said Poirot. “True.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“Inspector, would you mind coming with me for a moment? I
want to show you something.”

He led the way downstairs again, but instead of going into the
hall, he went into the small cloak-room.

“Look,” he said, pointing to the main switch.

The Inspector looked.

“Well?” he asked. “What about it?”

“You see this small piece of wire?”

He pointed to a tiny fragment of copper wire that was lying on
the floor.

“Someone has been tampering with the switch,” said Poirot.
“The lights were not turned off—they were _short-circuited_.”

“By Jove!” said the Inspector. “You’re right. But who could
have done it?”

“Someone who knew the house,” said Poirot. “Someone who had
access to this room.”

“One of the servants?”

“Perhaps. Or perhaps—someone else.”

He turned away and walked back into the hall.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to go to the inn and bring our
bags here. I think we shall stay the night after all.”

“But Lord Yardly said——”

“Never mind what he said. Go!”

I knew that tone of Poirot’s too well to argue. I went.

When I returned, half an hour later, I found the hall empty.
The Inspector and his man had gone, and Lord Yardly and Gregory
Rolf were upstairs.

Poirot was sitting by the fire. He looked up as I entered.

“Ah, Hastings! You have been quick. Good.”

“Where is everyone?” I asked.

“Upstairs. Lady Yardly is still very upset, and Miss Marvell
is in a state of collapse.”

“And the diamonds?”

“The diamonds, my friend, are still missing.”

“Do you think they will be found?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we shall find them—before
morning.”

“You have a clue?” I cried.

“I have more than a clue, Hastings. I have a _certainty_.”

“Who is it? The Chinaman?”

Poirot smiled.

“There was no Chinaman, Hastings.”

“But Lady Yardly saw him!”

“Lady Yardly saw—what she was meant to see.”

“Then who was it?”

“Think, Hastings. Who would benefit most by the disappearance
of the diamonds?”

“The thieves, I suppose.”

“And who are the thieves? Not two mysterious Chinamen who
appear and disappear like shadows. No, the thieves are much
nearer than that.”

“You don't mean——”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the whole thing was a
cleverly-planned comedy. The letters, the threats, the
appearance of the Chinaman—all were part of a scheme to
cover the real robbery.”

“But the diamonds were stolen!”

“Were they? Or were they only—_removed_?”

“I don't understand.”

“Listen, Hastings. Who is the person who is in great need of
money? Lord Yardly. Who is the person who is bitterly opposed
to the sale of the Star of the East? Lady Yardly. Who is the
person who has a great deal of money and wants the diamond?
Gregory Rolf.”

“You mean Gregory Rolf stole them?”

“Wait. Let us look at it from another point of view. Suppose
Lady Yardly had already sold the diamond—or pawned it?
Suppose she was afraid of her husband finding out? What more
natural than that she should arrange a mock robbery to account
for its disappearance?”

“But Miss Marvell’s diamond was stolen too!”

“Ah! That is the clever part of it. If only one diamond had
been stolen, suspicion might have fallen on the owner. But
if _both_ were stolen, then it must be the work of an
outside gang.”

“Then you think Lady Yardly and Mary Marvell are in league?”

“No, I do not think that. I think only one of them is
concerned. But which one?”

“Lady Yardly, of course. She was the one who saw the Chinaman.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “it was Miss Marvell who was so
insistent on coming here to-night. It was she who brought her
husband—the man who originally bought the Western Star.”

“You mean Gregory Rolf is the culprit?”

“Think, Hastings. He was the one who ‘found’ the switch. He
was the one who went out with the Inspector to search the
grounds. He had every opportunity to dispose of the jewels.”

“But why should he steal his own wife's diamond?”

“Perhaps it was not his wife’s diamond. Perhaps—it was a
_paste replica_.”

“A paste replica!”

“Why not? Miss Marvell has had the diamond for three years.
Gregory Rolf is an actor. He knows the value of publicity.
What better advertisement than the theft of the famous Western
Star?”

“But what about the other diamond—the Star of the East?”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is the question. Was that also a
replica? Or was it the real stone?”

“If it was the real stone, then he has committed a real robbery.”

“Exactly.”

“But how did he get it? Lady Yardly was wearing it.”

“In the darkness, Hastings, many things are possible. A
quick hand, a sharp pull—the thing is done.”

“But Lady Yardly saw the Chinaman!”

“In the dark, one sees what one expects to see. If you are
told there is a Chinaman in the room, you will see a Chinaman.”

“Then you think Gregory Rolf is the thief?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we shall soon know.”

He rose and walked towards the stairs.

“Come, Hastings. We must pay a visit to Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

We went upstairs and knocked at Gregory Rolf’s door. He
opened it at once. He was still in his evening clothes.

“Monsieur Poirot! Have you found anything?”

“I have found several things, Mr. Rolf. May we come in?”

“Certainly.”

He drew back and we entered the room. Miss Marvell was lying
on the bed, her face buried in the pillows. She did not look up.

“Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot, “I have been thinking about that
Chinaman. It was a very clever idea—very clever indeed.”

Gregory Rolf’s face hardened.

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. You see, Mr. Rolf, there is one thing you
forgot. Or rather, one thing you did not know.”

“And what is that?”

“That Hercule Poirot is not easily deceived. The piece of
black silk I found—it did not come from a Chinaman’s
sleeve. It came from _your_ coat, Mr. Rolf.”

Gregory Rolf laughed.

“Nonsense! My coat is perfectly all right. Look!”

He turned his arm to show the sleeve. It was quite intact.

“Ah!” said Poirot. “But this is not the coat you were wearing
this evening. You have changed it.”

“I have not! This is the same coat.”

“Then perhaps you will explain this?”

Poirot held out his hand. On the palm lay the tiny fragment of
black silk.

“It matches the lining of your sleeve, Mr. Rolf. You must
have torn it when you were tampering with the switch in the
cloak-room.”

Gregory Rolf’s face went white. He made a sudden movement
towards Poirot, but my friend was too quick for him. He
stepped back and drew a small revolver from his pocket.

“Stay where you are, Mr. Rolf. I am not alone. Captain
Hastings is here, and the Inspector is within call.”

Gregory Rolf stood still, his eyes flashing with rage.

“You think you’re very clever, don’t you? But you can’t
prove anything.”

“Can I not? We shall see. Inspector!”

The door opened and Inspector Miller entered.

“Have you got him, Monsieur Poirot?”

“I have, Inspector. Mr. Gregory Rolf is your man.”

“What about the diamonds?”

“I think you will find them in his pocket—unless he has
already hidden them.”

The Inspector stepped forward and searched Gregory Rolf. In a
few moments he drew out two small leather cases. He opened
them.

In each, a magnificent diamond lay and winked at us.

“The Star of the West and the Star of the East,” said Poirot
softly. “A very pretty pair.”

Gregory Rolf broke into a torrent of abuse, but the Inspector
silenced him.

“You’d better come with us, Mr. Rolf. Anything you say will
be taken down in evidence.”

As they led him away, Miss Marvell sat up on the bed. Her
face was tear-stained and she looked quite distracted.

“Gregory! Gregory! How could you?”

She burst into fresh sobs.

Poirot went over to her and patted her hand.

“_Tranquillisez-vous_, madame. It is a great shock, I know.
But it is better that you should know the truth now than
later.”

“But why did he do it? Why?”

“He needed money, madame. He has been playing high out West,
and he has lost. He thought that by stealing the diamonds
he could pay his debts and at the same time get a great deal
of publicity for you and himself.”

“And the letters—the Chinaman?”

“All a comedy, madame. He wrote the letters himself—or
had them written. He even hired two Chinamen to follow you,
so that the story would seem more plausible.”

“And Lady Yardly’s diamond?”

“He stole that in the darkness, as I suspected. He knew that
if both diamonds were stolen, suspicion would be less likely
to fall on him.”

“It’s—it’s horrible!”

“It is life, madame. But come, let us go and restore the
Star of the East to its rightful owner.”

We went to Lady Yardly’s room. Lord Yardly was still with
her.

“Lord Yardly,” said Poirot, “I have the pleasure of
restoring to you your family diamond.”

He handed the jewel to the astonished nobleman.

“But—but how? Where did you find it?”

Poirot explained the circumstances of the theft. Lord Yardly
listened in amazement.

“Gregory Rolf! I would never have believed it!”

“He is a clever actor, _milord_,” said Poirot dryly.

Lady Yardly sat up, her eyes shining with joy.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can we ever thank you?”

“By being more careful in future, madame,” said Poirot with
a little smile. “And perhaps—by not being so ready to
believe in mysterious Chinamen!”

He bowed to them both and we left the room.

Downstairs in the hall, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of our little adventure?”

“I think you were marvellous, Poirot! But how did you know
it was Gregory Rolf?”

“It was the lights, Hastings. When they went out, they went
out _instantly_. That could only be done by someone who
knew where the switch was, and who could get to it quickly.
Gregory Rolf was the only person who could have done that
without being noticed. And then, there was the piece of
silk. I did not find it on the floor, Hastings—I found it
_on the switch itself_! He must have caught his sleeve as
he turned it.”

“And the Chinaman Lady Yardly saw?”

“As I told you, she saw what she was meant to see. In the
darkness and the excitement, it was easy for her to imagine
the figure of a Chinaman by the window.”

“And the broken pane?”

“He must have broken it himself, either before or during the
scuffle. It was all very well planned.”

“But what about Miss Marvell? Did she know?”

“I think not. I think she was as much a victim as anyone.
But she will recover. She is a film star, and the publicity
of this affair will make her more famous than ever!”

He chuckled.

“And now, _mon ami_, let us go to bed. I am tired, and I
have a craving for my _tisane_.”

“One thing more, Poirot,” I said, as we went upstairs. “What
made you suspect Gregory Rolf in the first place?”

Poirot smiled.

“It was the recognition, Hastings! You remember how I said
that I recognized Mary Marvell, even though I had only seen
her once? Well, I also recognized Gregory Rolf. And I
remembered something about him—something that you had
forgotten.”

“What was that?”

“That before he was a film star, he was a very clever
_prestidigitateur_—a conjurer! And for a conjurer, the
stealing of a diamond from a lady’s neck is child’s play!”

I laughed.

“Poirot, you are really too marvellous!”

“_N’est-ce pas_?” said Poirot. “And now, good-night, Hastings.”

“Good-night, Poirot.”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


The next morning we left Yardly Chase and returned to London.
The affair of the Western Star was over, and once again
Hercule Poirot had triumphed.

As we sat in the train, I looked at my friend. He was
humming a little tune to himself, his eyes closed, a look of
supreme contentment on his face.

“What are you thinking of, Poirot?” I asked.

He opened one eye and looked at me.

“I am thinking, Hastings, that it is a very good thing for
the world that there is only one Hercule Poirot!”

And I could not help but agree with him.

“A telegram from Miss Marvell. She says she’s had a fourth letter,
and is coming down to-day instead of Friday. She’ll be here by
the seven-thirty train.”

Lady Yardly looked at him.

“To-day?” she echoed. “How very strange.”

Lord Yardly frowned. “Wait,” he said, looking at the telegram
again. “Is it? Yes, it’s dated this morning. It’s been delayed.”

He turned to Poirot. “Well, Monsieur Poirot, what do you make of
that? Does it mean the crisis has come?”

“I should not be surprised,” said Poirot gravely. “For me, I must
consult with the good Hastings. We go to our rooms. _N’est-ce
pas_, Hastings?”

In the privacy of our room, I turned to him. “What is it, Poirot?
Has the blow fallen? Is the Chinaman here?”

Poirot shook his head. “I do not think so. It is a very pretty
little comedy that is being played here, _mon ami_. But let us not
anticipate. One thing is certain—Miss Marvell and her diamond
will be here in an hour’s time.”

“Then you think the two diamonds will meet? But if they do, will
not the god return for his eyes?”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “And now, _mon ami_, your best clothes,
I pray of you. We must be _très chic_ for the dinner-table.”

Dinner that night was a somewhat silent meal. Lady Yardly was
obviously nervous, and her husband was distrait. From time to
time, one or other of them glanced at the clock.

“Seven-thirty,” said Lord Yardly. “The train is due now. She’ll
be here in twenty minutes.”

We sat in the hall, waiting. The minutes slipped by.

“A quarter to eight,” said Lady Yardly.

“Eight o’clock,” said Lord Yardly.

The door opened, and the butler appeared. “A car has just driven
up, my lord.”

In another minute Mary Marvell, followed by her husband, was
ushered into the hall. She was pale and trembling.

“Oh, Lady Yardly,” she cried, “I’m so frightened. It’s come! I’ve
had another letter. And—and I’m sure I saw a Chinaman in the
village as we drove through.”

Gregory Rolf was behind her, his face grim. “It’s true,” he said.
“I saw him too. I believe they’re shadowing us.”

Lady Yardly had risen. She was very pale. “I—I have had letters
too,” she said in a low voice.

“You?” Mary Marvell stared at her. “Then it is true? The god is
coming for his eyes?”

“The god is already here, perhaps,” said Poirot softly. “But let
us not be hysterical. We are all here together. We are safe.”

“Are we?” Mary Marvell’s voice rose to a shriek. “I tell you, I’m
frightened. I feel as though someone were watching me—someone
cruel and—and Eastern!”

“Come, come,” said Lord Yardly. “We must keep our heads. Let’s
have some dinner, and then we can talk things over.”

We went into the dining-room. It was a strange meal. Mary Marvell
scarcely touched a thing, and Lady Yardly was equally silent.
Gregory Rolf talked incessantly, but his gaiety seemed forced.

After dinner we returned to the hall. It was a dark, stormy night,
and the wind howled round the old house. Suddenly, there was a
loud report from outside.

“What was that?” cried Mary Marvell.

“Only a car back-firing,” said Gregory Rolf. “Don’t be nervous,
Mary.”

But the girl was trembling from head to foot. Suddenly, she
pointed to the window.

“Look!” she screamed. “There! At the window! A face—a Chinese
face!”

We all sprang to our feet. I rushed to the window and threw it
open. The terrace was empty.

“There’s no one there,” I said, looking back into the room.

But Mary Marvell had fainted. Gregory Rolf picked her up and
carried her to a sofa.

“This is getting serious,” said Lord Yardly. “I’ll have the
servants search the grounds.”

He rang the bell and gave his orders. Then he turned to Poirot.
“What do you advise, Monsieur Poirot?”

“I advise that the ladies retire to their rooms,” said Poirot.
“They will be safer there. And—I would suggest that the diamonds
be placed in a safe place.”

“I’ll put mine in the safe,” said Lord Yardly. “And Miss Marvell’s
too, if she’ll let me.”

“No!” cried Mary Marvell, who had recovered consciousness. “I
won’t let it out of my sight. I’ll keep it with me.”

“As you wish, madame,” said Poirot. “But I think you would be
wiser to trust Lord Yardly.”

“I won’t!” she said obstinately.

“Very well,” said Poirot. “But at least, let us see that the
windows are all securely fastened.”

He went round the room, examining the shutters and bolts. Then
he turned to us.

“And now, I think we should all retire. It has been a long and
trying day.”

We all moved towards the stairs. Lady Yardly and Mary Marvell
went up together, followed by Gregory Rolf. Lord Yardly stayed
behind to see to the lights.

I followed Poirot to our room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as he closed the door. “What do you think
now? Was it really a Chinaman at the window?”

Poirot did not answer. He was busy unpacking his bag.

“I wonder,” I continued, “if the diamonds are safe. It seems a
big risk to let Mary Marvell keep hers.”

“She is a very headstrong young woman,” said Poirot. “But perhaps
she is right. Who knows?”

He was silent for a moment, then he turned to me.

“Hastings, I have a little commission for you. Will you go down
to the hall and see if I have left my cane there? I remember
having it when we came in, but I do not see it now.”

“Certainly,” I said.

I went down the stairs. The hall was empty, the lights were
turned low. I looked round for the cane, but could not see it.
Suddenly, I heard a faint sound from the dining-room—the sound
of a window being cautiously opened.

I froze. Was it the Chinaman?

I crept to the dining-room door and looked in. The room was dark,
but I could see a dark figure silhouetted against the open
window. It was a man, and he was leaning over the sideboard.

I didn’t hesitate. I sprang upon him, and we fell to the floor
together.

“I’ve got you!” I cried.

“Let go, you fool!” cried a familiar voice.

It was Lord Yardly!

“Lord Yardly!” I exclaimed, releasing him. “I—I beg your pardon.
I thought you were a burglar.”

“I was just seeing that the window was fast,” he said gruffly.
“You’ve got a bit too much ‘deductive sense,’ Hastings.”

I felt a fool. “I’m very sorry,” I stammered.

I found Poirot’s cane and went back upstairs.

“Well?” said Poirot, as I entered the room. “Did you find it?”

“Yes,” I said, handing it to him.

I told him of my adventure in the dining-room. He listened
with a little smile.

“Ah, the good Lord Yardly! He is very careful of his
possessions. And now, _mon ami_, to bed. We must be up early
to-morrow.”

But we were not destined to have a quiet night. About two o’clock
in the morning, we were awakened by a piercing shriek.

I sprang out of bed and rushed into the passage. Poirot was close
behind me. The shriek had come from Mary Marvell’s room.

We burst in. Mary Marvell was standing in the middle of the room,
her face ashen. Gregory Rolf was beside her.

“It’s gone!” she gasped. “The diamond! It’s been stolen!”

“Stolen?” cried Poirot. “But how?”

“I don’t know,” she sobbed. “I was asleep, and then I felt
something—a hand—at my throat. I screamed, and whoever it was
fled through the window.”

I looked at the window. It was wide open.

“But I thought the windows were all fastened!” I cried.

“They were,” said Gregory Rolf. “But the thief must have climbed
up the ivy and forced the bolt.”

Lord Yardly and Lady Yardly had appeared in the doorway,
hastily clad in dressing-gowns.

“What’s happened?” asked Lord Yardly.

“The Western Star has been stolen,” said Poirot.

“Stolen?” Lord Yardly’s face went white. “But—but that’s
impossible!”

“It is very possible, it seems,” said Poirot dryly. “And now, if
you will excuse me, I should like to examine the room.”

He went to the window and looked out. Then he examined the floor
near the bed. Suddenly, he stooped and picked something up.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of silk,” said Poirot, holding it up. “Yellow silk.”

“A Chinaman!” cried Mary Marvell. “I knew it!”

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “And now, Lord Yardly, if I
might suggest it, perhaps we should see if your diamond is safe?”

Lord Yardly started. “The Star of the East! Of course!”

He rushed out of the room, and we all followed him. He went to
the safe in the library and opened it.

With a cry of despair, he fell back.

“It’s gone too!” he gasped. “The safe has been rifled!”

The scene was one of utter confusion. Mary Marvell was in
hysterics, Lady Yardly was weeping silently, and Lord Yardly
seemed turned to stone.

“Both diamonds!” I cried. “The god has his eyes back!”

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “A very remarkable coincidence.”

He looked from one to the other of the company. His eyes were
bright and searching.

“And now,” he said, “I think we should all go back to bed. There
is nothing more to be done to-night. In the morning, we shall
see what can be discovered.”

But I noticed that as he left the room, he was smiling to himself.

The next morning, Poirot was up early. I found him in the hall,
talking to the butler.

“Ah, Hastings,” he said. “You are just in time. I have been
making some inquiries.”

“Have you found anything?” I asked eagerly.

“Perhaps,” he said. “We shall see. And now, I think we should
have some breakfast. Then we will have a little talk with our
friends.”

After breakfast, Poirot requested the presence of Lord and Lady
Yardly, and Mr. and Mrs. Rolf in the library.

When we were all assembled, he began.

“Mesdames and messieurs, a very grave thing has happened. Two
famous diamonds have been stolen in one night. It is a mystery of
the most profound.”

“It’s that Chinaman!” cried Mary Marvell. “He’s got them both!”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But let us examine the facts. First,
we have the letters. They were sent to both Miss Marvell and Lady
Yardly. They were identical in tone. Then we have the appearance
of a Chinaman—both in London and here at Yardly Chase. And
finally, we have the theft of the diamonds, with a piece of
yellow silk left behind as a clue.”

“It’s as plain as a pikestaff!” said Gregory Rolf.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Let us see. To begin with, there is one
very curious thing. Miss Marvell’s letters were left by hand, by
a Chinaman. But Lady Yardly’s letters came by post.”

“What does that matter?” said Gregory Rolf.

“It matters a great deal,” said Poirot. “Because it suggests that
the person who sent the letters to Lady Yardly did not want to be
seen. Now, why should that be?”

He paused, but no one answered.

“Then,” continued Poirot, “we have the theft itself. Miss
Marvell’s diamond was stolen from her neck while she slept. The
thief entered by the window. But Lord Yardly’s diamond was
stolen from a safe—a safe that was not forced, but opened with
a key!”

Lord Yardly started. “A key? But I have the only key!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “Which suggests that the person who
opened the safe was someone who knew where the key was kept, or
who had a duplicate.”

He looked at Lord Yardly. The latter’s face was a study in
confusion.

“And now,” said Poirot, “we come to the most curious thing of
all. Miss Marvell, will you permit that I see the piece of silk
I found in your room?”

Mary Marvell handed it to him. Poirot looked at it closely.

“A very fine piece of silk,” he said. “But there is one thing
about it that is very strange. It is quite clean.”

“Clean?” I said. “Why shouldn’t it be clean?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “if it had been torn from the robe of a
thief who had climbed up the ivy and through the window on a
stormy night, it would surely be soiled, would it not?”

I saw the point. “By Jove, Poirot, you’re right!”

“So,” said Poirot, “we must ask ourselves: how did that piece of
silk get there? And why was it so clean?”

He looked round the room.

“The answer, I think, is simple. It was put there by someone
who wanted us to believe in the Chinaman. It was a—what you call—
a ‘red herring’!”

“Then there was no Chinaman?” cried Mary Marvell.

“Oh, I think there was a Chinaman,” said Poirot. “But he was not
a thief. He was an actor.”

He turned to Gregory Rolf.

“Mr. Rolf, you are a very good actor. But you made one mistake.
You were too anxious to see the Chinaman.”

Gregory Rolf started. “What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that it was you who arranged the whole
thing. You sent the letters to your wife. You hired a man to
dress as a Chinaman and follow her. You even arranged for him
to appear at the window last night.”

“That’s a lie!” cried Gregory Rolf.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why you were
seen in the village yesterday afternoon, talking to a man who
was later seen dressed as a Chinaman?”

Gregory Rolf went pale.

“And as for the theft,” continued Poirot, “that was very simple.
You stole the diamond from your wife yourself. You knew she
wouldn’t let it out of her sight, so you waited until she was
asleep.”

“But what about my diamond?” cried Lord Yardly. “He couldn’t
have stolen that! He doesn’t know where the key is kept!”

“No,” said Poirot. “He did not steal your diamond, Lord Yardly.”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“It was you, madame, who stole the Star of the East.”

Lady Yardly gave a cry and buried her face in her hands.

“Maude!” cried Lord Yardly. “It’s not true!”

“I’m afraid it is,” said Poirot. “You see, Lord Yardly, your wife
was in a very difficult position. She had been indiscreet in the
past—with Mr. Rolf, when she was in California. He was
blackmailing her. He demanded the diamond. She couldn’t give it
to him, because it was a family heirloom. So she devised a
plan. She would pretend it had been stolen by the same
Chinaman who was threatening Miss Marvell. She sent herself the
letters, and last night, when the alarm was raised, she took the
diamond from the safe and hid it.”

“But why?” gasped Lord Yardly.

“To pay the blackmailer,” said Poirot. “And also, I think, to
prevent you from selling it. She knew that if it were ‘stolen,’
you could not sell it to Mr. Hoffberg.”

There was a long silence. Then Lady Yardly looked up. Her face
was ravaged with tears.

“It’s true,” she sobbed. “He’s been blackmailing me for years.
I—I didn’t know what to do.”

Gregory Rolf made a movement as if to escape, but I was too
quick for him. I stepped in front of the door.

“Not so fast, Mr. Rolf,” I said.

Poirot turned to Mary Marvell.

“And you, madame, I think you have something to tell us? The
Western Star—it was not really stolen, was it?”

Mary Marvell looked down at her hands.

“No,” she whispered. “Gregory told me to pretend it had been
stolen. He said it would be great publicity for our new film.”

“I thought as much,” said Poirot. “A very pretty little comedy,
as I said.”

He turned to Lord Yardly.

“And now, _milord_, I think you will find your diamond hidden
in the back of the clock in Lady Yardly’s bedroom. As for Mr.
Rolf, I think the police will be very interested in his
blackmailing activities.”

Lord Yardly looked at his wife. Then he took her hand.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said softly. “We’ll get through this
together.”

Poirot and I walked out onto the terrace. The sun was breaking
through the clouds.

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “You’ve done it again. But how did you
know?”

“Psychology, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, tapping his forehead.
“Psychology. And also—I have a very good memory for faces. I
remembered seeing Mr. Rolf and Lady Yardly together in San
Francisco three years ago. When the story of the two diamonds
came up, I began to put two and two together.”

“But the Chinaman?”

“A very old trick, Hastings. The ‘curse of the East.’ It always
appeals to the romantic mind. But for Hercule Poirot, there is
only the truth—and the little grey cells!”

“Look at that, Monsieur Poirot. What do you make of it?”

Poirot took the telegram. I followed his eye as he read:

“_Shall be with you at half-past eight this evening._ GREGORY ROLF.”

Lord Yardly gave a short laugh.

“The plot thickens,” he said, not without a touch of grimness.
“I’ll tell you something, Monsieur Poirot. I had a letter from Mr.
Rolf only this morning. It was to tell me that he had changed his
mind, and that the film deal was off. Yet here he is, arriving at
half-past eight!”

“_C’est curieux_,” murmured Poirot. “Lady Yardly, you are
distressed?”

Lady Yardly was indeed very pale. Her eyes were fixed on the
telegram. She gave a start as Poirot spoke to her.

“I? Oh, no—I’m only surprised—amazed!”

The dressing-gong sounded again, and we went up-stairs to our rooms.
Poirot’s was next to mine, and we went in together.

“You see,” I cried, “the plot _does_ thicken. What on earth can
have brought Gregory Rolf down here? It looks as if something was
on the tapis.”

“I do not know—I do not know,” said Poirot. He shook his head.
“There are things—well, there are things! This _château_, it is
full of ghosts.”

“Ghosts?” I cried, startled.

“Oh, not the ghosts of the _spiritualistes_! No, the ghosts of the
past! Let us hope they will be laid.”

I did not know what to make of him. He was in an oddly solemn
mood. At dinner he was quiet and even thoughtful.

The meal was half-way through when we were interrupted. There was
a commotion in the hall outside, and a moment later a man burst
into the room. It was Gregory Rolf. He was in a state of great
agitation. Lord Yardly rose in surprise.

“What’s the matter, man?” he cried.

“The diamond! The Western Star! It’s been stolen!”

“Stolen?” I cried.

“Yes. My wife—she would wear it! I told her not to. But she’s so
headstrong. We were at the hotel. A man—a Chinaman—entered the
room. He must have been hiding there. He sprang upon her—tore the
jewel from her neck—and fled! The police are on his track.”

“A Chinaman!” I cried. “The very thing we feared! And it was
at——?”

“About seven o’clock.”

“Then,” I said, looking at my watch, “the thief may be here at
any moment now. He has had an hour and a half’s start.”

Lady Yardly had risen, and was standing as though turned to stone.

“The Star of the East!” she gasped. “He will come for that next!”

Lord Yardly sprang to his feet.

“Not if I know it! Maude, go and get the diamond at once. We’ll
place it in Monsieur Poirot’s hands.”

Lady Yardly left the room. We waited in a state of the utmost
tension.

Suddenly a piercing shriek rang out from the floor above.

“The diamond!” cried Lord Yardly. “He’s got it!”

We dashed out of the room and up the stairs. At the head of them
we met Lady Yardly. She was swaying to and fro, and her face was
ghastly.

“He—the Chinaman——” she gasped. “He was in my room—by the window!
The diamond—it’s gone!”

She fell in a dead faint on the floor. Lord Yardly dashed past
her into the room. I followed him. The window was open. The lace
curtains were torn and fluttering in the wind.

“Look!” I cried. “There he is!”

A dark figure was disappearing among the trees. I did not hesitate.
I leapt through the window, and dropped to the ground. It was a
drop of some twelve feet, but I landed safely. I was after the
man like a hound. I am a good runner, and I was gaining on him,
when I tripped over a low wire and fell headlong. By the time I
had picked myself up, the man had disappeared. I searched for
some time, but in vain.

I returned to the house, feeling very crestfallen. I found that
Lady Yardly had been carried to her room, and that Poirot was there
with her. Lord Yardly was in the hall, looking the picture of
despair.

“It’s gone!” he groaned. “The family diamond! It’s the end of
everything.”

“But the man?” I cried. “I saw him!”

“The police have been telephoned for,” said Lord Yardly. “Monsieur
Poirot is with my wife. He won’t let anyone in. He says she must
not be disturbed.”

“But the man?” I persisted. “What was he like?”

“I don’t know. I didn’t see him. I was too late.”

I told him of my pursuit.

“At least we know that there _is_ a man,” I said.

“Yes, but what does that help us? The diamond’s gone!”

We sat there in silence for some time. At last the door of Lady
Yardly’s room opened, and Poirot came out. He looked very grave.

“How is she?” asked Lord Yardly.

“She is better. She has told me all.”

“The Chinaman?” I asked.

“Yes, the Chinaman. It was as she said. He was in the room—by the
window. He snatched the diamond from her neck—and fled.”

“And the other? The one I saw?”

“That also was the Chinaman.”

“But what are we to do?” cried Lord Yardly. “The police——”

“The police will do their best,” said Poirot. “But I fear—I
greatly fear—that they will be too late. The diamond will have
been passed on.”

“But Gregory Rolf?” I asked. “Where is he?”

“He has gone back to London. He was in a state of great agitation
about his wife. He said he must go to her at once.”

“And Miss Marvell?”

“She is at the hotel. She is also in a state of great agitation.”

I could not help thinking that there was something very strange
about the whole business. The two diamonds stolen on the same
evening—and both by a Chinaman! It was too much of a coincidence.
And yet, I had seen the man myself.

The police arrived shortly afterwards, and we spent the rest of
the night in fruitlessly scouring the countryside. But of the
mysterious Chinaman there was no sign.

The next morning Poirot and I returned to London. My friend was
very silent, and I could see that he was thinking deeply.

“What do you make of it all, Poirot?” I asked at last.

“It is a very strange case, Hastings—a very strange case indeed.
There are things in it that I do not understand—things that do
not fit in.”

“But the Chinaman? I saw him!”

“Yes, you saw him. That is the most interesting thing about the
whole case.”

“But what do you mean?”

“I mean, my friend, that you have a very romantic imagination.
You saw what you expected to see.”

I was about to protest indignantly, but Poirot stopped me with a
gesture.

“Do not be angry, Hastings. I do not say that there was no man.
But was he a Chinaman? It was dark—you were some distance away—you
saw a figure. And because you had the idea of a Chinaman in your
head, you saw a Chinaman!”

“But Lady Yardly saw him too!”

“Precisely. She also had the idea of a Chinaman in her head.”

“But Gregory Rolf’s wife was robbed by a Chinaman!”

“So we are told.”

“But what do you think yourself, Poirot?”

“I think, Hastings, that we must use our little grey cells. We
must look at the facts—the hard, cold facts.”

“And what are they?”

“The facts are these: Two diamonds are stolen on the same evening.
In each case a Chinaman is said to be the thief. In one case, the
thief is seen by two people—one of whom is a very romantic young
man with a great deal of imagination!”

I flushed.

“And the other?”

“The other is a lady who is in a state of great agitation.”

“But what about the letters?”

“The letters? Ah, yes, the letters! They are very interesting,
those letters. They are so—how shall I say?—so _theatrical_!”

“Theatrical?”

“Yes. The ‘Great God,’ the ‘Two Eyes’—it is like a play, is it
not? A very bad play.”

“But what are you driving at, Poirot?”

“I am driving at this, Hastings. Who had the most to gain by the
theft of the diamonds?”

“The Chinese gang, of course!”

“But is there a Chinese gang? Have we any evidence of one—except
the letters?”

“But the man I saw?”

“As I said, you saw a man. But who was he? Was he a Chinaman? Or
was he—someone else?”

“Who else could he be?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

I was silent for a moment, thinking.

“You mean,” I said at last, “that the whole thing is a hoax? That
the diamonds haven’t been stolen at all?”

“Oh, no, they have been stolen right enough. But by whom?”

“But if Gregory Rolf didn’t do it—and he couldn’t have, because
he was in the room with us when the second diamond was stolen——”

“Was he? Are you sure of that, Hastings?”

“Of course I am! He came in just as we were half-way through dinner.”

“And the diamond was stolen—when?”

“About an hour later.”

“And where was Mr. Rolf during that hour?”

“He was in the room with us!”

“Are you sure? Think, Hastings, think!”

I thought back.

“Yes,” I said at last. “He was there all the time. He never left
the room.”

“And Lady Yardly? Did she leave the room?”

“Yes, she went to get the diamond.”

“And it was then that she was robbed?”

“Yes.”

“And you saw the man—when?”

“Just after she screamed.”

“And where was Lord Yardly?”

“He was with us in the dining-room.”

“So,” said Poirot, “we have three people who could not have
stolen the diamond—Lord Yardly, Mr. Rolf, and yourself. That
leaves—Lady Yardly.”

“Lady Yardly! But she was the one who was robbed!”

“So she says.”

“But I saw the man!”

“Again I say—you saw a man. But who was he? Was he a confederate
of Lady Yardly’s?”

“But why should she steal her own diamond?”

“Ah, that is the question! Why should she? Perhaps because she
had already sold it? Perhaps because she was being blackmailed?”

“Blackmailed? By whom?”

“By someone who knew her secret. Someone who knew that the diamond
she was wearing was not the real Star of the East—but a paste
imitation!”

“A paste imitation!” I cried. “But Poirot, you saw the stone
yourself!”

“I saw a stone, yes. But I am not an expert. And besides, I only
saw it for a moment.”

“But what about Miss Marvell’s diamond? Was that a paste imitation
too?”

“Ah, that is another matter. Miss Marvell’s diamond was real enough.
I would stake my reputation on that.”

“Then who stole that?”

“The same person, Hastings. The same person who planned the whole
business from beginning to end.”

“And who was that?”

“That, my friend, is what we are going to find out. And to do so,
we must go back to the beginning. We must go back to California—three
years ago.”

“California? But what happened then?”

“A great many things happened then, Hastings. Amongst others, Lady
Yardly met Gregory Rolf.”

“I know that. I told you so myself.”

“You did. And it is the most important fact in the case.”

“But I don’t see——”

“You will, Hastings, you will. In the meantime, I have a little
investigation of my own to make. Await me here.”

He was gone for several hours. When he returned, his face was
beaming.

“I have it, Hastings! I have it!”

“What have you found out?”

“I have found out the truth! The beautiful, simple truth! But
first, we must have a little meeting. I have invited Lord and Lady
Yardly, and Mr. and Mrs. Gregory Rolf, to meet me here this
afternoon.”

“But what for?”

“To restore to them their diamonds, Hastings! To restore to them
their diamonds!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“You have found them?”

“I have found them.”

He would say no more, and I was left to chew the cud of my
reflections until the arrival of our guests.

They arrived together, Lord and Lady Yardly looking pale and
anxious, and the Rolfs looking—well, much as usual, except that
Miss Marvell was in a state of great excitement.

“Now, Monsieur Poirot,” she cried, as soon as she was in the room.
“What’s all this? Have you really found my diamond?”

“I have, madame.”

“Then where is it? Give it to me!”

“In a moment, madame. But first, there are a few things that must
be cleared up.”

He turned to the others.

“Lord Yardly, I believe you wish to sell your diamond, the Star
of the East?”

Lord Yardly nodded.

“I do—or I did. But as it’s been stolen——”

“It has not been stolen, _milord_.”

“Not stolen? But I saw it taken myself!” cried Lady Yardly.

“You saw a man at the window, madame. But he did not take the
diamond. Because, you see, the diamond was not there to be taken.”

“Not there? What do you mean?”

“I mean, madame, that you had already given it away. You gave it
to Mr. Gregory Rolf three years ago in California!”

A gasp of astonishment went round the room. Lady Yardly had turned
as white as a sheet.

“It’s a lie!” she gasped.

“Is it, madame? I think not. Mr. Rolf was blackmailing you. He
had some—shall we say, indiscreet?—letters of yours. And the
price he asked for them was the Star of the East. You gave it to
him. But you were afraid to tell your husband. So you had a paste
copy made, and it was that that you have been wearing ever since.”

He turned to Gregory Rolf.

“And you, monsieur—you were not satisfied with one diamond! You
wanted both! So you conceived a very clever plan. You would steal
your own wife’s diamond, and at the same time you would steal the
other. And you would lay the blame on a mysterious Chinese gang!”

“It’s a lie!” cried Rolf, but his face was ghastly.

“Is it? I think not. You sent the letters yourself—both to your
wife and to Lady Yardly. You knew that Lady Yardly’s stone was a
paste imitation, but you also knew that it would be insured for
its full value. If it were stolen, the insurance company would
pay up, and Lord Yardly would be none the wiser. And in the
meantime, you would have the other diamond—the real Western
Star—to sell at your leisure!”

“But the Chinaman?” I cried. “The man I saw?”

“A confederate, Hastings. A simple confederate. Probably one of
the actors from Mr. Rolf’s company.”

He turned back to Rolf.

“And now, monsieur, if you will be so good as to hand over the
diamonds?”

For a moment Rolf looked as if he would defy him. Then, seeing the
hopelessness of his position, he reached into his pocket and drew
out two small packages.

“There they are,” he said sullenly. “And much good may they do
you!”

He turned and strode out of the room, followed by his wife, who
was in a state of collapse.

Lord Yardly was staring at the two diamonds in his hand.

“Then this one—the Star of the East—is the real one?”

“It is, _milord_,” said Poirot. “Mr. Rolf had it all the time.
He merely pretended to steal the other one to cover his tracks.”

“And the other one—my wife’s?”

“That, _milord_, is also the real one. Mr. Rolf had stolen it
from his wife earlier in the evening, as he said.”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“And now, madame, I think you have something to say to your
husband?”

Lady Yardly burst into tears.

“Oh, George, can you ever forgive me?”

Lord Yardly took her in his arms.

“There, there, my dear. It’s all over now. We’ll say no more about
it.”

He turned to Poirot.

“Monsieur Poirot, I don’t know how to thank you.”

“Do not thank me, _milord_,” said Poirot. “Thank my friend
Hastings. It was his—how shall I say?—_vivid imagination_ that
first gave me the clue!”

And with a twinkle in his eye, he bowed them from the room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when we were alone. “I must say, you’ve
surpassed yourself this time! But how on earth did you know?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, lighting a cigarette. “I did not know.
But I suspected. And as I have often told you, once you have
eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable,
must be the truth!”

“But the Chinaman?” I persisted. “I’m sure he looked like a
Chinaman!”

“Of course he did, Hastings! Of course he did! That was the whole
point of the disguise! But you must remember—to the eyes of
Hercule Poirot, things are not always what they seem!”

And he smiled at me with the utmost benevolence.

“Read this, Monsieur Poirot.”

Poirot took the slip of paper, and I too looked over his shoulder.

It was from Mary Marvell, and ran as follows:

“Just received another warning. Am terrified. Leaving for Yardly
Chase at once. Have the Star of the West with me. Hope you can
put me up. GREGORY.”

The message had been sent from London at four o’clock.

“_C’est ça_,” said Poirot, his eyes shining. “Wait for her, _milord_!
Whatever happens, do not leave your wife!”

The situation was tense. We all stood in a group. Then Lord Yardly
spoke.

“Is it any use, Monsieur Poirot? What could a handful of
Chinamen——”

“Who said Chinamen, _milord_? Do you not see it is some deep-laid
scheme? If you can protect your diamond and hers as well, you
will have outwitted them! But if you are not careful, _milord_,
neither will be saved!”

Lord Yardly nodded. “I see. All right, we’ll stick together.”

The next few hours passed in a state of suppressed excitement.
Dinner was a hurried meal, and we soon returned to the hall. Every
shadow seemed to hold a lurking figure, and the very wind in the
chimney sounded like a human voice.

It was just after nine o’clock when the sound of a motor-car was
heard outside. In a few moments the door opened, and Gregory Rolf,
looking pale and haggard, came into the hall.

“Where is Mary?” he cried. “She’s not here?”

“Not here?” Lord Yardly’s face fell.

“But the telegram?” I asked.

“What telegram? I sent no telegram!”
