“The one we received this afternoon.”

Gregory Rolf shook his head. “I know nothing of it. Mary left the
hotel at five o’clock. She said she was coming here. I was to
follow by the seven o’clock train. When I got here and found she
hadn’t arrived, I was nearly frantic.”

“_Sacré bleu!_” cried Poirot. “Then where is she?”

He had no time to say more. At that moment the lights went out,
and a woman’s scream rang through the air.

“The diamond! The diamond!”

Then followed the sound of a scuffle, a heavy fall, and a door
banging.

Lord Yardly’s voice was heard shouting for lights. When they were
brought, we found the room in confusion. Lady Yardly was lying
on the floor in a dead faint, her neck bare of the famous diamond.
Lord Yardly was bending over her.

“My wife! My wife! Are you hurt?”

She opened her eyes. “The Chinaman!” she gasped. “He came through
that door—he tore it from my neck!”

She pointed to a small side door which stood ajar. Gregory Rolf
and I rushed through it. It led into a small morning-room, the
French window of which was open.

“This way!” I cried. “He must have gone this way.”

We dashed out into the night, but could see no sign of any fugitive.
The moon was hidden behind a cloud. We returned to the hall to
find the household in an uproar. Lady Yardly had been carried to
her room, and Poirot was examining the little morning-room with
a flashlight.

“He must have been a very agile Chinaman,” he remarked dryly.

“But the diamond!” cried Lord Yardly. “What about the diamond? And
Mary—Miss Marvell?”

“As for the diamond, it is gone,” said Poirot. “As for Miss Marvell—I
fear she has been kidnapped.”

“Kidnapped?”

“It would seem so. But we must act! Hastings, to the telephone!
Ring up the police! Tell them to watch the roads. Mr. Rolf, you
had better go to the village and see if any suspicious characters
have been seen there.”

Gregory Rolf hurried away. Lord Yardly turned to Poirot.

“What can we do, Monsieur Poirot? Is there no hope?”

“There is always hope, _milord_,” said Poirot, his eyes fixed on
the floor. “But for the moment, we can only wait. Your wife—is she
better?”

“She is very much shaken. It has been a terrible blow to her.”

“Naturally. Will you permit that I see her for a moment? I wish
to ask her one or two questions.”

“Certainly. Come this way.”

We followed him upstairs. Lady Yardly was lying on a sofa in her
boudoir. She looked very pale and her eyes were red with weeping.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she sobbed. “It was too awful! That
terrible face! Those yellow eyes!”

“_Tranquillisez-vous_, madame,” said Poirot soothingly. “All will
be well. But tell me, was it a very large man who attacked you?”

“No—not very large. But so quick—so horribly quick!”

“I see. And you did not hear him coming?”

“No. I just felt his hands on my neck—and then I saw his face. Oh,
it was like a nightmare!”

“I understand. And now, _milord_, I think we can do no more tonight.
In the morning, the police will be here, and we can make a more
thorough investigation.”

We retired to our rooms, but I for one could not sleep. The
mystery of Mary Marvell’s disappearance, the theft of the Yardly
diamond—it was all so bizarre and incredible. What was the meaning
of it all? And where was Poirot? I had seen him steal out of his
room just as I was closing my own door.

I decided to follow him. I found him in the hall, looking out at
the moon which had now emerged from the clouds.

“Ah, Hastings! You too are wakeful? It is a beautiful night, is
it not?”

“Poirot, how can you talk of the night being beautiful? Don’t you
realize what has happened?”

“I realize everything, _mon ami_. And I also realize that there
is a great deal more to this case than meets the eye.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that things are not always what they seem.
But come, let us go to bed. To-morrow we shall see what we shall
see.”

The next morning brought a fresh surprise. A telegram arrived from
Mary Marvell!

“Safe and well. Will explain everything on arrival this afternoon.”

She arrived at three o’clock, looking quite her usual self.

“I’m so sorry if I’ve worried you all,” she said, as we gathered
round her in the hall. “But you see, I got another of those
horrible warnings, and I was so frightened that I decided to go
to a quiet little place in the country where no one would know me.
I thought it was the best way to keep the diamond safe.”

“And the diamond?” asked Lord Yardly. “You have it with you?”

“Of course! It’s right here.” She tapped her handbag.

“Then at least one of the diamonds is safe,” sighed Lord Yardly.
“But mine—mine is gone!”

“Gone?” cried Mary Marvell. “You mean it’s been stolen?”

Lord Yardly recounted the events of the previous evening. Mary
Marvell listened with wide eyes.

“How terrible!” she exclaimed. “And to think that mine might have
gone too if I hadn’t been so clever!”

Gregory Rolf, who had returned from the village, came forward and
embraced his wife.

“Thank God you’re safe, Mary! I’ve been nearly out of my mind.”

“Poor Gregory! But you see I was right after all.”

Poirot, who had been listening in silence, now stepped forward.

“And now, if you please, I would like to see the diamond—the
Western Star.”

“Certainly, Monsieur Poirot.” Mary Marvell opened her handbag and
drew out a small leather case. She opened it and handed it to
Poirot.

The little man took it and examined the stone with his magnifying
glass. Then he handed it back with a bow.

“A beautiful stone, madame. A very beautiful stone.”

“And now, Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord Yardly, “what do you propose
to do? The police have been here all morning, but they have found
nothing.”

“The police!” Poirot shrugged his shoulders. “They look for
Chinamen! They look for footprints! They do not use the little
grey cells!”

“Then you have a theory?” I asked eagerly.

“I have more than a theory, Hastings. I have the truth.”

“The truth?” we all cried.

“_Oui_, my friends. But first, let us all assemble in the hall.
I have something to say to you all.”

We followed him into the hall. Poirot took his stand by the
fireplace.

“Now,” he said, his eyes traveling from one to the other of us.
“Let us consider the facts. Two diamonds—the Star of the East and
the Star of the West. Both are said to be the eyes of a Chinese
god. Both are threatened with theft. And both are in the
possession of ladies who are—shall we say—not on the best of
terms?”

He paused, then continued.

“On Friday evening, the Star of the East is stolen. Lady Yardly
is attacked by a ‘Chinaman.’ The lights go out—the diamond is
gone. But is it? That is the question I ask myself.”

“What do you mean?” cried Lord Yardly. “Of course it’s gone! My
wife saw it stolen!”

“Did she, _milord_? Or did she only _say_ she saw it stolen?”

Lady Yardly turned pale. “Monsieur Poirot! What are you
suggesting?”

“I am suggesting, madame, that there was no Chinaman. I am
suggesting that the theft was a stage-managed affair, designed to
cover up the fact that the diamond was already gone!”

“Already gone?” I gasped.

“_Oui_, Hastings. Lady Yardly had already parted with the diamond.
She had been blackmailed—blackmailed by someone who knew a secret of
her past. And that someone was—Gregory Rolf!”

A gasp of astonishment went round the room. Gregory Rolf stepped
forward, his face dark with anger.

“That’s a lie! A damned lie!”

“Is it, Mr. Rolf? Let us see. Three years ago, you were in
California. So was Lady Yardly. You became—intimate. You gave her
the diamond which you had bought from a Chinaman—the Western Star.
But it was not a gift of love, Mr. Rolf. It was a gift with a
purpose. You knew that one day you would be able to use it against
her.”

“This is preposterous!” cried Lord Yardly. “My wife—and this man?”

“Wait, _milord_. Lady Yardly, in a moment of weakness, gave him her
own diamond—the Star of the East. In its place, she wore a copy.
But Gregory Rolf was not satisfied. He wanted more. He wanted
money. And so he began to blackmail her. He sent her the letters—the
letters with the scent of joss-stick. He knew that she would be
terrified, and that she would do anything to keep her secret.”

“And what about Mary Marvell?” I asked. “She received letters too.”

“Ah, Mary Marvell! She was the unconscious tool of her husband.
He sent her the letters to make the whole thing seem more
plausible. He even arranged for the ‘Chinaman’ to leave them. And
the story in _Society Gossip_—that too was his work. He wanted to
create an atmosphere of mystery and terror.”

“But the diamond?” cried Lord Yardly. “Where is it now?”

“It is here, _milord_.” Poirot reached into his pocket and drew
out a small object. It was the Star of the East!

“But how—where did you find it?”

“I found it, _milord_, in the morning-room—hidden behind a
shutter. It had never left the house. Lady Yardly, in her terror,
had tried to make it look like a theft. She had turned out the
lights herself, and then she had pretended to be attacked. She
had even staged the scuffle and the fall. But she had not had
time to dispose of the diamond. She had hidden it behind the
shutter, hoping to retrieve it later.”

Lady Yardly sank into a chair, her face buried in her hands.

“It’s true,” she sobbed. “It’s all true! He was blackmailing me—I
didn’t know what to do!”

Gregory Rolf made a dash for the door, but I was too quick for him.
I grabbed him by the arm and held him fast.

“Not so fast, Mr. Rolf! I think the police will be very
interested in what you have to say.”

Poirot turned to Lord Yardly.

“And now, _milord_, I have the honour to restore to you your family
diamond. As for the rest—I think you can safely leave it in my
hands.”

Lord Yardly took the diamond, his face a mixture of relief and
sorrow.

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. I—I don’t know how to thank you.”

“Do not thank me, _milord_. Thank the little grey cells. They
have once more proved their worth!”

And so the mystery of the Western Star was solved. Gregory Rolf
was arrested and charged with blackmail and theft. Lady Yardly’s
secret was kept, and she and her husband were eventually
reconciled. As for Mary Marvell, she returned to the States, her
faith in her husband shattered, but her own diamond—the Star of
the West—still in her possession.

And Poirot? He merely smiled and twirled his moustache.

“You see, Hastings,” he said, as we sat in his rooms the next
evening. “The simplest explanation is always the best. One only
has to use the little grey cells!”

“Read it, Monsieur Poirot.”

Poirot read:

“Star stolen. Full moon. The God has his own.
            “MARY MARVELL.”

“_Mon Dieu!_” cried Poirot. “The film star? Is it possible? She
has been robbed?”

“It is unbelievable!” cried Lady Yardly. “How? Where?”

Lord Yardly’s brow was gloomy.

“I told her not to take it with her. She should have left it at
the bank. And yet—the letter is from London. Let us see the
postmark.” He examined the telegram. “Sent from the West End at
five o’clock.”

Lady Yardly turned away with a shudder. “Oh, it is too horrible!”
she cried. “I am beginning to be afraid. What if _our_ diamond is
next?”

“_N’ayez pas peur, madame_,” said Poirot reassuringly. “Am I not
here?”

I looked at him in surprise.

“Then you think the danger is real, Poirot?”

“Decidedly.”

His tone was grave.

The dinner-gong sounded, and we were soon seated at the table.
Lord Yardly was distrait, his wife nervous and uneasy. At any
other time the old hall would have been a fascinating setting for
a meal, but to-night a shadow seemed to hang over the house. At
times I found myself glancing over my shoulder as though I too felt
the presence of some unseen danger.

Suddenly a scream rang out from the hall. We all started to our
feet. Lady Yardly was the first to reach the door.

“_C’est le Chinois!_” she gasped. “The Chinaman!”

She sank back, half-fainting. A tall figure in a blue robe, with
a pigtail and a mask, stood by the heavy velvet curtains that hung
across the door. For a moment he stood there, a sinister figure,
then with a swift movement he vanished into the darkness of the
hall.

With a shout, Lord Yardly dashed after him. Poirot and I followed,
but we were too late. The hall was empty, and the heavy front door
stood open.

“He went that way!” cried Lord Yardly. “After him, Hastings! I’ll
go round the other way.”

I dashed out into the night, but could see no sign of the fugitive.
The darkness was intense, and I stumbled more than once as I
searched the grounds. When I returned to the house I found the
whole household in an uproar. Lady Yardly had been carried to her
room, and Poirot was in the hall with Lord Yardly and the butler.

“He has escaped,” said Lord Yardly gloomily. “The fellow must know
every inch of the place.”

“And the diamond?” asked Poirot.

Lord Yardly’s face fell.

“It’s gone! The Star of the East has been stolen!”

“But how? Where?”

“It was in the jewel-case in my wife’s room. She had taken it out
to show it to the children, and then had replaced it. When the
alarm was raised she ran to her room—and found the case empty!”

Poirot nodded.

“The work of a master,” he murmured. “He must have been in the
house for some time. But tell me, _milord_, what of the other
diamond—the Star of the West?”

“I don’t know. We must wire to Miss Marvell at once.”

But Poirot shook his head.

“It is too late. The telegram we received was no hoax. The Star
of the West has already been stolen.”

“Then the two diamonds have met at last,” I said.

“_Oui_, my friend. And now they go back to the god.”

Lord Yardly turned to Poirot.

“What’s to be done? Can’t we do anything?”

“We can do much, _milord_. But for the moment—nothing. To-morrow
we shall see.”

“But the police?”

“If you like—but I should advise you to leave the matter in my
hands. I have my own methods.”

Lord Yardly hesitated, then he nodded.

“Very well. I’ll leave it to you.”

I must confess that I was disappointed in Poirot. He seemed to be
taking things very easily. I should have expected him to be up and
doing, searching for clues, questioning the servants. Instead of
which he spent the evening talking to the children’s nurse and
examining the locks on the doors.

The next morning he was up early, and I found him in the hall.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “have you found anything?”

“I have found much, Hastings. But before I tell you, I must see
Lord Yardly.”

He was with the peer for some time, and when he came out his face
was grave.

“We go back to London, Hastings,” he said.

“To London? But what about the diamond?”

“The diamond? Ah, _oui_, the diamond. We shall see.”

He would say no more, and we were soon on our way back to town.
As soon as we arrived at our rooms, Poirot sat down and wrote a
note.

“Take this, Hastings, to the Hotel Magnificent. It is for Mr.
Gregory Rolf. Bring him back with you if you can.”

I was lucky enough to find the actor in, and he accompanied me
back to our rooms. He seemed very much upset.

“It’s a bad business, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “Mary’s just
distraught. To think of that diamond being stolen—and after all
your warnings, too!”

“It was stolen, then?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, on Friday evening—just as we were getting ready for dinner.
A fellow dressed as a waiter came into the room, and before Mary
could say a word he’d snatched the jewel from the table and was
off. We chased him, of course, but he got away.”

“And the description of this waiter?”

“Oh, a regular Chinaman—pigtail and all.”

Poirot nodded.

“It is as I thought. And now, Mr. Rolf, I have a little surprise
for you.”

He went to his desk and took out a small box. Opening it, he held
up a magnificent diamond.

“The Star of the West!” cried Rolf. “Where did you get it?”

“I found it, monsieur. But that is not all.”

He took another stone from the box.

“The Star of the East!”

Rolf stared at him in amazement.

“But—but how?”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “The Star of the West was never
stolen.”

“What?”

“It was in my possession all the time. You see, Mr. Rolf, I had
my suspicions. I did not believe in those letters. They were too
like a ‘movie’ plot. So I took the liberty of substituting a
replica for the real stone when Miss Marvell showed it to me.”

“But the waiter?”

“A little piece of play-acting, monsieur—arranged by you and Miss
Marvell to give colour to the story. Is it not so?”

Rolf went pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“_Allons!_” said Poirot. “The game is up. You wanted to get the
insurance money, and at the same time to keep the diamond. A very
neat little plot, but you forgot one thing—Hercule Poirot!”

“And the other diamond?” I asked. “The Star of the East?”

“That was even simpler,” said Poirot. “It was never stolen either.”

“But we saw the Chinaman!” I cried.

“_Assurément_, we saw him. But he was not a Chinaman. He was Lord
Yardly!”

“Lord Yardly?”

“_Oui_, my friend. He too was in need of money. He had already
sold the real diamond to a dealer in Hatton Garden, and had replaced
it with a paste replica. Then, when he heard of the ‘Western Star’
mystery, he saw a way of explaining the disappearance of his own
diamond. He arranged the little scene in the hall, and then
‘stole’ the replica from his wife’s room. It was all very well
thought out—but he did not count on me.”

“But how did you find out?” I asked.

“By the exercise of my ‘little grey cells,’ Hastings! I knew that
Lord Yardly was in debt, and I knew that he was anxious to sell
the diamond. When the ‘theft’ occurred, I saw at once that it was
too well timed. And then I found a piece of blue silk in the hall—a
piece of the costume Lord Yardly had worn!”

He turned to Gregory Rolf.

“As for you, monsieur, I advise you to return the insurance money
and say no more about it. Otherwise——”

Rolf did not wait for the end of the sentence. He snatched up his
hat and bolted from the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings, how simple it all is when one uses the brain?
The two diamonds have indeed ‘met’—in the hands of Hercule Poirot!”

“But what about Lady Yardly?” I asked. “She seemed so upset.”

“Ah, _pauvre femme!_” said Poirot. “She knew nothing of her
husband’s plot. But I have seen Lord Yardly, and he has promised
to make amends. He will not sell Yardly Chase, and he will do his
best to make his wife happy. So, you see, it has all ended well.”

“And the diamonds?”

“They will return to the god, Hastings—or at least to the bank!
And now, I think we might have a little lunch. I know a place in
Soho where the _omelette_ is truly marvellous. . . .”

“Just a minute, Monsieur Poirot. I feel you ought to know about
this. It’s from Hoffberg. He thinks he’s found a customer for the
diamond—an American, sailing for the States to-morrow. They’re
sending down a chap to-night to vet the stone. By Jove, though, if
this goes through——” Words failed him.

Lady Yardly had turned away. She still held the telegram in her
hand.

At last the door opened and Lady Yardly entered. She was transformed. She wore a dinner gown of shimmering silver, and around her neck was a heavy, old-fashioned necklace of diamonds. In the centre, the great ‘Star of the East’ shone with a cold, white fire. It was a magnificent stone, though the setting was indeed, as she had said, somewhat clumsy and Victorian in style. Lord Yardly went forward to meet her, his eyes alight with a pride that was not unmixed with a certain greedy calculation as he remarked on the brilliance of the gem.

Suddenly a door banged, and a woman’s cry rang through the house.
Lady Yardly, her face deathly pale, her hands at her throat,
staggered into the room.

“The diamond!” she gasped. “It’s gone—stolen!”

“_Mon Dieu!_” cried Poirot.

Lord Yardly gave a smothered groan.

“What? How?”

“I was in my room, just going to put it on. The maid was out of the
room. Suddenly—a man—a Chinaman—jumped out from behind the
window-curtain. He—he sprang at me, and wrenched the necklace from
my neck. I fell—I—I think I fainted. When I came to, I was alone,
and the necklace—gone!”

She swayed as she spoke, and would have fallen if I had not caught
her. Lord Yardly was already running towards the door.

“Which way did he go? We must have the police!”

“_Wait!_” cried Poirot. “One moment. _Sacré_! What is this?”

He had bent down to the floor, and now he rose, holding something
in his hand. It was a small piece of silk, of a curious Eastern
design.

“The Chinaman, then, he exists!” he murmured. “He is not a myth!
But—how did he get in?”

We were all in the hall now. Lord Yardly was shouting for the
police, and his wife’s maid was weeping and hysterically
protesting her innocence.

“The window!” cried Poirot. “Was the window open, madame?”

“I—I think so. I’m not sure. No, I don’t know. I’m so confused.”

Poirot ran up the stairs to Lady Yardly’s room, and I followed
him. The window was wide open, and looked out upon the terrace.
Beneath the window were several shrubs. Poirot looked out, then
shook his head.

“The man must have been an acrobat! It is no easy task to climb
up that wall. See, the ivy—it is not disturbed!”

“There are the shrubs, Poirot,” I said.

“_C’est vrai_! He might have jumped from the terrace on to the
shrubs, and then up to the window-sill.”

He leaned out of the window, examining the wall closely.

“_Tiens_! What is this?”

He pointed to a small mark on the stone-work.

“It is a footprint!” I cried.

“_Oui_, it is a footprint. But what a small one! Decidedly, it is
a Chinaman who has been here!”

He looked about the room, his eyes sharp and birdlike. Suddenly he
pounced on something. It was a small piece of paper, with printing
on it.

“The god has his own!” he read.

I stood there, my brain reeling. The thing was too incredible!
A Chinaman in the heart of the English countryside!

“We must search the grounds,” I cried. “He cannot have got far.”

“_Assurément_,” said Poirot. “But first—where is the rest of the
necklace?”

He had picked up a small leather case from the floor. It was
empty.

“The necklace was in this?”

“Yes,” I said, “I suppose so.”

“But the Chinaman—he took the necklace? Why should he leave the
case? It is most curious.”

We descended the stairs again. Lord Yardly was in a state of
indescribable agitation.

“The police are on their way. I’ve telephoned to the local station.
They’re sending out a search party at once.”

“And the man from Hoffberg?” asked Poirot.

“He’s here. He arrived just after the—the robbery. He’s in the
library now.”

“I should like to see him,” said Poirot.

We followed Lord Yardly to the library. A small, dark man with
shrewd eyes rose as we entered.

“This is Mr. –er–”

“Levitt,” said the small man.

“Mr. Levitt. He has come from Hoffberg’s.”

“It’s a most unfortunate business, Lord Yardly,” said Mr. Levitt.
“My firm will be very much distressed.”

“They’re not so distressed as I am,” said Lord Yardly grimly. “The
diamond is gone, and that’s all there is to it.”

“You are sure it is the Star of the East that has been stolen?”
asked Poirot.

“Of course I’m sure! What do you mean?”

“Only that there are two diamonds, _milord_! The Star of the East
and the Star of the West. It would be a pity if the wrong one had
been taken!”

“The Star of the West belongs to Miss Marvell,” I said. “She is
not here.”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “I forgot.”

He turned to Mr. Levitt.

“You have seen the Star of the East?”

“Many times, monsieur. It is a very famous stone.”

“And you could identify it anywhere?”

“Certainly.”

“_Bien_! Then I have a request to make of you. Will you be so good
as to go to the _Magnificent_ Hotel, and ask for Miss Mary Marvell?
When you see her, ask her to show you the Star of the West. Then
come back here and tell us if it is the same stone as the one you
know as the Star of the East.”

“But, Poirot,” I cried, “what an extraordinary idea!”

“It is my idea, _mon ami_. Mr. Levitt, you will do this for me?”

“Certainly, Monsieur Poirot, if Lord Yardly has no objection.”

“Go by all means,” said Lord Yardly. “Though I don’t see what good
it will do.”

Mr. Levitt left the room, and we remained with Lord Yardly.

“And now, _milord_,” said Poirot, “I have another request to make.
I should like to speak to Lady Yardly alone.”

“Certainly,” said Lord Yardly. “I’ll go and see how she is.”

He left the room, and returned a few minutes later.

“My wife is in her boudoir. She will see you there.”

We followed him to a small, daintily-furnished room on the first
floor. Lady Yardly was lying on a sofa, her eyes closed. She
opened them as we entered.

“Monsieur Poirot,” she said, “this is a terrible business. Do you
think there is any hope of recovering the diamond?”

“I have every hope, madame,” said Poirot. “In fact, I am sure of
it.”

“You are?” she cried, sitting up. “How? Where is it?”

“It is in this house, madame.”

“In this house? But the Chinaman——”

“There was no Chinaman, madame.”

“But the piece of silk—the footprint—the note?”

“All very clever, madame, but they did not deceive Hercule Poirot!
No, it was a very pretty little comedy that was played here tonight.
And the actress—_was you_!”

“Poirot!” I cried, horrified.

Lady Yardly had turned a deathly white.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she faltered.

“I mean, madame, that there was no robbery. You took the diamond
yourself, and hid it. And then you made up this story of the
Chinaman to account for its disappearance.”

“But why—why should I do such a thing?”

“That is what I am going to tell you. You were being blackmailed,
madame. Three years ago, in California, you had a—shall we say, a
friendship?—with Mr. Gregory Rolf. You were—unwise enough to write
him some letters. And those letters, madame, he has been using
ever since to extort money from you.”

Lady Yardly buried her face in her hands.

“It’s true,” she sobbed. “Oh, God, it’s true! He’s a devil—a
perfect devil! He’s had thousands of pounds from me. And now—now
he’s demanding the diamond!”

“And so,” said Poirot, “you decided to ‘lose’ it. You would tell
your husband it was stolen, and then you would give it to Mr. Rolf
to satisfy his demands.”

“Yes,” she whispered. “That was my plan. I thought—I thought it
was the only way.”

“But it was a dangerous plan, madame. Very dangerous. If the
diamond had been found in your possession——”

“I know! I know! But what could I do? He threatened to show the
letters to my husband. And George—he would never forgive me! He
is so proud—so—so——” She broke off, sobbing.

“_Calmez-vous_, madame,” said Poirot kindly. “All is not lost.
Hercule Poirot is here! And now, if you will give me the diamond——”

“But I haven’t got it! I sent it to him—to Gregory Rolf—this
afternoon!”

“What?” Poirot’s face was a study. “You sent it to him? How?”

“By—by a messenger. A man he sent for it.”

“And the letters? Did he return the letters?”

“He said he would send them by post to-morrow.”

“_Sacré bleu_!” cried Poirot. “He has the diamond, and he still
has the letters! Madame, you have been—what you call—a ‘mug’!”

“I know! I know! But I was so frightened! He said if I didn’t
give him the diamond he would send the letters to George at once.”

“And now he has both! _Eh bien_, we must act—and act quickly!
Hastings, my friend, to the telephone! Ring up the _Magnificent_
Hotel. Ask for Mr. Gregory Rolf. If he is there, tell him—tell
him that Lady Yardly’s diamond has been stolen, and that the
police are on the track of the thief!”

I did as I was bid. In a few minutes I returned.

“Mr. Rolf is not at the hotel,” I reported. “He went out about an
hour ago.”

“_Tiens_!” said Poirot. “That is interesting. Where did he go?
Did they know?”

“No, they didn’t know.”

“_C’est dommage_! But wait—I have an idea! The man from Hoffberg’s!
He should be at the hotel by now. I will speak to him.”

He went to the telephone himself. After a few minutes he returned,
his face beaming.

“_Tout va bien_!” he cried. “Mr. Levitt has seen Miss Marvell.
And she has shown him the Star of the West. And, _mon ami_—it is
the same stone! The Star of the East and the Star of the West are
one and the same!”

“But how can that be?” I cried.

“It is very simple. There was only one diamond. Gregory Rolf had
it. He gave it to his wife, Mary Marvell, as a wedding present.
But he also—how shall I say?—gave it to Lady Yardly three years
ago in California!”

“You mean——”

“I mean that Mr. Gregory Rolf is a very clever man! He had the
diamond—it was a stolen one, no doubt—and he used it to further
his own ends. He gave it to Lady Yardly, and then, when he wanted
it back, he blackmailed her for it. But in the meantime, he had
already ‘given’ it to his wife! Of course, he couldn’t give it to
both of them at the same time. So he made Lady Yardly believe that
he still had her letters, and that he would return them if she
gave him the diamond. And all the time, the diamond was in the
possession of Mary Marvell!”

“But then—what was it that Lady Yardly ‘lost’ to-night?”

“A paste replica, _mon ami_! A very good one, no doubt, but still
a replica. Lady Yardly had it made some time ago, when she first
began to be blackmailed. She hoped to satisfy Mr. Rolf with it.
But he was too clever for her. He knew it was a fake. And so he
continued to blackmail her for the real stone—which he knew she
didn’t have!”

“Then why did he send for the fake to-night?”

“To get it out of the way! He knew that if the fake was found,
it would lead to questions—and the whole story might come out.
So he decided to have a ‘robbery’—a robbery that would point to
a Chinaman—and so divert suspicion from himself.”

“But the letters? What about the letters?”

“Ah, the letters! That is where Hercule Poirot comes in! I have
already telephoned to a friend of mine in the police. He will
pay a little visit to Mr. Gregory Rolf’s rooms at the _Magnificent_.
And I think—I think, _mon ami_—that he will find those letters!”

“And the diamond? The real diamond?”

“That, I am afraid, we cannot touch. It belongs to Mary Marvell.
She bought it—or rather, her husband ‘bought’ it for her—in good
faith. And since it was Gregory Rolf who ‘gave’ it to Lady Yardly
in the first place—well, it is a complicated legal question!”

“But Lady Yardly? What will happen to her?”

“Nothing, _mon ami_, nothing. Her husband need never know. The
‘robbery’ will be a mystery that is never solved. And Mr. Gregory
Rolf—well, I think Mr. Gregory Rolf will find it convenient to
return to America as soon as possible!”

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a marvel!”

“_Vraiment?_” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “And yet,
it was all so simple! The non-essentials, Hastings—always the
non-essentials! You saw a Chinaman—I saw a man who wanted a
diamond! You saw a romance—I saw a blackmailing scheme! It is
all a question of the ‘little grey cells,’ _mon ami_—the little
grey cells!”

Suddenly she appeared, a vision of beauty. Around her neck was
the heavy gold chain that supported the large diamond. It must have
been a stone of extraordinary brilliance. Even from across the
room its fire was almost blinding.

“Well, George,” she said, almost defiantly. “Here I am! Behold
the victim of the sacrifice!”

Her husband’s face went a shade redder.

“I only wish it hadn’t to be done,” he said shortly.

Lady Yardly turned to me.

“What do you think of our family treasure, Captain Hastings?”

She came across the room, and I stood up to examine the stone
more closely. It was truly a magnificent diamond, though the
setting, as she had said, was clumsy and Victorian in the extreme.

At that moment the door was thrown open and the butler announced
gravely:

“Mr. John Hoffberg, my lord.”

A small, dark man, with a very Jewish type of face, came into the
room. He bowed low to Lord and Lady Yardly.

“I have come down at the earliest possible moment, my lord,” he
explained. “It is a matter of hours if the deal is to go through.”

“Quite so,” said Lord Yardly. “Well, here is the stone. You would
like to examine it at once, I presume?”

“If your ladyship would permit?” said the diamond merchant.

Lady Yardly unclasped the necklace and handed it to him. He took
it to the light. I saw his eyes sparkle with professional interest.
Then a look of the most intense surprise crossed his face.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he ejaculated.

“What is it?” cried Lord Yardly.

Mr. Hoffberg looked from one to the other of us.

“This stone,” he said, in a voice that shook with excitement,
“it—it is a paste!”

“A paste!” Lord Yardly’s voice was a roar of anger. “What do you
mean, man? It’s been in our family for generations!”

“I cannot help that, my lord. The stone in this necklace is a
clever imitation—nothing more.”

“Maude!” Lord Yardly turned to his wife. “What does this mean?”

Lady Yardly had gone deathly pale. She swayed as she stood.

“I—I don’t know,” she gasped. “It—it must have been stolen.”

“Stolen!” shouted her husband. “When? How?”

“I don’t know,” she repeated. “I haven’t worn it for months. Not
since—not since—oh, I don’t know!”

“It was all right when I saw it last,” said Lord Yardly. “That
was just before we went to the States.”

Poirot stepped forward.

“_Pardon_,” he said, “but if I might be permitted to examine the
necklace for a moment?”

Mr. Hoffberg handed it to him. Poirot looked at it closely for a
minute or two, then he handed it back.

“Mr. Hoffberg is right,” he said quietly. “This is a paste
imitation.”

“But when was the real stone taken?” cried Lord Yardly.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“_Madame_,” he said, “I must ask you to be very frank with me.
When did you last wear this necklace?”

“I—I think it was at a dinner-party at the end of last season.”

“And since then?”

“It has been in my jewel-case.”

“And where do you keep your jewel-case?”

“In my bedroom.”

“Has it ever been unlocked?”

“Not to my knowledge.”

“Then the stone must have been taken some time ago. But by whom?”

Lord Yardly broke in.

“By some of those rascally servants, I’ll bound! I’ll have the
police in at once. I’ll have every one of them searched!”

“One moment, _milord_,” said Poirot. “Let us not be precipitate.
There are other possibilities. For instance, the letters?”

“The letters! Of course! The Chinese god business!”

“Exactly. If the stone has been stolen by the agents of this
mysterious Chinese society, they would naturally replace it with
a paste imitation so that the loss should not be immediately
discovered.”

“By Jove, you’re right!” cried Lord Yardly. “But how did they get
at it?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I intend to find out.”

He turned to the butler, who was still standing by the door.

“Tell me,” he said, “has any stranger been to the house lately?”

“No one, sir, except the usual tradesmen.”

“No one else? No—Chinaman, for instance?”

The butler started.

“Well, now you mention it, sir, there _was_ a Chinaman. He came to
the back door yesterday, hawking silk. I sent him about his
business pretty sharp, I can tell you.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes flashed. “A Chinaman! This is very interesting.”

He turned to Lord Yardly.

“_Milord_,” he said, “I think we have the clue we need. If you
will leave this matter in my hands, I have every hope of
recovering your diamond for you.”

“Of course, Monsieur Poirot, of course! We are entirely in your
hands.”

“_Bien!_ Then, if I might suggest it, I think we should all go to
dinner. We can discuss the matter further afterwards.”

Dinner was a somewhat silent meal. Lord Yardly was obviously
distressed, and Lady Yardly was pale and quiet. Only Poirot seemed
unaffected by the tragedy. He rattled on in his usual way,
telling stories of his past triumphs, and occasionally relapsing
into a brown study.

After dinner, he requested a private interview with Lady Yardly.
They were closeted together for some time. When they emerged,
Lady Yardly looked as though she had been crying, but Poirot
was as imperturbable as ever.

“And now, _mon ami_,” he said to me, “we must return to London.
There is much to be done.”

“But the diamond!” I cried. “Aren’t you going to stay and
investigate?”

“I have investigated,” said Poirot. “And now I must act. Come!”

As we drove back to London, I tried to get some information from
him, but he was unusually uncommunicative.

“Wait, Hastings, wait!” was all he would say. “The little grey
cells, they must work in silence.”

The next morning, we were sitting at breakfast when the door
opened and Miss Mary Marvell was announced. She was looking pale
and agitated.

“Monsieur Poirot!” she cried. “It has happened! The diamond is
gone!”

“Gone?” I ejaculated. “When? How?”

“Last night. I was at the theatre, and when I came back to the
hotel, I went to my jewel-case to put away some things, and—and
the diamond wasn’t there!”

“And the letters?” asked Poirot. “Did you get another one?”

“Yes. This morning. It was waiting for me when I woke up.”

She handed him a sheet of paper. On it was printed:

“The god has his own. The eyes are reunited.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “This is very interesting. And your
husband, what does he say?”

“He’s distracted! He’s gone off to Scotland Yard now.”

“I see. And you, madame, what do you want me to do?”

“I want you to find my diamond! Oh, Monsieur Poirot, you must!”

“I will do my best, madame. And now, if you will excuse me, I
have a call to make.”

He hurried out of the room, leaving me to console the distracted
actress. It was nearly two hours before he returned. He was
looking very pleased with himself.

“Well?” I asked. “Any news?”

“The best of news, Hastings. I have recovered the diamond.”

“Recovered it! But how? Where?”

“Wait a moment.” He turned to Mary Marvell. “Madame, if you will
come with me, I will restore your jewel to you.”

We drove to a small house in a quiet street. Poirot led the way
upstairs and into a room where a man was sitting at a table.
It was Mr. Gregory Rolf.

He looked up as we entered, and his face went white.

“What—what is the meaning of this?” he stammered.

“The meaning is very simple, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot. “I have come
for the Western Star.”

“I—I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“_Allons!_” said Poirot. “It is no use. I know everything. I know
that you stole the diamond from your wife’s jewel-case last night,
and I know why you did it.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Rolf.

“Is it? Then perhaps you can explain why you were seen leaving
the hotel with a small package at eleven o’clock last night,
and why you came straight to this house—the house of your
former wife!”

A woman had come into the room—a woman whom I recognized as
the one I had seen shadowing Mary Marvell on the day she first
came to Poirot’s rooms.

“It’s no use, Greg,” she said. “The game’s up.”

She turned to Poirot.

“He did it for me,” she said. “He wanted to give me enough
money to go away and start a new life. He’s been paying me
blackmail for years, ever since he married that—that woman.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And the Chinese letters? They were your
idea, I suppose?”

“Yes. I thought it would be a good way to cover up the theft.
I knew about the Yardly diamond, and I thought if I could
make it look like a Chinese plot, no one would suspect Greg.”

“And the Chinaman who left the letters?”

“That was me—in disguise.”

Poirot nodded.

“It was a clever plan,” he said. “But you forgot one thing—the
little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

He turned to Mary Marvell.

“Here is your diamond, madame,” he said, handing her a small
package.

She took it with a cry of joy.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“By being more careful in future, madame. And by not being so—
how shall I say?—so anxious to outshine your rivals.”

As we left the house, I turned to Poirot.

“But what about the Yardly diamond?” I asked. “Was that stolen
too?”

“No, Hastings. That was a different matter altogether.”

“But it was a paste imitation!”

“Exactly. And do you know why? Because Lady Yardly had sold
the real stone years ago!”

“Sold it! But to whom?”

“To Gregory Rolf! You see, Hastings, Lady Yardly had also been
a victim of Mr. Rolf’s—charms. He had some letters of hers—
very indiscreet letters—and he blackmailed her into giving
him the diamond. He then had it cut into two stones. One he
kept, and the other he gave to his new wife as a wedding
present!”

“But the Chinese letters Lady Yardly received?”

“She wrote them herself! She had heard about the letters
Miss Marvell was receiving, and she saw a chance to get her
diamond back—or at least to prevent her husband from selling
the imitation, which would have led to the discovery of her
secret. She hoped that by pretending her diamond had also been
stolen by the Chinese, no one would ever know the truth.”

“I see,” I said. “It was all very complicated.”

“Not to the little grey cells, Hastings! Not to the little
grey cells!”

And with a flourish of his cane, Poirot led the way back to
our rooms.

The door opened, and Lady Yardly entered. She was in evening dress, and around her neck was a heavy collar of diamonds, in the centre of which was a large stone of extraordinary fire and brilliance. Lord Yardly stepped forward, his eyes alight with a mixture of pride and greed. “By Jove, Maude,” he muttered, “it is a beauty.” Before she could respond, the butler reappeared at the door. “A Mr. de Pass, from Messrs. Hoffberg, has arrived, my lord. He says his business is most urgent.” Lord Yardly glanced at Poirot, who nodded slightly. “Show him into the library, Mullings. I’ll be there in a moment.” Lady Yardly’s hand went instinctively to her throat, her face paling. “Must it be tonight, George?” she asked softly, but her husband, occupied with the prospect of his debts being cleared, did not seem to hear her as he followed the butler from the room.

The door opened at last, and Lady Yardly swept into the room. She was transformed. Gone was the anxious mother; in her place stood a grande dame of the old school, her neck encircled by a glittering cascade of diamonds. In the centre, pulsing with a cold, blue light, was the Star of the East. Lord Yardly stepped forward, his eyes gleaming with a mixture of pride and calculation. “Magnificent, Maude, magnificent!” he exclaimed. “The Hoffberg fellow should be here any minute now to—” He was interrupted by a sudden, sharp ring at the front door bell which echoed through the silent house. We all stood immobile, caught in a tableau of expectation, as the heavy footsteps of the butler sounded in the hall, followed by a muffled colloquy.

Suddenly there was a low rustle, and Lady Yardly appeared framed
in the doorway, a radiant figure in a long white shimmering dress.
Round the column of her neck was a rivulet of fire. She stood there
with one hand just touching the necklace.

“Behold the sacrifice,” she said gaily. Her ill-humour seemed to
have vanished. “Wait while I turn the big light on and you shall
feast your eyes on the ugliest necklace in England.”

There was the sound of a struggle in the hall, a heavy fall, and
then the door was flung open once more. Lady Yardly was lying
insensible across the threshold, her white neck bare, the necklace
gone!

Poirot was the first to reach her.

“Is she hurt?” I asked.

“She has fainted,” he replied. “Stay here, Hastings. _Milord_, the
hall! Quick!”

Lord Yardly rushed out. I remained with the unconscious woman,
then she stirred and opened her eyes.

“Where is he?” she gasped. “The Chinaman—the man with the yellow
face!”

She looked around the room, then sank back as she realized that
her treasure was gone.

“The diamond!” she moaned. “It’s gone! The Star of the East!”

I helped her to a sofa. At that moment the lights went on again.
The butler was in the doorway. Behind him came Lord Yardly. He
was very pale.

“Not a sign of him,” he said. “The window in the little breakfast-room
was open. The scoundrel must have got out that way. The fellow
from Hoffberg’s has just arrived. He’s in the hall now. He met
nobody.”

Poirot’s face was very grave.

“This is a very serious business, _milord_.”

Lady Yardly sat up, her eyes flashing.

“I told you how it would be, George! I knew those letters meant
something!”

The nobleman’s face was a study in misery.

“I’m sorry, Maude. I suppose I ought to have believed you. But
it seemed so incredible.”

Poirot stepped forward.

“I should like to see this gentleman from Hoffberg’s,” he said.

The man was a tall, dark, rather saturnine-looking person, with
thick black hair. He appeared very much distressed.

“It is a most unfortunate thing,” he said. “I was to have seen the
diamond and report on its value. I arrived at the door only a few
minutes ago. As I came in I heard a scream, and then there was a
great deal of confusion. I’m afraid I have come at a most
unfortunate moment.”

“_Très bien_,” said Poirot. “You can go, monsieur. There is no
business for you to-night.”

The man bowed and left.

“The police must be informed at once,” said Lord Yardly. “I’ll go
and telephone.”

“One moment,” said Poirot. “_Attendez_ a little.”

Lord Yardly paused.

“Why?”

“There are one or two things I should like to ask Lady Yardly
first.”

The lady looked at him with surprise.

“You saw the man, madame?”

“Distinctly. He was a Chinaman, with a long pigtail, and he wore
a blue silk robe.”

“Where did he come from?”

“He must have been hiding behind the curtains. As I went to turn
on the light he sprang upon me. I think he must have used some
kind of drug, for I felt my senses leaving me.”

“And then?”

“Then he must have snatched the necklace from my neck and escaped.
The last thing I remember was his horrible yellow face.”

“One thing more, Lady Yardly. You had the necklace on when you
came into the room?”

“Yes, I had. You all saw it.”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “I saw it myself. Now, _milord_,
telephone to the police.”

While Lord Yardly was at the telephone, Poirot walked over to the
window and looked out. Then he came back and stood in the middle
of the room. His face was very thoughtful.

“It is a very strange case,” he said to me. “Very strange
indeed.”

“What is your theory?” I asked.

“I have no theory—yet. But I have certain ideas.”

The police arrived shortly, and their investigations were
thorough. But they led to nothing. No trace of the thief could be
found. The open window in the breakfast-room seemed the most
likely means of egress, but the ground outside was hard, and there
were no footprints.

The next morning Poirot and I returned to London. On the way he
was very silent. When we reached our rooms he sat for a long time
in his favorite chair, his eyes closed. At last he spoke.

“Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of Lady Yardly?”

“She’s a very beautiful woman,” I said. “And a very brave one.”

“_Vraiment?_ And you think she was telling the truth?”

“Of course! Why should she lie?”

“Ah, why indeed? That is the question. And yet—there were certain
things. For instance, did you notice the perfume in the room when
she fainted?”

“No, I can’t say I did.”

“It was very faint—but it was there. The perfume of the East.
Joss-sticks, Hastings! Just as in the letters she received.”

“But that only proves her story!”

“Or else it proves that she wished to _confirm_ her story. Why
should a Chinaman, who is a common thief, carry about with him
scented sticks?”

“To create an atmosphere, I suppose.”

“_Mon Dieu!_ you are of a romanticism! No, Hastings, there is
something here that I do not understand. And I must understand
it.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will pay a little visit to Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“What for?”

“To ask him a few questions. He was in California three years ago,
was he not? At the same time as Lady Yardly.”

“You think he may know something?”

“It is possible. At any rate, it is worth while to find out.”

He was away for some hours. When he returned his face was very
grave.

“Well?” I asked. “Did you see him?”

“I saw him. And I have learned several things. For one thing, he
denies ever having met Lady Yardly in California.”

“But Miss Marvell said he did!”

“Precisely. That is one of the things I find so interesting.
Someone is not telling the truth. And then there is the matter of
the letters. Miss Marvell’s letters were left by hand—by a
Chinaman. Lady Yardly’s came by post. Why the difference?”

“Perhaps the thief thought it safer.”

“Perhaps. But there is another possibility. Suppose there were no
letters?”

“What do you mean?”

“Suppose Lady Yardly invented the letters to provide a motive for
the theft?”

“But why should she want to steal her own diamond?”

“Ah, that is what I must find out. And I think I have a way.”

He would say no more, and for the next few days he was very busy.
He was out a great deal, and when he was at home he was
continually receiving and sending telegrams.

On Friday morning, the day Miss Marvell was due at Yardly Chase,
he came into the room with a look of triumph on his face.

“_Enfin!_” he cried. “I have it! The truth at last!”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“Wait, Hastings, wait. All will be revealed in due time. But first,
we must go to Yardly Chase.”

“To-day?”

“Yes. I have already telegraphed to Lord Yardly. We must be there
when Miss Marvell arrives.”

When we reached the Chase, we found the whole party assembled in
the hall. Lord and Lady Yardly, Miss Marvell and Gregory Rolf.
They all looked at us with surprise.

“Monsieur Poirot!” cried Lord Yardly. “What is the meaning of
this?”

“It means, _milord_,” said Poirot, “that I have come to restore to
you your diamond.”

There was a gasp of astonishment from everyone.

“You have found it?” cried Lady Yardly.

“I have found it,” said Poirot. He turned to Mary Marvell.
“Madame, I have to ask you a question. You have your diamond with
you?”

“Of course,” said the actress. She drew it from her bosom. “Here
it is.”

Poirot took it from her and looked at it closely. Then he turned to
Lord Yardly.

“And you, _milord_, have you the Star of the East?”

“But it was stolen!” cried the nobleman.

“Was it?” said Poirot. He reached into his pocket and drew out a
jewel. “Is this it?”

Lord Yardly stared at it in amazement.

“Yes! That is it! But how——”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “This stone was never stolen. It
was sent to Hoffberg’s for sale—by Lady Yardly!”

A dead silence followed his words. Lady Yardly had turned deathly
pale.

“It’s a lie!” she gasped.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I have the proof. Mr. Hoffberg has
identified you as the person who brought the stone to him. You
see, madame, you made one mistake. You thought that by
faking a theft you could sell the diamond and yet keep the money
for yourself. But you forgot that Mr. Hoffberg would recognize
you.”

Lady Yardly sank into a chair, her face hidden in her hands.

“It’s true,” she sobbed. “I had to do it. I was so much in debt—I
didn’t know which way to turn. And George was so determined to
sell it. I thought if I could sell it first, I could pay my debts
and he would never know.”

“But the Chinaman?” I asked. “The scream? The lights going out?”

“All a comedy, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “Lady Yardly arranged it
all. She turned out the lights herself, she screamed, she dropped
on the floor. It was very well done—very well done indeed. But she
forgot the perfume. That was the clue that led me to the truth.”

Lord Yardly went over to his wife and put his hand on her shoulder.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said gently. “I understand. We’ll get
through this somehow.”

He turned to Poirot.

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. You have saved us from a great deal
of trouble.”

“It is nothing,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse us, I
think we should be going.”

As we drove away, I looked at my friend with admiration.

“Poirot,” I said, “you are truly marvellous. How did you know?”

“It was the little grey cells, Hastings. The little grey cells.
They never fail.”

He sat back in the carriage and closed his eyes with a smile of
satisfaction.

The case was over. The mystery of the Western Star was solved.

We rushed for the door, which I had just time to note was
strangely heavy, as though something was being held against it.

In a minute we were into the hall, and the lights were turned on
there. But what a scene! Lady Yardly lay in a heap by the door,
her hands to her throat, her neck bare of all but her dress. The
necklace was gone.

“The window!” cried Poirot. “Is it not so?”

Lord Yardly rushed to it, and he and Poirot stood for a moment
leaning out.

“The flower-bed is trampled,” said Poirot. “But the thief has gone.”

I was at Lady Yardly’s side, she was slowly recovering.

“A Chinaman,” she gasped. “He—he sprang out from behind me—I
suppose as I went to turn the light on—and he snatched the
necklace. I—I thought he was going to kill me.”

“_Nom d’un nom!_” Poirot was at the other side of her. “And the
door—why was it so hard to open?”

“It was not locked,” she said, still shaking from the shock. “I
think he must have been leaning against it—that is why it felt so
heavy.”

“I’ll tell the police,” said Lord Yardly. “Wait, I’ll call them up.”

He rushed away.

Lady Yardly was still in a very nervous state.

“Oh, it’s horrible!” she moaned. “And Gregory Rolf will think—oh,
what _will_ he think?”

“Why Gregory Rolf?” asked Poirot.

“Because—oh, I don’t know why I said that. I was thinking of Miss
Marvell, I suppose.”

She rose to her feet, still trembling.

“Let me go to my room. I—I can’t stay here.”

The maid was summoned, and she was helped upstairs.

Poirot and I remained in the hall.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, his eyes very bright. “What do you think
of it?”

I was fairly bubbled with excitement.

“A Chinaman!” I cried. “The warnings! Everything! And Lord Yardly’s
bad luck! It is incredible, Poirot, but it has happened!”

“_Oui_,” said Poirot, “it has happened. It is very interesting.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said: “Come, we will go and
interview the butler.”

The butler was in a state of some agitation. He had heard the
scream, but had been unable to reach the scene of the crime
immediately, as the door into the dining-room had been locked on
the other side.

“You see,” said Poirot, “how well it was planned? The Chinaman,
he knew his way about the house. He knew where the switches were.
He knew which doors to lock.”

“Yes,” I agreed. “He must have been watching the house for some
time.”

Lord Yardly returned.

“The police will be here in a few minutes. I’ve told them everything.
It’s a most extraordinary business. I can’t understand it.”

“Neither can I,” said Poirot. “It is the most extraordinary
business I have ever come across. But I have hope. I have great
hope.”

“You think you can get the necklace back?”

“I have hope,” repeated Poirot.

“But what do you think? What is your theory?”

Poirot shook his head.

“Not yet, _milord_, not yet. Wait till I have seen the police.”

But the police could tell us nothing. They had found the flower-bed
trampled, but the marks were too confused to be of any use. They
had questioned the servants, but no one had seen or heard anything
unusual.

It was a late hour when we at last went to bed.

Poirot was still very silent. He would answer none of my questions,
but sat for a long time by the fire, his head on one side, as though
he were listening.

Early the next morning he was up and out. When he returned he was
in a state of great excitement.

“I have it, Hastings! I have it!”

“The necklace?”

“No, not yet. But I know who has it.”

“Who? For heaven’s sake, who?”

“Wait a little. I have still some work to do. But I will tell you
this—it is not a Chinaman!”

“Then who is it?”

“A very clever person, Hastings. A very clever person indeed. But
not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

I was more mystified than ever.

“But the scream? Lady Yardly’s story?”

“Ah! Lady Yardly’s story! That is the most interesting part of the
whole business. But come, we must go to London. I have an
appointment there.”

“With whom?”

“With Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“Gregory Rolf? But what has he to do with it?”

“More than you think, Hastings. Much more.”

I followed him, still more bewildered.

We arrived in London about midday. Poirot drove straight to the
Hotel Magnificent.

“Is Mr. Rolf in?” he asked at the desk.

“Yes, sir. He’s in his rooms.”

We were shown up. Gregory Rolf was alone. He looked surprised to
see us.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, what can I do for you? Any news of the
diamond?”

“Yes, Mr. Rolf. I have come to tell you that the Star of the East
has been stolen.”

Rolf started.

“Stolen? When? How?”

Poirot told him the story. Rolf listened with the greatest interest.

“And you have no idea who did it?”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “I know exactly who did it.”

Rolf looked at him keenly.

“And who was it?”

“It was you, Mr. Rolf!”

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then Rolf laughed.

“Me? You’re crazy, Monsieur Poirot! Why should I steal the
diamond? I don’t need the money.”

“No,” said Poirot, “you don’t need the money. But you wanted the
diamond. You wanted both diamonds!”

“Both diamonds? What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that there are not two diamonds. There is
only one!”

“One diamond?” I cried. “But I saw them both!”

“No, Hastings, you saw the same diamond twice. Or rather, you saw
one diamond, and you saw a very clever imitation of it.”

“But which was which?”

“The Star of the West was the real diamond. The Star of the East
was the imitation.”

“But Lady Yardly’s diamond was a family heirloom!”

“Was it, Hastings? Was it? That is what I began to doubt. And when
I heard that Lady Yardly had been in California three years ago,
and that she had known Gregory Rolf there—then I began to see light.”

“I don’t understand,” I said.

“It is very simple. Lady Yardly was in debt—very much in debt. She
had to have money. So she sold the Star of the East to Gregory
Rolf. But she couldn't let her husband know. So she had an
imitation made, and she wore that. But Gregory Rolf is a clever
man. He wanted the other diamond too—the Star of the West. So he
planned this little comedy. He sent the letters to his wife, and
he sent them to Lady Yardly. He knew that Lady Yardly would be
frightened, and that she would come to me. He wanted to make sure
that the story of the Chinese god was well known. Then, when the
time was ripe, he would ‘steal’ the diamond from Lady Yardly—or
rather, she would ‘steal’ it for him!”

“She stole it herself?” I gasped.

“Of course. It was she who turned out the lights. It was she who
screamed. It was she who hid the diamond—where, I do not yet know,
but I have no doubt I shall find it. She was being blackmailed,
you see. Gregory Rolf had the letters she had written to him in
California. He used them to force her to help him. He wanted the
Star of the West, and he knew that if the Star of the East were
stolen, Mary Marvell would be too frightened to keep her diamond.
She would give it to him for safe keeping—and then it would
‘disappear’ too! It was a very clever plan.”

Rolf was pale now, his eyes narrowed.

“You have no proof,” he said hoarsely.

“Haven’t I?” said Poirot. “We shall see. Lady Yardly is on her way
to London now. I think that when she knows that I know the truth,
she will be only too glad to tell it. She is a good woman at heart,
Mr. Rolf, and she loves her children. She will not want them to be
the children of a thief.”

Rolf stood for a moment, his face working. Then, with a sudden
movement, he thrust his hand into his pocket, drew out a small
package, and flung it on the table.

“There’s your diamond!” he snarled. “Take it and be damned to you!
But you’ll never prove anything against me.”

He strode out of the room, slamming the door behind him.

Poirot picked up the package and opened it. Inside was the Star of
the East—or rather, the Star of the West, for as Poirot had said,
they were one and the same.

“But Poirot,” I said, “how did you know?”

“It was the letters, Hastings. The letters that Lady Yardly said
smelt of joss-stick. Now, joss-stick is a very common thing in
California, but it is not so common in England. And then there was
the fact that the letters to Lady Yardly came by post, while those
to Miss Marvell were left by hand. Why? Because Gregory Rolf was
in London, and could easily leave the letters for his wife. But he
couldn’t go down to Yardly Chase to leave them for Lady Yardly,
so he had to post them. It was a small point, but a significant
one.”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“She will be all right, Hastings. She has her diamond back—for it
is her diamond, after all. And Gregory Rolf will not trouble her
again. He has too much to lose.”

“And Miss Marvell?”

“She will have to find another wedding present,” said Poirot with
a smile. “But I think she will be more careful in future. After
all, as I have always told you, it is the little things that
matter. The little things—and the use of the little grey cells!”

I sighed.

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I know it,” said Poirot simply. “It is my misfortune!”

He rushed across the dark room, and struggled with the door. To
no purpose—it was locked. We were all three trapped in the great
drawing-room.

“Wait!” cried Poirot. “I will open it.”

His hands were busy about the lock. In a second it flew open, and
we rushed into the hall.

Lady Yardly lay there unconscious.

Her husband was the first to reach her.

“Maude, Maude—my dear, what was it?”

The girl’s eyes slowly opened. Her hand went to her neck.

“Gone!” she gasped. “He’s got it!”

“The necklace? The diamond?”

“The diamond!” she groaned. “A man—a Chinaman—jumped out from the
shadows. I never saw him, but I felt his breath on my face. Then
he took the diamond from my neck, and disappeared.”

The butler was already at her side, followed by a footman. Lord
Yardly turned to them.

“Tell the men to search the grounds. At once! Don’t lose a second.
He can’t have gone far.”

The servants hurried away. Lady Yardly had recovered herself.

“No, no, George, let them go. I’m quite all right now. It was only
the shock.”

Suddenly Poirot leaned forward, and picked up a scrap of paper from
the floor.

“What is it?” I asked.

“The usual thing, _mon ami_. The diamond has returned to the god.”

Lord Yardly snatched the paper from his hand. It was exactly like
the letters I had seen.

“This is getting beyond a joke,” he growled. “The police must have
it at once.”

Poirot shook his head.

“Believe me, _milord_, the police will be of no use. Let us think.”

“But the diamond, man—the diamond!”

“Precisely. Let us think how to get it back. To do that we must
know where it is. To know where it is, we must use our little grey
cells. Is it not so, Hastings?”

“Yes, yes—of course. But really, Poirot——”

“You are right, it is a very serious matter. Madame, I pray of
you, go to your room and rest. It is a shock, _oui_, a great shock.
But all may yet be well. Lord Yardly, will you be so kind as to
accompany me to the hall? I should like to see exactly where the
accident happened.”

“Certainly.” Lord Yardly led the way.

Lady Yardly’s maid appeared at the head of the stairs, and Poirot
motioned to her to take her mistress to her room. We three followed
Lord Yardly.

“It was just here,” he explained, “where the rug is ruffled. Maude
was just going to turn on the lights when she was attacked.”

Poirot nodded, his eyes fixed on the floor.

“I see. And the Chinaman? Where did he come from?”

“I don’t know. There are so many hiding-places in this old house.
He might have been behind the curtains of the long gallery, or in
the little priest’s hole at the end of it.”

Poirot remained for a few moments in deep thought. Then he looked
up at Lord Yardly.

“One thing is certain, _milord_. Whoever took that diamond is still
in this house.”

“You think so? But the doors were all open.”

“_C’est possible_. But I have my reasons. Now, if you will excuse
me, I should like to have a few words with Lady Yardly.”

“She’s in no state for it, I’m afraid.”

“Only a few moments. It is essential.”

Lord Yardly gave way, and Poirot went upstairs. He was away about
ten minutes. When he returned his face was grave.

“Well?” I asked.

“Lady Yardly is naturally very much upset. But she has told me
what she could. It was as she said. A man’s hand, very yellow,
reached out from the darkness, and snatched the diamond from her
neck. She saw nothing else.”

“A Chinaman!” I cried. “The letters were right, then.”

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “And yet——”

He did not finish his sentence. For the next hour he was busy
examining the hall and the gallery. Then he announced his
intention of going for a stroll in the grounds. I went with him.

“What do you think of it all, Poirot?” I asked.

“What do you think of it, Hastings?”

“It seems to me perfectly clear. The Chinese gang have been as
good as their word. They’ve got the diamond.”

“And what about the other one—the Western Star?”

“I suppose they’ll get that too, if Miss Marvell isn’t careful.”

“_C’est possible_,” said Poirot. “But why should they want both?”

“The legend, of course. ‘The two diamonds which are the left and
right eye of the god shall return.’ It’s all very romantic,
Poirot.”

“_Romantique_—_oui_,” said Poirot. “But I do not like romance. I
prefer facts. And there are several facts in this case which are
not at all romantic.”

“Such as?”

“The fact that Lady Yardly’s diamond was not insured, for one.”

“But Lord Yardly said——”

“Lord Yardly said nothing about insurance. It was Miss Marvell’s
diamond that was insured for fifty thousand pounds. Lady Yardly’s
stone was an heirloom, and I doubt if it was even valued.”

“What does that matter?”

“It matters a great deal, _mon ami_. If you were going to steal a
diamond, would you choose one that was insured or one that was
not?”

“I don’t see that it makes any difference.”

“On the contrary, it makes all the difference in the world. If a
thing is insured, the insurance company will make a very thorough
investigation. If it is not, the police may be less energetic.”

“But the Chinese gang wouldn’t care about that.”

“Precisely. The Chinese gang would not care. But someone else
might.”

I stared at him. “What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that this case is not so simple as it looks.
There are several possibilities.”

“For instance?”

“Well, for instance, suppose there is no Chinese gang at all?”

“But the Chinaman—Lady Yardly saw him!”

“Lady Yardly saw a yellow hand. That is not quite the same thing.”

“But the letters?”

“Anyone can print letters on cheap paper.”

“You mean it’s a hoax, after all?”

“No, I do not think it is a hoax. The diamond has been stolen.
That is a very solid fact.”

“Then who stole it?”

“That is what we have to find out. There are four people who might
have done it.”

“Four? Who are they?”

“Mary Marvell, Gregory Rolf, Lady Yardly, and Lord Yardly.”

I gasped. “But Poirot, that’s impossible! Why should any of them
steal their own diamond?”

“Ah! Why indeed? That is the question. But consider the facts.
Lord Yardly is in desperate need of money. He wants to sell the
diamond, but his wife is against it. If the diamond is stolen,
and he can’t find the thief, he might be able to claim the
insurance—if there were any. But we have seen that there is not.
So that theory falls to the ground.”

“Then Lady Yardly?”

“Lady Yardly does not want the diamond sold. If it is stolen, it
cannot be sold. That is a possible motive.”

“But she was the one who was attacked!”

“So she says. But we did not see the attack. We only heard the
scream, and found her on the floor.”

“You mean she might have staged the whole thing herself?”

“It is a possibility. Then there is Miss Marvell. She wants to be
the only one to possess a ‘Star.’ If Lady Yardly’s diamond
disappears, hers becomes unique.”

“But she wasn’t even here!”

“She might have an accomplice. And finally, there is Mr. Gregory
Rolf. He has been out West, he knew Lady Yardly three years ago.
What if he has some hold over her? What if he is blackmailing
her?”

“But why should he steal the diamond?”

“Perhaps he didn’t steal it. Perhaps she gave it to him.”

“Gave it to him? Why?”

“To pay the blackmailer. It is a common enough story.”

“But the Chinaman?”

“A very convenient disguise. A little yellow paint on the hand,
and the trick is done.”

“Poirot, you are extraordinary! But which of them do you think it
is?”

“I do not think yet, Hastings. I observe. I collect facts. When
I have enough facts, then I think.”

We walked on in silence for a few minutes. Then Poirot stopped.

“One thing more, Hastings. Did you notice the perfume on Lady
Yardly’s letters?”

“Yes, she said it was like joss-stick.”

“Exactly. And did you notice any perfume in the hall just after
the diamond was stolen?”

I thought for a moment. “No, I can’t say I did.”

“I did,” said Poirot. “It was very faint, but it was there. And
it was not the smell of joss-stick.”

“What was it, then?”

“It was the perfume that Miss Mary Marvell uses. I noticed it when
she was in my rooms this morning.”

I whistled. “Then you think it was Mary Marvell?”

“I think nothing yet. But it is an interesting fact, is it not?”

We returned to the house. Lord Yardly was in the library, looking
very haggard and miserable.

“Any news?” he asked.

“None, _milord_,” said Poirot. “I have been looking at the
grounds, but it is too dark to see anything. To-morrow morning I
shall start my investigation in earnest.”

“The police will be here then,” said Lord Yardly. “I’ve just
telephoned them.”

“That is as it should be,” said Poirot. “In the meantime, I
suggest we all go to bed. We can do no more tonight.”

I must confess I did not sleep very well. The events of the evening
kept racing through my brain. Was it really a Chinese gang, or was
one of the four people Poirot had mentioned responsible? And what
about the perfume?

The next morning was bright and sunny. Poirot was up early, and
when I came down to breakfast I found him already at work. He was
examining the hall floor with a magnifying glass.

“Find anything?” I asked.

“A few grains of dust, Hastings. Very interesting dust.”

“Dust? What’s interesting about dust?”

“Everything, _mon ami_. To the trained eye, dust is as good as a
signature. But here is the inspector from the police.”

A tall, soldierly-looking man was being shown into the hall. He
introduced himself as Inspector Japp of Scotland Yard.

“I’ve heard of you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “Glad to have your
help on this case. It seems a bit of a mystery.”

“It is a very pretty little problem, Inspector,” said Poirot.
“But I think I can help you. First, let us see the room where
Lady Yardly was attacked.”

They went into the drawing-room, and Poirot explained the
circumstances of the theft. Japp listened attentively, making
notes in a little book.

“A Chinaman, eh?” he said. “We’ve had reports of a Chinese gang
operating in this area. It fits in.”

“Does it?” said Poirot. “I wonder.”

He spent the morning with the inspector, going over the house and
grounds. I followed them, but I couldn’t see that they were
making much progress. Lady Yardly remained in her room, and Lord
Yardly wandered about the house like a ghost.

At lunch time, a telegram arrived for Poirot. He read it, and a
smile spread over his face.

“_Bon!_” he said. “Now we shall see.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“A little information I was waiting for, Hastings. And now, I
think it is time we had a little talk with the members of this
household.”

He asked Lord Yardly to assemble everyone in the drawing-room.
Besides Lord and Lady Yardly, there were the butler and the
maid. Japp and I were also present.

Poirot stood in the centre of the room, looking very small but
intensely serious.

“_Mesdames et messieurs_,” he began. “I have been investigating
the theft of the Star of the East. It is a very interesting case,
very interesting indeed. At first it seemed like a simple matter
of a Chinese gang trying to recover a sacred jewel. But as I
looked deeper, I found that things were not what they seemed.”

He paused, and looked round the room.

“There were several things that puzzled me. First, why should the
thief choose to steal the Star of the East, which was not
insured, when the Western Star, which was insured for fifty
thousand pounds, was so much more attractive? Second, why was
there a smell of Miss Marvell’s perfume in the hall just after the
theft? And third, why did Lady Yardly say she saw a yellow hand,
when the letters she received had been sent by post and not left
by hand like Miss Marvell’s?”

Lady Yardly went very pale. Lord Yardly stared at Poirot in
amazement.

“What are you suggesting, Monsieur Poirot?” he asked.

“I am suggesting, _milord_, that there never was a Chinaman. The
whole story of the god’s eyes and the Chinese gang was a clever
invention.”

“But the letters?” cried Lady Yardly. “I received them!”

“_Oui_, madame, you received them. But you wrote them yourself!”

There was a gasp of astonishment. Lady Yardly started to protest,
but Poirot silenced her with a gesture.

“Wait, madame. Let me finish. You were being blackmailed. Three
years ago, in California, you were a little indiscreet. You fell
in love with a handsome young actor. You gave him your diamond,
the Star of the East, to pay a debt. Is it not so?”

Lady Yardly buried her face in her hands.

“Then, when your husband decided to sell the diamond, you were in
a hole. You didn't have the diamond to sell. So you invented this
story of the Chinese gang. You sent yourself the letters, and you
arranged the ‘theft’ last night. You even used Miss Marvell’s
perfume to cast suspicion on her, knowing she was coming here.”

“But the diamond!” cried Lord Yardly. “Where is it, then?”

“The diamond, _milord_, is in the hands of the man who has had it
for the last three years. The man Lady Yardly gave it to. The man
who has been blackmailing her ever since.”

“And who is that?” asked Japp.

“The man who is known as Gregory Rolf,” said Poirot.

At that moment, the door opened and Gregory Rolf walked into the
room. He looked from one to the other, his face a mask of
surprise.

“What’s going on here?” he asked.

“Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot, “I have been telling these good people
a little story about a diamond. Would you like to hear the end of
it?”

Rolf’s eyes narrowed. “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“I think you do. I think you have the Star of the East in your
possession at this very moment. And I think you also have the
Western Star, which you ‘stole’ from your wife this morning.”

“Stole? From Mary? You’re crazy!”

“Am I? We shall see. Inspector Japp, I think you will find both
diamonds in Mr. Rolf’s pockets.”

Japp stepped forward, but Rolf didn't wait. He turned and bolted
for the door. But he didn't get far. Two of Japp’s men were
waiting in the hall, and they quickly overpowered him.

A search of his person revealed two large diamonds.

“The Star of the East and the Western Star,” said Poirot
complacently. “A very pretty pair.”

Later, when we were back in our rooms in London, I asked Poirot
how he had known.

“It was the perfume, Hastings. That was the first clue. It was
too obvious. Lady Yardly wanted to suggest that Miss Marvell had
stolen the diamond, but she didn't realize that I would recognize
the perfume. Then there was the matter of the insurance. It was
much more likely that someone would steal the Western Star for the
insurance money than the Star of the East for no money at all.
When I found out that Gregory Rolf had been in California three
years ago, and that he was the one who had ‘bought’ the Western
Star from a Chinaman, the whole thing became clear. He had the Star
of the East all the time. He was blackmailing Lady Yardly, and he
used the story of the Chinese gang to cover up his own theft of
the Western Star.”

“But why did he steal the Western Star?”

“For the insurance, _mon ami_. Fifty thousand pounds is a lot of
money. He staged the ‘theft’ this morning, before they left for
Yardly Chase, and then he brought both diamonds down here,
intending to ‘steal’ the Star of the East as well, and so make
the whole story seem plausible.”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“She was a victim, Hastings. A victim of her own past
indiscretion. But I think Lord Yardly will forgive her. He is a
good-hearted man, and he was very much relieved to get his
diamond back.”

“And Miss Marvell?”

“She will get her insurance money, no doubt. And she will have
the satisfaction of knowing that her diamond was indeed the
twin of the Star of the East.”

“Poirot,” I said, “you are truly amazing.”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “But then,
as I have always told you, I am Hercule Poirot!”

We both dashed forward. The door was locked, but the three of us,
charging it together, burst it open.

The hall was empty. At the foot of the stairs, Lady Yardly lay
prostrate. She had fainted. Poirot bent over her, and her husband
and I were just about to do the same when a tall dark man appeared
breathlessly from the direction of the kitchens.

“What is the matter, my lord?” he asked.

“Who are you?” demanded Lord Yardly.

“I’m from Mr. Hoffberg, my lord. I came down by the six-forty. I
was just having some supper in the small dining-room when I heard
a scream, and I came at once.”

Lady Yardly was recovering. She opened her eyes, and they were
filled with a dazed terror.

“The Chinaman!” she gasped. “He was behind me. He tore the necklace
from my neck.”

Lord Yardly gave a roar of fury.

“The Chinaman! He’s in the house, then! We’ll catch the scoundrel.”

“Wait!” It was Poirot’s voice, sharp and authoritative. “He must
be in the house still. There is no other way out except through
this hall.”

We searched the house from top to bottom, but there was not a sign
of the intruder. We found one of the windows in the dining-room
open, and a series of muddy footprints on the sill.

The man from Hoffberg was still waiting. He seemed a quiet,
determined-looking fellow.

“I’m sorry, my lord,” he said, “but I’m afraid the stone is gone.
I’ve seen enough of it to be sure it was the real thing. I’m a
judge of diamonds, you know.”

Lord Yardly turned to Poirot. His face was white and drawn.

“This is a bad business, Monsieur Poirot. I wish I’d taken your
advice and put the diamond in a safe place. What are we to do?”

“_Eh bien_,” said Poirot, his eyes fixed on the man from Hoffberg.
“I will do my best. But it is a very difficult matter—very
difficult.”

We left him there with Lord Yardly, and I went upstairs to my room.
I was feeling very much depressed. I had expected so much of
Poirot, and he seemed to have failed so signally.

In about an hour’s time there was a knock at my door, and Poirot
entered.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?” he asked.

“I think it’s a very bad business,” I replied. “The diamond’s gone,
and we’ve no clue to the thief.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “I have a very good clue.”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“The perfume,” said Poirot. “The perfume of the joss-stick. It was
very strong in the hall when we found Lady Yardly.”

“But that only proves that it _was_ a Chinaman who stole the
diamond.”

“_Au contraire_,” said Poirot. “It proves that it was _not_ a
Chinaman.”

“What do you mean?”

“My dear Hastings, a Chinaman does not need to use the perfume of
the joss-stick to prove that he is a Chinaman! He is a Chinaman!
But a person who is _pretending_ to be a Chinaman—he uses the
perfume of the joss-stick to make people _think_ he is a Chinaman.”

“But the footprints on the windowsill?”

“They were made by a man’s boots, Hastings. And they were made from
the _inside_ of the room, not from the outside.”

“Then you think it was someone in the house?”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot.

“But who? Not Lord Yardly—he was with us in the drawing-room.”

“No,” said Poirot. “Not Lord Yardly.”

“Then who could it be?”

“There are only two people who could have done it,” said Poirot.
“The man from Hoffberg—or Lady Yardly herself.”
