“Lady Yardly! But she was the victim!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “She was the victim. And it is always the
victim who is the most suspect in these cases.”

“But why should she steal her own diamond?”

“Perhaps it was not her own diamond,” said Poirot. “Perhaps it was
a paste imitation, and she stole it to prevent the man from
Hoffberg from discovering the truth.”

“But he said he saw enough of it to be sure it was the real thing.”

“He may have been lying,” said Poirot. “Or he may have been
mistaken. Or perhaps he was in league with Lady Yardly.”

“It seems very unlikely,” I said.

“Everything is unlikely until it has happened,” said Poirot. “But
now, Hastings, I have a little task for you. I want you to go back
to London at once.”

“To London? Now?”

“Yes. I want you to go to the Hotel Magnificent and find out if
Mr. Gregory Rolf is there.”

“Gregory Rolf? What has he to do with it?”

“I do not know yet,” said Poirot. “But I have a little idea. A very
little idea, but it may lead to great things. Go, my friend, and
telephoning to me the result of your enquiries.”

I did as I was told, though I could not see what Gregory Rolf could
possibly have to do with the theft of Lady Yardly’s diamond.

When I arrived at the Hotel Magnificent, I was told that Mr. Gregory
Rolf was in his rooms. I went up and knocked at the door.

It was opened by Mr. Rolf himself. He looked surprised to see me.

“Why, it’s Captain Hastings!” he said. “What brings you here at
this time of night?”

“I have a message for you from Monsieur Poirot,” I said.

“From Poirot? What is it?”

“He wants to know if you have seen anything of a Chinaman lately.”

Gregory Rolf laughed.

“A Chinaman? No, I haven’t. Why does he want to know?”

“I don’t know,” I said. “He just asked me to find out.”

“Well, you can tell him from me that I haven’t seen any Chinamen.
Is that all?”

“Yes, that’s all,” I said.

I went back to the telephone and called Poirot.

“Well?” he asked. “What did he say?”

“He said he hasn’t seen any Chinamen,” I replied.

“_Bien!_” said Poirot. “That is very interesting. Now, Hastings,
I want you to do one more thing for me. I want you to find out if
Miss Mary Marvell is in the hotel.”

I went back to the desk and made enquiries.

“Miss Marvell is in her rooms, sir,” said the clerk. “She has been
there all evening.”

I telephoned this information to Poirot.

“_Merci_, Hastings,” he said. “That is all I wanted to know. You
can come back to Yardly Chase now. I think the mystery is solved.”

When I got back to Yardly Chase, I found Poirot in the hall. He was
looking very pleased with himself.

“Well?” I asked. “Who was the thief?”

“Come with me,” said Poirot. “I will show you.”

He led the way to the small dining-room. Lord and Lady Yardly were
there, and also the man from Hoffberg.

“Now, Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord Yardly. “You said you had
something to tell us.”

“I have,” said Poirot. “I have discovered the thief.”

“Who is it?” asked Lord Yardly.

Poirot turned to Lady Yardly.

“Lady Yardly,” he said. “I think you have something to tell us.”

Lady Yardly turned very pale.

“I? What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that it was you who stole the diamond.”

“I? That is ridiculous!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain why you have
the diamond in your possession at this moment.”

“I haven’t got it!”

“_Pardon_,” said Poirot. “But I think you have. It is hidden in
the heel of your shoe.”

Lady Yardly gave a cry and sank into a chair.

“How did you know?” she gasped.

“It was the perfume,” said Poirot. “The perfume of the joss-stick.
I noticed it when you came into the room. And I also noticed that
you were limping slightly. It was a very small limp, but to the
eyes of Hercule Poirot it was enough.”

Lord Yardly stared at his wife in horror.

“Maude! Is this true? Did you steal the diamond?”

Lady Yardly burst into tears.

“Yes,” she sobbed. “I did. But I only did it because I was being
blackmailed.”

“Blackmailed? By whom?”

“By Gregory Rolf,” said Lady Yardly. “He knew a secret of mine—a
secret from the time when I was in California. He threatened to
tell you if I didn’t give him the diamond. So I had a paste
imitation made, and I was going to give him that. But then the
letters started coming—the letters from the ‘Chinaman.’ I was
terrified. I thought he was going to steal the real diamond before
I could give him the imitation one. So I decided to steal it
myself, and make it look as though the Chinaman had done it.”

“But the man from Hoffberg?” said Lord Yardly. “He said the stone
was the real thing.”

“He was right,” said Poirot. “It _was_ the real thing. Lady Yardly
had already substituted the paste imitation for the real diamond,
and it was the imitation that she ‘stole’ from herself. But she
forgot one thing—she forgot that the man from Hoffberg would be
able to tell the difference.”

“But he said it _was_ the real thing!”

“Because I told him to say so,” said Poirot. “I had already found
the real diamond in Lady Yardly’s jewel-case, and I had substituted
it for the imitation one. So when the ‘Chinaman’ stole the diamond,
he was stealing the real one. But I had already taken it back from
him.”

“The Chinaman?” said Lord Yardly. “Who was the Chinaman?”

“There was no Chinaman,” said Poirot. “The letters were written by
Gregory Rolf. He wanted to frighten Lady Yardly into giving him the
diamond. But he didn’t know that she had already had an imitation
made. It was a very complicated plot, but it was not quite
complicated enough for Hercule Poirot!”

Lord Yardly looked at his wife. His face was full of pity.

“Maude,” he said. “Why didn’t you tell me? I would have helped
you.”

“I was ashamed,” she sobbed.

Poirot turned to the man from Hoffberg.

“I think, monsieur, that your business is finished. The diamond is
safe.”

As the man left the room, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of that? A very pretty little
case, was it not?”

“But Poirot,” I said. “What about Mary Marvell? Why did she get the
letters too?”

“Ah,” said Poirot. “That was the most clever part of the whole
business. Gregory Rolf wanted to make the story of the Chinese god
seem real. So he sent the letters to his own wife as well. He knew
that she would come to me, and that I would be drawn into the case.
It was a very clever piece of work—but he forgot the psychology of
Hercule Poirot!”

“And the diamond?” I asked. “What will happen to it now?”

“It will stay at Yardly Chase,” said Poirot. “Lord Yardly has
decided not to sell it. He is going to film the play after all—and
Gregory Rolf is going to pay him a very large sum of money for the
privilege!”

“But why should Gregory Rolf do that?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “if he does not, I shall tell the police
all about his little attempt at blackmail. I think Mr. Gregory Rolf
will be very glad to pay!”

And so, once again, the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot had
triumphed.

He dashed to the door, and with a violent effort wrenched it open.
From the hall came the sound of a heavy fall. A white figure lay
prostrate on the floor.

Lord Yardly gave a cry of horror. He fell on his knees beside her.

“Maude, Maude—my God!—it’s gone! The necklace—it’s gone!”

We followed him, but Poirot’s eye was on the floor. Something white
lay there—a little piece of paper. He picked it up and handed it
to me. It was a single sentence, carefully printed:

“The god has claimed his own.”

Lady Yardly was reviving. She began to moan, then she sat up
suddenly, her hands to her neck.

“It’s gone—gone! Oh, how horrible!”

Lord Yardly was almost past coherent speech.

“Maude, Maude—tell me. Who was it? What happened?”

She gave a little shudder.

“I was just going to turn on the light when I saw a figure—a
horrible, crouching figure—it seemed to come from nowhere. It
snatched at my throat. I screamed—and then I think I fainted.”

“Was it a—a _Chinaman_?” gasped Lord Yardly.

“I—I think so. I saw a yellow face.”

“My God!” cried the peer. “Then it’s true after all.”

He dashed to the bell, and rang it violently. The butler appeared,
running.

“Jenkins! Jenkins! A Chinaman has broken into the house! Ring up
the police—at once. Do you hear? At once.”

Then he turned to Poirot.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, what do you say to it now? You were right,
you see.”

Poirot’s face was very grave.

“I see,” he said. “I see. It is very strange. Will you permit that
I examine the hall?”

He did so with his usual meticulous care. But there was little to
be seen. A window at the end of the passage was open, and there
were some traces of mud on the sill.

“The fellow must have come in this way,” said Lord Yardly. “But
how could he have known?”

“_Ah!_ How indeed?” said Poirot. He looked at the open window
thoughtfully. “It is a very simple matter to enter a house in that
way. But to know the exact moment to strike——”

“He must have been watching the house,” I suggested.

“Without doubt,” said Poirot. “But even so——” He broke off. “Ah,
here are the police.”

A local inspector and a couple of constables arrived, and we spent
a busy hour. But nothing was found. The thief had vanished as
completely as though he had never existed. Lord Yardly was in a
state of collapse. Lady Yardly had been taken to her room, and
the doctor had been sent for.

Poirot and I were left alone in the hall. My friend was unusually
silent. He stood in the middle of the room, his brows knitted.

“What is it, Poirot?” I asked. “What are you thinking of?”

“I am thinking, Hastings, that there are certain points about this
case which are remarkably interesting. Why, for instance, did the
thief choose that particular moment? Why did he not wait until
Lady Yardly was alone? Why did he choose the one moment when three
men were within call?”

“I suppose because she had the necklace on then,” I suggested.

“_Peut-être._ But there are other things. That piece of paper, for
instance. It was very conveniently dropped. And the window—it was
open, yes, but there were no footprints on the flower-bed outside.”

“Then you think——” I began.

“I think many things, _mon ami_. But at present I say nothing. Let
us go to bed. To-morrow we shall see what we shall see.”

But the morning brought no new light on the mystery. Lord Yardly
was still in a state of nervous prostration, and Lady Yardly kept
her room.

“I think we may as well return to London,” said Poirot. “There is
nothing more for us to do here.”

I was surprised, for it was not like Poirot to give up so easily.
But I made no comment.

On our way back to the station, we ran into Gregory Rolf. He was
looking very much upset.

“I say, have you heard the news?” he cried. “It’s all over the
place. Lady Yardly’s diamond has been stolen! It’s the most
extraordinary thing I ever heard of. I’m just on my way to the
Chase now to see if there’s anything I can do.”

“You will find Lord Yardly in a very poor state,” said Poirot. “The
shock has been too much for him.”

“I don’t wonder. It’s a bad business. And on the very eve of our
deal, too. It’ll probably knock the whole thing on the head.”

“I fear so,” said Poirot. “Well, we must be getting on. Good-bye,
Mr. Rolf.”

“Good-bye, Monsieur Poirot.”

He hurried off in the direction of the Chase.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we settled ourselves in the
train, “I will tell you what I think of this case. It is a very
pretty little problem—very pretty indeed.”

“You have a theory?” I asked eagerly.

“I have more than a theory. I have a certainty. But we have still
a little way to go. To-morrow, _mon ami_, we shall know the truth.”

But the next day brought a fresh surprise. I was looking through the
morning paper when a paragraph caught my eye.

“THEFT OF THE WESTERN STAR! FAMOUS DIAMOND STOLEN FROM FILM STAR’S
HOTEL!”

I read the account aloud to Poirot. It seemed that Miss Mary Marvell
had also been the victim of a daring robbery. The diamond had been
stolen from her jewel-case while she was out at dinner. A
Chinaman had been seen hanging about the hotel, and a note had been
left behind in the jewel-case: “The god has claimed his own.”

“What do you say to that, Poirot?” I cried. “Both diamonds gone!
The Chinese god has his eyes back again.”

Poirot smiled.

“It is very convenient, is it not? Two diamonds stolen—two
Chinamen—two notes. It is almost too good to be true.”

“But what do you think?”

“I think, Hastings, that it is time we paid another visit to Miss
Mary Marvell.”

We found the film star in a state of high excitement.

“It’s just too perfectly wonderful!” she cried. “The most
marvellous publicity! Every paper in London has got it. And
Gregory’s so pleased. He says it’s the best thing that could have
happened.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “Mr. Rolf is pleased, is he? That is very
interesting. And you, madame, you are not distressed at the loss
of your diamond?”

“Oh, well, of course I’m sorry to lose it. But it was insured, you
know. And the publicity is worth more than the diamond.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, madame, I have a little request to
make. I want you to give me the name of the insurance company.”

“Why, certainly. It’s the Northern & Equitable.”

“Thank you, madame. And now, if you will excuse me, I have some
business to attend to.”

As we left the hotel, Poirot turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, for the final scene. I have all the threads in
my hand. To-night, we shall have the truth.”

“But how? Where?”

“At Yardly Chase. I have already telegraphed to Lord Yardly to meet
us there.”

“But what about the insurance company?”

“I shall see them on the way. It is a little formality, that is
all.”

It was a strange party that assembled in the library at Yardly
Chase that evening. Lord and Lady Yardly, Gregory Rolf and Mary
Marvell, and Poirot and myself.

Lord Yardly was looking pale and haggard. Lady Yardly was nervous
and restless. Gregory Rolf was as handsome and debonair as ever,
while Mary Marvell was evidently enjoying her position in the
limelight.

Poirot stood in the centre of the room, his eyes darting from one
to the other.

“Messieurs, mesdames,” he began, “I have asked you all to meet me
here to-night because I have something to tell you. The mystery of
the two diamonds is solved.”

A little gasp went round the room.

“You know who stole them?” cried Lord Yardly.

“I know who stole them—and I know why they were stolen. But first,
I must tell you a little story. It is a story of three years ago—in
California.”

I saw Lady Yardly start, and a look of terror come into her eyes.

“Three years ago,” Poirot continued, “a young English lady was
staying in California. She was a beautiful woman, and she was,
perhaps, a little—how shall I say?—_imprudente_. She made the
acquaintance of a handsome young actor. They became friends—more
than friends. The lady was so foolish as to write some letters—some
very foolish letters.”

Lady Yardly had sunk into a chair, her face buried in her hands.

“Then the actor married. He was ambitious, and he wanted money. He
remembered the letters. He began to blackmail the lady. She had
no money of her own, so she was forced to give him her jewels. At
last, he demanded the great diamond—the Star of the East.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Gregory Rolf, starting forward.

“It is the truth,” said Poirot calmly. “The lady was desperate. She
could not give up the diamond without her husband’s knowledge. So
she and the actor between them hatched a plot. The diamond was to
be stolen—by a Chinaman. The actor would then have the diamond,
and the lady would be free from her blackmailer.”

“It’s not true!” moaned Lady Yardly.

“But there was a complication,” Poirot went on. “The actor’s wife
also had a diamond—a very fine one, but not so fine as the Star of
the East. And the actor, he is a man of business! He saw a chance
of getting both diamonds. He told his wife the story of the Chinese
god, and he sent her the warning letters. Then he sent the letters
to Lady Yardly also. He knew that when the first diamond was
stolen, everyone would believe the story. And then—he stole his
wife’s diamond himself!”

“Gregory!” cried Mary Marvell, staring at her husband.

“Yes, madame,” said Poirot. “Mr. Rolf stole your diamond. He had
it insured for a large sum, and he intended to claim the insurance
money as well as keeping the diamond. It was a very pretty little
plan.”

“You can’t prove it!” shouted Rolf.

“Can I not?” Poirot’s voice was like silk. “I have just come from
the office of the Northern & Equitable. They were very interested
in my theory. And I think, Mr. Rolf, that when they find your
wife’s diamond in—shall we say, a certain safe deposit?—they will
be even more interested.”

Rolf went deathly pale. He made a movement as though to fly from
the room, but Poirot stopped him with a gesture.

“One moment, Mr. Rolf. There is also the matter of Lady Yardly’s
diamond. I think it would be better if you restored it to her—now.”

With a muttered oath, Rolf thrust his hand into his pocket and flung
a glittering object on the table. Then he turned and dashed from
the room.

Mary Marvell followed him, crying out his name.

There was a long silence. Then Lord Yardly rose and went over to
his wife. He put his arm round her shoulders.

“Maude,” he said softly. “Maude, my dear.”

She looked up at him with tear-filled eyes.

“Oh, George, can you ever forgive me?”

“Of course I can. We’ll forget all about it. The diamond’s back,
and that’s all that matters.”

Poirot stepped forward.

“I think, _milord_,” he said, “that it would be better if the
diamond were sold—at once. It has caused enough trouble.”

“You’re right, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll see Hoffberg about it
to-morrow.”

As we drove back to London, I looked at Poirot with admiration.

“You’re a marvel, Poirot!” I said. “How did you know?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the simplicity of the thing that
struck me. The Chinaman—the notes—it was all so like a melodrama!
And then, when I saw Lady Yardly, I knew she was being blackmailed.
She was so nervous—so terrified! And when she told me that Mary
Cavendish had sent her to me—well, I knew Mary Cavendish would never
have done such a thing unless there was something very wrong
indeed.”

“But the insurance company?”

“Ah, that was a little bluff, Hastings! But it worked, did it not?
And now, I think we have earned our sleep. It has been a long
day.”

I nodded. It had indeed been a long day—but a very successful
one. Once again, Hercule Poirot had triumphed.

We rushed blindly for the door, cannoning into each other in the
darkness. It was some minutes before we could find it. What a sight
met our eyes! Lady Yardly lay senseless on the marble floor, a
crimson mark on her white throat where the necklace had been
wrenched from her neck.

As we bent over her, uncertain for the moment whether she were dead
or alive, her eyelids opened.

“The Chinaman,” she whispered painfully. “The Chinaman—the side
door.”

We dashed out into the night, but the darkness was impenetrable. Yardly Chase is surrounded by dense shrubberies, and a hundred men could have hidden there with ease. We searched for a time, our hearts thumping, but there was no sign of a fleeing figure in a silken robe. At last, breathless and disappointed, we returned to the hall. Lady Yardly had been moved to a sofa, and Poirot was standing by her side, holding a small glass of water. His face was a mask of gravity, but I noticed his eyes—those cat-like eyes—were darting about the floor near the doorway where the incident had occurred.

But in vain we hunted through the grounds. There was no trace of
a living soul. We returned, somewhat crestfallen, to find that
Lady Yardly had been carried up to her room, and that a doctor had
been sent for. Poirot was in the hall.

“Well?” he demanded eagerly.

I displayed the necklace and the piece of silk, and recounted our
luckless search.

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot, and taking the silk he examined it
minutely.

At that moment the butler announced that a Mr. Mullings had arrived
from Mr. Hoffberg. Poirot gave a sudden skip of delight.

“_C’est magnifique!_ Let us see Mr. Mullings by all means.”

Mr. Mullings was a small, dapper man, wearing gold-rimmed
spectacles. He was visibly concerned to hear of the jewel robbery.

“I must wire at once to Mr. Hoffberg,” he said. “He will be greatly
distressed. It is a great blow to him. The Star of the East was
just what he wanted for his American client.”

“Wait,” said Poirot. “I would ask you, Mr. Mullings, to examine
this necklace—or what is left of it—and tell me if the other stones
are of any great value?”

The expert took the necklace.

“They are good stones,” he said, “but nothing out of the way. The
diamonds are of the second water, and some of them have a decided
yellowish tinge.”

“And the missing stone—the Star of the East—was it also of the
second water?”

“No, no—that was a diamond of the very first water. A most
beautiful stone. We have only seen it once, when it was brought
to us three years ago to be valued.”

“Three years ago?” I cried. “Is that so?”

“Yes, Captain Hastings. It was just before Lord Yardly’s visit to
the States.”

A low whistle escaped me.

“But what did it look like?” asked Poirot. “Can you describe it?”

“Certainly. It was a very large stone, somewhat pear-shaped, and
had a very slight—a very, very slight—blue tint.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is most interesting. And you would
know it again anywhere?”

“I could swear to it, Monsieur Poirot.”

“_Bien. C’est fini._ Good night, Mr. Mullings.”

As the expert left the room, Poirot turned to me.

“We must go to London at once, Hastings. At once, do you hear?
Not a moment to be lost.”

“But it’s nearly ten o’clock!”

“What does that matter? We will go by car. Come, _mon ami_, let us
be off.”

“But Lady Yardly?”

“She is in no danger. The doctor is with her, and her husband will
look after her. Come.”

I followed him out to the car. We reached London at one o’clock.
The next morning saw us at the Magnificent. Miss Marvell was not
yet up, but we were told that Mr. Rolf was in the breakfast-room.
We were shown in.

“How’s the detective business? Caught the Chinaman yet?” he asked
as he tucked into his bacon and eggs.

“Not yet,” said Poirot.

“What’s the news from Yardly Chase? My wife says she won’t go down
on Friday now.”

“The news from Yardly Chase,” said Poirot, “is that the Star of
the East was stolen last night.”

Gregory Rolf paused with his fork halfway to his mouth.

“You don’t say!” he cried. “Well, if that doesn’t beat everything!
What a stroke of luck for Mary!”

“Luck?” I asked.

“Why, yes. She’ll be the only one to have the stone now.”

“I’m not so sure of that,” said Poirot.

“What do you mean?”

“I have a fancy, Mr. Rolf, that your wife’s diamond will also be
stolen—within the next twenty-four hours.”

“What? Why, I’ve given orders that it’s not to be taken out of the
hotel safe.”

“You are wise,” said Poirot. “And yet—I have a fancy——”

Gregory Rolf laughed.

“Well, I’ll see that it’s not. I’ll go and have a look at it now.”

He left the room.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What is the meaning of all this? You don’t
really think the other stone will be stolen?”

“My friend, I am as sure of it as that I stand here!”

“But why?”

“Because, Hastings——” Poirot broke off as Gregory Rolf burst into
the room. He was pale and shaking.

“It’s gone!” he gasped. “The safe has been robbed! The Western
Star is gone!”

“What?” I cried. “Both of them?”

“Both of them,” said Poirot.

He turned to Rolf.

“Mr. Rolf, will you accompany us to our rooms? I have something I
wish to say to you.”

The actor complied, looking like a man in a dream. When we reached
our rooms, Poirot motioned him to a chair.

“Now, Mr. Rolf,” he said, “I will tell you what has happened.
Three years ago, you met Lady Yardly in California. You were then,
I believe, what is called a ‘cinematograph’ actor, and she was—well,
Lady Yardly. You had an affair—_n’est-ce pas_?”

Gregory Rolf nodded.

“And you gave her a diamond—the Star of the East. It was not a
very good diamond—Mullings has told us that—but it was a diamond.
Lady Yardly had it set in a necklace with other stones, and for
three years she has worn it. But then her husband began to get
into difficulties. He wanted to sell the diamond. Lady Yardly was
in a hole. She couldn’t sell a diamond that didn’t belong to her.
If she did, her husband would find out everything. What was she
to do? She must get hold of a diamond that was hers to sell.

“Then she heard that you were coming to England with your wife,
and that your wife had a diamond—the Western Star—which was
reputed to be the twin of the Star of the East. She saw a way
out. She would steal your wife’s diamond, and pretend that her own
had been stolen too. Then she would be able to sell the Western
Star as the Star of the East, and no one would be any the wiser.”

“But the letters?” I cried. “The Chinaman?”

“The letters were a clever touch of Lady Yardly’s. She knew that
if she could make it appear that there was a mysterious conspiracy
to steal the diamonds, it would be much easier to carry out her
plan. She wrote the letters to herself, and then, after she had
seen Miss Marvell, she wrote similar ones to her. The Chinaman was
also her invention. It was she who staged the scene in the hall,
she who extinguished the lights, she who dropped the necklace
(after removing the stone), and she who planted the piece of silk
in the door.”

“But the Western Star?” I asked. “How did she get that?”

“She didn’t get it,” said Poirot. “Gregory Rolf got it. He was
her accomplice. He had been blackmailing her for years, and when
she told him her plan, he saw a chance of getting the Western Star
for himself. He stole it from the hotel safe this morning.”

“Is this true, Rolf?” I asked.

The actor did not answer. He sat with his head in his hands.

“It is true,” said Poirot. “And now, Mr. Rolf, I have a proposition
to make to you. If you will return the Western Star to your wife,
and if you will promise to leave Lady Yardly alone in future, I
will say no more about the matter. If not—well, I think the police
would be interested in your career.”

Gregory Rolf looked up. His face was distorted with rage.

“You think you’re very clever, don’t you?” he snarled. “But you
can’t prove anything!”

“Can I not?” said Poirot. He drew a small object from his pocket.
“This is the piece of silk that I found in the door at Yardly
Chase. It is, as I thought, a piece of a Chinese robe. But it is
not, as you supposed, a piece of a real Chinese robe. It is a piece
of a theatrical costume. And on it is a small mark—the mark of a
well-known London costumier. I have been to see him this morning,
and he tells me that he supplied a Chinese costume to a Mr.
Gregory Rolf last week.”

There was a moment’s silence. Then Gregory Rolf rose to his feet.

“You win,” he said. “I’ll do as you say.”

He left the room.

“So it was Gregory Rolf after all,” I said. “And Lady Yardly.”

“_Oui, mon ami_,” said Poirot. “A very pretty little plot. But
they did not reckon with Hercule Poirot!”

“But Poirot,” I said, “there’s one thing I don’t understand. How
did you know that the Star of the East was not the real stone?”

“Because, Hastings, I have eyes! Did you not notice that when Lady
Yardly showed us the necklace, the stone was not pear-shaped, as
Mullings described it, but square? Lady Yardly had had the real
stone replaced by a paste one years ago, when she first needed
money. It was only when she heard that the real Star of the East
was likely to be sold that she became desperate. She had to have
a real stone to show the expert, and she thought she could steal
the Western Star for that purpose.”

“And the real Star of the East?” I asked. “Where is it now?”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is the most curious part of the whole
story. The real Star of the East was never in the Yardly family
at all. It was stolen from the temple in China, as the story said,
and it was brought to England by—Gregory Rolf! He sold it to a
dealer, who sold it to another, and finally it was bought by—Lord
Yardly’s father! But Lord Yardly, being in want of money, sold it
years ago to—Gregory Rolf! So you see, the stone had merely
returned to its original owner.”

“But then,” I cried, “the Western Star——”

“The Western Star,” said Poirot, “is the Star of the East! There
is only one stone, Hastings. Gregory Rolf merely invented the
story of the twin stones to make it easier for him to sell the
diamond twice over!”

“Well!” I said. “Of all the——”

But Poirot was not listening. He was carefully rearranging the
books on the top shelf.

But our search was fruitless. The winding paths and dense shrubberies of the Chase offered a thousand hiding-places, and the impenetrable darkness of the night made pursuit a mockery. We returned, breathless and disappointed, to find Poirot in the hall. He had not joined in our chase, but was instead meticulously examining the necklace and the scrap of silk I had recovered. His face was a mask of grave reflection, and he did not look up as we approached, though Lord Yardly began at once to recount our failure in a voice shaking with agitation.

But in vain we hunted through the grounds. There was no trace of
a living soul. We returned, somewhat dejectedly, to find Poirot
and the doctor, who had been sent for, wrapping Lady Yardly in
warm blankets. She was still faint and sobbing. Poirot, however,
was remarkably cool, his eyes darting about the hallway as if
memorizing the geometry of the crime. He picked up the mangled
remains of the necklace from the table where I had placed it and
turned it over in his hands with a curious expression. "A very
efficient thief," he murmured, more to himself than to us. "To
take only the center stone in such a whirlwind of darkness." He
then looked toward the side door, his eyebrows rising in a way
that usually preceded a very pointed question.

But in vain we hunted through the grounds. There was no trace of
the fugitive. We returned, somewhat crestfallen, to find that Lady
Yardly had been carried up to her room, and that a doctor had been
sent for. Poirot was in the hall.

“Well?” he demanded.

I displayed the silk fragment, and recounted our lack of success.

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “He was not there, the Chinaman? It is
strange, that.”

“Not at all,” I said. “He must have had a car waiting.”

“How did he enter the house?”

“Through the side door.”

“And it was not locked?”

“No.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to the ceiling. “It is very simple, is it
not?”

“It was a well-planned _coup_,” I said. “But he was nearly caught.
If it hadn’t been for the dark——”

“_Précisément!_” Poirot’s eyes were still fixed on the ceiling.
“How lucky that it was dark!”

“What do you mean?”

“The fuse, _mon ami_—the fuse had been cleverly tampered with. It
was no accident.”

“Exactly. It was all part of the Chinaman’s plan.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot again. He sounded slightly incredulous.

Lord Yardly was looking at the piece of silk.

“You’re sure it’s a Chinaman’s?” he asked. “I should have thought
it might have been a woman’s dress—from the feel of it.”

“No,” I said. “It is a piece of Chinese embroidery, without a
doubt.”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I had not noticed.”

I looked at him. Sometimes I feel that Poirot’s brain is not quite
what it was. He was staring at the floor now, with a completely
vacant expression.

“Monsieur Poirot,” I said, “there is one thing I should like to
know. Why were you not surprised? You seem to have expected this.”

“I did, Hastings.”

“But how? You said just now that you had no idea how the thief
entered the house.”

“I didn’t. I don’t now. But I knew the diamond would be stolen
to-night.”

“Because of the full moon?”

“Because of the full moon, Hastings. Also for other reasons.”

“But this is wonderful!” I cried.

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “The diamond was stolen to-night
because—well, to-night was the last chance.”

“The last chance?”

“_Mais oui_, my friend. To-morrow the diamond would have been sold
to this American. After that, it would have been much more
difficult to steal.”

“That’s true!” I cried. “I hadn’t thought of that. But why should
a Chinese gang care whether it was sold to an American or not?”

“Why, indeed?” said Poirot. He was still looking at the floor.
“Hastings,” he said suddenly, “I want you to do me a little favour.
Run up and see how Lady Yardly is, and if she could spare me a few
moments?”

I went. Lady Yardly was sitting up in bed. She looked pale and
shaken, but she was quite conscious.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she said. “Yes, let him come up by all means.”

I returned with the message. Poirot followed me into the room. He
went up to the bed.

“Madame,” he said, “I have a question to ask you. It is a very
important one. Will you answer it truthfully?”

Lady Yardly looked at him in surprise. “Of course. What is it?”

“Madame,” said Poirot, “did you ever receive any letters about the
diamond?”

Lady Yardly gasped. “Why, of course! You know I did. You were there
when I told Captain Hastings about them.”

“I was not there, madame,” said Poirot quietly. “And I did not
hear you tell Captain Hastings about them. I am asking you now—did
you ever receive any letters about the diamond?”

Lady Yardly’s face turned from white to a dull, angry red.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she stammered.

“I will tell you,” said Poirot. “Captain Hastings is a very
gallant gentleman. He is also—how shall I say it?—a little
imaginative. He told me a very pretty story about your being
blackmailed. I want to know if that story is true.”

Lady Yardly burst into tears. “It is true! It is true! Oh, Monsieur
Poirot, you don’t know—you don’t know!”

“I think I do,” said Poirot. He turned to me. “Hastings, would you
mind waiting outside for a few minutes?”

I went, a good deal puzzled. What was Poirot up to? What did he
mean by saying I had imagined the story about the letters? I had
repeated it to him almost word for word as Lady Yardly had told
it to me.

I waited in the corridor for what seemed an eternity. At last the
door opened and Poirot came out. He looked very grave.

“Well?” I asked.

“It is as I thought,” he said. “Lady Yardly has been very foolish—but
she has been more sinned against than sinning.”

“Then she _was_ being blackmailed?”

“Yes.”

“By a Chinaman?”

“No, Hastings. By a man she once knew in California—a man called
Gregory Rolf.”

“Gregory Rolf!” I cried. “The film actor?”

“Exactly. It seems that three years ago, when Lady Yardly was in
the States, she was—shall we say, a little indiscreet? She wrote
certain letters. Gregory Rolf has been using them to extort money
from her. And finally, he demanded the Star of the East.”

“But she couldn’t give it to him! It wasn’t hers to give.”

“Exactly. So she had to find a way out. She had heard about the
letters Miss Marvell was receiving—letters which Rolf himself had
sent, in order to create the necessary atmosphere—and she saw her
chance. She pretended that she, too, was being threatened. And
to-night, she staged a little drama. She turned out the lights,
banged the door, and screamed. Then she dropped the necklace—minus
the big diamond—and pretended she had been robbed by a Chinaman.”

“But the diamond?” I asked. “What has become of it?”

“She gave it to Gregory Rolf two days ago.”

“Two days ago! But she only saw him for a few minutes at the
theatre.”

“It was long enough. They had it all arranged.”

“And the piece of silk I found?”

“She put it there herself. She had cut it from an old Chinese
curtain.”

“But why did she do it?” I asked. “Why didn’t she just tell her
husband the truth?”

“Because she was afraid. Lord Yardly is a very proud man. He would
never have forgiven her.”

“And what are you going to do?”

“I have already done it,” said Poirot. “I have told Lady Yardly
that she must tell her husband everything.”

“And will she?”

“She has promised. It is the only way.”

He was silent for a moment, then he added:

“You see, Hastings, it was a very clever plot. Gregory Rolf gets
the diamond, and Lady Yardly gets her letters back, and no one is
any the wiser. Or so they thought. But they forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“They forgot Hercule Poirot!”

I looked at my friend with a new respect. Once again he had proved
himself to be the greatest detective of his age.

“But what about the American?” I asked. “The man who was coming
to buy the diamond?”

“There was no American, Hastings. That was another part of the
plot. Gregory Rolf sent that telegram himself, to force Lady
Yardly’s hand.”

“I see. And Miss Marvell? Was she in it, too?”

“I don’t think so. I think she was just a tool in her husband’s
hands. He used her to make the story of the Chinese god seem more
plausible.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a wonderful case. I should never have
guessed the truth.”

“No,” said Poirot, with a little smile. “But then, you have not the
benefit of my ‘little grey cells.’ Shall we go down to dinner?”

As we descended the stairs, we saw Lord and Lady Yardly coming out
of the library. They were walking hand in hand, and there was a
look of peace on Lady Yardly’s face that I had not seen there before.

Lord Yardly came up to Poirot and took his hand.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I don’t know how to thank you. My wife
has told me everything.”

“It was the only way, _milord_,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will
permit, I think we should all have some dinner. It has been a long
day.”

We went into the dining-room, and as we sat down, I saw Poirot
glance at the empty space on Lady Yardly’s neck.

“It is a pity about the diamond,” he said. “But after all, it is
only a stone. And happiness, _milord_, is worth more than all the
diamonds in the world.”

Lord Yardly nodded. “You’re right, Monsieur Poirot. Quite right.”

And as I looked at the happy couple, I couldn’t help thinking that,
for once, Poirot was right in more ways than one.

The mystery of the “Western Star” was solved.

_The End_

But in vain we hunted and searched. In the pitch darkness of the
night, the thief had found it easy to make his getaway. We returned
reluctantly, and Lord Yardly sent off one of the footmen post-haste
to fetch the police.

Lady Yardly, aptly ministered to by Poirot, who is as good as a
woman in these matters, was sufficiently recovered to be able to
tell her story.

“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and that you’ll preserve the diamond for him—and then it goes and
gets stolen right under your very nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, appearing much dejected. “It was a failure—a
_miserable_ failure.”

“So,” I continued, “it seems to me we’d be better out of the way.”

“And the police? We must await their arrival, _n’est-ce pas_?”

“Oh, the police!” I shrugged my shoulders. “What can they do? They
don’t know anything about the mysterious Chinaman. We do.”

“And what do we know about him?”

“Well, we know—at least we suspect—that he’s the same man who’s been
shadowing Mary Marvell. And we know that there’s a secret society
at work. The police will only laugh at such things.”

Poirot nodded. “They are very matter-of-fact, the police. It is
extremely probable that they will laugh. But we must not desert
Lord Yardly in his trouble. I shall stay.”

I was about to protest, but at that moment Lord Yardly burst into
the room. His face was distorted, and he was gesticulating wildly.

“The diamond!” he gasped. “The diamond!”

“What about it?”

“It’s here! He’s got it!”

“What?”

“The man from Hoffberg’s. He’s got it in his pocket.”

We stared at him in blank amazement.

“You mean he’s recovered it?” I asked.

“No, no! He’s always had it. He brought it with him from London.”

“But that’s impossible. You have the stone there in the necklace.”

“It wasn’t the stone. It was a paste replica. He’s had the real
stone for three years.”

“What?” I cried.

Lord Yardly was almost choking. “He showed me his credentials.
There’s no doubt about it. He’s the man Hoffberg’s sent. And he
brought the diamond with him for me to see—the diamond I sent them
three years ago to be reset!”

“But why didn’t they return it to you?”

“Because I’ve never paid the bill for the resetting! And they knew
I was hard up, so they kept it as security. But they’ve found a
purchaser now, and they sent a man down to-night to get my final
sanction to the sale.”

I felt my head spinning.

“But then—what was the stone that was stolen to-night?” I gasped.

“The paste replica I told you of,” said a voice behind us.

It was Lady Yardly. She was standing in the doorway, her face deadly
pale.

“I’m sorry, George,” she said in a low voice. “I ought to have
told you—but I was so afraid. I was so dreadfully afraid.”

“Afraid of what, Maude?”

“Afraid of the blackmailers. You see, when we were in California
three years ago, I—I was very foolish. I had some—some letters.
They were used against me. The price of their return was the Star
of the East. I had to give it up. I had a paste replica made, and
it was that which I have been wearing ever since. Then when these
Chinese letters began to come, I was terrified. I thought that some
one had discovered the secret of the diamond—and I didn’t know what
to do. I was afraid to tell you.”

Lord Yardly took her hands in his.

“There, there, Maude,” he said soothingly. “It’s all right. Why
didn’t you tell me? I’d have understood.”

“I—I was so ashamed.”

I looked at Poirot. He was looking at Lady Yardly with a very
curious expression.

“So,” he said, “the mystery is explained. The Star of the East was
never here at all. It was the paste replica that the Chinaman
stole.”

“The Chinaman?” Lady Yardly shuddered. “I shall never forget his
face.”

“It was a strange business,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “Very
strange. But I think, Hastings, that we may now return to London.”

“But aren’t you going to help the police to find the thief?”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“I do not think the police will have much difficulty in finding
him, _mon ami_. He is a very well-known character.”

“You know who he is?”

“_Mais oui_! He is the same man who shadowed Mary Marvell, who left
the letters for her, and who, finally, stole the paste diamond
from Lady Yardly. He is a man of many parts.”

“But who? Who?”

“His name,” said Poirot, “is Gregory B. Rolf.”

I stared at him.

“Gregory Rolf? The actor? But why? What could he have to gain by
it?”

“A great deal, _mon ami_. You see, it was Mr. Gregory Rolf who
blackmailed Lady Yardly three years ago. It was he who had the
diamond. But he couldn’t sell it—it was too well known. So he hit
on this ingenious plan. He would make it appear that the diamond
was stolen by a mysterious Chinese gang. Then he could sell the
diamond in America with a clear conscience, and no one would ever
suspect the truth. He even went so far as to create a ‘Chinese’
atmosphere for the benefit of Miss Marvell—and incidentally of
ourselves. The letters, the ‘Chinaman’ shadowers—all were part of
the same clever scheme.”

“But the Chinaman who stole the diamond to-night?”

“Mr. Rolf is a very clever actor, Hastings. A little ‘make-up,’ a
Chinese robe—and the thing is done! He was staying at the inn,
remember. It was easy for him to come here, slip in at the side
door, and—well, you saw the rest.”

“But how did you know?”

Poirot smiled.

“Because, _mon ami_, I am Hercule Poirot! I have the little grey
cells. When I hear of two diamonds, both the ‘eyes’ of a god, and
both coming from the East, I say to myself: ‘This is too much of
a coincidence!’ And then I find that Mr. Gregory Rolf is the
husband of the lady who owns one diamond, and the former
acquaintance of the lady who owns the other. At once, the truth
becomes clear to me. The ‘Chinese’ business was a very old-fashioned
trick—but it is the old tricks that are the most successful.”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“She was his victim. He knew she would be too afraid to tell the
truth. But he did not account for Hercule Poirot!”

And, with a magnificent flourish of his hand, my friend led the
way out into the night.

“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and that you’ll preserve the diamond for him—and then it goes and
gets stolen right under your nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, with a somewhat rueful face. “It was not a
triumph for me, no. The little grey cells, they have not functioned
as they should.”

I felt sorry for him. “He is getting old,” I thought. “His powers
are declining.” Aloud I said: “Don’t worry. You’ll have better luck
next time.”

“Then we remain?”

“Well, I’d like to see the end of it. But it’s rather awkward
staying on like this.”

“Oh, as for that, Lord Yardly will not mind. He is only too anxious
to have us. What did he do with that necklace, by the way?”

“I’ve got it here.” I pulled it from my pocket.

Poirot took it and examined it. “I might as well take care of it
for him,” he remarked, and slipped it into his own pocket.

His manner was so nonchalant that I was surprised. But before I
could say anything, Lord Yardly burst into the room. He looked
more distracted than ever.

“The man from Hoffberg’s. What do you think?”

“Yes?”

“He says the stone is a paste one!”

“What?” I cried.

But Poirot only smiled, and said: “I thought as much.”

“But, man alive, if it’s paste, it can’t have been stolen! And if
it’s paste, where is the real stone?”

“_À la bonne heure!_” said Poirot. “You find your little grey cells
at last. Where _is_ the real stone?”

“It’s been in the family for generations,” moaned Lord Yardly. “It
can’t be paste.”

“But Lady Yardly told us that she had always wanted it reset,”
reminded Poirot. “Why was that? Because she had already had it
reset—with paste! The real stone was sold years ago.”

“Sold? Sold? Who sold it?”

“You should be able to answer that question better than I,
_milord_,” said Poirot. “But I will suggest to you that it was
the person who had the best right to do so, and who also had a very
urgent motive.”

“You mean——”

“I mean Lady Yardly.”

“But why?”

“You told us yourself, _milord_, that you had been—shall we say,
a little wild? That you were head over ears in debt? Lady Yardly,
like a good wife, wished to help you. She sold the diamond, and
substituted paste. But then, as you say, Gregory Rolf appeared on
the scene.”

“Gregory Rolf?”

“_Oui._ He was in California three years ago—at the same time as
Lady Yardly. He knew the story of the diamond. He may even—who
knows?—have been the person to whom she sold it. At any rate, when
he came to England, and saw a chance of acquiring the second
diamond, he saw also a chance of—shall we say—a little
blackmail?”

“Blackmail?”

“_Précisément._ He knew the stone Lady Yardly was wearing was paste.
He also knew she wouldn't want you to find out. So he began
sending those letters—to his wife as well as to Lady Yardly—to
create the atmosphere of a Chinese plot. Then, to-night, he
arranged for a confederate to ‘steal’ the paste stone. Lady Yardly
was in the plot, of course. She had to be. It was the only way
to explain the disappearance of the diamond which she knew you
were about to sell.”

“And the real stone?” I asked.

“The real stone,” said Poirot, “is at this moment in the possession
of Mr. Gregory Rolf. He bought it from Lady Yardly three years ago.
And now, if I am not mistaken, he is about to ‘find’ it—or rather,
his wife’s stone—and the two will be ‘returned’ to the god together.
A very pretty little drama!”

“But we must stop him!” I cried. “We must arrest him!”

“_Doucement, mon ami._ We have no proof. And besides, think of the
scandal. No, I have a better way. Lord Yardly, if you will give
me _carte blanche_ for one hour, I think I can settle this matter
to your satisfaction.”

Lord Yardly looked at him for a moment, then he nodded. “Go ahead,”
he said.

Poirot turned to me. “Come, Hastings. We must return to London.
We have an appointment at the Hotel Magnificent.”

As we hurried to the waiting car, I asked: “But Poirot, how did
you know it was paste?”

“_Mon cher_, it was simple. When I examined it this morning, I saw
at once that it was a very good imitation—but an imitation. And
when Lady Yardly came to me with the same story of letters and
Chinamen—well, the coincidence was too great! Then there was the
perfume on the letters—the joss-stick. That was a little too much
‘local colour,’ as you say. And finally, when I saw Lady Yardly
with her children—well, I knew then that she was a good woman,
and that if she had done something wrong, it was for the sake of
those she loved.”

“But the Chinaman?”

“A myth, Hastings! A creature of the imagination. The piece of
silk? Placed there by Lady Yardly herself. The darkness? The banged
door? All part of the play.”

“And now?”

“And now we go to see Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

We found the great actor in his suite at the Magnificent. He
received us with his usual easy charm.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot? Any news of the missing diamond?”

“I have much news, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot quietly. “In fact, I have
come to ask you to return it.”

Gregory Rolf’s face went white. “I don't know what you mean.”

“I think you do. I mean the Star of the East—the real Star of the
East—which you bought from Lady Yardly in California three years
ago.”

“You’re crazy!”

“Not at all. I have the facts. And I have also the paste necklace
from which the Star of the East was ‘stolen’ to-night. If I go to
Scotland Yard——”

“Wait!” Rolf’s voice was hoarse. “What do you want?”

“I want the diamond. In return, I give you this.” He held out the
paste necklace. “You can ‘find’ it—and the stone—and no one will
be any the wiser. Lady Yardly will be saved from scandal, and
Lord Yardly will have his diamond back—for I do not think you will
risk keeping it now.”

Gregory Rolf looked at Poirot for a long moment. Then he turned,
went to a small safe in the wall, and took out a shimmering stone.

“You’re too smart for me, Monsieur Poirot,” he said with a wry
smile. “Here it is.”

Poirot took the stone, and bowed. “I thank you, monsieur. You have
chosen the wiser course.”

As we left the hotel, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They do not fail one.”

“But Poirot,” I said, “what about the Western Star—Miss Marvell’s
diamond?”

Poirot chuckled. “Ah, that is the best part of the joke! There
_is_ no Western Star. There never was. Gregory Rolf invented the
whole story to give more ‘éclat’ to his wife’s career. The stone
she wears is also a paste imitation! He couldn't afford a real one
of that size.”

“Then Lady Yardly’s was the only real diamond?”

“Exactly. And now she has it back again. A happy ending, _n’est-ce
pas_?”

“And the Chinese god?”

“He must wait for his eyes a little longer, I fear,” said Poirot.
And, hailing a taxi, he gave the address of our rooms in
Bury Street.

“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and that you’ll preserve the diamond for him—and then it goes and
gets stolen right under your very nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, looking very depressed. “It was a failure—a
_miserable_ failure.”

“So,” I proceeded, “it seems to me we should be better away.”

“And the policeman who is on his way—you do not think he would
like to ask us some questions—the little Belgian who is so clever
and his friend who is so—what is the word you use?—re-markable?”

“Oh, come now, Poirot!” I said, feeling slightly uncomfortably
warm. “I’m not as good as that. But I’ll tell you what I’d like to
do—have another look at that little side door.”

Poirot acquiesced.

I examined the door with a fine professional air.

“You see,” I pointed out, “it’s an old-fashioned lock. A common
skeleton key would open it. The man must have been hidden in the
shrubbery, and watched his opportunity.”

“_Assurément_,” agreed Poirot. “It is all very simple. As you say,
it was a _miserable_ failure. But take heart, my friend, we will
return to London, and I will seek to console myself by the further
study of Miss Mary Marvell’s diamond.”

“You think that will be stolen too?” I asked eagerly.

“I am almost sure of it.”

I could not help thinking that Poirot was being a little
disingenuous. He must have known more than he was letting on. At
all events, his words proved true. The next morning the papers were
full of the sensational theft of “the Western Star.” It had been
taken from the hotel safe in the middle of the night. The
circumstances were very similar. A Chinaman had been seen escaping
by the fire-escape.

Poirot was profoundly interested. He hurried off to the Magnificent,
and I accompanied him. We found Gregory Rolf and his wife in a
state of high excitement. The police had already been there, and
it was evident that they were fairly baffled.

“What a set of incompetents!” cried Gregory Rolf. “It’s the same
story everywhere. The official police are no good. They don’t know
how to handle a case like this.”

“I agree with you,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “They
lack—psychology! To-day is Friday—the day of the full moon, is it
not?”

“That’s so,” said Mary Marvell. “And both the diamonds have gone.
It’s too mean for words. My beautiful diamond!” She almost sobbed.

“Do not despair, madame,” said Poirot. “I have a little idea.”

“What is it?” they both cried.

“It is a secret. Hastings, we must be off.”

He hurried me out of the room.

“Where are we going?” I asked.

“To Hatton Garden. To Mr. Hoffberg’s.”

We were some time at Mr. Hoffberg’s, and when we came out Poirot’s
face was very thoughtful. He would not answer any of my questions.

“_Patience, mon ami_. The case is almost complete. There is but
one point that is not quite clear.”

“What’s that?”

“The letters. I must see those letters again.”

“But they were stolen from Miss Marvell’s room, along with the
jewel.”

“I have the copies I made of them. But I wish to see the originals.”

“How can you, when they’ve been stolen?”

“They may not have been stolen. It is possible that they were
mislaid.”

I looked at him in surprise, but he would say no more.

When we reached our rooms, Poirot went straight to the little
almanac that I had handed him on the previous morning. He appeared
to be making some calculation. Then he looked up at me with a
smile.

“Hastings, I have a little job for you. I want you to go down to
Yardly Chase again.”

“What for?”

“To fetch Lady Yardly here. Tell her that it is of the utmost
importance, and that I have news of the diamond.”

“But will she come?”

“I think so. Yes, I think so.”

I was not so sure, but I did as he requested. Lady Yardly was very
reluctant to come, but I eventually persuaded her.

When we arrived, Poirot was not in the room. He came in a few
minutes later, carrying a small box in his hand.

“Lady Yardly,” he said, “I have sent for you because the matter is
urgent.”

“You have news of the diamond?” she asked breathlessly.

“I have more than news, madame. I have the diamond itself!”

“What?”

He opened the box. There, on a bed of white wool, lay a magnificent
diamond.

“The Star of the East!” cried Lady Yardly.

“No, madame,” said Poirot, “this is ‘the Western Star.’”

“But how—how did you get it?”

“That is my little secret. And now, madame, I will ask you to be
so good as to give me the Star of the East.”

Lady Yardly drew back, her face very pale.

“I—I don’t understand.”

“I think you do, madame. I think you understand very well.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, madame, that there never was any Chinaman at Yardly Chase.
You staged that little scene yourself. You extinguished the lights,
you screamed, you dropped the necklace where it would be easily
found—minus the big diamond. You had already removed the diamond.”

“It’s a lie!”

“Is it? Then why did you do it? I will tell you. You were being
blackmailed. You had to have money—at once. You were going to sell
the diamond to Mr. Hoffberg. But your husband had the same idea.
He had already arranged to sell it. You had to act quickly. So you
staged the robbery.”

Lady Yardly sank into a chair, her face hidden in her hands.

“It’s true,” she moaned. “It’s true. I was desperate. I didn’t know
what to do.”

“And the letters?” I asked. “Who wrote the letters?”

“I did,” said Lady Yardly. “I wanted to make it look like a Chinese
plot.”

“But Miss Marvell? She received letters too.”

“I know. I wrote those too. I knew she had a similar diamond, and
I thought that if she were also receiving warnings, it would make
the whole thing more plausible.”

“And the robbery at the Magnificent?” I asked. “Who did that?”

“I did,” said a voice from the doorway.

We turned to see Gregory Rolf standing there.

“You?” I cried.

“Yes,” he said, coming into the room. “I saw a way of getting hold
of Mary’s diamond and making a bit of money at the same time. I knew
about the Chinese letters—I’d seen them in her room—and I thought
I’d follow suit. I staged the robbery at the hotel, and made it
look like a Chinaman had done it.”

“So,” said Poirot, “we have two robberies, two Chinamen, and two
diamonds—and yet there is only one diamond!”

“What do you mean?” I asked.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that there is only one Western Star. The
other—the Star of the East—is a fake. It has been a fake for many
years. Lord Yardly’s father sold the original and had a paste
replica made. Lady Yardly did not know this. She thought she was
selling a valuable diamond, whereas she was only selling a piece
of glass!”

He turned to Gregory Rolf.

“As for you, monsieur, your little plot was more successful. You
have the real diamond. But I think you will find it better to
return it to your wife. It is, as you said, a very fine stone.”

Gregory Rolf looked at him for a moment, then he turned and left
the room.

Lady Yardly rose to her feet.

“Monsieur Poirot,” she said, “I don’t know how to thank you.”

“Do not thank me, madame. It was a very simple case. It only
required a little—psychology!”

When she had gone, I turned to Poirot.

“Well,” I said, “you’ve certainly cleared that up. But tell me, how
did you know that Lady Yardly had written the letters?”

“_Mon ami_, it was the perfume. You told me yourself that the
letters had a curious perfume—something like joss-stick. Now,
joss-stick is a very common perfume in China, but it is not often
found in England. But there is a perfume that is very like it—a
perfume that is much used by a certain class of society. It is
called ‘Nuit de Chine.’ And that, _mon ami_, was the perfume that
Lady Yardly was wearing when she called on us!”

“And the piece of silk?”

“A little piece of an old Chinese robe that I happened to have in
my pocket. I dropped it when you were not looking!”

I looked at him in amazement.

“Poirot,” I said, “you are—re-markable!”

“Am I not?” said Poirot. “And now, _mon ami_, let us go and have
some dinner. I am very hungry!”

“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and that you’ll preserve the diamond for him—and then it goes and
gets stolen right under your very nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, appearing much dejected. “It was a failure—a
_miserable_ failure.”

“So,” I continued, “it seems to me we’d be better out of it.”

“And the policeman who is on his way? And the gentleman from Mr.
Hoffberg’s?”

“Oh, Lord Yardly can look after them. What can you say to them?”

Poirot looked at me. “Hastings,” he said, “I shall stay. I am a
dog who has been given a bone, and you give me the credit for
letting it be taken from me so easily?”

“But you _did_ let it be taken!”

“_Patientez_,” said Poirot dryly.

He went into the library. I followed. Lord Yardly was talking to
a tall, sharp-looking man.

“This is Monsieur Poirot,” said the peer. “This gentleman is from
Mr. Hoffberg’s. He has come about the diamond.”

“Mr. Mullis?” asked Poirot.

The man bowed. “That is my name.”

“You have not seen the stone yet?”

“No, sir.”

“You have seen it, have you not, _milord_?”

“Yes,” said Lord Yardly. “I’ve seen it often.”

“Is it a very large stone?”

“It is a magnificent stone.”

“How did you come by it, _milord_?”

“It has been in the family for some generations.”

“I see.” Poirot turned to Mr. Mullis. “I should like you to see
it.”

“I was just about to ask Lord Yardly if I might do so,” said the
 Hatton Garden man.

“A little moment,” said Poirot. He went out of the room, and
returned in a few seconds with the necklace. He handed it to the
jeweller. “The great center stone is missing, as you see. But I
should like your opinion on the other stones.”

Mr. Mullis took the necklace and went to the light. He took a small
magnifying glass from his pocket and moved it from stone to stone.
A queer smile came over his face.

“I’m afraid Lord Yardly has been misinformed,” he said. “These
stones are very clever, but they are only paste.”

“Paste!” cried Lord Yardly, starting up. “You’re mad!”

The jeweller shrugged his shoulders. “I’m sorry, m’lord, but there
is no doubt about it. I’ll stake my reputation on it.”

“And the big stone—the Star of the East?” asked Poirot.

“That was a diamond, I presume?”

“The Star of the East,” said Mr. Mullis, “was also a paste
imitation.”

Lord Yardly sank back into his chair as though he had been shot.

“But this is incredible!” he gasped. “My father—my grandfather—they
always said——”

“It is a very common story,” said Poirot. “The original jewels are
sold, and clever paste imitations are put in their place. Often the
heads of the family are quite unaware of the fact.”

“But Maude?” cried Lord Yardly. “Does she know? I must go and find
her.” He hurried from the room.

Poirot turned to Mr. Mullis. “You are quite sure of what you say?”

“Absolutely.”

“Then it would be as well, I think, if you returned to town at
once.”

When the jeweller had gone, Poirot turned to me with a twinkle in
his eye.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s a most extraordinary business,” I said. “Who can have
stolen the jewels? And when?”

“The ‘when’ is easy enough to answer,” said Poirot. “The original
Star of the East was stolen—or rather, sold—three years ago.”

“Three years ago! But how do you know?”

“_Mon cher_, do you not remember what Mary Marvell told us? That
Gregory Rolf bought the Star of the West from a Chinaman in San
Francisco three years ago? And what did we see in _Society Gossip_?
‘One eye shall go West, the other East, till they shall meet once
more.’ Hastings, the Star of the West and the Star of the East are
one and the same stone!”

“But how did Gregory Rolf get hold of it?”

“He did not get hold of it. He bought it. He bought it from—Lady
Yardly!”

“Lady Yardly!”

“Exactly. You remember I told you that Lady Yardly’s name was
coupled with that of Gregory Rolf in California three years ago?
_Eh bien_, it was then that she sold him the diamond. She was in
financial difficulties—I have no doubt she had been ‘going the
pace,’ as you say. She sold him the diamond, and had a paste
imitation made. But Lord Yardly, also in financial difficulties,
decides to sell the family jewel. What is Lady Yardly to do? She
is in a hole. At any moment the fact that the diamond is a fake
may be discovered. So she invents this story of the Chinaman and
the warning letters. She has seen Gregory Rolf, and knows that his
wife has the diamond. She uses that fact to give a colour of truth
to her story. She gets you to tell her all about Miss Marvell’s
letters, and then she goes home and ‘receives’ some herself! She
is clever—but she is not clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

“But the robbery to-night?” I asked, bewildered. “The Chinaman—the
darkness?”

“All a little comedy, Hastings! It was Lady Yardly herself who
turned off the light, and then she dropped the necklace (all but the
big stone) where it would be found. And the big stone?”

“Yes, where is the big stone?”

“It is here,” said Poirot. He held out his hand. In the palm of it
lay the great diamond.

“But where did you get it?”

“I picked it up from the floor where Lady Yardly had dropped it—or
rather, where she had _meant_ to drop it. You see, Hastings, she
had the stone in her hand all the time. When the light went out,
she simply wrenched the necklace from her own neck, and then, as
she fell, she let the stone drop. But she missed her aim—it rolled
under a chair. I, who have the eyes of a cat in the dark, saw it.
And I also saw something else.”

“What was that?”

“I saw Lady Yardly’s face when the light went out. It was not the
face of a woman who is afraid—it was the face of a woman who is
acting a part! And now, Hastings, we will go and find Lady Yardly.”

We found her in the library with her husband. She was pale and
trembling.

“Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, “I have something to say to you.”

He then, with the utmost delicacy, told her what he had discovered.
When he had finished, she burst into tears.

“It is true,” she sobbed. “I was so desperate. Gregory Rolf—he
blackmailed me. He had some letters of mine—he said he would show
them to George unless I gave him the diamond. So I gave it to him.
And then, when George wanted to sell it, I didn’t know what to do.
I thought if it were stolen, George would never know that it was
only paste.”

Lord Yardly stepped forward and put his arm round his wife.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said. “I’ve been a bit of a brute
to you. I ought to have known. We’ll start again, and we’ll get
through somehow.”

Poirot turned to me. “You see, Hastings? The ‘Star of the East’
and the ‘Star of the West’—they have met at last. And now, they
must return to the god!”

“You mean——”

“I mean that the diamond must be returned to Mary Marvell. Or rather,
it must be sold, and the money must go to Lord and Lady Yardly.
As for Gregory Rolf—I think he will not trouble them again. I have
a little something here”—he tapped his pocket—“that will ensure
his silence.”

“And the Chinaman?” I asked.

Poirot smiled. “The Chinaman, Hastings, was a very useful piece of
fiction. But the piece of silk you found in the door—that was a
masterstroke! I saw Lady Yardly tear it from her own tea-gown as
she went out of the room!”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a most extraordinary case.”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “But it had its points. And now,
Hastings, let us return to London. I have a great desire for some
of those little cakes that one gets at the pâtisserie in the
High Street.”

“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and that you’ll preserve the diamond for him—and then it goes and
gets stolen right under your nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, with a sudden sparkle in his eyes. “It was
not a very brilliant success. You would propose, then, that we
withdraw, _sur la pointe des pieds_?”

“That is my idea.”

“The ideas of the good Hastings are always excellent,” said Poirot,
and I thought I detected a trace of a smile on his face. “But,
alas! it cannot be. I have stayed the night at the inn, but I
promised to be at the Chase to-morrow morning. And Hercule Poirot
never breaks his word.”

I thought he was making a great mistake, but I said no more.

We were up early the next morning. After breakfast, Poirot asked
for a few minutes’ private conversation with Lord Yardly. The
latter looked weary and distraught.

“Anything you like,” he said. “But the police are here, and I must
give them all the help I can. This is a terrible business.”

“It will only be for a few moments,” promised Poirot.

We were ushered into the library. Poirot closed the door.

“_Milord_,” he began, “I have a little confession to make to you.
I have been in your house under false pretences.”

“What?” Lord Yardly stared.

“I am not here to investigate the affair of Miss Marvell. I am
here because I suspected that a crime would be committed.”

“You suspected? Then why didn’t you prevent it?”

“Because it was necessary to let the crime be committed.”

“What on earth do you mean?”

“I will explain. There were two diamonds—two ‘Stars.’ One of them
is a magnificent stone—a gem of the first water. The other is——”

“Well?”

“A paste imitation.”

Lord Yardly’s face went a curious mottled colour. He sank into a
chair.

“How did you know?” he whispered.

“Because I am Hercule Poirot. And I know also who has the real
stone.”

Lord Yardly sprang up. “You know? Who? Where is it?”

“It is in the hands of the man who found a buyer for it in America.”

“Hoffberg?”

“No, no, not Hoffberg. The man I mean is Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“Gregory Rolf? The actor?”

“Exactly.”

“But—but—how? You are mad!”

“I am never mad,” said Poirot. “Listen. Mr. Rolf had a very clever
plan. He would buy a fine diamond, have a paste copy of it made,
and then—well, he would manage to get the original back again.
It was he who sent those letters to his wife. He knew she would
come to me. He wanted the story of the Chinese god to be well
established. Then, at the right moment, he would steal the stone
from her—and everyone would believe it was the work of the
Chinaman.”

“But Lady Yardly’s diamond? How does that come in?”

“Ah! that was the cleverest part of all. You see, Lady Yardly had
parted with her diamond some years ago.”

“What?” Lord Yardly was almost speechless.

“She was in difficulties, and Mr. Rolf, whom she had known in the
States, helped her. He took the diamond, and gave her a paste
reproduction in its place. He also, no doubt, promised to be silent.
But lately he has been in want of money. He hit upon this scheme.
He knew that the two diamonds were almost exactly alike. He
arranged for the story of the ‘twin’ diamonds to be revived.
The person who sent the letters to Lady Yardly—was Mr. Gregory
Rolf. He knew that, in her terror, she would do anything he
suggested. He probably told her that the only way to avoid a
scandal was to have the stone ‘stolen’ by a Chinaman. She would be
forced to agree. He provided the ‘Chinaman.’ He was the ‘Chinaman’
himself! He staged the whole scene—the lights out—the scream—the
dropped necklace—the piece of silk. It was all very well thought
out. And he has the real Star of the East now!”

“It is impossible!” gasped Lord Yardly. “My wife—she could not——”

“Ask her,” said Poirot.

He stepped to the door and called. In a minute Lady Yardly entered
the room. She looked from one to the other of us. Her face was
deadly pale.

“Maude,” said Lord Yardly. “Is this true?”

She looked at him for a moment, then she sank on her knees and
burst into a passion of weeping.

“I did it for the children, George,” she sobbed. “I was so
unhappy—I didn’t know what to do. And he—he blackmailed me. He
threatened to tell you everything.”

Lord Yardly went to her and put his hand on her shoulder.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said huskily. “Don’t cry. We’ll get
through somehow. Monsieur Poirot, I—I don’t know what to say to
you.”

“There is nothing to say,” said Poirot. “I have been able to serve
you—that is enough. As for Mr. Gregory Rolf, I think we shall find
that he has decided to leave the country—without the Star of the
East.”

“You have it?”

“I have it here,” said Poirot, and he drew the great diamond from
his pocket. “I took the liberty of removing it from the necklace
myself, when I was ministering to Lady Yardly. I thought it would
be safer in my pocket than in that of a ‘Chinaman.’”

He handed the stone to Lord Yardly with a bow.

“And now, Hastings,” he said, turning to me, “I think we may return
to London. Our work here is finished.”

As we were being driven to the station, I turned to Poirot.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said. “How on earth did you
find it all out?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I have often told you that it is the
little things that matter. When Miss Marvell showed me her letters,
I noticed that they were not posted. That was the first point.
Then, when Lady Yardly came, she told me her letters _had_ been
posted. Why the difference? Because Gregory Rolf was on the spot
to deliver his wife’s letters by hand, but he had to post Lady
Yardly’s. Then there was the perfume—the joss-stick. A little
_trop de zèle_, that! And the piece of silk—it was too convenient.
No, Hastings, it was a clever plot, but it could not deceive Hercule
Poirot!”

“But why did you tell Lord Yardly that Gregory Rolf had the diamond?
You had it yourself all the time.”

“It was more dramatic so,” said Poirot. “And besides, it was
necessary to make Lady Yardly confess. Without her confession, I
could have proved nothing. Ah, _mon ami_, the psychology—it is a
great thing!”

I was silent. I was thinking of the look on Lord Yardly’s face when
Poirot had handed him the diamond.

“At any rate,” I said at last, “you’ve saved the Yardly diamond.”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “And yet—do you know, Hastings?—I find
myself a little sorry for Gregory Rolf. He had a great talent—a
very great talent. It is a pity it was not better directed.”

I did not answer. I was still marveling at the genius of my
extraordinary friend.

“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and all will be well—and then the diamond vanishes from under your
very nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, rather crestfallen. “It was not one of my most
striking triumphs.”

This way of describing events almost caused me to smile, but I
stuck to my guns.

“So, having—pardon the expression—rather made a mess of things,
don’t you think it would be more graceful to leave immediately?”

“And the dinner, the without doubt excellent dinner, that the
_chef_ of Lord Yardly has prepared?”

“Oh, what’s dinner!” I said impatiently.

Poirot held up his hands in horror.

“_Mon Dieu!_ It is that in this country you treat the affairs
gastronomic with a criminal indifference.”

“There’s another reason why we should get back to London as soon
as possible,” I continued.

“What is that, my friend?”

“The other diamond,” I said, lowering my voice. “Miss Marvell’s.”

“_Eh bien_, what of it?”

“Don’t you see?” His unusual obtuseness annoyed me. What had
happened to his usually keen wits? “They’ve got one, now they’ll
go for the other.”

I shook my head dubiously. The Chinaman’s methods were so
unconventional that I did not feel easy.

Dinner was a funereal meal. Lord Yardly was naturally downcast.
Lady Yardly had been too shaken to appear. Poirot, however, seemed
to have regained his usual spirits. He prattled away in a light-hearted
fashion that I felt to be distinctly in bad taste.

“_En avant_!” he cried, as he pulled the last walnut towards him.
“The little grey cells, they have worked! Lady Yardly, she is
better—_n’est-ce pas_?”

“She’s resting,” said Lord Yardly. “I’ve told her that it’s no use
crying over spilt milk—but it’s a pretty bad business for me.”

“The case is not yet finished, _milord_,” said Poirot. “You see,
there are several things that are curious.”

“I’ll say they are,” I put in.

“For instance,” continued Poirot, “there is the matter of the
light-switch. Lady Yardly, she was just about to turn it on when
the lights went out. That means that the switches were _inside_
the room, but the Chinaman, he was _outside_ in the hall. How did
he manage to reach them? Then there is the piece of silk. It is a
very important clue, that! And there is the fact that the side
door was found unlocked. Who unlocked it?”

“The Chinaman, of course,” I said.

“But if it was always kept locked, Hastings, he would have had to
possess a key. Where did he get a key? No, no, _mon ami_, we must
seek the person who unlocked that door from the _inside_.”

“What do you mean?” Lord Yardly stared at him.

“I mean,” said Poirot, his voice dropping to a whisper, “that there
was an accomplice—in this very house!”

Lord Yardly went white. “An accomplice? One of the servants? It’s
impossible! I’ve known them for years.”

“Nevertheless,” said Poirot, “the facts are there. Let us go and
visit the scene of the crime.”

We followed him to the hall. Lady Yardly was just descending the
stairs.

“Maude,” said her husband, “Monsieur Poirot has a theory. He thinks
there was someone in the house who helped the thief.”

Lady Yardly gripped the banister. “Someone in the house? Who?”

“That is what I intend to find out,” said Poirot. He looked at her
with a strange, searching gaze. “Madame, I will ask you once more—are
you sure you cannot remember anything else about the man who
attacked you?”

She shook her head. “Everything happened so quickly. I told you
everything I saw.”

“And you, _milord_,” Poirot turned to Lord Yardly, “you saw nothing?”

“Nothing at all. I was in the drawing-room with you and Hastings.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “But I, _milord_, I saw something!
When the lights went out, I did not rush for the door like you and
Hastings. No, I stood quite still. And in the darkness, I saw a
shadow—a shadow that did not belong to a Chinaman!”

“What do you mean?” cried Lady Yardly.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the person who took the diamond was
not a Chinaman at all. It was someone who wanted us to _think_ it
was a Chinaman. Someone who used a piece of silk and a pigtail as
a disguise.”

“But who?” gasped Lord Yardly.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I will show you. But first, I must
ask you to accompany me to London. We must visit Miss Mary Marvell.”

“Miss Marvell?”

“Precisely. If I am not mistaken, she holds the key to the mystery.”

Lord Yardly looked bewildered, but he agreed. We set off for London
in his car. It was late when we reached the hotel, but Poirot
insisted on seeing Miss Marvell at once.

We were shown up to her suite. Gregory Rolf was there, looking
rather surprised to see us.

“Monsieur Poirot! And Lord Yardly! What’s the trouble?”

“The trouble, Mr. Rolf, is that the Star of the East has been
stolen,” said Poirot.

“Stolen!” cried Mary Marvell, coming forward. “Then the warning was
true!”

“It was true, madame,” said Poirot. “But the thief did not go to
China. He came here.”

He turned to Gregory Rolf.

“Mr. Rolf, I believe you have something that belongs to Lord Yardly.”

Rolf laughed. “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“No?” Poirot’s voice was like silk. “Then perhaps you will permit
me to examine your luggage?”

“Luggage? What for?”

“For a certain necklace—and a certain diamond.”

Mary Marvell looked from one to the other, her face pale. “Gregory,
what does he mean?”

Rolf’s face had turned a dull, angry red. “He’s crazy! That’s what
he is!”

“Am I?” Poirot smiled. “Then perhaps you will explain why you were
at Yardly Chase this evening?”

“I wasn’t at Yardly Chase!”

“_Au contraire_,” said Poirot. “I saw you. It was your shadow I
saw in the hall when the lights went out. You see, Mr. Rolf, you
are a very tall man—much taller than any Chinaman. And you have
a very characteristic way of moving.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Rolf.

“Is it?” Poirot turned to Lord Yardly. “_Milord_, I think you will
find your diamond in Mr. Rolf’s possession. He and Lady Yardly
planned this ‘robbery’ together.”

“Maude!” cried Lord Yardly. “It can’t be true!”

“It is true, _milord_,” said Poirot. “Lady Yardly was being
blackmailed by Mr. Rolf. He knew something of her past—something
that happened three years ago in California. He forced her to help
him steal the diamond. She provided the key to the side door, she
turned off the lights, and she pretended to be attacked. Then she
dropped the necklace where it would be found—minus the Star of the
East, which Mr. Rolf had already taken.”

Lady Yardly, who had followed us to London and entered the room
unnoticed, sank into a chair, sobbing.

“It’s true, George! He threatened to tell you everything! I didn’t
know what to do!”

Gregory Rolf made a sudden movement towards the door, but I was
too quick for him. I blocked his way.

“Not so fast, Mr. Rolf,” I said.

Poirot stepped forward and deftly removed a small object from
