Rolf’s pocket. It was the Star of the East.

“So,” said Poirot, “the two eyes of the god have met at last. But
they will not return to China. They will return to their rightful
owners.”

He handed the diamond to Lord Yardly.

“And Miss Marvell’s diamond?” I asked.

“Ah!” Poirot smiled. “Miss Marvell’s diamond was never in any
danger. You see, Hastings, the letters she received were not from
a Chinaman. They were from Mr. Rolf himself. He wanted to create
an atmosphere of mystery and terror, so that when the real robbery
occurred, everyone would blame the ‘Chinaman.’ It was a very clever
scheme—but he forgot the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

Mary Marvell was staring at her husband in horror. “Gregory! How
could you?”

Rolf did not answer. He knew the game was up.

Lord Yardly turned to his wife. His face was grave, but not unkind.

“We’ll talk about this later, Maude. For now, let’s just be thankful
that the diamond is safe.”

As we left the hotel, I turned to Poirot.

“You were marvellous, Poirot! But how did you know it was Rolf?”

“It was the piece of silk, Hastings. It was not from a Chinaman’s
robe at all. It was from a very expensive dressing-gown—the kind
of dressing-gown that a successful film actor might wear. And then
there was the perfume—not joss-stick, but a very particular brand
of cigar that I noticed Mr. Rolf was smoking when he visited my
rooms. After that, it was just a matter of logic.”

I sighed. “I suppose it was. But I must admit, you had me fooled
with that Chinaman story!”

Poirot chuckled. “_Mon ami_, you are an incurable romantic! But
never mind. You have your own talents. For instance, you are a
very good witness—even if you do not always know what it is you
are witnessing!”

And with that, we walked home through the quiet London streets.

I shook my head dubiously. The Chinaman’s methods were so
unconventional that I did not feel easy.

Dinner was a funereal meal. After it Poirot requested a few minutes’
private chat with Lord Yardly. I was not included in the conference.
I wandered out into the hall, and stood looking out of the open
door into the night. My mind was busy with the events of the evening.
I could not help thinking that it was a very lucky thing for Gregory
Rolf that the Yardly diamond had been stolen. The film deal was now
almost certain to go through. But then I felt ashamed of my
suspicions. After all, the man was a gentleman, and he had been
staying at the Magnificent Hotel in London at the time of the
robbery. 

My thoughts were interrupted by Poirot. He came out of the library,
beaming and rubbing his hands.

“Now, my friend,” he cried. “To the inn, and to bed. To-morrow we
return to London. To-morrow shall be a day of great activity! I
have it all—how do you say?—taped out.”

We reached London on the following afternoon. I had thought that
we should go straight to Poirot’s rooms, but he directed the taxi
to the Magnificent Hotel.

“We must see Miss Marvell,” he explained.

We found Gregory Rolf in the lounge. He looked very much upset.

“Thank goodness you’ve come, Monsieur Poirot,” he cried, as soon
as he saw us. “The most terrible thing has happened!”

“What is it?”

“The diamond! It’s gone!”

“What? Stolen?”

“Yes. This morning.”

“How?”

“Mary was in her room. She’d just been looking at the jewel. She’d
laid it on the dressing-table for a moment while she went into the
next room—the bathroom. When she came back, it was gone!”

“Was the door to the corridor locked?”

“No. But the maid was in the little hallway of the suite. She
swears no one passed her. Yet the jewel is gone!”

“Any Chinamen about?” I asked, with a slight smile.

Gregory Rolf looked at me in surprise.

“Why, how did you know? The elevator boy says he took up a
Chinaman to this floor about the time of the robbery.”

I looked at Poirot. He seemed quite unruffled.

“_Bien_,” he said. “The two eyes of the god have returned. The
romance is completed. Let us congratulate ourselves.”

“Congratulate ourselves! When my wife’s fifty-thousand-pound
diamond has been stolen?”

“Be comforted, monsieur. I feel sure that you will eventually
recover your fifty thousand pounds from the insurance company.”

Mr. Rolf stared at him.

“I’d much rather have the jewel back.”

“I do not doubt you,” said Poirot, smiling. “But tell me, when did
the theft take place?”

“About eleven-thirty.”

“_Bien_. I shall have a word or two with the manager.”

We stayed at the hotel for about an hour. Poirot seemed to spend
most of his time talking to various employees. When we finally left,
I was bursting with curiosity.

“Well?” I asked. “What have you discovered?”

“I have discovered, Hastings, that Gregory Rolf is a very fine
actor—but not quite fine enough for Hercule Poirot!”

“What do you mean?”

“The diamond was not stolen at eleven-thirty, my friend. It was
taken much earlier—probably before Miss Marvell even got out of
bed.”

“But the Chinaman?”

“There was no Chinaman. The elevator boy was bribed to say he saw
one.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait, Hastings, wait! The case is not yet complete. There is
another little trip we must take. To Hatton Garden this time.”

I shook my head dubiously. The Chinaman’s methods were so
unconventional that I did not feel easy.

Dinner was a funereal meal. After it we took our departure. Poirot
was very silent, and I felt for him. He was no doubt deeply
chagrined. I tried to cheer him up by suggesting various theories.

“Looking at it plainly,” I said, “the person who has most to gain
is Gregory Rolf. But then he’s in London. If he could have stayed
in town and yet managed the theft, it would be a master-stroke.”

“_Vraiment_,” agreed Poirot. “But he was in London, as you say.”

“Could he have some assistant? A Chinaman?”

“Now you are being romantic again! It is a great disadvantage to
possess a mind of a romantic cast. No, I do not think Mr. Rolf has
anything to do with this.”

“Well, then, who has?”

“_Mon ami_, I have a little idea—not a very big one yet—but it
develops. To-morrow I shall know if it is a good one or not.”

He would say no more, and we retired to rest.

The following morning I was out and about early. When I returned
to our rooms, I found Poirot just finishing his breakfast. He was
beaming with good-humour.

“You are very debonair this morning,” I remarked. “Then your little
idea is a good one?”

“It is excellent.”

“Will you tell me?”

“I have a little question to ask you, Hastings. One, two, three,
and it is done. Is it not that you told me that Lady Yardly told
you that she had been advised by Mary Cavendish to come to me?”

“Yes, she said so.”

“_Tiens!_ That is strange.”

“Why?”

“Because I saw Mary Cavendish yesterday, and she had never heard
of the Star of the East!”

I stared.

“That’s very odd!” I said.

“_N’est-ce pas?_ And there is another small thing. You told me
Lady Yardly’s letters were impregnated with a smell of joss-stick?”

“Yes, I’m sure of it.”

“And you are a great admirer of the ladies, Hastings. You have a
keen eye for the detail of their _toilette_. Tell me, was Lady
Yardly wearing any perfume when you sat so close to her?”

“She had a very subtle and delicious scent,” I replied
enthusiastically. “I don’t know its name, but it was very
distinctive.”

“It was not—joss-stick?”

“No, indeed.”

Poirot nodded and began to hum a little tune.

“Are we going to the hotel to see Mary Marvell?” I asked.

“What for?”

“To warn her.”

“I have already warned her. She will not listen.”

“Well, then, to keep a watch.”

“I have much more important things to do. But I am going to the
hotel. If you like to accompany me, _je ne dis pas non_.”

We found Gregory Rolf in the hall of the _Magnificent_. He looked
very worried.

“Look here,” he said. “Mary’s got it into her head that she’s going
to be robbed to-day. She’s in a state of blue funk.”

“I thought the date was Friday?” I remarked.

“So it is. But Mary thinks they’ll come earlier. She’s locked
herself in her room, and she won’t see anyone.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. He went to the telephone box. In a
few minutes he returned. “Everything is arranged. Mr. Rolf, I wish
you to do exactly as I say. Do not go near your wife’s room. If you
like, you can go for a walk with Captain Hastings. I see that he
is just about to suggest it to you.”

I was, as a matter of fact, doing nothing of the kind, but I fell
in with Poirot’s plan, and the two of us spent a very pleasant
morning together in the Park. Gregory Rolf was a most interesting
companion, and we had much in common.

We returned to the hotel for lunch. Poirot met us. He was beaming.

“Everything is arranged!” he whispered.

“What is arranged?” I asked, but Poirot only winked at me.

After lunch, we sat in the hall for some time. Gregory Rolf was
called away to the telephone, but returned in a few minutes.

“Mary has a most extraordinary idea,” he said. “She wants to see
Monsieur Poirot. She’s heard something that has frightened her
worse than ever. But she’ll only see _him_.”

Poirot rose.

“I will go to her at once. Stay here, I pray of you.”

He was absent for about twenty minutes. When he returned, he looked
very grave.

“Mr. Rolf,” he said, “I must ask you to come upstairs with me. Your
wife has a most extraordinary story to tell.”

We all three went up together. Miss Marvell was sitting on the bed.
She was very pale, and she was shaking all over. As we entered she
gave a little cry.

“Gregory, I’ve been so frightened—oh, so frightened!”

“There, there, Mary,” he said, going to her and putting his arm
round her. “It’s all right. Monsieur Poirot is here.”

“Tell us, madame,” said Poirot.

In a trembling voice, the girl told her story.

“I was sitting here,” she said, “when I heard a little noise—a sort
of scratching. I looked at the door. It was being opened very, very
slowly. Then a hand came round the door—a yellow hand—and then I
saw his face—a Chinaman with a pigtail. I tried to scream, but I
couldn’t. He came right into the room. He had a long knife. He
came up to me, and he said: ‘The diamond—give me the diamond.’ I
was so scared I just gave it to him. Then he went out as he had
come.”

“This is a most extraordinary story,” said Gregory Rolf. “Why, it’s
exactly like Lady Yardly’s.”

“You are right,” said Poirot. “It is very like Lady Yardly’s.”

“But the diamond is gone!” cried the actor. “Monsieur Poirot, what
can we do?”

“We can do nothing,” said Poirot. “The diamond is gone. That is
certain.”

“But the police?”

“The police will be no use.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that I know who stole the diamond.”

“You know? Then who was it?”

“It was not a Chinaman,” said Poirot. “It was Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“Gregory!” cried Mary Marvell.

“What the devil do you mean?” shouted the actor.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that you have been very clever—but not
clever enough for Hercule Poirot.”

The actor laughed. “You must be mad! Why, I’ve been with Captain
Hastings all the morning.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That was your little mistake. You see,
it was not this afternoon that you stole the diamond—it was three
days ago!”

“Three days ago?”

“Precisely. You stole it from your wife then, and you substituted
a paste replica. Then you arranged this little scene to account
for its disappearance. It was very well done—but you should not
have been so anxious to be with Captain Hastings all the morning.
It was too much of an alibi.”

“You can’t prove it!” said Rolf, but his face had gone very white.

“Can I not? We shall see. I have a little idea that if I were to
search your pockets——”

With a sudden movement, Rolf sprang for the door, but Poirot was
too quick for him. In a moment he was struggling in the grasp of
two sturdy men whom Poirot had evidently had in readiness.

“Aha! You see? My friends from Scotland Yard were waiting for you.
It is a pity, Mr. Rolf, but there it is.”

When the actor had been removed, Mary Marvell turned to Poirot.
She was no longer shaking, and her eyes were very hard.

“So Greg’s a thief!” she said. “I might have known it. Well, what
about my diamond?”

“I am afraid,” said Poirot, “that you will never see it again. You
see, it was not really your diamond.”

“Not mine?”

“No. It was Lady Yardly’s.”

“Lady Yardly’s?”

“Precisely. You see, three years ago, when Lord Yardly was in the
States, he had an affair with a certain young lady. To buy her
silence, he gave her the Star of the East. That young lady was
yourself, Miss Marvell.”

The girl didn’t answer. She just stared at him.

“Lord Yardly,” continued Poirot, “has been trying to get it back
ever since. When he found that Gregory Rolf had married you, he
saw his chance. He knew that Rolf was a crook, and he made a deal
with him. Rolf was to steal the diamond from you and return it to
Lord Yardly, and in return Lord Yardly was to give him a large sum
of money. But Rolf was even more of a crook than Lord Yardly
realized. He decided to keep the diamond for himself, and to
pretend it had been stolen by a Chinaman. He had already stolen
the other diamond—the one that really belonged to the Yardly
family—and he intended to keep them both.”

“But the Chinaman at Yardly Chase?” I asked. “Who was he?”

“There was no Chinaman,” said Poirot. “That was Lady Yardly’s
little contribution. You see, she knew that her husband was trying
to get the diamond back, and she was terrified that he would
succeed. She had already sold the real Star of the East to pay her
own debts, and she had a paste replica in its place. She knew that
if her husband ever got his hands on it, he would find out it was
paste. So she arranged the little scene with the Chinaman to
account for its disappearance. It was a very clever idea—but she
forgot that joss-sticks have a very strong smell!”

“And the letters?”

“Gregory Rolf wrote those. He wanted to create an atmosphere of
mystery and Chinese gods. It was all very romantic—as you would
say, Hastings—but it did not deceive Hercule Poirot.”

“But how did you find out?” I asked.

“My friend, I have my methods. And then there was the perfume.
Lady Yardly was wearing a very expensive and very modern perfume—but
her letters smelt of joss-stick! It was a mistake—a very great
mistake. And then there was the fact that Mary Cavendish had never
heard of the Star of the East. That was the finishing touch.”

He turned to Mary Marvell.

“And now, mademoiselle, if I were you, I would return to the States.
I do not think you will find it very comfortable in England.”

The film star rose. She looked at Poirot for a moment, and then
she laughed.

“You’re a clever little man,” she said. “I’ll give you that. Come
on, let’s get out of this.”

When she had gone, I looked at Poirot.

“Well,” I said, “you’ve certainly cleared that up. But I must say
I feel sorry for Lord Yardly.”

“Do not distress yourself, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “Lord Yardly
has his diamond back—or at least, he will have when the police
have finished with Mr. Rolf. And Lady Yardly has her secret—for
I do not think Lord Yardly will ever know that his diamond was a
paste one. So everyone is happy—except perhaps Mr. Gregory Rolf.
And even he will have plenty of time for reflection!”

He smiled at me, and began to arrange his breakfast things with
meticulous care.

“Order and method, Hastings,” he said. “Order and method. That is
the secret of Hercule Poirot!”

I shook my head dubiously. The Chinaman had a way of appearing
when least expected. I felt that Miss Marvell’s diamond was in
imminent danger. Poirot, however, was adamant. He would not leave
Lord Yardly’s dinner.

The meal was a strained one. Lord Yardly was obviously preoccupied,
and Lady Yardly still appeared shaken by her experience. The
representative from Hoffberg’s had been informed of the robbery,
and had departed to report the disaster to his firm. Poirot was the
only one of the party who appeared at his ease. He chatted
incessantly, and his conversation was as varied as it was
entertaining. He seemed to have forgotten the loss of the diamond
entirely.

When we retired to bed, I was too restless to sleep. The events
of the day had left me keyed up to the highest pitch. I felt that
we were on the eve of further developments. If only I could persuade
Poirot to return to London!

Suddenly I sat up in bed. Was it my imagination, or had I heard a
faint sound in the corridor outside my door? I listened intently.
Yes, there it was again—the sound of stealthy footsteps.

In an instant I was out of bed. I crept to the door and opened it
cautiously. The corridor was in darkness, but as I watched, a
dimly-defined figure passed me. I followed it on tip-toe. It led
the way towards the small side door. As the figure reached it, the
moon, which had been obscured by clouds, shone out brilliantly
through the window. The man in front of me was a Chinaman!

With a shout I sprang upon him. He was surprisingly strong, and
we struggled together in the darkness. I felt his fingers at my
throat. I was losing consciousness when suddenly the lights were
switched on.

It was Lord Yardly, followed by Poirot and several of the servants.

“What on earth is the matter?” cried his lordship.

I pointed to the man I was still grappling with. “The Chinaman!”
I gasped.

But it was no Chinaman. It was Gregory Rolf!

I shook my head dubiously. The Chinaman’s methods were so
unconventional that I did not feel easy.

Dinner was a lugubrious meal. Lord Yardly and his wife were equally
depressed. Poirot, however, was in his best form. He prattled
cheerfully, and seemed once more to be completely himself. I
realized that his dismay of a few moments ago had been but
momentary.

He had just started on a story of a royal personage when the butler
once more crept to Lord Yardly’s side.

“Mr. Rolf has just arrived, m’lord. He was most anxious to see
you, so I have shown him into the library.”

Lady Yardly gave a low cry. “Gregory Rolf!”

“The film actor?” I asked, surprised.

Lord Yardly had risen. “I’ll go and see him. Wonder what he wants.”

He was absent for some time. When he returned his face was pale
and his hand shook.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said in a low voice. “I have a most
extraordinary thing to tell you. Miss Marvell’s diamond has been
stolen.”

“What?” I cried, springing up. “And the full of the moon not until
Friday!”

Poirot looked at me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings, I was right. There is no time to be lost. Tell
us the manner of the robbery, _milord_.”

“It happened at the hotel. Miss Marvell was in her room. She had
had the diamond out, and was just about to lock it away when a
Chinaman sprang from behind a screen and snatched it from the table.
He got away through the window.”

“At what time did this occur?” asked Poirot.

“About seven o’clock.”

“Then,” I cried, “the two robberies were almost simultaneous!”

“That is very interesting,” said Poirot. “And how did Mr. Rolf
come to be here?”

“He came down by the 6.30, and on his arrival at the station
received a telegram from his wife telling him what had happened
and saying that she was coming down by the next train. He came up
here at once to see if we were all right. He was terribly upset
about it.”

“I should think so,” I said. “He’s lost a diamond worth fifty
thousand pounds. No wonder he’s upset.”

“It’s a very strange business,” said Lord Yardly. “But I can’t
understand why Maude should be so upset.”

His wife’s face was indeed ashen. She looked like a woman who had
seen a ghost.

“I—I was thinking of the letters,” she gasped. “It’s all so
horrible.”

“_Don’t_ think about it, dear,” said Lord Yardly. “Monsieur Poirot,
what do you advise us to do? I’ve seen the Hoffberg man, and he’s
in a terrible state. He’s gone back to town to see his chief. He
says the whole thing is most fishy. What do you think?”

“I think, _milord_,” said Poirot, “that I should like to see Mr.
Rolf for a few moments.”

“Certainly.” Lord Yardly led the way to the library.

Gregory Rolf was pacing up and down, his handsome face marred by
lines of anxiety. He came forward eagerly.

“Monsieur Poirot? I’ve heard of you, of course. This is a terrible
business. My poor Mary is distracted. She’s coming down by the
next train.”

“I’m sorry to hear that, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot gravely. “There
are several things I want to ask you. First of all, would you mind
letting me see that telegram?”

Rolf produced it from his pocket. It had been despatched from the
Strand at 7.15.

“And now, Mr. Rolf, another question. Where is the Star of the
West at this moment?”

Gregory Rolf looked at him as though he were mad.

“Stolen, of course!”

“But no, it is here,” said Poirot. He dived his hand into his
pocket and produced a large diamond.

“My God!” cried Rolf. “Where did you get it?”

“I found it where the thief had dropped it,” said Poirot calmly.

He turned to Lord Yardly. “I have a little confession to make to
you, _milord_. When I told you I would preserve the diamond for
you, I meant what I said. I have had it in my pocket ever since
I arrived this afternoon.”

“But the necklace——”

“Was a very good imitation, _milord_. It belonged to a little
friend of mine who is on the stage. I borrowed it for the evening.”

Lord Yardly’s face was a study.

“Then the stone the Chinaman stole was——”

“A paste one, _milord_. Also the piece of silk I found. I put it
there myself.”

Gregory Rolf had been watching him with a very curious expression.

“You’re a very clever man, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “But I don’t
quite see your point.”

“Don’t you, Mr. Rolf? It is very simple. I wanted to see what
happened. And I have seen.”

He turned to the door.

“And now, Hastings, I think we may return to town. We have done
our work. Good night, Lord Yardly. I will send you a full report
in a few days.”

We were some way on our journey before I recovered my speech.

“Poirot,” I said, “I’m absolutely bewildered. What on earth does
it all mean?”

Poirot chuckled.

“It means, _mon ami_, that I have been a little more clever than
our friend the film actor. You see, he is a very good actor, but
he is not a very good thief.”

“Gregory Rolf a thief?”

“Precisely. It was he who stole his wife’s diamond—or rather, it
was never stolen at all! He and his wife arranged the whole thing
between them.”

“But why?”

“For the insurance money, of course! They were hard up—and the
stone was insured for a huge sum. They invented the story of the
Chinaman and the god’s eye. Then they heard that Lady Yardly had
a similar stone, and they saw a chance of getting hold of that,
too. Rolf had been a friend of Lady Yardly’s in the past—you
remember the gossip you told me? He blackmailled her into giving
him the stone. She was to pretend it had been stolen by a Chinaman
in the same way. That would divert suspicion from him. It was a
very pretty little plot.”

“But the letters?”

“All part of the game. They sent them to themselves, and Rolf
suggested they should come to me—to give a sort of official air
to the thing. But he didn’t know that Lady Yardly had already been
to see me. When I saw them both together I realized that they were
working in collusion. Lady Yardly was scared to death—I could see
that. She was being driven into it against her will.”

“But how did you know the stone she wore was the real one?”

“I didn’t. I just took a chance. I guessed that Rolf would try to
get hold of it before it was sold to the American. My little
theatrical display was designed to make him show his hand. And he
did! He was so sure the stone had been stolen that he didn’t even
trouble to check the news of his wife’s robbery. He just came down
here to see how things were going. And he fell right into my trap.”

“It’s wonderful,” I said. “Simply wonderful. But what will happen
to them?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“Lord Yardly will get his diamond back, and the Rolfs will have
to find some other way of paying their debts. I don’t think they’ll
try the Chinaman trick again! But it was a pretty little case,
Hastings, a very pretty little case.”

I shook my head dubiously. The full of the moon theory left me
entirely cold. I had my way with Poirot, however, and we departed
immediately, leaving behind us a note of explanation and apology
for Lord Yardly.

In the morning Poirot appeared to be still in a lethargic mood. At
last I managed to drag him out. On the way to the _Magnificent_,
we stopped at a newsagent’s and I bought a bundle of morning
papers. As I had expected, the news of the daring robbery at Yardly
Chase was in all of them. The theft was a most mysterious one. I
pointed the headlines out to Poirot. He nodded.

“_Oui_, they make a great stir. And yet they do not tell us much
that is new. Never mind, the little grey cells, they will work the
better in the quiet.”

“What about the little grey cells of the police? They don’t seem
to have done much.”

“They have not the same method of attack. At the _Magnificent_?
_Bien_. Let us ask for Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

We were ushered into the sitting-room of the film star. He came
forward to meet us. His usual hearty manner was overcast by a
cloud of anxiety.

“I guess you’ve come about this business at Yardly Chase, Monsieur
Poirot? It’s hit us hard. Mary’s just all broke up over it. This
Chinese gang means business. It’s their diamond they’re after, and
they don’t care a hang how they get it.”

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “Is Madame Marvell visible?”

“I’ll see.” He went into the next room and returned a moment or
two later. “Come right in.”

Miss Marvell was sitting up in bed propped with pillows. She was
looking pale and wan.

“Have you heard?” she cried. “Oh, Monsieur Poirot, what shall I
do? I’m scared to death!”

“There is no need to be scared, madame,” said Poirot soothingly.
“No harm shall happen to you.”

“But the diamond? They’ll get that!”

“Not if you do as I say. Listen, madame. I want you to give me that
diamond. I will take it away and keep it in a place of safety.”

The actress’s face went even paler than before.

“Oh, I daren’t! I’ve been so terrified. I sent Gregory to the safe
deposit for it this morning. He’s got it there in that small jewel-case
on the table.”

Poirot walked over to the table and picked up the small black
morocco case. He opened it. There, on its bed of white velvet, lay
the Western Star. Poirot examined it, then snapped the lid to, and
slipped the case into his pocket.

“Now, madame, you can rest in peace. I will answer for the safety
of the jewel.”

“Oh, thank you, thank you, Monsieur Poirot! You’ve taken a load
off my mind.”

“Wait a moment,” I said. “I’ve just thought of something. Mr. Rolf,
did you see a Chinaman at the hotel this morning?”

Gregory Rolf shook his head. “Can’t say I did. Why?”

“There’s one in the hall now,” I said. “I noticed him as we came
through.”

“What?” Rolf sprang to the door. “I’ll get him. If he’s one of the
gang——”

He dashed out.

“He’ll never catch him,” I said. “He was just going out when I saw
him.”

“_N’importe_,” said Poirot. “He did not get what he came for, that
is the great thing. Now, madame, I will wish you a good morning.”

We went out, and I caught sight of the back of Gregory Rolf as he
turned the corner of the corridor.

“One moment, Hastings,” said Poirot. “I have a little word to say
to the manager of the hotel.”

I waited for him. When he returned, he was beaming.

“Now, Hastings,” he said. “To the post-office. I wish to send a
telegram.”

“To Lord Yardly?”

“No.”

He would say no more, and after we had despatched the wire, he
insisted on my going with him to a small out-of-the-way cinema.
He seemed to be enjoying himself hugely, and it was only with the
greatest difficulty that I could get him to discuss the case at
all.

“The case? Oh, that is practically finished!”

“Finished?” I cried. “You know who the thief is?”

“_Mais oui_! It is very simple.”

“Then why don’t you have him arrested?”

“My dear Hastings, I am not the police! I work for my own glory.
Wait until to-morrow, then you shall see what you shall see!”

I was forced to be content with this. But I must say I found Poirot’s
air of mystery very trying.

The following morning we received a visit from Lord Yardly. He
looked very much better than on the previous day.

“Got your telegram, Monsieur Poirot. What is it? You’ve got the
diamond?”

“No, _milord_.”

Lord Yardly’s face fell. “Oh, I thought from your wire——”

“I have something better. If you will be so good as to accompany
me to the _Magnificent_? I have an appointment there with Mr. and
Mrs. Rolf.”

“They’ve got it, then?”

“You shall see.”

When we arrived at the _Magnificent_, we were shown at once to Miss
Marvell’s suite. She was up and dressed, and looked much better.
Gregory Rolf was with her.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “what’s the news? You’ve got our
man?”

“I have not got the man, Mr. Rolf, but I have got the diamond.”

“The Star of the East?” cried Lord Yardly.

“No, the Western Star.”

He drew the jewel-case from his pocket and opened it. The great
diamond lay there in its bed of white velvet.

“But that’s mine!” cried Mary Marvell. “You took it away yesterday!”

“Exactly, madame.”

“Then where is the other? The Star of the East?”

“There is no other,” said Poirot quietly.

There was a moment of dead silence. We all stared at him.

“What do you mean?” gasps Lord Yardly.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that there has only been one diamond—the
one you see before you. Let me reconstruct the story. Three years
ago, Lord Yardly, you were in California. There you met a certain
lady—and you were not very discreet. In fact, you gave her some
very compromising letters. Later, you wanted to get those letters
back. The lady was willing to part with them—for a price. That
price was the Star of the East. You gave it to her, and to account
for its absence you had a clever paste imitation made, which you
gave to your wife. Is it not so?”

Lord Yardly’s face was a study. He did not speak.

“Now, three years later,” continued Poirot, “this lady, who is none
other than Miss Mary Marvell, comes to England. She has the
diamond. She is also about to visit Yardly Chase. It is a dangerous
situation. What does she do? She and her husband, Mr. Gregory Rolf,
invent this story of the Chinese god. They send letters to
themselves—and to Lady Yardly. They know that she has the
imitation, and they believe that she will be too afraid of her
husband to say anything. But they make a mistake. Lady Yardly is
braver than they thought. She goes to a detective—the great Hercule
Poirot!” He bowed. “Mr. Rolf, who has been watching her, sees her
at my rooms. He realizes that he must act quickly. He arranges the
robbery at Yardly Chase. It is he who is the ‘Chinaman.’ He enters
the house by the side door, which he has previously seen to be
unlocked. He stages the scene with Lady Yardly, and then he
‘finds’ the necklace with the diamond—the paste diamond—missing.
And all the time he has the real diamond—the Western Star—which
his wife is supposed to have. It is a very clever plot—but it did
not deceive Hercule Poirot!”

“It’s a lie!” cried Gregory Rolf, but his face was livid.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I have just come from the manager’s office.
He tells me that you were seen in the hotel on the morning of the
robbery—the morning when you were supposed to be in London. And,
further, I have a little piece of silk here—the piece of silk that
was found in the door at Yardly Chase. It is a very interesting
piece of silk. It is not Chinese. It is a piece of a dressing-gown—a
very handsome dressing-gown—which I saw in your room this morning!”

Gregory Rolf made a sudden movement towards the door, but Lord
Yardly was before him.

“No, you don’t!” he cried. “You’ve played your little game, and
you’ve lost. Now, I’ll have my letters back—or I’ll call the
police!”

Gregory Rolf hesitated for a moment, then he drew a bundle of
letters from his pocket and threw them on the table.

“Take them!” he snorted. “They’re no use to me now.”

He and his wife went out of the room, their faces black with rage.

Lord Yardly picked up the letters. His hand was shaking.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I don’t know how to thank you. You’ve
saved me from ruin.”

“_It is nothing_,” said Poirot. “And now, if I might suggest it—give
the diamond to Lady Yardly. It is hers by right, and I think she
has earned it.”

Lord Yardly took the diamond from the case.

“You’re right,” he said. “I’ll go to her at once.”

As he left the room, I turned to Poirot.

“How on earth did you find it all out?” I asked.

“My dear Hastings, it was very simple. From the first, I was struck
by the fact that the two diamonds were so exactly alike. And then,
when Lady Yardly came to see me, I saw that she was terrified—not
of the Chinaman, but of something else. What could it be? Only
one thing—that her husband should find out the truth. And then,
the robbery! It was too well staged—the lights going out, the
scream, the ‘Chinaman’ disappearing. And the piece of silk! It was
too much! It was intended to be found. No, it was all very
transparent. But, _n’importe_, it has ended well. And now, my
friend, let us go and have some lunch. I have a great hunger.”

And as we walked down the street, Poirot hummed a little tune to
himself, looking the very picture of satisfaction. He had added
another triumph to his long list, and he was well pleased with
himself and with the world.

On the following morning, we were sitting at a late breakfast when
the door was burst open and Gregory Rolf dashed into the room.
He was ashy pale, and his great frame shook with emotion.

“It’s gone!” he shouted. “It’s gone!”

Poirot rose. “What is gone?”

“The diamond! The Western Star!”

“Impossible!” I cried. “And Friday not yet here!”

Gregory Rolf sank into a chair. “I laughed at the whole thing,” he
groaned. “But she was terrified. She hid the jewel herself—wouldn’t
even tell me where. And now it’s gone! She’s well-nigh distracted.
The police are there now.”

“How did it go?”

“She must have been followed yesterday. She went to some little
private hotel—I don’t know why.”

“The _St. Mary’s_ in Carlton Gardens?” suggested Poirot.

“That’s it. How did you know? She went there to see a friend, she
says. While she was there, a man broke into her room and ransacked
her jewel-case. She only discovered the loss this morning.”

Poirot looked at his watch. “Ten-thirty. Hastings, my friend, a
taxi. Mr. Rolf, I will accompany you to the hotel.”

On the following morning, Poirot was ahead of me. He greeted me
with a smile, and a telegram which he tossed across the table. It
was from Lord Yardly, and announced the further loss of the diamond
necklace, which had been stolen from the table in the library
during a few minutes’ absence on the part of the man from
Hoffberg’s.

“A good haul for the gentleman from China,” I remarked. “Two
robberies in one night! They are doing well.”

“_Ce n’est pas mal_,” said Poirot. He was checking some figures in
a little book. “_Ce n’est pas mal du tout_.”

“What are you doing, Poirot?”

“I am making a little calculation, Hastings. It is a little whim
of mine.”

“Is it about the value of the diamonds?”

“No, it is not about the value of the diamonds. But, see, here is
the paper. Let us see if there is any news of our friends.”

I took the paper. There was a short account of the robbery at Yardly
Chase, but no mention of any other.

“And now, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, shutting his little book and
putting it in his pocket, “we will go to the _Magnificent_.”

Mary Marvell was in her suite. She was as adorable as ever in a
wonderful morning gown of foaming lace.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot?” she cried. “What about it?”

“Madame, I have to tell you that the Star of the East has been
stolen.”

“Stolen!” she cried. “Then the Yardly diamond _is_ gone?”

“_Oui_, madame.”

“And the Chinaman?”

“The Chinaman was there. Lady Yardly was knocked down and
senseless.”

“Oh!” The girl’s eyes were wide with terror. “Gregory, do you hear?
It’s true! They’ve got it. I shall be the next!”

“Now, Mary, don’t get all worked up,” said Gregory Rolf, coming in
from the next room. “I guess we can look after ourselves. I’m not
taking any chances. I’ve been in touch with a firm of private
detectives, and we’ve got their men on duty day and night. If any
Chink shows his nose in this hotel, he’ll get his head shot off
before he can say ‘knife.’”

Poirot turned to him. “May I ask, Monsieur, why you did not employ
these men before?”

“I didn’t believe in the danger. I do now.”

Poirot nodded. Then he turned to the actress.

“Madame, I would like to see the diamond.”

The girl hesitated a moment, then she went into the bedroom and
returned with a small jewel-case in her hand. She unlocked it and
handed it to my friend.

Within, on its bed of blue velvet, lay the scintillating gem.
Poirot took it out, studied it for a moment, and then replaced it
with a low bow.

“A wonderful stone, madame,” he said. “You are quite sure it is
the same one that I saw three days ago?”

The girl laughed. “Why, of course!”

“I am not so sure,” said Poirot. “You see, I have a little secret
to tell you, madame. I had my suspicions of the Star of the East.
I had an idea that it might be—a paste replica. It occurred to me
that Lord Yardly might have had it made some years ago, when he was
short of money, and have sold the real stone then.”

“Is that so?” said Gregory Rolf, interested.

“It was only a suspicion, you understand,” continued Poirot. “But
it was because of it that I wished to see your diamond. If yours
were the same, I should know that it, too, was a replica.”

“Well?” asked the girl. “Is it?”

“No,” said Poirot, “it is the real stone.”

The actress gave a sigh of relief.

“But I must have it,” continued Poirot. “If I do not, it will be
stolen before the night is out.”

“I’ve got my own men watching,” said Gregory Rolf.

“They will not be of any use,” said Poirot. “No, madame, the stone
must be given into my keeping.”

He spoke with so much authority that the actress was visibly
impressed.

“I—I don’t know,” she wavered.

“_Ecoutez_, madame. I will take the diamond to my rooms. There I
will place it in a safe. At the moment when the Chink thinks he is
stealing it, he will find it is gone.”

The girl laughed. “All right, Monsieur Poirot, you shall have it.
But mind you look after it!”

“I will do that, madame.”

She handed him the little case, and Poirot, with a bow, prepared
to depart.

At the door he turned. “By the way, madame, have you still got
those letters that you received?”

“I think so. Gregory, where did I put them?”

“In the little bureau, I think,” said her husband.

She went to it, and brought them to Poirot. He looked at them and
nodded.

“_Merci_, madame. I will keep these for a little while.”

When we were outside, I expressed my surprise.

“I didn’t know you had a safe, Poirot?”

“I have not, _mon ami_.”

“Then why did you tell her so?”

“Because it sounds better. Now, we must hurry. I have much to do.”

He hailed a taxi. “Scotland Yard,” he said.

At the Yard, he was absent for some time. When he came out, he
seemed well pleased with himself.

“And now,” I asked, “are we going back to our rooms to wait for
the Chinaman?”

“No, my friend, we are going to Yardly Chase.”

“What?” I cried in astonishment. “But the diamond is here!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. He took the jewel-case from his pocket and
opened it. To my horror, it was empty!

“Poirot!” I cried. “The diamond! It has been stolen!”

“Not at all, _mon ami_. I have it here.” He produced a small tissue
paper parcel from another pocket.

“Then why——”

“You will see, Hastings, you will see. For the moment, I must
concentrate. There is much to do.”

We arrived at Yardly Chase late in the afternoon. Lord Yardly was
not there, but Lady Yardly received us. She looked pale and
haggard.

“I am glad you have come, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “Everything
is in such a muddle here. The police—and that man from Hoffberg’s—it
is all very trying.”

“I can understand, madame,” said Poirot sympathetically. “But I
have news for you. I have recovered the Star of the East!”

“What?” She stared at him, her eyes wide with astonishment.

“_Oui_, madame. Here it is.” He produced the diamond.

She took it from him, her hands trembling. “Is it—is it really it?”

“Without doubt, madame.”

“But how—where did you find it?”

“That is my little secret, madame. And now, I have a request to
make. Will you wear this diamond to-night?”

“Wear it? Now? But after what has happened——”

“I beg of you, madame. It is necessary for my plans.”

She hesitated, then she gave in. “Very well, Monsieur Poirot, I
will do as you wish.”

“_Merci_, madame. And now, I must see Lord Yardly.”

“He is in the library. He has just come in.”

We found Lord Yardly with a tall, thin man who was introduced to
us as Mr. Henderson, from Hoffberg’s.

“Glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord Yardly. “But what’s
all this about the diamond? My wife tells me you’ve found it?”

“That is so, _milord_.”

“But where? How?”

“It is a long story, _milord_. But the diamond is safe. That is
the main thing, is it not?”

“Of course, of course. But I don’t understand——”

“You will understand everything in time, _milord_. For the moment,
I must ask you to be patient. I have a little surprise for you
to-night.”

The evening passed quietly. At dinner, Lady Yardly wore the diamond.
It shone with a brilliant light, but I noticed that she seemed
nervous and uneasy.

After dinner, we all assembled in the drawing-room. Poirot seemed
to be in a state of suppressed excitement. He kept looking at his
watch, and glancing at the door.

Suddenly, the door opened, and the butler announced:

“Mr. and Mrs. Gregory Rolf.”

There was a moment of stunned silence. Lord Yardly rose to his
feet, his face flushed with anger.

“What is the meaning of this?” he demanded. “What are these people
doing here?”

Gregory Rolf stepped forward. He looked calm and self-possessed.

“I guess we have a right to be here, Lord Yardly,” he said. “We’ve
come for our diamond.”

“Your diamond?” cried Lord Yardly. “What do you mean?”

“I mean the Western Star,” said Gregory Rolf. “The stone that your
wife is wearing at this moment!”

Lady Yardly gave a cry and clutched at her throat.

“It’s a lie!” she cried. “This is the Star of the East! It has been
in my husband’s family for generations!”

“Is that so?” said Gregory Rolf. “Then maybe you can explain how
it comes to be exactly like the one that was stolen from my wife
this morning?”

“Stolen?” cried Lord Yardly. “Mary’s diamond was stolen?”

“It was,” said Gregory Rolf. “And Monsieur Poirot here was the
last person to have it.”

All eyes turned to Poirot. He was standing in the middle of the
room, a little smile on his lips.

“It is true,” he said. “I did take the diamond from Miss Marvell.
But I did so with her permission.”

“But where is it now?” demanded Gregory Rolf.

“It is here,” said Poirot. He pointed to the diamond on Lady
Yardly’s neck.

A gasp of astonishment went round the room.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What are you saying? You said you had recovered
the Star of the East!”

“So I had, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “But the Star of the East and
the Western Star are one and the same!”

“What?” cried Lord Yardly.

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “Lord Yardly, as he told us, was
in great need of money. Some years ago, he sold the Star of the
East to a certain person. To hide the loss from his wife, he had
a paste replica made, which she has been wearing ever since. The
real stone, meanwhile, passed through several hands until it was
bought by Mr. Gregory Rolf, who gave it to his wife as a wedding
present.”

“But that’s impossible!” cried Lady Yardly. “I’ve had the diamond
all the time!”

“No, madame,” said Poirot. “You have had the paste replica. And
you knew it. That is why you were so opposed to your husband
selling it. You knew that as soon as a lapidary saw it, the fraud
would be discovered.”

Lady Yardly sank into a chair, her face buried in her hands.

“But what about the robbery?” I asked. “And the Chinaman?”

“There was no Chinaman, Hastings,” said Poirot. “It was a little
piece of acting, staged by Lady Yardly herself. She knew that her
husband was determined to sell the stone. If it were stolen, he
could not do so. So she arranged the scene in the drawing-room.
She turned out the lights, screamed, and dropped the necklace—from
which she had already removed the stone. The ‘Chinaman’ was a touch
of local colour, suggested by the letters she had been receiving.”

“But who sent the letters?” I asked.

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is the most interesting part of the case.
The letters were sent by—Mr. Gregory Rolf!”

“Gregory!” cried Mary Marvell.

“_Oui_, madame,” said Poirot. “Mr. Rolf is a very clever man. He
knew the history of the diamond. He knew that Lord Yardly had sold
it, and he guessed that there was a replica at Yardly Chase. He
wanted to get hold of that replica.”

“But why?” I asked.

“Because,” said Poirot, “he had already sold the real diamond!
The stone he gave to his wife was also a paste replica! He wanted
the other one so that, if any questions were ever raised, he could
produce it and say it was the original.”

Gregory Rolf made a movement towards the door, but two men stepped
forward and intercepted him. I recognized them as the detectives
I had seen at Scotland Yard.

“Gregory B. Rolf,” said one of them, “I arrest you for the theft
of the Western Star diamond.”

As they led him away, Mary Marvell burst into tears. Lady Yardly,
too, was weeping quietly. Lord Yardly stood by her, his hand on
her shoulder.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said. “We’ll get through this
somehow.”

Poirot and I walked out into the night.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you’ve done it again. But how did you
know?”

“It was the letters, Hastings. The letters sent to Miss Marvell
spoke of the ‘left eye’ of the god. The letters sent to Lady Yardly
spoke of the ‘right eye.’ But both sets of letters were written
on the same typewriter! And that typewriter, as I discovered at
the _Magnificent_, belonged to Mr. Gregory Rolf!”

“And the perfume?” I asked. “The joss-stick?”

“A little touch of ‘atmosphere,’ _mon ami_. Mr. Rolf is an actor,
remember!”

We walked on in silence for a moment.

“You know, Poirot,” I said, “it’s a bit of a disappointment. I
was looking forward to a real Chinese mystery.”

“_Que voulez-vous_, Hastings? Life is like that. One expects a
romance, and one finds—a fraud!”

He sighed, and then his face brightened.

“But the dinner, _mon ami_! We have missed the dinner of Lord
Yardly, but we will have a dinner of our own! A dinner that will
make us forget all the diamonds in the world!”

And, linked arm in arm, we went in search of a restaurant.

THE END

On the following morning, we were sitting at a late breakfast when
the door flew open and Gregory Rolf dashed into the room. He was
ashen-pale, and his great frame shook with emotion.

“It’s gone!” he gasps. “The diamond’s gone!”

Poirot poured himself out another cup of chocolate.

“Which diamond?” he asked placidly.

“The ‘Western Star.’ Mary’s diamond. It’s been stolen.”

“How?”

“Last night. She was in her room at the hotel. She’d stayed in,
not feeling very well. I’d gone out to a big dinner at the Savoy.
Just as she was sitting down to a light supper, there was a tap
on the door, and a waiter came in with a note. He stood there
waiting for an answer. As she was reading it, he tripped her up,
and while she was still dazed by the fall, he had the jewel-case
out of her hand and was out of the room. He hadn’t even bothered
to lock the door behind him. When she screamed he was gone
completely.”

“What about the waiter?”

“The real waiter was found gagged and bound in a linen closet. The
other man was a ringer—heaven knows how he got into the hotel.
He was a Chinaman, or at least he looked like one—made up, I
suppose. Anyway, the stone’s gone. It’s a bad business.”

Poirot looked at him for a moment with a very curious expression.

“It is a great misfortune,” he said. “And what is the health of
Madame Marvell this morning?”

“She’s naturally prostrate—heartbroken. It’s a terrible loss to
her.”

“And you, Monsieur Rolf? You too are heartbroken?”

“I? It’s a big loss, of course. But I’m thinking of Mary.”

Gregory Rolf went back to the hotel, and Poirot and I were left
alone.

“Well,” I cried, “I was right! Now they’ve got both!”

Poirot smiled.

“My friend, things are not always as they seem.”

“What do you mean?”

“The Western Star was never stolen.”

“But Mr. Rolf has just said so!”

“Precisely. He has just said so. Therefore, I know it is not true.”

“But why should he say so?”

“Ah, _mon ami_, why? Let us go and see Miss Marvell.”

At the hotel, we found the actress in bed. She was indeed prostrate.
She could only repeat the same story over and over again.

“It was the Chinaman, Monsieur Poirot. Just like in the letters.
He came in, and before I knew what was happening, he had the
jewel-case.”

“And you saw his face, madame?”

“It was all yellow—horrible! He was a Chinaman.”

“And the note he brought you?”

“Here it is.” She handed him a crumpled piece of paper. It
contained the same printed words we had seen before.

“And you, Monsieur Rolf?” asked Poirot, turning to the actor.
“What do you make of it?”

“It’s a mystery to me,” said Rolf. “I’ve no idea how the fellow
managed to get into the hotel. But he did.”

Poirot nodded. As we left the room, he beckoned to me.

“Hastings, I have a little commission for you. Go to Yardly Chase.
Tell Lord Yardly that I must see him and his wife at my rooms at
six o’clock this evening. Do not take no for an answer.”

“And you?”

“I have a little visit to pay—to a jeweler in Hatton Garden.”

I did as I was told. Lord and Lady Yardly were surprised at the
summons, but I managed to persuade them to come. When they arrived
at Poirot’s rooms at six o’clock, they found Mary Marvell and
Gregory Rolf already there. The two women looked at each other
with a good deal of curiosity.

Poirot rose and bowed.

“I have asked you all to come here,” he said, “because the mystery
of the two diamonds is at an end.”

“You’ve found them?” cried Mary Marvell.

“One of them, madame. The other was never lost.”

“What?”

“Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, “will you be so good as to tell us
the truth?”

Lady Yardly turned pale.

“I don’t know what you mean,” she faltered.

“I think you do. Three years ago, in California, you met Mr. Gregory
Rolf.”

Mary Marvell started, and looked at her husband.

“You became—shall we say, friends? You were very unhappy with your
husband. You let Mr. Rolf have—the Star of the East. Is it not so?”

Lady Yardly bowed her head in her hands.

“He blackmailed me,” she sobbed. “He told me he would tell George
everything—unless I gave him the diamond. I had a copy made in
paste. George never knew. And then, when he wanted to sell the
diamond to pay his debts, I was in despair. I didn't know what to
do.”

“I will tell you what happened,” said Poirot. “Mr. Rolf, having
the real diamond, decided to create a little diversion. He gave
the diamond to his wife as a wedding present—calling it the Western
Star. But then the time came when Lady Yardly's husband wanted to
sell his diamond. Mr. Rolf saw a danger there. If the two diamonds
were ever compared, it would be seen that one was a fake. So he
invented the story of the Chinese god. He sent the letters to his
wife, and then he saw to it that Lady Yardly received similar
letters. He hoped that, in the panic, both diamonds would be
‘stolen’ by a mysterious Chinaman. Then no one would ever know the
truth.”

“But the diamond that was stolen at Yardly Chase?” I asked.

“The ‘stolen’ diamond was the paste copy, my friend. Lady Yardly,
at my suggestion, played her part. She ‘lost’ her diamond to a
mythical Chinaman. And Mr. Rolf, on his part, ‘lost’ the Western
Star—which was, of course, the real Star of the East.”

“And where is it now?” asked Lord Yardly.

Poirot reached into his pocket and drew out a small box. Inside
it, the great diamond sparkled and shone.

“I took the liberty of recovering it from the ‘Chinaman,’” he said
with a smile. “Or, to be more precise, from the safe deposit where
Mr. Rolf had placed it.”

Gregory Rolf started to speak, but the look on Poirot’s face
silenced him.

“I think, Monsieur Rolf,” said Poirot, “that it would be better if
you and your wife were to leave England as soon as possible. The
climate, it is not healthy for you.”

The actor and his wife left the room without a word.

Lord Yardly stepped forward and took Poirot’s hand.

“I don’t know how to thank you,” he said. “You’ve saved my family’s
honour.”

“It was a small thing,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, what do
you say to a little dinner? I think we have earned it.”

As we walked to the restaurant, I turned to my friend.

“Poirot,” I said, “how did you know?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the simplest thing in the world.
When Lady Yardly came to see us, she said that her letters had a
smell of joss-stick. But the letters of Miss Marvell had no such
smell. Why? Because the ‘Chinaman’ who left them was none other
than Mr. Gregory Rolf. He had not thought of the scent! And then,
at Yardly Chase, I saw Lady Yardly’s face when she looked at her
children. A woman who loves her children as she does, she does not
let herself be blackmailed for a trifle. I knew then that there
was a secret in her past—a secret that involved Mr. Rolf.”

“And the Hatton Garden jeweler?”

“He confirmed my suspicions. He had made the paste copy of the
diamond for Lady Yardly three years ago.”

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I know it, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “I know it.”

Is there anything else I can help you with?

In the morning Poirot appeared to be still in a very lethargic
mood. It was past eleven when we finally arrived at the hotel.

“It is possible that the lady is not yet up,” observed Poirot, as
he presented his card.

After a few minutes, the page returned and informed us that Miss
Marvell was in the sitting-room.

As we entered, a man rose from a desk by the window and came to
meet us. It was Gregory Rolf.

“Mr. Poirot? I’m sorry my wife can’t see you. She’s prostrated by
this morning’s news.”

“What news?” I asked, a sudden foreboding cold at my heart.

For answer he handed me the paper he had been reading.

“Sensational Theft of Famous Diamond!” I read. “The Star of the
West Stolen from Miss Mary Marvell!”

I gasped.

“When? How?”

“Last night. About nine o’clock.”

I looked at Poirot. He seemed quite unruffled, not a bit distressed.

“Aha!” I said. “Nine o’clock! At the same time that the other was
being stolen at Yardly Chase!”

“What?” Rolf cried. “The Star of the East was stolen last night?”

“It was,” I said, and recounted the circumstances.

Rolf seemed thunderstruck.

“This is the most amazing thing I ever heard. It’s a colossal
conspiracy.”

“But how was your diamond stolen, Monsieur?” asked Poirot
placidly.

“My wife has been very nervous lately. Last night she decided to
hand the jewel over to me to take to the safe deposit. She was
just passing it to me, when suddenly the lights went out, and
somebody springing out of the darkness snatched the jewel from her
hand. By the time I’d got the lights on again, the thief had
vanished. But we found a clue. Look!” He went to the desk and
brought out a small piece of embroidered silk.

It was the exact duplicate of the piece I had found at Yardly
Chase!

“I suppose you’ve been to the police?” I asked.

“Sure. And I’ve given them the clue, too. But I’m not hoping for
much. It’s a well-organized gang, that’s what it is.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “It is very similar. Yes, it is very
similar. Do you mind if I go and say a few words to Madame?”

“I’m afraid she’s pretty upset. She’s in her bedroom, and she
wouldn’t even see the police.”

“Still, she will see me. Tell her that I have a message for her
from Lady Yardly. It is very important.”

Rolf hesitated, and then went into the inner room. He returned
after a minute or two.

“Step in, sir. She’ll see you.”

Poirot passed into the room. I followed him. Miss Marvell was
lying on her bed, her eyes red with weeping.

“This is a terrible thing, Monsieur Poirot,” she sobbed.

“Do not distress yourself, Madame,” said Poirot. “It is a great
loss, but I—Hercule Poirot—tell you that all is not yet lost.
Perhaps I can even now recover your jewel.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Only that I have a theory. Hastings, _mon ami_, go and see if Mr.
Rolf has a copy of the _Daily Mirror_ there. I want to see a
paragraph in it.”

I complied. The sitting-room was empty, but I found the paper
Poirot wanted. I returned with it.

My friend was standing by the window.

“Ah, let me see. Yes, yes, I thought so. Now, Madame, I will bid
you _adieu_.”

We left the hotel, and I expressed my surprise that Poirot should
be so little affected by the double loss.

“You don’t seem to care a bit, Poirot!”

“Why should I, my friend? Have I not told you that I will recover
the diamonds?”

“You really think so?”

“I am sure of it. Listen, Hastings. I want you to go down to Yardly
Chase at once. Tell Lord Yardly that I have high hopes, and ask
Lady Yardly to be so kind as to come up to London to-morrow. She
should be at my rooms at eleven o’clock. Can you do this?”

“Certainly. But why don’t you come too?”

“I have much to do here. Matters of the most important.”

I felt that Poirot was once more his old self. He was on the track.
His somewhat incomprehensible conduct of the previous day was
explained.

I duly carried out his instructions. Lord Yardly was eager for news,
and Lady Yardly promised to be at Poirot’s rooms at the time
specified.

I returned to town, and was with Poirot at eleven o’clock the next
morning. He was very silent, and would say nothing of his
intentions.

At a few minutes past eleven, Lady Yardly was announced. Poirot
greeted her with great respect.

“Madame,” he said, “I have sent for you because the time has come
to speak the truth.”

Lady Yardly stared at him.

“The truth? I don’t understand.”

“I think you do. You know where the Star of the East is at this
moment.”

“I?” Lady Yardly turned very pale.

“_Oui_, Madame. It is there!” He pointed to the jewel-case that
stood on the table.

With a cry, Lady Yardly sprang forward.

“My diamond! You have found it! Oh, Monsieur Poirot!” She took the
case in her hands.

“A moment,” said Poirot, his hand on hers. “Is that your diamond,
Lady Yardly?”

“Of course. Why do you ask?”

“Is it the Star of the East?”

Lady Yardly did not answer. She stood as though turned to stone.

“Lady Yardly,” said Poirot, and his voice was very kind. “I know
everything. There were no Chinamen. There was no attack. You wished
your husband to sell the diamond to Gregory Rolf, and you invented
the story of the letters and the Chinaman to make him more willing
to do so. But Gregory Rolf knew that the stone was a paste replica.
The real Star of the East was pawned by you in South Africa three
years ago. You were in great straits—I will not ask why. Gregory
Rolf knew. He has been blackmailing you ever since. You are his
victim. It was he who suggested that you should pretend the stone
was stolen. He had a duplicate of his wife’s diamond made—a paste
one—and it was this that was stolen from Miss Marvell. The real
Western Star has never left her possession.”

“How did you know?” whispered Lady Yardly.

“It was the perfume on your letters—the same that Miss Marvell
uses. That was the first clue. Then your story of the Chinaman.
You and Miss Marvell told the same story, because it was Gregory
Rolf who had suggested it to you both. And finally I found this.”

He held up a small object. It was a shirt-stud.

“I found it on the floor at Yardly Chase—near where you fell. It
belongs to Gregory Rolf. He was at Yardly Chase that night. He was
the ‘Chinaman’ who ‘attacked’ you. It was a well-planned little
comedy, Madame. He intended to get the insurance money for his
wife’s diamond, and at the same time he would have the Star of the
East—which he could then sell. He is a very clever man, Gregory
Rolf!”

Lady Yardly had buried her face in her hands.

“What are you going to do?” she sobbed.

“For you, Madame—nothing. If you will go back to Yardly Chase, and
tell your husband the truth, I think he will forgive you. He is a
good fellow, Lord Yardly. As for Gregory Rolf, I have a little
account to settle with him.”

Lady Yardly rose. She was very pale, but she looked like a woman
who had been eased of a great burden.

“I will do as you say, Monsieur Poirot. You have been very kind.”

When she had gone, I turned to Poirot.

“So Gregory Rolf was the thief!”

“_Précisément_, my friend. A very pretty little plot. He had to
be at Yardly Chase to ‘rob’ Lady Yardly, and at the same time he
had to be at the _Magnificent_ to ‘rob’ his wife. But he managed
it. It was his wife who staged the scene at the hotel—the lights
going out and all the rest of it. She is an actress, remember!”

“But how did you find the diamond?”

“I did not find it, _mon ami_. I have never had it. That jewel-case
I showed to Lady Yardly was empty. I only wanted to see her face
when I told her the diamond was there. It was a little ‘bluff,’
you see.”

“And Gregory Rolf?”

“I think that Mr. Gregory Rolf will find it convenient to leave
England very soon. He is a clever man, but he is not so clever as
Hercule Poirot!”

And Poirot, with a satisfied smile, began to arrange his
ornamental china cats in a perfectly straight line.

In the morning Poirot seemed strangely disinclined to stir out. I
began to suspect that, having made a mistake to start with, he was
singularly loath to proceed with the case. In answer to my
persuasions, he pointed out, with admirable common sense, that as
the details of the affair at Yardly Chase were already in the
morning papers the Rolfs would know quite as much as we could tell
them. I gave way unwillingly.

I turned to the manager. “When did the robbery occur?”

“About an hour ago,” he said, looking at his watch. “As Monsieur
Rolf says, it was very daring. A man representing himself as coming
from Lord Yardly, with a note for Miss Marvell, was shown up to
her room. She was alone at the time, her husband being out. He
seems to have been a person of very plausible address, for he
persuaded her to give him the diamond to take back with him,
ostensibly for the purpose of making some comparison between the
two stones.”

My face showed my disgust at the transparency of the trick.

“Wait,” said the manager. “The most extraordinary part is still to
come. This man—whoever he was—actually had the audacity to write
out a receipt on the hotel stationery.”

He handed a slip of paper across the desk. I read it with amazement.

“Received from Miss Mary Marvell, one diamond (the Western Star),
to be returned to-morrow. (Signed) J. de C. Yardly.”

“Lord Yardly’s signature!” I cried. “It’s a forgery, of course.”

“Without doubt,” said Poirot, who had been listening with the
greatest interest. “But what a very simple-minded thief! To leave
such a trace behind him!”

Gregory Rolf broke in. “Simple-minded or not, he’s got the diamond!
And how did he know that Mary had it with her? We’ve kept it pretty
dark.”

Poirot’s eyes met mine. I knew what he was thinking. The same
thought was in my own mind. Lady Yardly! She had known that Mary
Marvell was bringing the diamond to Yardly Chase. She had been in
the room when the telegram from Hoffberg arrived. Could it be
possible that she—no, the idea was too preposterous. And yet—Lord
Yardly had said she was bitterly opposed to the sale of the Star
of the East. If she could get hold of the other diamond, she might
be able to prevent the sale of her own. But it was a wild,
improbable theory.

“What about the man who brought the note?” I asked the manager.
“Can he be described?”

“The page-boy who took him up says he was a tall, dark man with a
military bearing.”

“That doesn’t help much,” I said. “There must be thousands of men
in London who answer to that description.”

Poirot had been very quiet. He now spoke.

“One little question, Mr. Rolf. When did you last see the diamond?”

“Just before I went out, about half-past eleven. Mary was wearing
it.”

“And you, monsieur?” Poirot turned to the clerk. “When did this
man arrive?”

“At twelve-thirty, sir.”

“And you saw him?”

“Yes, sir. I was at the desk when he came in. He asked for Miss
Marvell.”

“Should you know him again?”

“I think so, sir. He was—as the boy said—tall and dark, with a
small black moustache. He wore a grey suit and a Homburg hat.”

Poirot nodded. “I see. And the note—was it in Lord Yardly’s
handwriting?”

“It appeared to be, sir. I have seen his lordship’s signature once
or twice in the hotel register.”

Poirot turned to the Scotland Yard men. “You are taking steps to
trace this man?”

“Naturally, Monsieur Poirot. We have his description, and we’re
keeping a sharp look-out at all the railway stations and ports.
He can’t have gone far yet.”

“That is good,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse us, I
think there is nothing more that we can do here.”

As we walked away from the hotel, I noticed that Poirot seemed
deeply in thought.

“A very strange case, Hastings,” he said at last. “Very strange
indeed.”

“The audacity of it!” I cried. “To go to the hotel and ask for the
diamond in Lord Yardly’s name!”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “It was—how do you say it?—of a cool
nerve! And the receipt—the receipt was the most extraordinary part
of all. To sign Lord Yardly’s name—it was almost as though he
_wanted_ to be caught.”

“Perhaps he did,” I said jokingly. “Perhaps he’s a kleptomaniac.”

Poirot did not smile. “No, Hastings, I do not think he is a
kleptomaniac. I think he is a very clever man—a very clever man
indeed.”

He relapsed into silence, and did not speak again until we reached
our rooms.

Once there, he threw himself into his armchair and sat with his
eyes closed, his forehead wrinkled in thought. I knew the signs.
The ‘little grey cells’ were at work. I did not disturb him.

After a long interval, he opened his eyes.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have a fancy to see Lord Yardly again. I
think we will go down to Yardly Chase this afternoon.”

“But, my dear Poirot,” I protested, “what is the use? We know all
that he can tell us. And besides, he’ll be in a towering rage after
our sudden departure last night.”

“Nevertheless,” said Poirot firmly, “we go. There is a train at
four o’clock. We shall just catch it.”

On our arrival at the Chase, we were informed that Lord Yardly was
in the library. He received us with a surprised, and none too
friendly, expression.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “this is an unexpected visit.
I thought you had returned to London.”

“I ask a thousand pardons, _milord_,” said Poirot with a humble
bow. “Our departure was—shall we say—a little abrupt. But I have
found out something that I think will interest you.”

Lord Yardly’s face cleared. “Indeed? What is it?”

“It concerns the theft of your diamond,” said Poirot. “And also
the theft of the ‘Western Star.’”

“The ‘Western Star’!” cried Lord Yardly. “Has that been stolen
too?”

“It has,” said Poirot. “This morning, in London.”

He proceeded to give a brief account of the robbery at the
_Magnificent_. Lord Yardly listened with an expression of the
uttermost astonishment.

“But this is incredible!” he cried. “A man in my name—with my
signature! It’s—it’s a most damnable outrage!”

“Quite so, _milord_,” said Poirot. “And now, if I might see Lady
Yardly for a moment?”

“My wife? What has she to do with it?”

“I should like to ask her a few questions about the man who
attacked her last night,” said Poirot.

Lord Yardly hesitated, then rang the bell. “Ask her ladyship to
come here for a moment, Mullings.”

In a few minutes Lady Yardly entered the room. She looked pale and
agitated.

“Monsieur Poirot!” she said. “I did not know you were here.”

“I have come to ask you a question, madame,” said Poirot. “A very
important question. When you were attacked last night, did you
really see a Chinaman?”

Lady Yardly stared at him. “Why, yes—of course. I told you so.”

“And yet,” said Poirot softly, “the side door was locked on the
inside, was it not?”

“I—I don’t know. I thought——”

“It was locked, madame. I examined it myself this morning. And the
piece of silk—the embroidered silk that was caught in the door—it
was from a lady’s scarf, was it not? A scarf that I saw you
wearing yesterday?”

Lady Yardly’s face went deathly white. She sank into a chair.

“What—what do you mean?” she whispered.

“I mean, madame,” said Poirot, “that there was no Chinaman. There
was no attack. You took the diamond from the necklace yourself,
and dropped the rest of it by the door, where you had previously
placed the piece of silk from your scarf.”

Lord Yardly sprang forward. “Poirot! What are you saying? Are you
mad?”

“No, _milord_,” said Poirot, “I am not mad. I am only telling you
the truth. Lady Yardly, why did you do it?”

Lady Yardly burst into tears. “I had to! I had to! He was
blackmailing me!”

“He? Who?” cried Lord Yardly.

“Gregory Rolf,” said Poirot quietly.

We all stared at him in amazement.

“Gregory Rolf!” I cried. “But he’s a famous actor! Why should he
blackmail Lady Yardly?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “three years ago, when Lord and Lady Yardly
were in California, Lady Yardly had a—shall we say—a friendship
with Mr. Rolf. It was a very close friendship—so close that Lady
Yardly gave him her diamond, the ‘Star of the East,’ to pay some
of his debts.”

“Maude!” cried Lord Yardly in horror.

Lady Yardly sobbed heart-brokenly. “It’s true, George. I was a
fool—a wicked fool. But I was so young—and he was so—so—oh, I
can’t explain it! And then, when you wanted to sell the diamond,
I didn’t know what to do. I knew it wasn’t there—that the stone in
the necklace was only a paste replica. I had to do something to
hide the truth. And then those letters started coming—the letters
about the Chinese god. I thought it was a way out—if the diamond
was stolen, you would never know it was a replica.”

“But the letters?” I asked. “Who wrote them?”

“Gregory Rolf,” said Poirot. “He wanted to get hold of the other
diamond—the ‘Western Star’—and he saw a way to do it by using the
story of the twin stones. He knew that if he could get Miss Marvell
to bring her diamond to Yardly Chase, he could find a way to steal
it, and the blame would be laid on the mysterious Chinaman.”

“But the robbery this morning?” I said. “He was at the hotel with
us when we heard about it.”

“He was,” said Poirot. “But he had an accomplice—a man who looked
like Lord Yardly, and who could forge his signature. A man who
is, I suspect, also an actor.”

“But why did he come to you, Poirot?” I asked. “Why did he bring
Miss Marvell to you?”

“Because,” said Poirot with a smile, “he wanted to make the story
more convincing. He knew that if the great Hercule Poirot was
involved, no one would doubt the existence of the Chinese plot.
It was—as I said—a very clever plan. But he made one mistake. He
forgot that Hercule Poirot has—the little grey cells!”

Lord Yardly stood silent for a moment, his face a mask of misery.
Then he went to his wife and put his hand on her shoulder.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said huskily. “We’ll get through it
somehow. I’ve been a bit of an ass myself, you know.”

Lady Yardly looked up at him with eyes full of gratitude.

“And the diamond, Poirot?” I asked. “What will happen to it?”

“The ‘Western Star’ will be returned to Miss Marvell,” said Poirot.
“Mr. Rolf and his accomplice will, I think, find it convenient to
leave the country. And as for the ‘Star of the East’—well, it is
already in the hands of Mr. Hoffberg. I took the liberty of
sending it to him this morning, after I had—shall we say—recovered
it from Mr. Rolf’s rooms.”

“You recovered it?” I cried. “How?”

“By a very simple method, Hastings. I knew that Rolf had the stone,
and I knew that he would not dare to keep it on him. So I—how do
you say it?—I ‘burgled’ his rooms while he was at the hotel with
us. It was—as I have often told you—a matter of _method_!”

I looked at my friend with a new respect. He had certainly lived
up to his reputation.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I think we will go and have that
dinner. I am—how do you say?—famished!”

As we walked away from Yardly Chase, I couldn’t help feeling a
little sorry for Lady Yardly. She had made a terrible mistake, but
she had certainly paid for it.

“Poor woman,” I said. “It must have been a nightmare for her.”

“_Oui, mon ami_,” said Poirot. “But she is lucky to have a husband
who—how do you say?—understands. It is a rare thing, Hastings.
A very rare thing.”

He fell into a thoughtful silence, and we walked on in the quiet
evening air, the mystery of the “Western Star” finally solved.

The story was a simple one. About half-past eleven that morning,
the clerk at the reception-desk had received a telephone call from
Miss Marvell, asking for her jewel-case to be sent up to her room.
She had given the secret password, which had been arranged between
the hotel and herself as a special precaution. A page-boy had
thereupon been dispatched with the case. He had been met at the
door of Miss Marvell’s suite by a man who had taken the case from
him, and given him a tip. The man was described as being small,
dark, and having a somewhat foreign appearance. He had not been
seen since.

Miss Marvell herself, on returning to her room about an hour later,
had been horrified to find the jewel-case missing. She had
immediately communicated with the manager.

The case was found later in an empty room on the same floor. It
had been forced open and the diamond was missing. All the other
jewels were intact.

“But the password?” I cried. “How did the man know that?”

Rolf shook his head.

“That’s the mystery. I don’t believe Mary has ever told it to a
soul but me. I’m certain she hasn’t. And I haven’t breathed it to
anyone.”

Poirot’s face was a study in perplexity. He looked from one to
another.

“But there is something more, _n’est-ce pas_?” he asked.

The manager nodded.

“There is. About five minutes after the case had been delivered,
another call came from Miss Marvell. The same request, and the
same password! Naturally, we told her that the case had already
been sent up.”

“_Ma foi!_” cried Poirot. “This is a very clever thief! He must
have been on the watch. He must have overheard the password when
it was first arranged.”

“That’s what the police think,” said Rolf. “They’re following up
a clue now. They think they know the man.”

I turned to Poirot. “The Chinaman again!”

Poirot nodded. “_Sans doute_,” he murmured. “The Chinaman of Yardly
Chase!”

He seemed strangely uninterested. I could not understand it. He
lounged about the room, his eyes wandering from one object to
another. Suddenly he pounced on a small object which was lying on
the floor. He picked it up and examined it with some interest.

“_Tiens!_” he said. “A piece of silk. And the embroidery is
unmistakable. It has been torn from a Chinaman’s robe.”

I gave a cry of triumph.

“The same clue! Then it _was_ the same man. We’ve got him now.”

But Poirot only shook his head.

“I am not so sure,” he said. “It is too simple—too very simple!”

He turned to the manager.

“I should like to see the room where the jewel-case was found.”

The manager led the way. It was a small, unoccupied bedroom. Poirot
looked round him. He went to the window and looked out. Then he
examined the door.

“It was not locked?”

“No.”

“And the jewel-case—where was it?”

“Under the bed.”

Poirot knelt down and looked under the bed. He stayed there for
some time. When he emerged his face was very red. He was puffing
and blowing.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he gasped. “But I am getting old. My joints, they
stiffen.”

He brushed his knees carefully.

“Well,” I said, as we left the hotel. “What do you think of it
now?”

“I think, Hastings, that we have been very much deceived.”

“You mean that it was not a Chinaman at all?”

“I mean that there was no Chinaman at Yardly Chase, and no Chinaman
at the _Magnificent_.”

“But the piece of silk?”

“A plant, _mon ami_—a plant! To-morrow is Friday—the full of the
moon. We shall see what we shall see.”

“You think something more will happen?”

“I think that we shall have a very interesting day.”

And with that I had to be content.

On the Friday morning, Poirot was in his most enigmatic mood. He
refused to answer any questions, and spent most of the time
polishing his moustaches.

About twelve o’clock the door opened and Lord Yardly was announced.
He looked pale and haggard.

“I’ve had another letter, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “Look at
this.”

He handed a sheet of paper to my friend. On it was printed:

“To-night the two eyes shall meet. At the full of the moon they
shall return to the god.”

“What does it mean?” cried Lord Yardly. “They’ve got my diamond—now
they’re going for the other. But they’ve got that, too! What does
it mean?”

“It means, _milord_,” said Poirot, “that we must act—and act
quickly. Hastings, my hat. We go to the _Magnificent_.”

We found Gregory Rolf and his wife in their sitting-room. They
looked surprised to see us.

“We’ve come about the diamond,” said Poirot. “I have reason to
believe that it is still in this hotel.”

“What?” cried Rolf. “But the police——”

“The police,” said Poirot, “are very good at finding what is there.
I find what is _not_ there! Miss Marvell, I must ask you to be
so good as to come with me to your bedroom.”

Mary Marvell looked at him with wide, frightened eyes.

“What do you mean?” she whispered.

“I will show you,” said Poirot.

We followed him to the bedroom. Poirot went straight to the bed.
He knelt down and felt along the valance. Suddenly he gave a cry
of satisfaction. He drew out a small, dark object. It was the
jewel-case!

“But it’s empty!” cried Rolf. “The police found it empty.”

“_Assurément_,” said Poirot. “It was empty then. It is not empty
now.”

He opened the case. There, on the white velvet, lay the two
diamonds—the Star of the East and the Western Star!

There was a moment of absolute silence. Then Mary Marvell gave a
piercing shriek and fell fainting into her husband’s arms.

“What does it mean?” gasped Lord Yardly. “My diamond! But how——”

Poirot turned to him with a little bow.

“It is very simple, _milord_. The Star of the East was never
stolen from Yardly Chase.”

“But I saw it! I saw the Chinaman!”

“You saw what you were meant to see. Lady Yardly is a very clever
actress. She staged the whole thing. She extinguished the lights,
she screamed, she dropped the necklace. But the Star of the East
was already in her pocket.”

“But why—why?”

“Because, _milord_, she had already sold the diamond! She was in
debt—blackmailed, perhaps—and she had to have money. She sold the
diamond to Mr. Gregory Rolf three years ago in the States. The
stone she wore was a paste replica.”

I saw Rolf’s face go a sickly grey.

“When she heard that the diamond was to be sold, she was
distracted. She knew that the fraud would be discovered. So she
devised this plan. She and Mr. Rolf were in it together. He had
the real stone—the one he had bought from her. He also had his
wife’s stone. The plan was to ‘steal’ both stones, and then, after
the full of the moon, to ‘find’ them again—or perhaps to let the
insurance company pay. The letters, the Chinaman—it was all a
theatrical display, for which Mr. Rolf provided the materials.”

“You mean,” I gasped, “that Gregory Rolf——”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “He is the true culprit. He and Lady
Yardly together. But he was the master mind. He played on his
wife’s fears, and on Lady Yardly’s necessity. It was a very clever
scheme, but he forgot one thing.”

“What was that?” I asked.

“He forgot,” said Poirot, drawing himself up, “the grey cells of
Hercule Poirot!”
