And as we walked home together, Poirot explained the clues that
had led him to the truth—the piece of silk that was ‘too simple,’
the perfume on the letters, and above all, the psychology of the
characters involved.

“It was a great case, Hastings,” he said, twirling his moustache.
“One of my most interesting. But now, let us find a place where
we can have a really excellent lunch. The affairs gastronomic, they
must not be neglected!”

The story was soon told. Miss Marvell had left the diamond in the
hotel safe for the night, intending to wear it for some function
in the evening. That morning, between ten and eleven, her husband
had gone into the office and asked for it. It had been handed to
him without hesitation, as it had been on many previous occasions.
He had then gone out, and not returned until an hour later, only
to deny all knowledge of the transaction. The clerk had been sent
for, and had at once identified him as the man who had received
the jewel.

“The funny thing is,” said Rolf, “that I was out with my wife the
whole morning. We didn’t get back until half-past eleven.”

“Can any one identify you?” asked one of the detectives.

Rolf thought. “Well, let me see. We were at the photographer’s,
Elliott and Fry’s, at half-past ten. They’d be able to say.”

“That’s so,” said the detective. “It’s a case of personation, that’s
what it is. And a pretty clever one, too.”

The clerk was still sticking to his story.

“I’m sure it was Mr. Rolf,” he said, with a bewildered look.

“That’s where the cleverness comes in,” said the detective. “A
first-class make-up, and there you are! Why, I could almost take
my oath it was Mr. Rolf myself.”

“And it was not a Chinaman?” Poirot asked the clerk.

“No, sir, it was Mr. Rolf himself, as I’ve said.”

Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings, it was not a Chinaman this time. Decidedly,
the plot thickens.”

“But what do you make of it?” I asked, as we were being driven
back to our rooms.

“What do you?”

“I? Oh, I’m quite in the dark. It’s a most extraordinary case.”

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “I agree with you. It is _most_
extraordinary.”

He had relapsed into his most enigmatic mood, and I knew that it
was quite useless to question him further.

I was surprised, however, on our arrival, to find a visitor
awaiting us. It was no other than Lady Yardly. She looked pale and
anxious.

“I had to come,” she said. “I couldn’t rest. Tell me, Monsieur
Poirot, is there any news?”

“None, madame,” said Poirot, “except that Miss Marvell’s diamond
has also been stolen.”

“Also?” Lady Yardly gave a little cry. “Then it is true, after all!
The two stones have been reunited. But how? What happened?”

Poirot told her. She listened with the most intense interest.

“It is incredible,” she said, when he had finished. “And you have
no clue to the thief?”

“None, madame.”

“And—and my stone? Is there no chance of its being recovered?”

“I fear not, madame. It has probably been smuggled out of the
country by now.”

Lady Yardly sighed.

“It is a great blow to my husband,” she said. “He had so hoped to
be able to sell it. Now all his plans are ruined.”

“I am sorry, madame,” said Poirot. “But I have done my best.”

“I know you have, Monsieur Poirot. I—I think I will go now. I
only wanted to know if there were any news.”

As soon as she had left the room, Poirot’s whole manner changed.
He became suddenly alert and business-like.

“Hastings,” he said, “I must ask you to do something for me. Go
to the _Magnificent_ and find out from the hall-porter if a
Chinaman has been seen there this morning. Also, I want you to go
to the photographer’s, Elliott and Fry, and find out at what time
Mr. and Mrs. Rolf were there this morning.”

“But, Poirot——”

“Do as I ask you, _mon ami_. I have my reasons.”

I went, though I could not see the use of it. When I returned,
Poirot was sitting in his chair with his eyes closed. He opened
them as I entered.

“Well?”

“The hall-porter says no Chinaman has been seen this morning. As
for the photographers, Mr. and Mrs. Rolf were there at half-past
ten exactly. So that’s that.”

“_Bien!_” said Poirot. “That is what I expected.”

“But I don’t see how it helps you. If Rolf was at the photographer’s
at half-past ten, he couldn’t have been at the hotel at the same
time.”

“Precisely, _mon ami_. And yet the clerk is sure it was he.”

“A clever impersonation,” I suggested.

“_Peut-être_,” said Poirot. “But there is another possibility.”

“What is that?”

“That it _was_ Mr. Rolf.”

“But he was at the photographer’s!”

“Is it not possible to be in two places at once? No, I suppose
not. And yet—if one had a twin brother?”

“Rolf hasn’t a twin brother,” I said.

“No,” said Poirot. “I suppose not. But he has a wife.”

“What do you mean?”

“Suppose it was not Mr. Rolf who went to the photographer’s?”

“But I saw her myself—Mary Marvell!”

“Are you sure, Hastings? You have seen her on the screen many
times, but you did not recognize her in the street. Is it not
possible that some one else—a woman of the same height and build—could
have impersonated her?”

“But who?”

“That is the question,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, I am
going to Yardly Chase. Will you come with me?”

“To Yardly Chase? But why?”

“Because I have a little experiment I want to try.”

He would say no more, and we started off at once. On our arrival
at the Chase, we were told that Lord Yardly was in the library.
We were shown in to him.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “You have news for me?”

“Not exactly news, _milord_,” said Poirot. “But I have a little
theory I should like to test. You will permit me?”

“Certainly, certainly. Anything you like.”

Poirot went to the side door through which the thief had escaped.
He examined it closely.

“It was through this door that the Chinaman went, was it not?”

“Yes,” said Lord Yardly.

“And it was here that the necklace was found?”

“Yes.”

“And here,” Poirot continued, “that this piece of silk was found?”
He held up the fragment of embroidery.

“Yes.”

“_Bien!_” said Poirot. “And now, _milord_, I will tell you what
really happened.”

Lord Yardly stared at him.

“What really happened?”

“Yes. There was no Chinaman, _milord_.”

“No Chinaman? But my wife saw him!”

“Lady Yardly was mistaken,” said Poirot quietly. “Or rather, she
was—shall we say—under a delusion?”

“I don’t understand you.”

“It is very simple, _milord_. The necklace was never stolen.”

“Never stolen? But the Star of the East is missing!”

“Precisely. It is missing because it was never there.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, _milord_, that the Star of the East was sold three years
ago.”

Lord Yardly went deathly pale.

“Sold? Three years ago? What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that Lady Yardly sold the diamond in
California three years ago, and had a paste replica made. It was
this replica that she was wearing last night.”

“Is this true?” gasped Lord Yardly.

“It is the truth,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will permit me,
I will show you how the ‘robbery’ was committed.”

He went to the door and turned out the lights. In the darkness,
we heard him move towards the drawing-room. Then came the sound
of a fall, and a piercing scream.

“The Chinaman!” Poirot’s voice rang out. “The Chinaman—the side
door!”

He turned on the lights again.

“You see, _milord_? It was Lady Yardly herself who staged the
scene. She snatched the necklace from her own neck, dropped it by
the side door, and—fainted. The Star of the East was already gone—she
had only to remove the paste stone from its setting, which she did
later.”

“But why?” cried Lord Yardly. “Why should she do such a thing?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “she was being blackmailed. Gregory Rolf
knew her secret. He had bought the real diamond from her in
California three years ago. When he came to England, he saw a
chance of getting even more money out of her. He threatened to
tell you the truth unless she gave him—the Star of the West.”

“The Star of the West? But that belongs to his wife!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is why he staged the ‘robbery’
at the hotel. He wanted to get possession of his wife’s diamond
without her knowing it, so that he could give it to Lady Yardly
in exchange for—his silence.”

“But this is incredible!” said Lord Yardly.

“It is the truth,” said Poirot. “And if you want proof, you will
find the Star of the West in Lady Yardly’s jewel-case at this very
moment.”

Lord Yardly rang the bell and sent for his wife’s jewel-case. It
was brought, and Poirot quickly found a secret compartment. In
it, wrapped in a piece of silk, was a magnificent diamond.

“The Star of the West,” said Poirot.

At that moment, the door opened and Lady Yardly entered the room.
She looked from one to the other, and then her eyes fell on the
diamond in Poirot’s hand. With a cry, she fell on her knees.

“Forgive me, George!” she sobbed. “I did it for the children’s
sake! I didn’t want you to know!”

Lord Yardly went to her and raised her to her feet.

“It’s all right, Maude,” he said huskily. “I—I understand.”

Poirot and I went out quietly and left them together.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we were driving back to London. “You’ve
done it again. But how did you know?”

“Psychology, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, patting his forehead. “I
knew that Lady Yardly was lying from the first. Her story was too—what
shall we say?—theatrical. And then, there was the scent of the
joss-stick on the letters. That was a mistake. No real Chinaman
would be so—obvious.”

“But what about Gregory Rolf?”

“Ah, Gregory Rolf! He is a clever man, that one! He saw a chance
of getting both diamonds. He would have Lady Yardly’s secret, and
his wife’s diamond as well. He is a _scélérat_, Hastings, but a
clever one!”

“And Mary Marvell?”

“She is an innocent victim. She will get her diamond back, and
she will never know how near she came to losing it.”

“It’s a wonderful case, Poirot,” I said. “One of your best.”

“It has its points,” said Poirot modestly. “It has its points.
But, after all, it was very simple. As I always tell you, Hastings,
it is the little things that matter. The little things!”

The story of the theft was soon told. Miss Marvell had decided to
go to her bank and deposit the diamond there, and had asked the
waiter to call a taxi. A few moments later he returned to say the
taxi was at the door, and that a gentleman from Monsieur Poirot’s
was waiting to see her. A small man, with a very large black
moustache, had been ushered into the room, and had presented a note
signed “Hercule Poirot” to the effect that a plot had been
discovered to rob Miss Marvell of her diamond on her way to the
bank, and that she was to hand it over to the bearer who would be
responsible for its safety.

“And she did?” I cried.

“She did,” said Gregory Rolf. “She was quite unsuspicious, and gave
it to the man at once.”

The clerk broke in. “I saw him go out. I’ll never forget him. He’d
a most extraordinary-looking moustache.”

I looked at Poirot. He seemed quite unmoved.

“_Bien!_” he said at length. “_C’est fini_.”

He turned to the door.

“And what do you propose to do now, Monsieur Poirot?” asked one
of the detectives, with a suspicion of a sneer.

Poirot drew himself up to his full height.

“I? I go to Yardly Chase.”

“To Yardly Chase?” I cried. “But why?”

“Because, _mon ami_, it is there that I shall find the Star of the
West.”

“But it’s at Yardly Chase already! That is, the Star of the East is.”

“The Star of the West _also_, Hastings.”

I followed him from the room, and as we went down the corridor
encountered Mary Marvell herself. She was looking very white and
scared.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she cried, “have you heard?”

“I have heard, madame. And I have just told the good Hastings that
I go to Yardly Chase to find your diamond.”

“To Yardly Chase? But how can it be there?”

“That is my little secret, madame.”

I followed him to the taxi in a state of the most complete
bewilderment.

“Look here, Poirot,” I said, as we drove off, “what is this new
theory of yours? It seems to me the most extraordinary one I’ve ever
heard.”

“_Ma foi_! but it is the only one that fits the facts.”

“But what facts?”

“One very important one, Hastings. Do you not remember that I took
Miss Marvell’s diamond in my hand?”

“Well, what of that?”

“Well, _mon ami_, I am not an expert in jewels, but I have a
certain knowledge, and the stone I held in my hand was—a
paste!”

“A paste?” I gasped. “Then why didn’t you say so?”

“Because it would have been of no use. I wanted to see what would
happen. And now I see.”

“But I don’t.”

“Wait, and you shall see.”

“But the Yardly diamond? Is that a paste too?”

“No, that is the real stone.”

I shook my head in despair. The more Poirot explained, the more
confused I became.

“Wait,” was all he would say. “Wait and see.”

  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

At Yardly Chase we found everything in a state of the greatest
excitement. The police were there, and Lord Yardly was in a state
of collapse.

“My diamond!” he cried. “My diamond! It’s gone. It’s been stolen.”

“Calm yourself, _milord_,” said Poirot. “I have come to restore it
to you.”

“To restore it? Then you’ve got it?”

“Not yet, but I know where it is.”

“Where? Where?”

“In the possession of the person who stole it.”

“And who is that?”

“Wait!”

We were in the library. Poirot went to the door and called.

“Will you come here a moment, Lady Yardly?”

Lady Yardly entered, looking very pale and anxious.

“You wanted me, Monsieur Poirot?”

“Yes, madame. I wanted to tell you that I have found the Star of
the West.”

“The Star of the West? But I thought that was Miss Marvell’s
diamond.”

“So it was, madame. But it is now in this house.”

“In this house? But where?”

“In your possession, madame.”

Lady Yardly drew herself up. “Monsieur Poirot, what do you mean?”

“I mean, madame, that three years ago, when you were in California,
you had a—shall we say, a friendship?—with Mr. Gregory Rolf. And
that, to pay certain debts, you gave him the Star of the East, and
had a paste replica made to take its place.”

Lady Yardly gave a cry and sank into a chair.

“It is true!” she sobbed. “It is true!”

“Then,” continued Poirot, “Mr. Rolf, being a man of business,
re-sold the diamond to another—shall we say, customer?—who
happened to be his wife, Miss Mary Marvell. But recently, you see,
Lord Yardly began to talk of selling the diamond. What was to be
done? You were in despair. Then came the news of Miss Marvell’s
arrival in England. A plan occurred to you. You would pretend that
your diamond also had been threatened by the same Chinese gang.
You thought that, in the confusion, you might be able to steal Miss
Marvell’s diamond, and so replace the one you had lost. But Mr.
Rolf had the same idea! He, too, wanted to get hold of the real
diamond. And so it was he who sent the letters to his wife, and
who finally stole the diamond from her, using a disguise that would
suggest—well, shall we say, a certain Belgian detective? But, alas
for him, the diamond he stole was—the paste one! And now, madame,
I must ask you for the Star of the East.”

Lady Yardly rose, and with trembling fingers drew a small packet
from her bosom.

“Here it is,” she whispered. “But oh, Monsieur Poirot, do not tell
my husband! It would break his heart.”

“Be at ease, madame,” said Poirot. “Your secret is safe with me.
Lord Yardly shall have his diamond, and no one shall be the wiser.”

He turned to the door.

“And now, Hastings, let us go. We have a train to catch.”

In the taxi, I turned to him.

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a marvel! But tell me, how did you know
that Lady Yardly had the diamond?”

“It was very simple, _mon ami_. When I saw the two stones, I
realized that they were both paste! And then I knew that the real
diamond must be—somewhere else! And as Lady Yardly was the only
person who could have had it . . .”

“But you said the Yardly diamond was real!”

“Did I, Hastings? Ah, then I must have been mistaken! But it is
real now, _n’est-ce pas_?”

And with a little chuckle, the great detective settled himself back
in his seat.

  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

The true culprit, as you have seen, was Lady Yardly, who had
originally sold the diamond to Gregory Rolf, and then attempted to
recover it.

He was obviously in a state of some excitement, and as he
proceeded, his story was quite as dramatic as any of his film
productions.

“You’ve heard, I suppose, what happened last night?”

I nodded.

“The Star of the East was stolen from Yardly Chase.”

“Exactly. Well, this morning about eleven o’clock, a man came here
and asked for Mary. He gave his name as Monsieur Hercule Poirot.”

He paused, and I gave an exclamation of astonishment. Poirot sat
perfectly still, but his eyes were very bright.

“He told her,” Rolf continued, “that he had had a lucky inspiration,
and that he had come for the diamond, to take it to a place of
safety.”

“Good heavens!” I cried.

“Mary, being a bit scared after what had happened last night, didn’t
hesitate. She fetched the diamond, and gave it to him.”

“Without a thought of any possible trickery?”

“Why should she? The man was Monsieur Poirot. She had seen him
before, remember.”

“But surely——” I began, but Poirot silenced me with a gesture.

“Go on, Mr. Rolf.”

“Well, it wasn’t ten minutes after he had gone that I came in. Mary
told me what she had done. I saw through it at once. I got the
manager, and we went to the desk. The clerk there had seen a man
leave the hotel a few minutes before, and he’d noticed something
queer about him. We’ve got his description.”

The manager took up the tale. “The man was short, and had a very
remarkable pair of moustaches. He was also slightly lame.”

I looked at Poirot. He seemed quite unruffled.

“And you have no idea who this man was?” I asked.

The manager shook his head. “None. But we’ve got a clue. He
dropped a glove as he went out. It’s an evening glove, and inside
is the name of a well-known firm of London outfitters.”

He held it up as he spoke.

“But this is extraordinary!” I cried. “The thief must have known
Monsieur Poirot’s appearance perfectly.”

“That’s so,” said Rolf. “And he must have known also that Mary
would be likely to be at home at that hour.”

“Wait a minute,” said Poirot, speaking for the first time. “There
is one thing I do not understand. How did the thief know that the
Star of the East had been stolen last night? The news was only in
the morning papers.”

“He might have seen it there,” suggested the manager.

“No,” said Poirot, shaking his head. “He must have known it before.
Otherwise he would not have been so sure of his welcome.”

“That’s true,” said Rolf. “But how could he have known?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He rose to his feet.

“I have seen enough. Hastings, we will go.”

Outside in the street, I turned to him in some excitement.

“You have a clue?”

“A very good one, _mon ami_.”

“What is it?”

“The glove.”

“The glove? But what can that tell you?”

“A great deal. For one thing, it is a very small glove. Almost
small enough for a woman.”

“A woman!” I cried. “You think it was a woman in disguise?”

“It is possible. But there is another thing. Did you notice the
perfume?”

“Perfume?”

“Yes. A very faint, but very distinctive perfume. The same perfume
that Lady Yardly noticed on her letters.”

“Then it was the same person!”

“Undoubtedly.”

“But who?”

“That,” said Poirot, “we shall see.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said: “We will go to Hatton
Garden, Hastings. I want to have a little talk with Mr. Hoffberg.”

Mr. Hoffberg was a small, dark man with a very keen eye. He
received us with some curiosity.

“I’ve heard of you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “What can I do for
you?”

“I want to ask you a few questions about the Star of the East,”
said Poirot.

“Ah! A very fine stone. A very fine stone indeed. It’s a pity it’s
been stolen.”

“You were going to buy it, I believe?”

“I was—if it proved to be all that was claimed for it.”

“And you sent a man down to Yardly Chase last night to see it?”

“I did.”

“What was his name?”

“Mr. Abelstein.”

“And did he see the stone?”

“No. He arrived just after the robbery had taken place.”

“I see. And you have no idea who could have stolen it?”

“None. It’s a very mysterious business.”

“One more question, Mr. Hoffberg. Have you ever seen the Star of
the West—the diamond belonging to Miss Mary Marvell?”

“I have.”

“How does it compare with the Star of the East?”

“They are almost identical. In fact, if they were placed side by
side, it would be very difficult to tell them apart.”

“I thought as much,” said Poirot. “Thank you, Mr. Hoffberg. You
have been most helpful.”

As we left the office, Poirot’s face was very grave.

“Hastings,” he said, “we must go back to the _Magnificent_.”

“Why?”

“I want to see Mr. Gregory Rolf again.”

When we arrived at the hotel, we found Rolf in his sitting-room.
He looked surprised to see us.

“Found out anything?” he asked.

“A great deal,” said Poirot.

He sat down and looked Rolf straight in the eyes.

“Mr. Rolf,” he said, “where is the Star of the West?”

Rolf stared at him. “What do you mean? It’s been stolen, as you
know.”

“No,” said Poirot, shaking his head. “It has not been stolen.”

“But——”

“It has not been stolen, because it was never here.”

“I don’t understand you.”

“It is very simple. The stone that you gave to the man who
pretended to be me was not the Star of the West. It was a
worthless imitation.”

Rolf sprang to his feet. “What are you saying?”

“I am saying,” said Poirot, “that the Star of the West has been in
your possession all the time. You bought it three years ago, as
you said. But you did not give it to your wife. You kept it
yourself.”

“This is preposterous!” cried Rolf.

“Is it? Then perhaps you will explain why you were so anxious to
have it stolen?”

“I wasn’t!”

“Oh, yes, you were. You and Lady Yardly.”

“Lady Yardly!”

“Yes. You and she were in this together. It was a very clever
scheme. You wanted the money from the insurance, and she wanted the
money from the sale of her diamond. So you arranged that both
diamonds should be ‘stolen’ by a mysterious Chinaman. That way,
no one would suspect either of you.”

Rolf sank back into his chair, his face pale.

“How did you know?” he whispered.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “In the first place, there was
the perfume. The same perfume on Lady Yardly’s letters and on the
glove dropped by the ‘thief.’ That suggested a connection between
the two cases. Then there was the fact that the Star of the East
was stolen just when Mr. Hoffberg’s man was expected. That was
very convenient for Lady Yardly, as it prevented the stone from
being examined. And finally, there was the ‘thief’ who pretended
to be me. Only someone who knew me well, and who knew that I was
away from London, could have carried out that plan. And you, Mr.
Rolf, knew both those things.”

Rolf was silent for a moment. Then he said: “You’re too clever for
me, Monsieur Poirot. It’s true. Lady Yardly and I were—well, we
were very good friends in California three years ago. I gave her
the Star of the West then. But lately she’s been in need of money,
and so have I. So we thought of this plan. She was to ‘lose’ her
diamond, and I was to ‘lose’ mine. We thought the Chinese story
would make it all seem very romantic and mysterious.”

“And the Chinaman at Yardly Chase?” I asked.

“That was Lady Yardly herself,” said Poirot. “She had the
embroidered robe and the pigtail ready. It was she who put out the
lights and pretended to be attacked. Then she dropped the
necklace—minus the diamond, which she had already removed—and
slipped back into the room.”

“And the piece of silk?”

“She put that there herself,” said Poirot.

“Well,” said Rolf, with a sigh, “I suppose the game’s up. What
are you going to do?”

“I am going to do nothing,” said Poirot. “Provided,” he added,
“that the diamonds are returned to their rightful owners.”

“They will be,” said Rolf. “I promise you that.”

“Then,” said Poirot, rising, “I think there is no more to be said.”

As we walked back to our rooms, I looked at Poirot with admiration.

“You are marvellous!” I said. “To think that you saw through it all
from the beginning!”

“Not quite from the beginning, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, with a
twinkle in his eye. “But as soon as I realized that the ‘thief’
had a pair of moustaches almost as fine as my own, I knew that he
could be no ordinary criminal!”

A very few minutes sufficed to give us the facts. Mr. Rolf had gone
out of the hotel at 11.15. At 11.30, a gentleman, so like him in
appearance as to pass muster, entered the hotel and demanded the
jewel-case from the safe deposit. He duly signed the receipt,
remarking carelessly as he did so: “Looks a bit different from my
ordinary one, but I hurt my hand getting out of the taxi.” The
clerk merely smiled and remarked that he saw very little difference.
Rolf laughed and said: “Well, don’t run me in as a crook this time,
anyway. I’ve been getting threatening letters from a Chinaman, and
the worst of it is I look rather like a Chink myself—it’s something
about the eyes.”

“I looked at him,” said the clerk who was telling us this, “and I
saw at once what he meant. The eyes slanted up at the corners like
an Oriental’s. I’d never noticed it before.”

“Darn it all, man,” roared Gregory Rolf, leaning forward, “do you
notice it now?”

The man looked up at him and started.

“No, sir,” he said. “I can’t say I do.” And indeed there was
nothing even remotely Oriental about the frank brown eyes that
looked into ours.

“To Lord Yardly, _mon ami_.”

I stared. “What do you want to say to him?”

“Oh, merely a little question—_une petite question_,” said Poirot
flippantly. “And then we dine. To-night, _mon ami_, we dine as we
have never dined before!”

“You are in a very good humour,” I observed, rather nettled.

“_C’est vrai!_ I am always in a good humour when I have been right.”

“But you weren’t right!” I cried. “You’ve been wrong all along!”

Poirot smiled. “Wait, my friend! Wait!”

The next morning, Poirot handed me a telegram. It was from Lord
Yardly, and ran:

“Certainly. Five years ago. In California.”

I stared at it. “What on earth does this mean?”

“It means, _mon ami_, that I have been right! All the same, I must
make a little journey to Yardly Chase. It is better to have everything
cleared up.”

“Then you aren’t coming with me?” I asked.

“Whither do you go?”

“To the _Magnificent_.”

“What for?”

“To offer my condolences to Miss Marvell.”

“_Tiens!_ but that is a very good idea,” said Poirot. “I will go
to Yardly Chase, and you shall go to the _Magnificent_.”

“But don’t you want to see her too?”

“Not yet, _mon ami_, not yet. I have a little business to settle
with Lord Yardly.”

I set off on my mission of sympathy. I found Mary Marvell much
calmer than I had expected. She was sitting up in bed, and her
maid was brushing her hair.

“It’s too bad,” she said, in answer to my condolences. “And Gregory’s
so upset about it. He says he feels it’s his fault for not having
taken better care of it.”

“It must be a great loss to you,” I said sympathetically.

“I’ll say it is! It was such a beautiful stone. But there, I
suppose it’s no use crying over spilt milk.”

I was just leaving when Gregory Rolf came in. He looked very
haggard and worn.

“Any news?” I asked.

He shook his head. “None. And I don’t expect any. Those Chinks are
too clever for us.”

I returned to our rooms, to find Poirot just arrived from his
expedition. He looked tired but triumphant.

“_Eh bien_,” he cried, “I have seen _milord_ and _milady_! I have
cleared up the mystery of the Star of the East!”

“Then you know who stole it?”

“I do.”

“And who was it?”

“Lord Yardly.”

I stared. “Lord Yardly?”

“Precisely. He stole his own diamond.”

“But why?”

“To get the insurance money, of course! He is, as he told us, in
debt, and his wife would not hear of his selling the stone.”

“But—the Chinaman?”

“There was no Chinaman. It was Lady Yardly herself who invented
him.”

“What?”

“Listen, _mon ami_. Three years ago, Lady Yardly was in California.
She was then Miss Maude Stopperton. She met Gregory Rolf. They
became—well—more than friends. He gave her a diamond—the Star of
the East. In return she gave him—certain things. A year later, she
married Lord Yardly. Gregory Rolf also married—Miss Mary Marvell.
But he did not forget Lady Yardly. He began to blackmail her. He
threatened to tell her husband everything, and to show him the
letters she had written him—unless she gave him back the diamond.”

“But it was a family jewel!”

“It was not. It was his gift to her. But she had told her husband
it was a family jewel. She was in a hole. She couldn’t give it back
without her husband’s knowledge. Then Rolf arrived in England.
He and his wife were to visit Yardly Chase. Lady Yardly was in
despair. Then she had a brilliant idea. She would pretend that
the diamond had been stolen by a Chinaman! She wrote the letters
to herself—and also to Mary Marvell—to give colour to the story.
She knew that Gregory Rolf would not dare to say anything for fear
of incriminating himself. He had the diamond—he had had it for some
time—but he wanted to make sure that Lady Yardly would not give
him away. That is why he came to me—to see if I suspected anything.
If I had not been so clever, he would have got away with it. But
I was too much for him!”

“But how did you find out?”

“By the exercise of my little grey cells, _mon ami_! I saw at once
that the story of the Chinaman was a lie. Why should a Chinaman
wait three years before trying to get the diamond? And why should
he write letters beforehand? It was not the Chinese way. Then I
saw Lady Yardly. She was a woman with a secret—a woman who was
afraid. I saw Gregory Rolf. He was a man who was also afraid. I
put two and two together. Then I saw the piece of silk. It was a
piece of Lady Yardly’s own tea-gown! She had torn it off herself
and left it in the door! After that, it was easy. I telegraphed
to Lord Yardly to ask if his wife had been in California five years
ago. He replied that she had. That settled it.”

“But what about the other diamond—Miss Marvell’s?”

“Ah! that was also the work of Gregory Rolf. He saw how well Lady
Yardly’s plan had worked, and he thought he would do the same.
He stole his wife’s diamond, and made it appear that the same
Chinaman had done it! He knew that the insurance company would
pay up, and he would have the diamond as well! It was a very pretty
little plot—but he did not reckon with Hercule Poirot!”

“And what are you going to do about it?”

“Nothing, _mon ami_. Lord Yardly has his diamond back—I found it
in Gregory Rolf’s rooms this morning—and Lady Yardly has her
letters. As for Gregory Rolf, he has lost both the diamond and
the letters. I think that is enough punishment for him.”

“And Mary Marvell?”

“She has her husband—such as he is! And she will get the insurance
money. So everyone is happy—except perhaps the insurance company!
But they can afford it.”

He smiled and began to polish his nails.

“After all, _mon ami_,” he said, “it was a very simple case. But
it had its points—it had its points!”

“To Lord Yardly, _mon ami_.”

“What about?”

“To tell him the Star of the West is safe.”

“Safe?” I cried, thunderstruck. “What do you mean?”

“Just what I say, _mon ami_.”

I knew Poirot’s methods, and the futility of questioning him.

At last, on our return to our rooms, he began his explanation.

“The problem, as I see it, is very simple. We have here two famous
diamonds. They were both stolen by a Chinaman. Who is the
Chinaman? Miss Marvell says she was shadowed by one—but her
husband says he did not see him. Lady Yardly says she saw one
through the door—and as confirmation of her story a piece of silk
is found in the door.”

“Wait a moment,” I cried. “That proves that there _was_ a Chinaman.”

“It proves that there was a piece of silk, _mon ami_—it does not
necessarily prove that there was a Chinaman.”

I began to see light.

“You mean——”

“I mean that there was no Chinaman at Yardly Chase. It was a plant.
Lady Yardly, who is ‘bitterly opposed to her husband selling the
diamond,’ as she tells him—_mais oui_, she tells him—has a very
different reason for not wanting the stone to be seen by an expert
from Hatton Garden!”

“You mean she has already sold it?”

“Exactly. Three years ago she was in California—so was Gregory
Rolf. Gregory Rolf had the stone—the ‘Western Star’—for which he
said he had paid a tenth of its value to a ‘Chink’ in San Francisco.
What a story! Is it not more likely that Lady Yardly, in some
financial difficulty, sold him the ‘Star of the East’ and had a
paste replica made to take its place in the Yardly collection?”

“But then there were two stones!”

“There was only one, _mon ami_—the Yardly diamond. Rolf had it.
He and his wife, between them, hatched the story of the two
diamonds and the ‘Star of the West.’ It was a magnificent piece of
advertisement for Miss Marvell—and it also gave Rolf a chance of
stealing the stone from his own wife and thus claiming the
insurance money!”

“But how did he steal it?”

“I will tell you. He was the man who went to the safe deposit this
morning. He is a ‘movie’ actor, remember. It was the simplest
thing in the world for him to make himself up to look like a
Chinaman—hence the ‘slanted eyes’ the clerk noticed.”

“But the clerk said his eyes were not slanted when he looked at
him just now!”

“Naturally not. He had removed his make-up. It was a very simple
trick, but it worked.”

“And what about the ‘Star of the East’ at Yardly Chase?”

“That was the paste replica. Lady Yardly knew she couldn’t let the
Hatton Garden expert see it, so she had to ‘steal’ it herself!
She knew the story Rolf was putting about, so she simply copied
it. She wrote herself the letters, and then, at the right moment,
she turned out the lights, ‘stole’ the necklace, and dropped it
where it would be found—minus the stone, of course, which she had
already removed.”

“But the piece of silk?”

“She put it there herself, _mon ami_.”

“And how did you know?”

“Psychology, Hastings, psychology! When I saw Lady Yardly with her
children, I knew she was a ‘bonne mère.’ A woman like that does
not sell her family jewels unless she is in some great trouble. I
guessed that she was being blackmailed—by Gregory Rolf! He had
her in his power because he knew she had sold him the diamond
clandestinely.”

“And what did you say to him just now?”

“I told him that I knew everything, and that if he did not return
the diamond to me at once, I would go straight to the police. He
saw that the game was up, and—well, here it is!”

He drew a glittering stone from his pocket.

“I shall return it to Lady Yardly, and I think we can trust her to
see that it is not sold to an American sailing to-morrow!”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must say you’ve come out of it better
than I expected. But you must admit that the ‘full of the moon’
was a bit of a bloomer!”

Poirot smiled.

“Perhaps, _mon ami_—perhaps! But you will admit that it was a
very ‘full’ moon for Mr. Gregory Rolf!”

“To Lord Yardly.”

I made a gesture of impatience. “My dear Poirot, can’t you leave
that unfortunate man alone?”

“Wait!” he said, his eyes dancing. “You shall see.”

A long-drawn sigh escaped from him as we emerged from the post
office.

“Now, Hastings, to the Yardly Chase. We shall arrive just in time
for the tea!”

“What?” I cried. “We’re not going to Yardly Chase?”

“But yes, my friend. It is my little joke, you see. I think this
afternoon we will meet all our friends at the Chase—Lord and Lady
Yardly, Miss Marvell, and Gregory Rolf.”

“I don’t understand you, Poirot.”

“_Ma foi!_ but it is simple. The diamonds have both been stolen.
They are in the hands of the Chinaman. What should he do but return
them to the god? And where should the god be, but at Yardly Chase,
where the first diamond was stolen?”

I began to think Poirot had taken leave of his senses.

“But what do you think you’re going to do?”

“_Attendez, mon ami_! You shall see.”

On our arrival at Yardly Chase, we found that Lord and Lady Yardly
were at home, and that Miss Marvell and Gregory Rolf had only just
arrived.

“This is an unexpected pleasure, Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord
Yardly, with a rather forced smile. “You have some news?”

“I have much news, _milord_,” said Poirot, with a little bow. “And
if you will all follow me into the library, I will tell you what
it is.”

We all trooped into the library, and Poirot took his stand in the
middle of the room. He looked from one to the other of us with his
bright, searching eyes.

“Now,” he said, “I will tell you the story of the two diamonds.
They were both stolen, as you know, by a Chinaman. But who was this
Chinaman?”

He paused, and we all waited with bated breath.

“He was a man,” continued Poirot, “who was very clever, very
daring, and very well acquainted with the habits of his victims.
He knew that Lord Yardly was in debt, and that he wanted to sell
his diamond. He knew that Miss Marvell was a film star, and that
she was very fond of her jewels. And he knew that Lady Yardly was
very attached to her diamond, and did not want to part with it.”

“What are you talking about, Poirot?” I cried.

“Wait!” he said, with a gesture of the hand. “This man, he had a
very simple plan. He would steal both diamonds, and then he would
sell them to a rich American who was looking for just such stones.
But first he had to get them into his possession. And so he
invented the story of the Chinese god, and the letters, and the
Chinaman who left them by hand.”

“But the Chinaman was seen!” cried Lord Yardly. “Lady Yardly saw
him herself!”

“Did she?” said Poirot, with a curious smile. “Let us ask her.”

He turned to Lady Yardly, who was sitting very pale and still in
her chair.

“Lady Yardly,” he said, “will you tell us the truth?”

She looked up at him with wide, frightened eyes.

“The truth?” she whispered.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “The truth. You did not see a Chinaman, did
you?”

There was a moment of intense silence. Then Lady Yardly’s head
dropped, and she began to sob.

“No,” she wailed. “I didn’t! There was no Chinaman! It was all a
lie—a horrible, wicked lie!”

We all stared at her in amazement.

“But the necklace!” cried Lord Yardly. “The gap in the necklace!”

“The diamond was not stolen, _milord_,” said Poirot quietly. “It
had been gone for some time.”

“Gone?” gasped Lord Yardly. “What do you mean?”

“It was sold three years ago,” said Poirot, “when you and Lady
Yardly were in California. It was sold to a certain Mr. Gregory
Rolf.”

A cry of rage broke from Gregory Rolf.

“It’s a lie!” he shouted. “A damned lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain how you came
to have the Star of the East in your possession three years ago,
and why you gave it to your wife as a wedding present?”

“The Western Star!” I cried. “Then the Western Star and the Star
of the East are the same stone?”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “There never were two diamonds. There was
only one. Lady Yardly sold it to Gregory Rolf three years ago to
pay her debts, and it was replaced by a paste replica. But when
she heard that Miss Marvell was coming to England with the real
diamond, she was terrified that the fraud would be discovered. And
so she invented the story of the Chinese god and the letters,
hoping to frighten Miss Marvell into staying away. But when that
failed, she had to think of something else. She had to make it
appear that her diamond had been stolen, so that no one would ever
know that it was only a paste replica.”

“But the theft at the hotel!” I cried. “How do you explain that?”

“That,” said Poirot, “was the work of Mr. Gregory Rolf. He saw his
chance to get the diamond back and at the same time to get the
insurance money. He knew all about the letters and the Chinaman,
and he used them to his own advantage. He was the man who went to
the hotel and claimed the jewel-case, and he was the man who made
up his eyes to look like a Chinaman’s.”

Gregory Rolf made a sudden movement towards the door, but the two
Scotland Yard men, who had been waiting outside, stepped into the
room and intercepted him.

“Gregory Rolf,” said one of them, “I arrest you for the theft of
the Western Star diamond.”

As they led him away, Mary Marvell turned to Poirot with tears in
her eyes.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she sobbed, “how can I ever thank you? You
have saved my diamond!”

“And you, _milord_,” said Poirot, turning to Lord Yardly, “I think
you will find that your diamond is also safe. It is in the hands
of the insurance company, and I have no doubt that they will be
only too glad to return it to you—for a consideration!”

Lord Yardly took his wife’s hand in his.

“Maude,” he said, “can you ever forgive me?”

She looked up at him through her tears.

“Oh, George!” she whispered.

And as we walked out into the evening air, Poirot turned to me
with a smile.

“You see, my friend,” he said, “it is as I told you. In this world,
one must always look for the simplest explanation. And what could
be simpler than that?”

I shook my head. “You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“_Ma foi!_” he said. “I know it!”

“To Lord Yardly. I wish to know if he has sold his diamond.”

“But, Poirot——”

“_Ta-ta-ta_! My little ideas! They are so foolish! But, you see,
I have been wrong—so many times—and I would be quite sure.”

About an hour later we received a reply from Lord Yardly.

“Stone sold to Hoffberg’s man last night. Lord Yardly.”

Poirot’s eyes shone with delight.

“And now,” he said, “we will go to Yardly Chase. We will arrive in
time for dinner.”

“What on earth are we going there for?” I asked.

Poirot only smiled.

It was nearly eight when we arrived. Lord and Lady Yardly were
both in the hall, and they welcomed us with considerable
embarrassment.

“Look here, Monsieur Poirot,” began the former, “the diamond’s
found, you know. I got a wire from the police this afternoon.”

“_Vraiment!_” said Poirot, with an air of great surprise. “Where
did they find it?”

“On a man they arrested at the docks—a Chinaman. He was just
sailing for the East.”

“_Tiens!_ How very remarkable.”

Lady Yardly had come forward, her eyes bright with excitement.

“Isn’t it too wonderful, Monsieur Poirot? And to think that my
husband has sold it after all.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “I would like to speak to you—_en
particulier_—for one moment.”

He led the way into the small morning-room, and Lady Yardly and I
followed him. Closing the door, he turned to her.

“Madame,” he said, “I have a little story to tell you. It is the
story of a young and beautiful woman, who, three years ago, in
California, was so unfortunate as to find herself in a very
difficult position. She was being blackmailed. Is it not so?”

Lady Yardly turned a ghastly white.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“_Pardon_! But I think you do. And the blackmailer—he was a man
you had known in the old days—one Gregory Rolf. He wanted your
diamond—the Star of the East. He had a use for it—a very special
use. He had another diamond—a smaller and less valuable one—which
he called ‘the Western Star.’ He intended to give it to the lady
he was about to marry—but he wanted a better one. He wanted yours.
So he blackmailed you. He made you give him your diamond, and he
gave you ‘the Western Star’ in exchange. Is it not so?”

Lady Yardly was gasping for breath.

“No—no—it’s not true!”

“And then,” continued Poirot, “came the news that he was coming
to England—bringing his wife with him. And she would wear the
diamond. You were terrified. You knew that your husband would be
sure to see it—and that he would realize it was yours. So you
invented this story of the Chinese god. You wrote the letters to
yourself—and then you told your husband about them. You knew that
if he thought there was a plot to steal the diamond, he wouldn't
be surprised if it were stolen. You had to have it stolen—you
understand? Because Gregory Rolf was coming here—to Yardly Chase—and
he would be wearing the diamond—no, his wife would be wearing it.
You couldn't let your husband see it on her.”

Lady Yardly had sunk into a chair. She was sobbing convulsively.

“It’s true—it’s true! He had a letter of mine—a foolish,
indiscreet letter—and he threatened to show it to George. George
is so—so—he wouldn't have understood. He’d have—oh, I don’t know
what he’d have done! I had to give it to him. And then, when I
heard he was coming here, I was nearly mad with terror. I thought
of the Chinese story—it seemed so plausible. And I stole my own
diamond—at least, it wasn't the real diamond—it was the one he’d
given me—the Western Star.”

“And you were the Chinaman!” I cried. “You wore an embroidered silk
wrap, and you put on a pigtail—and you staged that scene in the
drawing-room!”

Lady Yardly nodded. “I thought it was the only way. I didn't know
George was going to sell the diamond.”

“_Ma foi_,” said Poirot. “It was a very clever little plot. But
Gregory Rolf, he is a clever man, too! He saw his chance to get
both diamonds. He staged a robbery of his own diamond—and then
he was going to claim the insurance money! But he didn't know that
Papa Poirot was on his trail!”

He turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings, it was all very simple. The moment I saw Lady
Yardly, I knew she was the woman Gregory Rolf had known in
California. And when I heard about the Chinese god, I knew it was
a romance. People do not send Chinamen to steal diamonds in real
life—except in the ‘movies.’ And Gregory Rolf, he is a ‘movie’
actor—it was his own atmosphere!”

“But what about the diamond the police found?” I asked.

Poirot chuckled. “They didn't find any diamond, my friend! I sent
that wire myself!”

“You!”

“_Mais oui_! I wanted to see how Lady Yardly would take it. And
when she showed such delight—well, then I knew!”

He turned to Lady Yardly.

“And now, Madame, I have a little advice for you. Tell your husband
the truth. He is a good fellow, and he will understand. And as for
Mr. Gregory Rolf—I think we can leave him to the insurance
companies!”

Lady Yardly stood up. She looked at Poirot with a new expression
in her eyes.

“I will,” she said. “I’ll tell him everything. Thank you, Monsieur
Poirot.”

As we drove back to London, I looked at Poirot with admiration.

“You really are a marvel,” I said. “I don’t know how you do it.”

“It is the little grey cells, my friend,” said Poirot, tapping his
forehead. “The little grey cells!”

We sat in silence for a few minutes. Then Poirot spoke again.

“There is one thing that worries me, Hastings.”

“What is that?”

“The Star of the West—it is a very fine diamond. It is a pity it
should belong to such a _scélérat_ as Gregory Rolf.”

“Oh, well,” I said, “you can’t have everything.”

“No,” said Poirot. “I suppose not. But all the same—it is a pity!”

He sighed, and relapsed into silence.

I, too, was silent, thinking over the strange events of the last
few days. It had been a most remarkable case—and Poirot had come
out of it with flying colours. Once again, he had proved that he
was indeed the greatest detective in the world.

And as the lights of London came into view, I felt a sense of
satisfaction and well-being. It was good to be back—and it was
good to have Poirot for a friend.

For, as he would say himself, there is no one quite like Hercule
Poirot!

“To Lord Yardly, _mon ami_.”

I stared. “What on earth for?”

Poirot only smiled. “I have told him to come here at once.”

“What?”

“The Star of the West—it is a most remarkable stone.”

I stared at him. He seemed to have taken leave of his senses.

“The Star of the East is also a remarkable stone.”

“What does all this mean, Poirot?”

“It means that I, Hercule Poirot, have failed, but that I am at
last on the right track. My friend, the case is more subtle than
it appeared. We have to do with a very clever person—one who has
studied the ‘Western Star’ to some purpose.”

The evening was nearly over when Lord Yardly arrived. Poirot and
I were already at the _Magnificent_. Lady Yardly was with her
husband. She looked pale and worn, but her eyes were bright.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” she said, “you have some news for us?”

“_Madame_,” said Poirot, bowing low, “I have the pleasure to
restore to you the Star of the East.”

I gave a gasp of amazement.

“Where did you find it?” I cried.

“It was not far to seek, _mon cher_ Hastings. Now, Lord Yardly, if
you will be so good as to step this way.”

He led the way to the lift. We all followed him.

“I have taken the liberty,” said Poirot, “of taking a small room
on the third floor. I think it will be more private.”

As we entered it, I saw Mary Marvell sitting by the window. She
rose as we came in.

“This is Miss Mary Marvell,” said Poirot, with a wave of the hand.
“Lady Yardly—Miss Marvell.”

The two women looked at each other. Then Mary Marvell’s eyes
dropped.

“I guess I’ve made a mistake,” she said in a low voice.

“A mistake, _madame_?” Poirot’s voice was like a knife-edge. “That
is a very mild word to describe a very cold-blooded and calculated
theft.”

“Theft!” I cried. “Poirot, what do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that the Star of the East was never stolen. It
was in the possession of Lady Yardly all the time.”

“But the Chinaman?” I gasped.

“A myth, _mon ami_—a myth created by Lady Yardly to account for
the disappearance of the diamond which she had already disposed of!”

“Disposed of?” Lord Yardly’s voice was like a thunder-clap. “What
do you mean, Maude?”

Lady Yardly had sunk into a chair, her face buried in her hands.
Poirot took up the tale.

“Three years ago, _milord_, when you were in the States, you were,
as you have told us, in difficulties. To save the situation, Lady
Yardly consented to the sale of the Star of the East. It was sold
to Mr. Gregory Rolf.”

“Gregory Rolf!” I cried.

“_Précisément_. But there was a condition—that it should not be
shown or spoken of for three years. At the end of that time, Mr.
Rolf intended to give it to his wife as a wedding-present. Lady
Yardly, on her side, had a paste replica made, which she wore on
all state occasions. But as the time drew near when the diamond
would be shown in public, she became more and more uneasy. She
knew that a comparison with the real stone would at once reveal
the fraud. Then she saw the paragraph in _Society Gossip_. It gave
her an idea. She would pretend that her stone, also, was being
claimed by the Chinese god. She wrote the letters to herself, and
then, hearing that Miss Marvell had also received warnings, she
saw her way to a still more daring stroke. She would pretend that
her stone had been stolen, and would then be able to claim the
insurance money!”

“But the Chinaman?” I persisted. “I saw the piece of silk in the
door.”

“Lady Yardly placed it there herself. As for the man you saw—there
was no man! Lady Yardly herself turned out the lights, and threw
the necklace where you found it—after having already removed the
paste stone.”

“And the robbery here?” I asked, still bewildered.

“Ah! that was a very different matter. That was a real robbery.
Mr. Gregory Rolf is a very clever man. He saw that if he could
obtain possession of both stones, he could then sell them as a
pair for an enormous sum. He knew that Lady Yardly had a paste
replica. He also knew that she would be afraid to denounce him.
So he staged the robbery at the hotel, using his own resemblance
to a Chinaman to suggest the same Orientals who were supposed to
be after the stones.”

“But the clerk?” I cried. “He said the man had slanting eyes.”

“Mr. Rolf is an actor, _mon ami_! A little piece of transparent
plaster at the corners of the eyes—it is easily done! And he took
care to suggest the idea to the clerk beforehand.”

“But where is the diamond now?” asked Lord Yardly.

“It is here,” said Poirot. He drew from his pocket a small box.
Opening it, he revealed a magnificent diamond. “I found it in Mr.
Rolf’s possession. He had not had time to dispose of it.”

“And the other stone?” asked Mary Marvell.

“The other stone, _madame_,” said Poirot, “is also here.” He drew
another diamond from his pocket. “The Star of the West. It was,
as you said, in the hotel safe deposit. But it was not stolen by
Mr. Rolf. It was stolen by Lady Yardly!”

“Lady Yardly!” we all cried.

“_Oui_. She followed Mr. Rolf to the hotel, and while he was
getting the jewel-case from the safe deposit, she managed to
abstract the Star of the West from his pocket. She thought that
by doing so she would be able to blackmail him into returning her
own diamond. But she did not reckon with Hercule Poirot!”

Lady Yardly rose to her feet. She looked like a woman who had
passed through a long and painful illness.

“It is true,” she said, in a low, dead voice. “I was desperate.
I didn’t know what to do. And then—this man appeared. He told me
he could help me—that he would get my diamond back for me. I didn’t
know he was a thief himself.” She looked at Gregory Rolf, who had
entered the room unobserved.

The actor laughed. “A very pretty story, Lady Yardly. But I’m afraid
it won’t hold water. You see, I have a witness.”

He stepped aside, and a woman entered the room. It was the
middle-aged woman I had seen following Mary Marvell on the day she
first came to Poirot’s rooms.

“This is my secretary, Miss Henderson,” said Rolf. “She was with
me all the morning. She can testify that I never left the hotel.”

Poirot smiled. “Ah! Miss Henderson. I think I have seen you before.
In fact, I have a little description of you here.” He drew a piece
of paper from his pocket. “Middle-aged, grey hair, spectacles.
Yes, it fits perfectly. But there is one thing you have forgotten,
Mr. Rolf.”

“What is that?”

“The little matter of the perfume. The letters which Lady Yardly
received were impregnated with the scent of joss-sticks. And so,
it appears, is Miss Henderson!”

The woman turned pale. “It’s a lie!” she cried.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain how it is
that this piece of silk, which was found in the door at Yardly
Chase, matches exactly with the robe you were wearing on the night
of the robbery?”

He held up the piece of silk I had found. Then he drew another
piece of silk from his pocket—a larger piece, evidently torn from
a garment. The two pieces matched perfectly.

“You see, Mr. Rolf,” said Poirot, “it was not Lady Yardly who
staged the robbery at Yardly Chase. It was you and your accomplice,
Miss Henderson. You knew that Lady Yardly had a paste replica, and
you saw your way to getting possession of it—and the insurance
money as well! You were the ‘Chinaman’ who was seen at Yardly Chase.
And it was you who stole the ‘Western Star’ from the hotel safe
deposit, using your own appearance to disarm suspicion.”

Gregory Rolf's face was a study in rage and fear. He made a sudden
dash for the door, but Poirot was too quick for him.

“No, no, Mr. Rolf. I have a couple of friends from Scotland Yard
waiting outside. I think they would like to have a word with you.”

As the door closed behind the actor and his accomplice, Poirot
turned to Lady Yardly.

“And now, _madame_,” he said, “I think you have a little
confession to make to your husband.”

Lady Yardly looked at Lord Yardly. Then she held out her hands to
him.

“George—can you ever forgive me?”

Lord Yardly took her hands in his. “Of course, Maude. We’ve both
been fools. But it’s all over now.”

Poirot beamed on them. “_C’est bien_,” he murmured. “_Tout est
bien qui finit bien_.”

“But, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to our rooms, “how did
you know it was Gregory Rolf? You seemed so sure it was a
Chinaman.”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “it is always the simplest explanation
that is the most likely. A Chinaman in the middle of the English
countryside? It is too romantic—too like a story-book! No, I knew
it must be someone who had an interest in the diamonds. And who
had a greater interest than the man who had already bought one of
them, and who stood to gain so much by the possession of both?”

“But the eyes?” I persisted. “The clerk said they were slanted.”

“Mr. Rolf is an actor, _mon ami_! As I told you, a little piece of
transparent plaster is easily applied. And he had already
prepared the mind of the clerk by his remarks about his own
appearance.”

“And the piece of silk?”

“A very old trick, Hastings! But a very effective one. It
suggested the Orient at once. And as for the perfume—well, that
was a little mistake on the part of Miss Henderson. She should not
have been so fond of joss-sticks!”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“Ah! Lady Yardly. She was a very foolish woman. But she has
learnt her lesson. And I think, _mon ami_, that the ‘Western Star’
and the ‘Star of the East’ will not meet again for some time to
come!”

We had reached our rooms. Poirot sat down in his comfortable chair
and sighed with satisfaction.

“A very pretty little problem, Hastings! And one that required all
the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot!”

I looked at him. He was quite his old self again.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I know it, _mon ami_,” he replied placidly. “I know it!”

“Lord Yardly.” He discounted further inquiries by slipping his arm
through mine. “Come, come, _mon ami_. I know all that you feel
about this miserable business. I have not distinguished myself!
You, in my place, might have distinguished yourself! _Bien!_ All
is admitted. Let us forget it and have lunch.”

It was about four o’clock when we entered Poirot’s rooms. A figure
rose from a chair by the window. It was Lord Yardly. He looked
haggard and distraught.

“I got your wire and came up at once. Look here, I’ve been round
to Hoffberg, and they know nothing about that man of theirs last
night, or the wire either. Do you think that——”

Poirot held up his hand.

“My excuses! I sent that wire, and hired the gentleman in question.”

“_You_—but why? What?” The nobleman spluttered impotently.

“My little idea was to bring things to a head,” explained Poirot
placidly.

“Bring things to a head! Oh, my God!” cried Lord Yardly.

“And the ruse succeeded,” said Poirot cheerfully. “Therefore,
_milord_, I have much pleasure in returning you—this!” With a
dramatic gesture he produced a glittering object. It was a great
diamond.

“The Star of the East,” gasped Lord Yardly. “But I don’t
understand——”

“_Oui_, my friend. And why not? He’s a clever fellow, this Gregory
Rolf. He had only been in London a few days when he heard of this
Star of the East, and he knew it was the duplicate of his own
Western Star. He was also a friend of Lady Yardly’s. He’d known
her in America three years ago. At that time she had been indiscreet
and he had letters of hers in his possession. He used these to
extort the Star of the East from her. She didn’t dare tell her
husband, and she’d given the diamond to Rolf. The ‘Chinese’
letters were an invention of his to divert suspicion. He’d already
given the diamond to his wife as a wedding present. He didn’t think
they’d ever be likely to meet.”

“But they did meet!” I cried. “And you——”

“I—_mon cher_—guessed it when I saw that Mary Marvell was wearing
it. She’d probably insisted on wearing it to show off before Lady
Yardly, whose diamond was only a paste replica. I guessed it then.
And I knew Gregory Rolf was behind it all. He’s a fine actor, and
he’d played his part with the greatest skill. But when he found
that I was onto him, he preferred to return the diamond rather
than face a scandal.”

“And Miss Marvell’s diamond?” I asked.

“My dear Hastings, there never _was_ a second diamond! There was
only one—the Western Star. Gregory Rolf had had it all the time.
He merely invented the story of the second stone to make his wife’s
diamond seem even more valuable. It was a very clever piece of
bluff.”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“Ah, Lady Yardly! She was only too glad to get her diamond back
without any more fuss. She’ll be more careful of her letters in
future, I fancy!”

“It’s a wonderful case, Poirot!” I cried.

“_Pas mal_,” said Poirot, with a modest shrug. “But it was a
simple problem—a very simple problem—to one who knows how to
think!”

“Precisely. He had it on him.”

“But he didn’t steal it?”

“No, _mon ami_. He _gave_ it to me.”

“Gave it to you?”

“Why, yes! You see, Gregory Rolf is a person of a very great
imagination. He have his little plan—and it was a very clever little
plan. He think: ‘I will steal the diamond of Mary, and also I will
steal the diamond of Lady Yardly—and so I will have both diamonds!
But I cannot steal the diamond of Lady Yardly—it is already
gone!’”

“Gone?” I echoed.

“_Oui_, my friend. Lady Yardly have no diamond. She have only a
paste imitation. She have sell the real diamond three years ago—to
Gregory Rolf!”

“But why——”

“To pay her debts, _mon cher_. She was very hard pressed. And Mr.
Rolf, he was very galant—he buy the diamond, and then he say to
her: ‘I will keep the diamond, and you shall have the paste
imitation—and no one will know the difference!’”

“But the letters—the Chinaman?”

“The letters? _C’est magnifique_, that! Mr. Rolf, he have a great
talent for the theatre. He write the letters to Mary, and he send
the Chinaman to leave them. Then he think: ‘If I send letters also
to Lady Yardly, she will be too frightened to say anything when I
steal her diamond! For she will think it is the Chinaman who has
stolen it!’”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“She was in a great state of mind when she come here. She did not
know what to do! She think: ‘If the diamond is stolen, George will
find out that it is only paste!’ So she come to seek the advice
of Poirot. But I am out, and she see instead the great Hastings!
And he—he put the idea into her head! He say: ‘You have received
blackmailing letters?’ And she say: ‘_Oui_.’ She catch at the
straw! And when I come back, I see at once that something is
wrong—that Lady Yardly is hiding something.”

“But the scene at Yardly Chase?” I asked, still puzzled.

“Ah! _ca!_ That was where I had my little idea! I send the telegram
from Hoffberg, and I send the man to vet the stone. And then Lady
Yardly, she is in a great taking! She think: ‘Now all will be
discovered!’ So she make her little plan. She turn out the lights,
she scream, she drop the necklace—and she keep the diamond! But
she do not know that I am watching her! And when I see her pick
up the diamond and hide it in her dress—then I know!”

“And what did you do?”

“I say to her: ‘Madame, I know all. Give me the diamond, and I
will see that no one knows. But you must tell me the truth.’ And
she tell me. And then I go to Mr. Rolf, and I say to him: ‘Monsieur,
I have the diamond of Lady Yardly. If you do not give me the
diamond of Mary Marvell, I will tell the police all that I know!’
And he—he is a man of business, and he see that the game is up.
So he give me the diamond.”

“But why did he steal his wife’s diamond?”

“Ah! _mon cher_, he is a very extravagant man, is Mr. Rolf! And
he have many debts. And he think: ‘If the diamond is stolen, I
will have the insurance money, and I will also have the diamond!’”

“But what about the Chinaman at the door?”

“There was no Chinaman, _mon ami_. Lady Yardly, she have the great
talent for the theatre also! She tear the piece of silk from her
own gown, and she drop it by the door!”

“And the clerk at the hotel—the slanting eyes?”

“Mr. Rolf, he have the great talent for the make-up, as I told
you! It was very simple for him to change his appearance slightly.”

I sighed. “It seems very simple now you explain it.”

“It is always simple—when one uses the little grey cells of the
brain!” said Poirot, with a smile.

“And what will happen now?”

“Lady Yardly have her diamond back—and she have no more debts. And
Mr. Rolf—well, I think Mr. Rolf will find it convenient to return
to America as soon as possible! And Mary Marvell—she have a very
good advertisement for her new film!”

“And the ‘Western Star’?”

“It is where it always was—in the possession of its rightful
owner.”

“But which is the rightful owner?”

Poirot smiled. “That, _mon ami_, is a question that I do not
propose to answer!”

“But what about the god with the two eyes?”

“The god? _Ah, le bon Dieu!_ I think he is very well content! He
have his two eyes back again—or at least he think he has! And in
this world, _mon ami_, it is the illusion that counts!”

I looked at Poirot. He was smiling to himself, and his eyes were
shining with a gentle light.

“You are a very great man, Poirot,” I said.

“_Mais oui_,” said Poirot, “I know it well!”

I laughed. “And you are also a very conceited one!”

“What will you? When one is unique, one knows it! And now, _mon
ami_, let us go and have that dinner of which I spoke! I have a
great hunger!”

And so, arm in arm, we went out into the night.

“_Oui!_” Poirot laughed. “He stole it from the hotel. He was the
man who walked in at 11.30. He was the man who had been shadowing
the girl that first morning—though she did not know it! He saw the
whole thing—including the letters he himself had written!”

“I don’t follow.”

“_Ma foi_, it is so simple! It was Gregory Rolf who had the diamond,
the Western Star. He had already sold it to some one else, and
this was his way of getting it back. He knew that the two diamonds
were so much alike as to be indistinguishable. So he chose the
Yardly diamond to be stolen first, and then his own. Then he would
claim the insurance money on the Western Star, and no one would
be any the wiser.”

“But the Chinaman?” I asked.

Poirot laughed again. “There was no Chinaman. That was Gregory
Rolf in a clever disguise. It was he who was seen by Lady Yardly.”

“And Lady Yardly? Why did she tell us such a tale?”

“Ah, that is the most interesting part of the story! You see, she
too was in a hole. She had already sold the diamond herself to
Gregory Rolf three years ago! She was being blackmailed by him,
and she saw in this story of the Chinaman a way out of her
difficulties.”

“Then she never had the diamond at all?”

“_Si_, she had a very clever imitation—made by Gregory Rolf. He
it was who suggested the whole idea to her.”

“And you found all this out?”

“By the exercise of my little grey cells, _mon ami_! And now, if
you will excuse me, I must attend to my correspondence.”

And the little man sat down at his desk and began to write, leaving
me more than ever impressed by the genius of my friend.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


The Adventure of the Western Star had reached its conclusion, and
once again Hercule Poirot had proved himself to be the greatest
detective of the age. I looked at him with admiration as he sat
there, his head slightly to one side, his eyes fixed on some distant
point, no doubt already planning his next triumph. As for me, I
was content to be his humble follower, ever ready to chronicle
his exploits and marvel at his extraordinary powers of deduction.
The mystery of the two diamonds was solved, and justice had been
done. Truly, as Poirot would say, there is nothing like the little
grey cells for solving the most complex of problems!

“Precisely. You did not observe my little talk with him? I had a
clever assistant—a little Chinaman whom I keep for such occasions.
When he jumped out from behind a screen and said ‘_Ah!_’ Mr. Rolf’s
face was a study! He gave up the diamond at once. It was he who
stole it from Lady Yardly, and he who had the other one—all the
time!”

I gasped.

“You mean he never bought it in San Francisco?”

“Never. He was Lady Yardly’s lover three years ago, when she was
out West. She was a little fool—she gave him the diamond. Then she
wanted it back. He wouldn’t give it. He blackmailed her—and she
paid. Then he became Mary Marvell’s husband, and she wanted to wear
the stone. Lady Yardly had a duplicate made—a paste one. Rolf
suspected this. He wanted the real stone. He and his wife arranged
the whole thing—the letters, the Chinaman—it was all a plant to
get Lady Yardly to show the real stone. She did, and he took it.
But she had the presence of mind to say a Chinaman took it, and
to drop her own necklace in the hall—where you found it, Hastings.
Then Rolf had to make it look as though his wife’s stone was stolen,
too—so he stole it himself!”

I was still gasping.

“But how did you know?”

“I have a little method of my own,” said Poirot, smiling. “It is
psychology, _mon ami_. I saw Mary Marvell—she is not the woman to
believe in Chinese gods. Therefore the whole thing was a fake.
Rolf is a great actor—but he is not a great detective. He made one
mistake. He told me he knew Lady Yardly three years ago. Lady Yardly
denied it. Then I knew one of them was lying. And I believed—the
woman!”

“And the ‘full of the moon’?”

“A little touch of the local colour, _mon ami_. It was a very
pretty case.”

“But you’ve let Rolf go?”

“_Ma foi_! yes. I have no evidence—and besides, there is Lady
Yardly to be considered. No, the case is ended. But it was
interesting—_tout de même_.”

“And the other diamond—Miss Marvell’s?”

“That, _mon ami_, was the real Star of the West. It has been in the
possession of the god for many centuries—and now it has returned
to him. For I have sent it back to China—by a very safe hand!”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You are a most extraordinary man!”

“I am unique,” said Poirot. “I have always told you so.”

He began to brush his hat with a little silk handkerchief.

“And now, _mon ami_, let us go to the Ritz. I have a little hunger.
_Allons!_”

“_Oui_, my friend. The thief of the Western Star—the so-called
theft. Gregory Rolf, alias the Chinaman! Oh, I know I must explain
all that.”

He settled himself in his chair and began his narrative.

“It was simple, _mon ami_. Figure to yourself that this was a crime
of two parts. The theft of the Star of the East from Lady Yardly,
and that of the Western Star from Mary Marvell. Now, as to the
latter, that was a very simple matter. Rolf, the actor, has played
many parts. To play that of himself was easy. He merely walked in,
demanded his wife’s jewel-case, and walked out again. Then he threw
the case in a corridor, and kept the diamond.”

“But the Star of the East?” I interrupted.

“Ah! that was more complicated. Rolf and Lady Yardly had met out
West, three years ago. There was a little—how shall I put it?—a
_tendresse_ between them. And Rolf, the scoundrel, had got her into
his power. He had some letters of hers—letters that her husband
must not see. You remember that Lord Yardly had been rather a dog
in his youth?”

I nodded.

“_Bien!_ So had Lady Yardly. She had been indiscreet. And Rolf
blackmailed her. He gave her the choice of paying him a large sum
of money, or of having the letters sent to her husband. She had
no money of her own, so he suggested the diamond.”

“But she told us it was stolen by a Chinaman,” I cried.

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “That was his idea. He was to provide
the ‘Chinaman’—himself in disguise. Thus the theft would be
accounted for, and the stone would pass into his hands. But then
came the news of the Western Star. To Gregory Rolf, it was an
inspiration! He would have _two_ diamonds instead of one. He began
to send the letters—to his wife and to Lady Yardly.”

“But why to his wife?”

“To provide an alibi for himself! To show that a Chinese gang
really _was_ at work. He knew that she would come to me, and that
thus the story of the Chinese god would be given a wide publicity.
He also knew that Lady Yardly would see the paragraph in _Society
Gossip_ and that she would also come to me. He hoped that I should
be able to ‘protect’ the stones, and that when they were ‘stolen’
in spite of my efforts, no one would dream of suspecting him!”

“And Lady Yardly?”

“She was a tool in his hands. He forced her to tell the story of
the Chinaman. He himself was the ‘Chinaman’ who appeared at Yardly
Chase. He had only to slip into the house, snatch the necklace,
and disappear. The piece of silk was a clever touch, which he had
prepared beforehand.”

“But the diamond you have just given back to Lord Yardly? Where did
that come from?”

“That, _mon ami_, was the Star of the East. Rolf had it. When I
charged him with the theft this morning, he was—how you say?—all
of a heap! He saw that the game was up, and he was only too glad
to give up the stone on condition that I should not prosecute.
The letters, also, are in my possession.”

“But the Western Star?” I cried. “What of that?”

Poirot’s face clouded. “Ah! there I have been less fortunate.
That stone, I fear, we shall never see again. Rolf has no doubt
already disposed of it. It was, as I suspected from the first,
the only real stone of the two.”

“The only real stone?”

“_Mais oui_. Lady Yardly’s diamond was a paste replica. She had
sold the real one years ago to pay some of Rolf’s earlier
blackmailing demands. That was why she was so opposed to her
husband’s selling the jewel—she knew that the fraud would be
discovered as soon as it passed into the hands of an expert like
Hoffberg.”

“And you knew all this?”

“I suspected it, _mon cher_, from the moment that Lady Yardly told
you that her letters came by post, and were scented. A Chinaman,
my friend, does not use a joss-stick to scent his letters! That
was a touch of ‘local colour’ added by a woman’s imagination.
Then, when I saw the two women together—the one so simple and
childlike, the other so—how shall I say?—so _torturée_—I began to
see the truth. And when I found that Gregory Rolf had been in
California at the same time as Lady Yardly—_enfin_, the case was
clear.”

I sat in silence for a few moments, marvelling at my friend’s
perspicacity. Then a thought struck me.

“But what about the ‘Western Star’?” I asked. “If it was the only
real stone, why did Rolf steal it from his own wife?”

Poirot smiled. “Because, _mon ami_, it was not his wife’s to steal!
It belonged to—Lady Yardly!”

“Lady Yardly?”

“_Parfaitement_. It was the original Star of the East, which she
had sold to Rolf three years ago. He, in turn, had given it to his
wife as a wedding present. You see the irony of the situation?
The two stones had indeed ‘met once more,’ as the prophecy
foretold!”

I gasped. “And you are not going to tell Mary Marvell?”

“_Ma foi, non!_ Why should I? She has her husband—and she will
soon have another diamond, no doubt! As for the other——” He
shrugged his shoulders. “I have saved a family from ruin, and I
have preserved the ‘honour’ of a noble name. It is enough for
Hercule Poirot.”

He paused, and then added with a twinkle: “But I think, _mon ami_,
that in future I shall stick to my ‘little almanac’ for the dates
of the full moon! It is more—how you say?—more reliable than the
imagination of a Gregory Rolf!”

“_Mais oui!_ The warning letters, the Chinaman, the article in
_Society Gossip_, all sprang from the ingenious brain of Mr. Rolf!
The two diamonds, supposed to be so miraculously alike—bah! they
did not exist. There was only _one_ diamond, my friend! Originally
in the Yardly collection, for three years it has been in the
possession of Mr. Rolf. He stole it this morning with the assistance
of a touch of grease paint at the corner of each eye! Ah, I must
see him on the film, he is indeed an artist, _celui-là_!

“But why should he steal his own diamond?” I asked, puzzled.

“For many reasons. To begin with, Lady Yardly was getting restive.”

“Lady Yardly?”

“We saw something—_quoi_? A necklace that looked like it, because
she told us it was so. But let us consider the facts. To start
with, did you ever see a woman of any sense carry about fifty
thousand pounds worth of jewellery in a handbag as Miss Marvell
professed to do? And for the second—have you never noticed that a
necklace may look very different indeed in the light of the fire
from how it does in the bright glare of an electric light? Lady
Yardly knew her business. She would not have the bright lights
switched on until the diamond—the real diamond—was safely out of
it. And _enfin_, the Chinaman. Why did he not take the necklace
as well? Because he did not exist, my friend! It was a fairy story
to cover the disappearance of the stone. Lady Yardly herself
dropped the necklace where we found it. And the piece of silk? Ah,
_mon ami_, I am a man of sentiment. It was I who picked it up
from the floor, and I who placed it in the door to make the story
complete.”

“You did?”

“_Mais oui!_ I was always of the opinion that the Chinaman was
superfluous. So I supplied one myself!”

“But why did you tell Lord Yardly it was Rolf?” I asked, confused.

“I did not. I said the diamond was preserved to him. I did not say
by whom. I think it will be better that his lordship never knows.
Lady Yardly has had a lesson, and I think she has learnt it. As
for Rolf, he will not speak! No, he will be very silent indeed!”

“But how did you get it from him?”

“Very simply. I have a little acquaintance with the police. I had
Mr. Rolf watched, and I found out that he was disposing of a stone
answering to the description of the Star of the East. I also found
that he was being shadowed by a real Chinaman—doubtless some agent
of the temple! I hinted to him that I had certain proofs—and he
gave up the stone. He did not want to go to prison, you see. Also
I think he was a little afraid of the Chinaman!”

“And the ‘Western Star’?” I asked.

“It will return to the temple. I have already seen to that. But
Miss Marvell will have her fifty thousand pounds insurance money,
so she will not be so very much the loser. It is a good thing to
have the imagination, _mon ami_, but it must be kept in its place.
One must always be guided by the little grey cells—the _little grey
cells_!”

And Poirot smiled at me with his own peculiar blend of vanity and
kindness.
