“_Non, mon ami_, we did not! We saw a necklace, yes! It was around
her neck, yes! But was it the _same_ necklace?” Poirot smiled.
“No, it was not! That was the paste replica. The real one was
already in her pocket. She had only to wait for a moment’s
darkness to make the change. When we find the necklace on the
floor, she has already removed the large stone. A few minutes
later, while her husband is talking to the ‘expert’ from Hoffberg’s,
she hands the diamond to me. It was a risk, but she was desperate.
She knew that I knew the truth, and she trusted to my—what do you
call it?—_noblesse oblige_!”

“But how did you get it from Rolf?”

“Ah, that was a little more difficult! I went to see him, as you
saw. I told him that Lady Yardly had told me all. I pointed out to
him that his little plan had failed. If he persisted in his claim
for the insurance money, I should be forced to tell the whole
story to the police. As it was, if he handed over the diamond to
me at once, I would say nothing. He is a man of sense, _ce
monsieur_! He saw that the game was up, and he gave in. He is now
on his way to find a more ‘healthy’ climate! For he knows that
Hercule Poirot—he does not forget!”

I drew a long breath.

“It’s a most extraordinary story,” I said. “But tell me, Poirot,
why did you send that wire to Lord Yardly?”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“To see if my ‘psychology’ was correct, _mon ami_. I wished to see
if Lady Yardly would indeed have the courage to ‘steal’ her own
diamond. And she had! _Une femme de tête, cette milady!_”

“And the ‘full of the moon’?” I asked, laughing.

“Ah! _par exemple_! I could not allow you to have _all_ the credit,
Hastings! I had to have a little ‘mystery’ of my own! But come,
let us have tea. I have a fancy for those little pink cakes!”

And so the case of “The Western Star” was ended. It had not been,
perhaps, one of Poirot’s most brilliant successes, but it had
certainly been one of his most interesting ones. As for me, I
learned once more the lesson that with Hercule Poirot nothing is
ever quite what it seems!

“_Si, si_, my friend, but only after she had had time to adjust it!
The pliers, they were in the pocket of her gown. _Tout simple_, is
it not? The story of the Chinaman, it was of a charming
simplicity! The piece of silk—the finishing touch! But she was not
content to let it rest at that. She must needs come to town to
tell me her tale. And I, being the little Poirot, am not deceived!
I let the farce continue. I let Rolf play his part. The diamond
expert, he was a little friend of mine from Hatton Garden. I
informed him that he was only to look for the paste replica. _En
vérité_, it was not there! For Lady Yardly had given it to Rolf.
He was to restore it to her in London. That was her price for her
silence! Then what does he do? He steals it from the _Magnificent_!”

“But why?”

“To get the insurance money, of course. He would naturally keep
the stone for himself, but I think I managed to convince him that
to give it up to me was his only hope of escaping a term of penal
servitude! He saw the force of my argument.”

“You are a marvel, Poirot,” I said admiringly. “What was the point
of the ‘full of the moon’?”

“_Ah, mon ami_! That was the most clever stroke of all! If you wish
to hide a thing, you hide it behind something else. Mr. Rolf knew
well that I should be on my guard on the Friday. Therefore he chose
another day. Also he knew that I should be on the lookout for a
Chinaman. Therefore he made himself into one. He is a truly
great artist, _ce monsieur_!”

And Poirot leaned back in his chair, and smiled at me with his
usual benignity.

“It was a near thing, Poirot,” I said. “He might easily have
escaped you.”

“_Jamais!_” said Poirot firmly. “Not when it is Hercule Poirot who
hunts! But you, Hastings, you must learn to think with your head,
and not with your imagination. It is a great thing, the
imagination—but not in a detective.”

I said no more. I felt that I had already sufficiently
distinguished myself.

“_Pardon, mon ami_, we saw a necklace! _A_ necklace, yes—but not
necessarily _the_ necklace! Lady Yardly had already substituted
a paste replica. That was why she was so anxious for the dark!
The necklace she threw into the hall was the real one. In the
struggle the diamond had been lost, but not by a Chinaman! Oh, no,
Lady Yardly herself had removed it. She had it in her hand all the
time. When I bent over her she was still clutching it. I took it
from her then and there! That was why I was so anxious to leave.
I wanted to get to London to see Mr. Rolf. I tell him I know all.
He is a man of business, he see that the game is up. He hand over
the diamond—and the letters. The insurance money, he must forgo
that, but he is a wise man, he know when to stop. Lady Yardly
will be happy now, she has her diamond, her husband is satisfied,
and no one will ever know.”

I looked at him in silence.

“You do not admire my methods?”

“I am thinking of the Chinaman,” I said.

“_Le pauvre_!” said Poirot, with a twinkle. “I feel for him too.
But, after all, he was only a piece of grease-paint.”

“And Miss Marvell’s diamond?”

“Ah, I see you have it! The ‘Western Star’ and the ‘Star of the
East’—the left eye and the right—they were one and the same! A
pretty romance, _n’est-ce pas_?”

“And the full of the moon?”

“_Ma foi!_” said Poirot. “I am not an astronomer. I cannot tell
you.”

I shook my head.

“Poirot,” I said. “You’re a wonderful man.”

“_Mais oui!_” he replied, with his usual modest smile. “I am
unique. All the world knows it.”

“And the true culprit?” I asked.

“Ah, Hastings, you must decide that for yourself. Was it the
blackmailer, or the woman who was his victim? Or was it, perhaps,
the man who first stole the stone from the temple in the East?
Who shall say? The little grey cells, they have done their work.
Let us go to dinner.”

“Wait, _mon ami_. The lights were not on, _n’est-ce pas_? And she
held the necklace with her hand. It was easy for her to conceal
the missing stone. I guessed as much when I found that she had
dropped the necklace on the floor! Why? Because she did not want
Lord Yardly to examine it closely. If it were found in the passage,
the loss of the diamond would be at once attributed to the
Chinaman. I sent a little note to our friend Rolf this morning.
I told him that I had certain proofs which would be interesting
to the insurance company, and I suggested that he should return
me the diamond of which he had so cleverly robbed himself. He saw
that the game was up, and, with the sang-froid of a great artist,
he sent me the diamond by messenger. It arrived just before Lord
Yardly.”

“And you think he will leave the country?” I asked.

“Without doubt. The game is played out in this part of the world.
He will find another victim, believe me. Lady Yardly will be more
careful in future. She has had a lesson. Lord Yardly will think
it was indeed a Chinaman—and so all is for the best in the best of
possible worlds!”

“What about Miss Marvell?”

“She will go on playing to the gallery—it is her métier. But she
will find that she has lost her diamond!”

I shook my head. “I’m afraid I don’t understand, Poirot. How could
there be only one diamond? You said they were alike.”

“_Mais non_, _mon ami_, they were _identical_. The ‘Western Star’
and the ‘Star of the East’ are one and the same diamond. It was
originally in the Yardly collection. Gregory Rolf stole it from
Lady Yardly three years ago, when she was out in California, and
he has been wearing it himself ever since as ‘the Western Star.’”

“But the insurance?”

“_Eh bien_, he would have got that too—if it had not been for
Hercule Poirot! You see, he had insured ‘the Western Star’ for
fifty thousand pounds. When it was ‘stolen,’ he would have claimed
the money. It was a very pretty little plot.”

I sighed.

“It’s a very wicked world,” I said.

“_C’est vrai_,” agreed Poirot, “but it has its redeeming features.
The dinner of Lord Yardly, for example. I shall always remember
it with pleasure.”

“But you didn’t stay for it!”

“No,” said Poirot, “but I had a very good lunch! Come, Hastings,
let us go and have some tea. My work is finished, and I feel a
great desire for a _tisane_.”

As we walked along, I could not help reflecting on the amazing
cleverness of my little friend. And yet, I had been right about
the ‘full of the moon’ after all! It just goes to show that even
the greatest minds can be misled by a little bit of romanticism.

“Poirot,” I said, “you really are a very remarkable man.”

“_Mais oui_,” said Poirot, with his usual modest smile. “I am
Hercule Poirot! There is no one else like me in the world.”

And with that, we went to tea.

“I demand pardon, my friend. Her hand concealed the part of it
where the gap would have shown. To place a piece of silk in the
door beforehand is child’s play! Of course, as soon as Rolf read
of the robbery, he arranged his own little comedy. And very well
he played it!”

“What did you say to him?” I asked with lively curiosity.

“Naturally. He wanted his own theft to be a part of the grand
Chinese scheme! He has a great imagination, that Rolf. But what
a magnificent artist! And what an advertisement! Even the
detective Hercule Poirot, he cannot save ‘the Western Star’!”

I laughed.

“Oh, Poirot, you are too much!” I cried. “And you have given the
real diamond to Lord Yardly?”

“Yes.” Poirot chuckled. “And it is his. Let us hope he will find
some other way of paying his debts.”

“And the paste one?”

“Is in the safe deposit of the _Magnificent_ Hotel. Mr. Rolf did
not stop to find that out. He was in too much of a hurry to make
his escape!”

“I suppose you’re right,” I said. “He’s a scoundrel, but a clever
one.”

“_Assez bien_,” admitted Poirot. “But not so clever as Hercule
Poirot!”

“No, I sent those,” said Poirot, “I wanted to see her reaction.
And I saw it!” He broke off. “_C’est fini!_ The case is over.”

“But you haven’t told me who the real culprit was!” I cried.
“Which one of them actually did it?”

Poirot looked at me with an indulgent smile, as one might at a
child.

“My dear Hastings, have you not been listening? There were _two_
culprits, and yet in a sense, there was only one. The real thief
was Gregory Rolf. He had the diamond all the time! He only ‘stole’
it from himself to get the insurance money and to hide the fact
that he had already had the stone for three years. But the first
theft—the theft of the ‘Star of the East’ from Lady Yardly—that
was done by Lady Yardly herself! She ‘stole’ her own diamond to
prevent its sale, which would have revealed that the stone in her
necklace was only paste. It was a comedy of errors, _mon ami_!”

“But what about the Chinaman?” I asked, still a little confused.

“There was no Chinaman,” said Poirot. “He was a product of Mr.
Rolf’s fertile imagination—and Lady Yardly’s. They both found him
a very convenient person to blame!”

He leaned back in his chair, his eyes twinkling.

“And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as to reach me that
large volume from the top shelf—the one you put back so
untidily—I will continue my study of the Peerage. It is a most
interesting work!”

“Precisely. _Voyez-vous_, it was a very clever little comedy. He
intended both diamonds to be stolen—one by Lady Yardly herself,
to cover up his track, and the other by himself. He would have the
jewel and the money. Lady Yardly would have a clear conscience,
and Mary Marvell—well, as I said, she would have a _réclame_
unsurpassed. All would have been for the best in the best of all
possible worlds—if it were not for the little grey cells of Hercule
Poirot!”

“I suppose you’re right,” I said. “It was a very pretty little
comedy.”

Poirot looked at me.

“It was a tragedy, my friend. A tragedy that nearly ended in a
shattered home. And the villain of the piece? Not the poor Lady
Yardly, driven to desperation. Not the Lord Yardly, whose past
follies came back to haunt him. No, the true culprit was the man
who pulled all the strings from the beginning.”

I looked at him, waiting.

“Gregory Rolf,” said Poirot. “He was the one who planned the
blackmail, the substitution, and the final daring theft. He played
upon the fears of one woman and the vanity of another. A most
accomplished scoundrel.”

“Naturally. He would not have her left behind. If she had remained
in London, her first action would have been to take the diamond
out of the safe and it would have appeared at once that there were
two diamonds—one real and one paste. In her ignorance of the
situation she would have had no motive for concealing her
knowledge. She would have said to Lady Yardly: ‘But you have
_my_ diamond, _ma chère_! I gave it to Gregory Rolf three years
ago!’ No, that would not do at all. So he must get her to Yardly
Chase with the paste replica. She is to be frightened into taking
the fake stone down with her, then he can steal it and it will go
at once into the melting pot—of course I speak figuratively. And
then she gets fifty thousand pounds insurance money!”

I shook my head.

“It was a very daring and clever scheme,” I said.

“No, no, _mon cher_,” said Poirot with a long sigh. “Not clever!
Simply—_psychological_!”

“But why did you tell Lord Yardly you had sent that telegram?” I
asked. “Surely he’ll think it very strange?”

“Ah, _mon ami_, you are as usual too literal! I told him that the
expert was sent by me—and that it was all a little ruse of mine
to bring matters to a head. He will never know that the expert
was really from Hoffberg’s and that the whole thing was a most
fortunate coincidence!”

“And Lady Yardly? Will she tell him?”

“_Ma foi_,” said Poirot, “I think it is very unlikely! But she is
a woman—who can say? But I have no doubt that she will be a very
devoted wife and mother for the future! Let us hope so, at any
rate.”

“And Gregory Rolf?”

“Ah, he will return to America with his wife. He is a very clever
actor, as I have already said! I think he will find it more
profitable to stick to the screen in future. After all, fifty
thousand pounds is not a bad haul!”

“But he didn’t get it!” I reminded him.

“True,” said Poirot. “He did not get it. But he has his reputation.
The stolen diamond—it is a wonderful advertisement!”

I laughed.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“_Pas du tout!_” said Poirot, with his usual modest air. “I am
merely—Hercule Poirot!”

“Precisely. He wished her to be on her guard, to believe that her
diamond was in danger. Thus she would the more easily accept his
story of the robbery. A clever rogue, _ce_ Monsieur Rolf! But he
had the misfortune to meet Hercule Poirot!”

Poirot smiled at me with his old, beaming self-confidence.

“And I, my friend, I had the misfortune to be at fault!” he added,
his eyes twinkling. “I did not realize that there was only _one_
diamond! You see, the name, it was the same! ‘The Star of the
West’—‘The Star of the East’—it was too simple. But I admit it.
I was for the moment—what do you call it?—_blind as a bat_!”

“Well, you’ve come out of it with flying colours,” I said
admiringly. “I never should have thought of it.”

“That is because you are so romantic, Hastings! To you, a Chinaman
is always a mystery, a figure of romance! But for me—I see only
facts! It is the little grey cells, my friend, the little grey
cells!”

He tapped his forehead.

“And now, _mon ami_, let us have a little lunch. I have a fancy
for a _crême de volaille_ and perhaps a _petit_ soufflé. Order, I
pray of you!”

And while I did so, Poirot sat in his armchair, a look of sublime
satisfaction on his face. He had saved a family from ruin, and he
had outwitted a clever scoundrel. What more could the heart of
Hercule Poirot desire?

I sighed.

“What is it, Hastings?”

“I was only thinking,” I said. “That after all, it was a very
simple case.”

“Everything is simple—when it is explained,” said Poirot. “But to
arrive at the explanation—that is not always so simple! However,
let us eat! The _gastronomie_, it is a great science! One should
treat it with respect.”

And with a flourish of his napkin, he prepared to do justice to the
admirable lunch that Mrs. Murchison was even then bringing into the
room.

“_Pas du tout_,” said Poirot briskly. “She came by the advice of
Mary Cavendish to seek my aid in her dilemma. Then she heard that
Mary Marvell, whom she knew to be her enemy, had been here, and
she changed her mind, jumping at a pretext that _you_, my friend,
offered her. A very few questions sufficed to show me that _you_
told her of the letters, not she you! She jumped at the chance your
words offered.”

“I don’t believe it,” I cried, stung.

“Come, come,” said Poirot, “do not be an infant. See, I have saved the honour of a noble house, and I have prevented a rogue like Gregory Rolf from enriching himself at their expense. Is that not enough? And for you, Hastings, you have had a most interesting experience in the methods of Hercule Poirot. One day, perhaps, you will write of it, and then you will see how necessary it was that I should act as I did. As for the ‘Western Star’ and the ‘Star of the East,’ they are once more one—and that is as it should be. In the meantime, let us go to dinner. I heard of a new restaurant in Soho where the _omelette aux fines herbes_ is said to be—superb!” And with a gay little laugh, he led me from the room, his good humour completely restored.

“Come, come, Hastings,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling with suppressed mirth as he patted me on the shoulder. “Do not be an infant. Is it not enough that the ‘Western Star’ has set in the West and the ‘Star of the East’ has returned to its rightful—if slightly foolish—home? Order and method, my friend, and a little knowledge of the human heart—they are the only tools of the great Hercule Poirot. And now, let us go and lunch sumptuously; I feel that my stomach, no less than my brain, has earned a reward for its labours!”

I was not to be appeased so easily, and for some time I sat in a moody silence, reflecting on the many occasions Poirot had allowed me to pursue a false scent. Poirot, however, was in the highest of spirits, skipping about the room as he restored a wayward ornament to its symmetrical position on the mantelpiece. “Come, come, Hastings,” he said at last, with a twinkle in his eye. “Do not be the bear. The mystery is solved, the ‘Western Star’ is restored to its rightful heaven, and the Yardly family is saved from the clutches of a most ingenious scoundrel. Mr. Gregory Rolf is indeed a great artist of the cinema, but he has found that even the most dazzling star must pale before the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot!” And with a magnificent flourish of his hand, he sat down to his chocolate, perfectly satisfied with himself and the world.

“And after all,” he added, with a twinkle in his eye, “was it not a most ingenious problem? To see through the greasepaint of the actor Gregory Rolf, the terror of the lady, and the greed of the blackmailer—it is all in a day's work for the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot! The ‘Western Star’ may be a myth of the movies, but the Star of the East is a reality that remains with its rightful owners. Come, Hastings, do not look so black. Let us go to dinner; I hear that at the Ritz they have a new chef who understands the delicacy of a _vol-au-vent_ as few others do. We shall celebrate the triumph of method and order!”

“Calm yourself, Hastings,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eyes. “The truth, it is often a bitter pill, but it cures the indigestion of the mind! Gregory Rolf, he is a great actor, yes—but he forgot that Hercule Poirot also knows how to play a part. He sought the insurance, the diamond, and the silence of a lady; instead, he has the exposure and the empty hands. As for the ‘Western Star,’ it returns to the rightful setting of the Yardly family, and the ‘Star of the East’—well, as I said, they were always one and the same! Come, let us go to the Ritz. I feel that a glass of _sirop de cassis_ is necessary to restore the equilibrium of my stomach after such a display of British temper!”

“I’m fed up!” I went out, banging the door. Poirot had made an
absolute laughing-stock of me. I decided that he needed a sharp
lesson. I would let some time elapse before I forgave him. He had
encouraged me to make a perfect fool of myself!
